claim: Robinovitch and colleagues analysed 227 falls from 130 residents, captured on video between 2007 and 2010 in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada.
supporting_passage: We did this observational study between April 20, 2007, and June 23, 2010, in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada. Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways). ... We captured 227 falls from 130 individuals (mean age 78 years, SD 10).
safe_wording: Researchers filmed 227 falls by 130 residents of two care homes in British Columbia, Canada, between 2007 and 2010.
qualifications: Say 'care homes' (long-term care facilities); say cameras were in shared areas only.

claim: The commonest cause of falling was incorrect shifting of body weight (41%); trips or stumbles caused 21% and slips only 3%.
supporting_passage: The most frequent cause of falling was incorrect weight shifting, which accounted for 41% (93 of 227) of falls, followed by trip or stumble (48, 21%), hit or bump (25, 11%), loss of support (25, 11%), and collapse (24, 11%). Slipping accounted for only 3% (six) of falls.
safe_wording: About 4 in 10 of the filmed falls (93 of 227) came from shifting body weight the wrong way during an ordinary movement. About 1 in 5 (48) came from a trip or stumble, and 6 from a slip.
qualifications: These are shares of falls filmed in shared areas, not of all falls in the homes. Causes were judged by a research team watching the videos.

claim: Falls happened most often during forward walking, standing quietly and sitting down; about a fifth happened during transfers.
supporting_passage: The three activities associated with the highest proportion of falls were forward walking (54 of 227 falls, 24%), standing quietly (29 falls, 13%), and sitting down (28 falls, 12%). Compared with previous reports from the long-term care setting, we identified a higher occurrence of falls during standing and transferring, a lower occurrence during walking ... 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs. ... The activities associated with fewest falls were standing and reaching, standing and turning, and seated or wheeling in a wheelchair (table 4).
safe_wording: The commonest moments were walking forward (54 falls), standing still (29) and sitting down (28). About 1 in 5 falls happened while moving to or from a chair or bed.
qualifications: Do not list turning as a common moment: standing and turning was among the activities with the fewest falls. These are counts of falls, not risk per minute spent on each activity (the study did not measure time spent in each activity).

claim: Cameras were only in common areas, not bedrooms or bathrooms, so the findings describe falls in shared spaces.
supporting_passage: Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways); Delta View had a network of 216 cameras, and New Vista had 48. No cameras were located in bedrooms or bathrooms. ... In 2010, at Delta View, 45% of falls documented on incident report occurred in common areas, of which 65% were captured on video. At New Vista, 34% of documented falls occurred in common areas, of which 28% were captured on video. ... We did not measure (and were unable to incorporate in a risk analysis) the amount of time spent doing the various activities associated with falls. ... We stress that our results summarise the situational context of falls in common areas of the long-term care environment.
safe_wording: The cameras were in lounges, dining rooms and corridors only. Falls in bedrooms and bathrooms, where many care home falls happen, were not filmed.
qualifications: Put this limitation on the chart itself. Do not state what share of all care home falls happen in bedrooms; the paper gives only that 45% and 34% of documented falls at the two sites were in common areas in 2010.

claim: Falls prevention in care homes should give as much attention to transfers and sitting down as to trip hazards.
supporting_passage: Our findings emphasise the need to target each of these activities in fall risk assessment and prevention strategies. ... We showed that 25% of trips occurred due to the foot being caught on a chair or table leg, suggesting the need for improved staff awareness of this hazard, and improvements in environmental planning and furniture design. 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs.
safe_wording: The authors suggested strength exercise and better support when moving to and from chairs, and noted that a quarter of trips were over chair or table legs. We should give sitting down, standing up and transfers the same attention as clearing trip hazards.
qualifications: Mark the position as judgement drawn from the finding ('We should...'), not a tested intervention. Keep the furniture-leg point so the post does not dismiss trip hazards.

claim: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of onset are a core feature (P1, highest certainty level) in the MDS criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy; 'backward' falls are not part of the criterion wording.
supporting_passage: Table 2, Postural instability, Level 1: "P1: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years". Table 4 definition: "Spontaneous loss of balance while standing, or history of more than one unprovoked fall, within 3 years after onset of PSP-related features." Discussion: "We are also aware of several other clinical signs that have been proposed to indicate the diagnosis of PSP, for example, retropulsion with spontaneous backward falls ... Whereas these signs may indeed be helpful to raise suspicion about PSP, we found no clear evidence suggesting that they would indeed contribute reliable information to substantiate the diagnosis of PSP." Table 5: Probable PSP = "(O1 or O2) + (P1 or P2)", "PSP with Richardson's syndrome".
safe_wording: In the Movement Disorder Society criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of the first symptoms are a core feature. Combined with slowed or restricted up-and-down eye movements, they support a diagnosis of probable PSP.
qualifications: Carousel label: 'Repeated falls without a clear cause in the first 3 years: think PSP'. Do not write 'early backward falls: think PSP' as if it were the criterion; backward falls are a traditional sign that the criteria authors found no clear evidence for.

claim: Recurrent falls due to impaired balance within 3 years of onset are a red flag against Parkinson's disease in the 2015 MDS criteria, and in autopsy-confirmed cases they were documented far less often in PD than in atypical parkinsonism.
supporting_passage: Red Flags were described as negative features which are potential signs of alternate pathology, but with lower or uncertain specificity. Red Flags rule out probable PD only when they cannot be counterbalanced by supportive criteria ... Table 1: "Recurrent falls (>1 per year) within first 3 years". Results: "'Recurrent falling because of impaired balance within 3 y' was reported in 3.8% of 124 PD cases and 28% in 19 DLB cases. In 274 MSA cases, these early falls were reported in 28.8%, in 33.6% of 28 PSP cases and in 22% of 27 CBD cases." Discussion: "Items with less clear discriminative value were 'rapid progression of gait impairment', 'recurrent falls', and 'bilateral symmetric Parkinsonism', as these features were reported in 3.8–17.6% of PD cases."
location: Introduction; Table 1; Results, Red Flags; Discussion
safe_wording: Repeated falls from poor balance in the first 3 years of a Parkinson-like illness are a warning sign in the Movement Disorder Society criteria that the illness may be something other than Parkinson's disease. In people whose diagnosis was confirmed after death, such early falls were recorded in about 4 in 100 with Parkinson's disease and about 1 in 3 with PSP.
qualifications: A red flag, not an exclusion: it can be outweighed by features supporting PD. Autopsy numbers are small for PSP (28 cases) and come from retrospective notes. The same review advises making sure dopamine treatment is adequate before relying on early falls as a red flag.

claim: The gait of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is small-stepped, magnetic (feet barely lifted) and broad-based, and becomes unstable on turning.
supporting_passage: Gait disturbance in iNPH has three characteristics: small-step gait, magnet gait, and broad-based gait. Walking becomes unstable and slow. ... When changing directions, steps are small and unstable. ... pathological gait features, such as small-step gait (short length of stride), broad-based gait (increasingly large step intervals), instability, difficulty in changing directions, frozen gait (no first step taken), and shuffle (dragging of feet and decreased elevation)
location: Chapter 1, Characteristics and evaluation of gait disturbance; Chapter 3, CSF drainage test
safe_wording: Normal pressure hydrocephalus typically causes short, wide-based steps with the feet barely lifted, which become more unsteady on turning.
qualifications: Carousel label: 'Short, wide-based steps, feet barely lifted, unsteady on turning: think NPH'.

claim: Gait disturbance is the commonest symptom of NPH; bladder symptoms and cognitive change are common but the full triad is often incomplete.
supporting_passage: The percentage of gait disturbance is 94–100%, which is consistent in almost all studies and is seen in almost all iNPH cases. The rates reported for cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction vary, being 78–98% and 60–92%, respectively. Consistently, gait disturbance is the most common symptom of iNPH, followed by cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence. Many reports state that the triad is complete in approximately 60% of cases. Meanwhile, a large-scale questionnaire survey conducted in Japan in 2012 revealed that the full triad was present in only 12.1% of 1524 patients. ... Urge incontinence associated with an overactive bladder is characteristic of dysuria in patients with iNPH.
safe_wording: Almost everyone with NPH has the walking problem. Bladder urgency and slowed thinking are common too, but many people do not have all three.
qualifications: Do not imply urgency and slowed thinking must be present before NPH is considered.

claim: Shunt surgery is effective for NPH and many people improve, with walking improving most.
supporting_passage: CSF shunt intervention is effective for treating iNPH. Recommendation Grade 1, Level of Evidence B ... Symptoms usually improve after surgical intervention. ... The degree of improvement in gait disturbance is the highest, followed by cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction. ... Based on evaluations such as mRS, improvement rate after shunt intervention is reported to be approximately 39–81% in 3–6 months, 63–84% in 1 year, 69% in 2 years, and approximately 60–74% in 3–6 years. ... gait disturbance showed the highest rate of improvement ... approximately 60–77%.
location: Chapter 4, CQ-10; Chapter 5, CQ-14 and prognosis
safe_wording: Shunt surgery helps many people with NPH who are selected for it; in reported series, roughly 6 to 8 in 10 were better a year later, and walking improved most.
qualifications: Applies to selected patients (usually after a positive tap test and typical imaging); outcomes depend on comorbidity, disease duration and complications.

claim: Marked unsteadiness with eyes closed (a positive Romberg test) points to loss of position sense, for example from neuropathy, but also occurs with loss of inner-ear balance function; it is not a test of cerebellar function.
supporting_passage: In clinical neurology, the Romberg test is traditionally used to assess postural stability by altering visual input, thereby unmasking disequilibrium in patients with sensory ataxia caused by proprioceptive deficits. ... The classic Romberg test primarily evaluates proprioceptive function, particularly the integrity of the posterior columns of the spinal cord. ... It is not a test of cerebellar function, as cerebellar dysfunction typically leads to balance impairment regardless of visual input. ... While the Romberg test is standard, it fails to clearly differentiate vestibular from sensory ataxia. (Anagnostou 2025) / ... sensory ataxia, as both conditions typically present with a positive classical Romberg test. (Anagnostou 2025 abstract) / We conclude that the Romberg test ... had an unsatisfactory classification value in terms of distinguishing patients from healthy controls. Instead, it should be interpreted within the comprehensive context of the broader neurological examination and the electrodiagnosis of peripheral nerve function. (Anagnostou 2024 abstract)
location: Anagnostou 2025 Abstract and Introduction; Anagnostou 2024 Abstract
safe_wording: If someone is much more unsteady standing with eyes closed than open, they are relying on vision to balance. Think of loss of position sense in the feet and legs (for example from neuropathy) or loss of inner-ear balance function.
qualifications: Carousel label: 'Much worse with eyes closed: think loss of position sense (for example neuropathy) or inner-ear balance loss'. The test is a pointer, to be read with the rest of the examination.

claim: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and spinal cord degeneration, sometimes without anaemia, and damage can become permanent if untreated.
supporting_passage: Table 2 Neurological: "Peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the cord and autonomic eg bowel/urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction" ... "No particular correlation between haematological and neurological features has been demonstrated, such that those with neurological symptoms may have no haematological abnormalities, and vice-versa." ... "Sequelae of untreated vitamin B12 deficiency includes not only permanent neurological symptoms, but also osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease."
location: Table 2; When should vitamin B12 deficiency be suspected?; Learning points
safe_wording: One treatable cause of neuropathy to check is vitamin B12 deficiency, which can damage nerves and the spinal cord even when the blood count is normal.
qualifications: The source does not mention the Romberg sign; link B12 to neuropathy and spinal cord damage, not to the sign directly.

claim: Gait disorders in older people are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing but point to underlying diseases that need specific tests.
supporting_passage: Another relevant message is that gait disorders are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing, but implicate the presence of underlying diseases that warrant specific diagnostic tests.
safe_wording: A walking problem in later life usually has a cause that can be named. 'Old age' is not a diagnosis.
qualifications: Expert review statement; frame the clinical instruction (watch every person who falls walk, turn and stand with eyes closed) as the post's recommendation.

claim: In a 1997 study of 58 residents of sheltered accommodation in Umea, Sweden, 10 of the 12 who stopped walking when a conversation started fell within 6 months, compared with 11 of the 46 who kept walking.
supporting_passage: 58 residents in sheltered accommodation in Umea, Sweden, were included. All were able to walk with or without aids and able to follow simple instructions (mean age [SD] 80·1 [6·1] years; 72% women). The most common diagnoses (some had more than one) were dementia (n=26), depression (25), and previous stroke (20). ... The staff registered falls indoors during a followup of 6 months. ... 12 people stopped walking when a conversation started and ten of them fell during the 6-month follow-up. 21 people fell at least once. ... The positive predictive value of “stops walking when talking” was 83% (10/12) and the negative predictive value was 76% (35/46). (Lundin-Olsson 1997, letter text) / Lundin-Olsson and colleagues12 13 reported that this test demonstrated good specificity (95%) as well as acceptable positive predictive values (PPV, 83%) and negative predictive values (NPV, 76%) with moderate sensitivity (48%) in predicting falls. (Hyndman 2004, Introduction)
location: Lundin-Olsson 1997 letter (text via Consensus record); Hyndman 2004 Introduction
safe_wording: In a small 1997 study of 58 older people in sheltered housing in Sweden, 12 stopped walking when someone started talking to them. Ten of those 12 fell in the next 6 months, compared with 11 of the 46 who kept walking.
qualifications: Tiny study (12 people with the sign), one setting, many participants with dementia, depression or stroke. The '11 of 46' is 46 minus the 35 true negatives in the letter. The counts were read in the Consensus reproduction of the letter; the percentages are also in the Hyndman full text.

claim: Stopping walking when talking was highly specific but insensitive for later falls: most people who fell had kept walking.
supporting_passage: The specificity was high (95%; 35/37) but the sensitivity was low (48%; 10/21). (Lundin-Olsson 1997 letter text) / Lundin-Olsson and colleagues12 13 reported that this test demonstrated good specificity (95%) ... with moderate sensitivity (48%) in predicting falls. (Hyndman 2004) / The pooled odds ratio for falling was 5.3 (95% CI, 3.1-9.1) when subjects had changes in gait or attention-demanding task performance whilst dual tasking. ... The predictive value for falling was particularly efficient amongst frail older adults compared with healthy subjects. Two prospective studies challenged the usefulness of the dual-task paradigm as a significant predictor compared to single task performance and three studies even reported that gait changes whilst dual tasking did not predict falls. (Beauchet 2009 abstract)
safe_wording: In that study, only 2 of the 37 people who did not fall had stopped walking, so the sign was rarely a false alarm. But 11 of the 21 people who fell had kept walking, so its absence was weak reassurance.
qualifications: The specific-but-insensitive finding comes from the original 1997 study itself. Do not attribute 'high specificity, low sensitivity' to the Beauchet 2009 review: its abstract reports that dual-task changes in general were linked with falls (pooled odds ratio 5.3), especially in frail people, and does not give sensitivity or specificity for the sign.

claim: Later studies in other populations found the sign less accurate or not linked with falls.
supporting_passage: Twenty six subjects stopped walking when a conversation was started and 16 of them fell during the six month follow up period ... For all fallers (>=1) the positive predictive value of SWWT was 62% (16/26), the negative predictive value 62% (23/37), specificity 70% (23/33) and sensitivity 53% (16/30). ... Although the SWWT test was easy to use, its clinical usefulness as a single indicator of fall risk in identifying those community dwelling people with stroke most at risk of falls and in need of therapeutic intervention is questionable. ... In summary, although the SWWT test has shown promising results in predicting falls among frail elderly subjects, these findings could not be repeated among people with PD. (Hyndman 2004) / SWWT was rare (2.8%), yet associated with higher motor DTCs but not falls, suggesting compensatory strategy. ... SWWT (β=0.01, p = .951) ... were nonsignificant. ... First, the cross-sectional design inherently limits causal inferences. (Zhou 2026)
location: Hyndman 2004 Abstract and Introduction; Zhou 2026 Abstract, Results, Limitations
safe_wording: The sign has not held up equally everywhere. In 63 people with stroke living at home, it missed about half of those who fell and gave more false alarms. In over 4000 healthy older volunteers, fewer than 3 in 100 stopped walking, and stopping was not linked with past falls. A 2000 report found it did not predict falls in Parkinson's disease.
qualifications: The Parkinson's point is reported second-hand in Hyndman 2004 (the Bloem 2000 letter has no abstract). Zhou 2026 looked at past falls, not future falls.

claim: Gait that deteriorates when a second task is added is linked with future falls, though it may add little to ordinary walking speed.
supporting_passage: Changes in gait under dual-task testing are associated with future fall risk, and this association is stronger than that for single-task conditions. Limitations in the available literature preclude development of detailed recommendations for dual-task gait testing procedures in clinical practice to identify and stratify fall risk in older adults. (Muir-Hunter 2016) / The meta-analytic findings indicate single and dual task tests of gait speed are equivalent in the prediction of falls in older people (Menant 2014)
safe_wording: Walking that gets worse when a person has to think at the same time is linked with later falls, but reviews disagree on whether it tells you more than ordinary walking speed.
qualifications: Optional background only; not essential to the post.

claim: In nursing and residential care, providing hip protectors probably reduces hip fractures slightly: about 11 fewer people per 1000 (from about 60 to about 49 per 1000 over about a year).
supporting_passage: Pooling of data from 14 studies (11,808 participants) conducted in nursing or residential care settings found moderate quality evidence for a small reduction in hip fracture risk (risk ratio (RR) 0.82, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.67 to 1.00); the absolute effect is 11 fewer people (95% CI, from 20 fewer to 0) per 1000 having a hip fracture when provided with hip protectors. / Summary of findings: Hip fractures at 1 year older people living in institutions, Follow-up: 6-24 months; No hip protectors provided: Moderate risk 60 per 1000; Hip protectors provided: 49 per 1000 (40 to 60); RR 0.82 (0.67 to 1.00); 11808 (14 studies); moderate. / Plain language summary: In older people living in nursing care facilities, providing a hip protector - probably decreases the chance of a hip fracture slightly
location: Abstract, Main results; Summary of findings table 1; Plain language summary
safe_wording: In care homes, offering hip protectors probably prevents a small number of hip fractures. Over about a year, roughly 60 in every 1000 residents without them would break a hip, compared with about 49 in 1000 offered them: about 11 fewer.
qualifications: The effect is of offering protectors (intention to treat), not of wearing them. The 60 per 1000 is the review's assumed baseline risk. The range runs from about 20 fewer to no difference, so the benefit could be very small. Moderate certainty.

claim: For older people living at home, hip protectors probably have little or no effect on hip fracture.
supporting_passage: There is moderate quality evidence when pooling data from five trials in the community (5614 participants) that shows little or no effect in hip fracture risk (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.58); the absolute effect is two more people (95% CI 2 fewer to 6 more) per 1000 people having a hip fracture when provided with hip protectors. / In older people living at home, providing a hip protector - probably has little or no effect on hip fractures
location: Abstract, Main results; Plain language summary; Summary of findings (10 versus 12 per 1000)
safe_wording: For people living in their own homes, trials found little or no difference in hip fractures when hip protectors were offered.
qualifications: Moderate certainty; hip fracture was less common in these trials (about 10 per 1000 a year), so any benefit would be small.

claim: Poor acceptance and adherence limit hip protectors; whether the benefit is concentrated in people who wear them consistently has not been shown by randomised comparisons.
supporting_passage: Adherence, particularly in the long term, was poor. ... Poor acceptance and adherence by older people offered hip protectors is a barrier to their use. (Cochrane abstract) / The proportion of people who adhered to the hip protector intervention ranged from 24% to 80% ... In view of the different ways in which estimates of acceptance and adherence were presented, we did not attempt any summary estimate of frequency of use. (Cochrane SoF and Results) / For the 334 nursing home residents with greater than 80% adherence to hip protector use, the incidence rate of hip fracture on protected vs unprotected hips did not differ (5.3%; 95% CI, 2.6%-8.8% vs 3.5%; 95% CI, 1.3%-5.7%; P = .42). Overall adherence was 73.8%. (Kiel 2007) / In the hip-protector group, four subjects had a hip fracture (among 1034 falls) while wearing the protector, and nine subjects had a hip fracture (among 370 falls) while not wearing the protector (Kannus 2000)
location: Cochrane Abstract, Summary of findings, Results (Acceptance and adherence); Kiel 2007 Abstract; Kannus 2000 Abstract
safe_wording: Many people stop wearing hip protectors: in the trials, the share who kept to them ranged from about 1 in 4 to 8 in 10. It makes sense that protectors can only help when worn, but trials have not shown that consistent wearers get most of the benefit; one large trial found no benefit even among residents who wore them over 80% of the time.
qualifications: Do not state that the benefit is 'mostly among people who wear them consistently'. The Kannus within-group comparison (fractures when worn versus not worn) is observational.

claim: Hip protectors may slightly increase pelvic fractures (low-certainty evidence).
supporting_passage: However, the risk ratio for pelvic fractures is RR 1.27 (95% CI 0.78 to 2.08); this is an absolute effect of one more person (95% CI 1 fewer to 5 more) per 1000 having a pelvic fracture when provided with hip protectors. ... However, hip protectors may slightly increase the small risk of pelvic fractures. / Summary of findings: Pelvic fractures at 1 year: 5 per 1000 versus 6 per 1000 (4 to 10); RR 1.27 (0.78 to 2.08); 12,408 (9 studies); low.
safe_wording: The review found a possible small rise in pelvic fractures (about 1 more per 1000), but this is uncertain.
qualifications: Either omit or state as uncertain; low certainty; the confidence interval includes no effect.

claim: Hip protectors do not reduce falls or other fractures, so they do not replace falls prevention or bone treatment; side effects such as skin irritation are uncommon.
supporting_passage: There is probably little to no effect on falls (rate ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.16) or fractures other than of the hip or pelvis (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.07). ... The incidence of adverse events while wearing hip protectors, including skin irritation, ranged from 0% to 5%.
safe_wording: Hip protectors do not stop falls and showed no clear effect on other fractures. They are an extra, not a replacement for exercise, medicines review or bone treatment.
qualifications: 'Not a replacement' is a judgement that follows from the evidence; the review did not test protectors against falls prevention or bone drugs.

claim: Barriers to wearing hip protectors in care homes include discomfort, acute illness, staff shortages and staff beliefs.
supporting_passage: Twenty-eight articles met our inclusion criteria, and facilitators and barriers were clustered into 4 socio-ecological levels: system (eg, facility commitment, staff shortages), caregiver (eg, belief in the efficacy of protectors, negative perceptions), resident (eg, clinical risk factors for falls and related fractures, acute illness), and product (eg, soft shell, discomfort). (Korall 2015) / Chan 2000 ... reported a compliance of 50%, with dementia given as a reason for non-compliance. (Cochrane Results)
location: Korall 2015 Abstract; Cochrane Results (Acceptance and adherence)
safe_wording: Whether protectors get worn depends on comfort, the person's health, and whether the home has the staff and commitment to help.
qualifications: Continence and dressing are not named in the abstracts opened; do not list them as evidenced barriers unless another source is opened.

claim: Chronic subdural haematoma is especially common in older people, and its incidence rises steeply with age.
supporting_passage: The overall incidence rate was 8.2/100,000 persons ... Overall, the highest incidence rate was 64.2/100,000 persons in patients 80–89 years old. (El Rahal 2023) / Chronic subdural haematoma (CSDH) is one of the most common neurological disorders, and is especially prevalent among elderly individuals. (Kolias 2014) / The median age of patients admitted was 77 years (range 20-99). (Brennan 2017)
location: El Rahal Results, Incidence of cSDH; Kolias Abstract; Brennan Results
safe_wording: This kind of bleed is much more common in later life. In Switzerland, people in their 80s were treated for it about 8 times as often as the population overall.
qualifications: Swiss figures count surgically treated cases only.

claim: It often follows a head injury, which may be minor and may not be remembered or mentioned; about 4 in 10 people have no recalled or recorded recent head injury.
supporting_passage: Head injury is a common risk factor and in a study of 1000 patients, 61.7 % recalled a recent one. (Shapey 2016) / 62% (514/823) had a documented history of head injury in the preceding 3 months. (Brennan 2017) / Moreover, in the context of a usual brain injury, which can pass unobserved and may frequently be ignored, the chronic subdural haematoma has a latent period until the appearance of the clinical symptoms ... Therefore, the main element that can lead to the diagnosis of chronic subdural haematoma is the minor brain injury; however, it should not be forgotten that it is seriously taken into account only by some of the patients or their families. (Iliescu 2015)
location: Shapey Pathophysiology; Brennan Results; Iliescu Clinical diagnosis
safe_wording: About 6 in 10 people with this bleed have a recent knock to the head on record. The rest have none recorded, often because the knock seemed too small to mention or was forgotten.
qualifications: The 'often forgotten or dismissed' explanation is from a narrative review; the 6 in 10 figure is measured.

claim: Symptoms usually develop over days to weeks, and the haematoma often shows itself weeks or months after the original bleed.
supporting_passage: CSDHs often present several weeks or months after the index bleed, because as the initial acute haematoma liquefies it enlarges. ... Patients with chronic subdural haematomas can present in a variety of ways, and symptom onset and progression may range from days to weeks. (Shapey 2016) / Chronic subdural hematoma – the clinical manifestations appear after 21 days (Iliescu 2015, Definition)
location: Shapey Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation; Iliescu Definition
safe_wording: The bleed can grow slowly, so problems often appear weeks after the fall, and can creep on over days to weeks.
qualifications: None beyond variability.

claim: Common presenting problems include unsteadiness or falls, headache, weakness on one side, slower or muddled thinking and drowsiness; in older people it can look like a stroke or rapidly worsening dementia.
supporting_passage: Gait disturbance was the most common clinical presentation in 362 (58.6%) patients, followed by headache in 286 (46.4%) patients, focal neurological deficits in 252 (40.7%) patients, and cognitive deterioration in 246 (39.8%) patients. ... Table 1: Drowsiness/coma 109 (618) 17.6 (El Rahal 2023) / Cognitive impairment was the most frequent presenting symptom of transferred patients (58%), followed by hemiparesis (41%) and headache (41%) (Brennan 2017) / Elderly patients frequently present with multiple symptoms that may mimic a stroke or rapidly progressive dementia. (Shapey 2016)
location: El Rahal Results and Table 1; Brennan Results; Shapey Clinical Presentation
safe_wording: In a Swiss study, the commonest problem was unsteadiness or falls (about 6 in 10 people), then headache (about 5 in 10), weakness or other one-sided signs (about 4 in 10) and worse thinking (about 4 in 10). Some people became drowsy. In older people it can look like a stroke or dementia getting quickly worse.
qualifications: Both cohorts are people treated in neurosurgical units, so milder cases are under-represented. Describe the thinking change as 'slower or muddled thinking'; do not frame it as delirium.

claim: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet medicines are risk factors, and many people with the condition take them.
supporting_passage: Other risk factors include coagulopathy, use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant medication ... Anticoagulant and antiplatelet use are both implicated in CSDH development and recurrence. (Shapey 2016) / Of the patients transferred, 356/823 (43%) were prescribed anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication at the time of referral: 171 aspirin (21%), 160 warfarin (19%), 36 clopidogrel (4%) (Brennan 2017) / Anticoagulant and antiplatelet use are commonly indicated in older people with SDH, but few data inform decision-making surrounding these agents in the context of intracranial bleeding. (Rickard 2023)
location: Shapey Pathophysiology and Anticoagulation section; Brennan Results, Perioperative clotting; Rickard Abstract
safe_wording: Blood thinners, such as anticoagulants and aspirin-type medicines, make this bleed more likely. In a UK study, over 4 in 10 people treated for it were taking one.
qualifications: Do not advise stopping blood thinners; decisions balance bleeding against clot risk (Rickard 2023). The 43% is prevalence among patients, not a risk estimate.

claim: It is diagnosed with a brain scan (CT or MRI), and symptomatic cases are often treatable, mainly by surgical drainage through burr holes.
supporting_passage: The suspicion of expansive intracranial injury makes us perform a paraclinical investigation (CT or MRI), which makes the diagnosis clearer by evidencing the iso- or hypodense subdural collection. (Iliescu 2015) / Surgical evacuation is the mainstay of management for symptomatic patients or haematomas exerting significant mass effect. (Kolias 2014) / However, burr hole drainage can be safe and effective in older adults with symptomatic chronic SDH (cSDH). Such patients need careful assessment to ensure symptoms arise from cSDH and not from coexisting medical pathology. (Rickard 2023) / Criteria on mortality (2%), rate of recurrence (9%), and unfavorable functional outcome (22%) were met ... Increasing patient age (p < 0.00001) ... independently predicted unfavorable functional outcomes (Brennan 2017) / A good outcome was seen in 81% of patients (El Rahal 2023)
location: Iliescu Clinical diagnosis; Kolias Abstract; Rickard Abstract; Brennan Abstract; El Rahal Abstract
safe_wording: A brain scan shows it. When it causes symptoms, it is often treatable, usually by draining it through small holes in the skull. In a UK study, about 1 in 10 needed a second operation, and outcomes were worse in the oldest patients.
qualifications: Say 'often treatable', not 'treatable'. Not everyone needs surgery; some small collections are watched. Outcomes are poorer with older age and frailty.

claim: A large UK trial found dexamethasone led to fewer good outcomes and more adverse events than placebo.
supporting_passage: a favorable outcome was reported in 286 of 341 patients (83.9%) in the dexamethasone group and in 306 of 339 patients (90.3%) in the placebo group (difference, -6.4 percentage points [95% confidence interval, -11.4 to -1.4] in favor of the placebo group; P = 0.01). Among the patients with available data, repeat surgery for recurrence of the hematoma was performed in 6 of 349 patients (1.7%) in the dexamethasone group and in 25 of 350 patients (7.1%) in the placebo group. More adverse events occurred in the dexamethasone group than in the placebo group.
safe_wording: Steroid tablets (dexamethasone) were tested in a large UK trial and led to worse recovery overall, so they are not a routine treatment.
qualifications: Dexamethasone did reduce repeat operations; the overall balance was unfavourable. Most trial patients also had surgery.

claim: Blocking the middle meningeal artery (embolisation), added to standard treatment, reduced recurrence in two 2024 trials; a third did not show a clear difference.
supporting_passage: Hematoma recurrence or progression leading to repeat surgery occurred in 8 patients (4.1%) in the treatment group, as compared with 23 patients (11.3%) in the control group (relative risk, 0.36 ...). ... Further study is needed to evaluate the safety of middle meningeal artery embolization (EMBOLISE) / a primary-outcome event occurred in 19 of 120 patients (16%) in the embolization group, as compared with 47 of 129 patients (36%) in the control group ... Further study of longer-term safety outcomes is warranted. (STEM) / Symptomatic recurrence or progression of subdural hematoma within 90 days occurred in 24 patients (6.7%) in the embolization group and in 36 (9.9%) in the usual-care group (between-group difference, -3.3 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -7.4 to 0.8; P = 0.10). The incidence of serious adverse events was lower in the embolization group (MAGIC-MT) / the emerging treatment of middle meningeal artery embolisation offers a well-tolerated, minimally invasive intervention which may reduce the risks of rebleeding in older adults (Rickard 2023)
safe_wording: A newer procedure that blocks the artery feeding the membrane around the bleed is being used alongside drainage to lower the chance of it coming back. Two of three large 2024 trials found fewer recurrences.
qualifications: Adjunct, not a replacement for drainage in most people. Longer-term safety still being studied; two trials were industry funded.

claim: Families should mention a recent fall or knock to the head, even a minor one, if new unsteadiness, headache, drowsiness, weakness or slower thinking appears in the following weeks, and ask whether a scan is needed.
supporting_passage: Therefore, the main element that can lead to the diagnosis of chronic subdural haematoma is the minor brain injury; however, it should not be forgotten that it is seriously taken into account only by some of the patients or their families. ... If the CT examination is currently very easily accessible, the diagnosis of chronic subdural haematoma has become quite simple, the main condition being that you only have to think about such a diagnosis. (Iliescu 2015) / Elderly patients frequently present with multiple symptoms that may mimic a stroke or rapidly progressive dementia. (Shapey 2016)
location: Iliescu Clinical diagnosis; Shapey Clinical Presentation
safe_wording: If new problems appear in the weeks after a fall, tell the doctor about the fall, even if it seemed too minor to mention, and ask whether a brain scan is needed.
qualifications: Practical advice drawn from the evidence, not a guideline quotation. Sudden severe symptoms need emergency care, not a routine GP appointment. NICE head injury guidance could not be opened; do not cite it.

claim: Looking down at a kerb or step through bifocals or varifocals means looking through the lower (reading) part of the lens, which blurs objects at that distance and impairs depth and edge perception.
supporting_passage: VISIBLE (Introduction): "The lower lenses of all types of multifocal glasses blur distant objects in the lower visual field, and this factor in particular may represent an important problem for older people." Lord 2002 (Abstract): "Eighty-seven subjects (55.8%) were regular wearers of multifocal (bifocal, trifocal, or progressive lens) glasses. These subjects performed significantly worse in the distant depth perception and distant edge-contrast sensitivity tests in conditions that forced them to view test stimuli through the lower segments of their glasses."
location: Haran 2010 Introduction (full text); Lord 2002 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: When you look down at a kerb or step ahead through bifocals or varifocals, you are looking through the lower, reading part of the lens, and that part blurs things at walking distance. In laboratory tests, older people who wore these glasses judged depth and saw edges less well when they looked through that part of the lens.
qualifications: Laboratory measures in one Australian study; describes how the lenses work, not a trial result.

claim: Regular multifocal wearers had more falls over one year, especially trips, falls outside the home and on stairs.
supporting_passage: "Multifocal glasses wearers were more than twice as likely to fall in the follow-up period than nonmultifocal glasses wearers (odds ratio (OR) = 2.29, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.06-4.92), when adjusting for age, poor vision, reduced lower limb sensation and strength, slow reaction time, and increased postural sway. Multifocal glasses wearers were also more likely to fall because of a trip (OR = 2.79, 95% CI = 1.08-7.22), when outside their homes (OR = 2.55, 95% CI = 1.14-5.70), and when walking up or down stairs (P <.01)."
safe_wording: In the same study, people who regularly wore multifocal glasses had more falls over the following year, especially trips, falls outside the home and falls on stairs, even after allowing for other risk factors. This was an observational link in 156 people and does not prove the glasses caused the falls.
qualifications: Association, not causation. Do not turn the odds ratio into 'twice as likely' (STYLE 9), even though the authors did. Small sample with wide confidence intervals.

claim: In the VISIBLE trial, giving regular multifocal wearers single-lens distance glasses for walking outdoors did not clearly reduce falls overall.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "606 regular wearers of multifocal glasses (mean age 80 (SD 7) years). Inclusion criteria included increased risk of falls (fall in previous year or timed up and go test >15 seconds) and outdoor use of multifocal glasses at least three times a week." ... "In the 299 intervention and 298 control participants available to follow-up, the intervention resulted in an 8% reduction in falls (incidence rate ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.73 to 1.16)." Results: "In the 597 participants who completed calendars, fall rates did not differ significantly between the groups." Table 2, All falls, Overall: intervention 299, fallers 170 (57), total falls 461, rate 1.54; control 298, fallers 175 (59), total falls 496, rate 1.66; IRR 0.92 (0.73 to 1.16).
location: Abstract; Results (Effect of intervention on falls); Table 2
safe_wording: In the VISIBLE trial in Australia, 606 people with an average age of 80 who wore bifocals or varifocals outdoors were randomly given either a separate pair of single-lens distance glasses for walking outside, with advice, or usual care. Over 13 months the trial did not show a clear difference in falls overall: about 1.5 falls per person with distance glasses and about 1.7 with usual care, a gap that could have been chance.
qualifications: State this overall result first (judge's sharpen). Participants were at raised falls risk and already wore multifocals outdoors at least three times a week.

claim: In a pre-planned subgroup of people who regularly took part in outdoor activities, distance glasses reduced falls, outdoor falls and injurious falls.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Pre-planned sub-group analyses showed that the intervention was effective in significantly reducing all falls (incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.42 to 0.87), outside falls, and injurious falls in people who regularly took part in outside activities." Results: "Significant interactions were evident between the intervention and self reported baseline outdoor activity levels (assessed with the Adelaide activities profile) for the outcomes of all falls, falls outside the home, and injurious falls (P<0.001)." Table 2, All falls, High AAP level: intervention 148, fallers 77 (52), total falls 187, rate 1.26; control 113, fallers 68 (60), total falls 244, rate 2.16; IRR 0.60 (0.42 to 0.87).
location: Abstract; Methods (Statistical analysis: three pre-planned subgroup analyses); Results; Table 2
safe_wording: Among people who went out a lot (above the middle score on a questionnaire about outdoor activities), those given distance glasses had fewer falls: about 1.3 falls per person over 13 months, against about 2.2 with usual care. Outdoor falls and falls causing injury were also lower. The researchers planned this comparison before the trial, but it is still a subgroup of one trial.
qualifications: Pre-planned (one of three planned subgroup analyses; the other two, by physiological risk and previous falls, showed no interaction: P=0.31 and P=0.19). Subgroups defined by a median split of a self-reported score. Single trial, not replicated. Tinted lenses were encouraged and may have contributed. Do not quote the paper's number needed to treat of 1.1 (it counts falls, not people, and misleads).

claim: In people who took part in little outdoor activity, distance glasses increased falls outside the home.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "A significant increase in outside falls occurred in people in the intervention group who took part in little outside activity." Results: "In contrast, in those who had Adelaide activities profile outdoor subtotal scores less than or equal to the median, intervention group participants had a non-significant increase in all falls and injurious falls and a significant increase in falls outside the home; the number needed to harm was 4.5." Table 2, Outside falls, Low AAP level: intervention 151, fallers 77 (51), falls 102, rate 0.92; control 185, fallers 66 (36), falls 76, rate 0.59; IRR 1.56 (1.11 to 2.19). All falls, Low AAP level: rate 1.81 vs 1.36; IRR 1.29 (0.95 to 1.75). Conclusions: "The intervention may be harmful, however, in multifocal glasses wearers with low levels of outdoor activity."
safe_wording: Among people who went out less, falls outside the home went up with the distance glasses, from about 0.6 to about 0.9 per person over 13 months. Their total falls also rose (from about 1.4 to 1.8 per person), but that difference could have been chance. The authors concluded the change may be harmful for people who wear multifocals and rarely go out.
qualifications: Same subgroup caveats as C01-23-d. The authors suggest frailer, housebound people may find switching glasses confusing, or gain false confidence; they found no falls at the moment of switching.

claim: Only about half of those given distance glasses used them as advised for most of the year, and non-fall injuries were more common in the intervention group.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "162 (54%) of the intervention group reported satisfactory use of distance glasses for walking and outdoor activities for at least 7/12 months after dispensing." Adverse events: "Seventy-seven (26%) intervention participants had one or more non-fall injuries (laceration, lifting or twisting injury, burn/scald, eye injury, collision, pedestrian injuries) compared with 51 (17%) controls (χ=6.61,df=1, P=0.01)." Discussion: "Intervention group participants were more likely to have non-fall injuries. However, these injuries were generally minor and not related to increased healthcare use."
safe_wording: Swapping glasses is a habit to learn: only about half of those given distance glasses used them as advised for 7 months or more of the year. More people in the distance-glasses group had injuries other than falls (26 in 100, against 17 in 100 with usual care); most were minor.
qualifications: Adherence self-reported.

claim: The World Falls Guidelines 2022 support active older people avoiding multifocal glasses outdoors, and include checking multifocal use in a falls assessment.
supporting_passage: Vision interventions: "Evidence from randomised controlled trials and prospective studies indicates cataract surgery for the first eye, [] and both eyes [] and achieving optimal safe functional vision by active older adults avoiding the wearing of multifocal glasses when outside [] are effective fall prevention strategies." ... "In fact, it is recommended that optometrists counsel their clients about likely short-term increased fall risk when dispensing new prescription glasses." Assessment table: "Objective assessment of visual problems and acuity and appropriate use of glasses (including check multi−/bifocal glasses)If indicated, refer to ophthalmologist or optometrist"
location: Full text, Vision interventions (Recommendation details and justification); multifactorial assessment table (Sensory function)
safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines list active older people avoiding multifocal glasses when outside as an effective falls prevention strategy, and say a falls assessment should check how bifocal or multifocal glasses are used. They also advise optometrists to warn people about a possible short-term rise in falls risk when new glasses are dispensed.
qualifications: The guideline statement rests mainly on VISIBLE; the word 'active' carries the qualification.

claim: The trial authors recommend separate distance glasses outdoors for people who are often out, and one pair of multifocals for those who rarely go out.
supporting_passage: Policy and practice implications: "Secondly, older people with considerable correctable distance refractive error who take part in frequent outdoor activities should use single lens distance glasses when outdoors and in other unfamiliar settings." ... "Thirdly, older regular wearers of multifocal glasses with considerable correctable distance refractive error who take part in little outdoor activity should use multifocal glasses for most activities (rather than using multiple pairs of glasses)." Conclusions: "clinicians should be conservative in eyewear prescription, particularly in frail older people who do not often leave their homes."
location: Discussion, Policy and practice implications; Conclusions
safe_wording: The trial's authors suggest a separate pair of distance glasses for walking outside for people who are often out and about, and staying with one pair of multifocals for people who rarely go out. That makes it a conversation to have with your optometrist, not a change for everyone.
qualifications: Authors' recommendations, not a formal guideline.

claim: In the 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for community-dwelling older people, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% and the number of people having one or more falls by 15%.
supporting_passage: "Exercise reduces the rate of falls by 23% (rate ratio (RaR) 0.77, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.71 to 0.83; 12,981 participants, 59 studies; high-certainty evidence)." ... "Exercise also reduces the number of people experiencing one or more falls by 15% (risk ratio (RR) 0.85, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.89; 13,518 participants, 63 studies; high-certainty evidence)." Plain language summary: "Exercise reduces the number of falls over time by around one‐quarter (23% reduction)." ... "Exercise also reduces the number of people experiencing one or more falls (number of fallers) by around one‐sixth (15%) compared with control."
location: Abstract, Main results (Exercise (all types) versus control); Plain language summary
safe_wording: In the 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for older people living at home, exercise cut the number of falls by about a quarter (23%) but cut the number of people who fell at least once by about a sixth (15%). Both results are high-certainty evidence from dozens of trials.
qualifications: Relative effects; give the absolute figures (C01-02-b) first on the visual. The two outcomes come from overlapping but not identical sets of trials (59 and 63 studies).

claim: The review's absolute illustration: 850 falls per 1000 people followed for a year becomes about 195 fewer falls with exercise; 480 fallers per 1000 people becomes about 72 fewer fallers.
supporting_passage: "Based on an illustrative risk of 850 falls in 1000 people followed over one year (data based on control group risk data from the 59 studies), this equates to 195 (95% CI 144 to 246) fewer falls in the exercise group." ... "Based on an illustrative risk of 480 fallers in 1000 people followed over one year (data based on control group risk data from the 63 studies), this equates to 72 (95% CI 52 to 91) fewer fallers in the exercise group."
safe_wording: Picture 1000 people like those in the trials, followed for a year. Without exercise they would have about 850 falls between them; with exercise, about 195 fewer. Without exercise, about 480 of the 1000 would fall at least once; with exercise, about 72 fewer, so about 408. The first number counts falls; the second counts people.
qualifications: The denominator is '1000 people followed over one year', not '1000 person-years' as the candidate wrote. These are illustrations built from average control-group risks, so label icon arrays 'illustration based on Cochrane 2019'. The 408 is simple subtraction (480 minus 72). The fallers figure is closer to the question 'will I fall this year?', but it is still an average across trial participants, not a prediction for one person (judge's concern).

claim: Falls are recurrent events: some people fall more than once, so a count of falls and a count of people who fell measure different things.
supporting_passage: Robertson 2005: "These techniques a) allow for the fact that falls are frequent, recurrent events with a non-normal distribution; b) adjust for the follow-up time of individual participants; and c) allow the addition of covariates." Fleming 2008 (Results): "There were 265 reported falls in total as most people fell at least twice." Cochrane 2019: "850 falls in 1000 people" versus "480 fallers in 1000 people followed over one year".
location: Robertson 2005 Abstract; Fleming 2008 Results (Falling in different residential settings); Cochrane 2019 Abstract
safe_wording: Falls repeat. A person who falls three times counts three times in the number of falls but once in the number of people who fell. So a programme can prevent some repeat falls without changing whether a person falls at all, and the two figures from the same trials will differ.
qualifications: Do not claim that 'a minority of people have most falls': no opened source quantified this. The gap between a rate ratio and a risk ratio is partly a property of counting 'at least one fall' rather than every fall, not only of repeat fallers; keep the explanation to what each number counts.

claim: Some falls interventions reduce the rate of falls without clearly reducing the number of people who fall; the 2026 Cochrane review of multifactorial interventions is the clearest example.
supporting_passage: Swarnalatha 2026: "Multifactorial interventions may reduce falls rate (RaR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; I² = 92%; 29 trials, 9442 participants; low-certainty evidence) and the risk of recurrent falls (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.98; I² = 45%; 17 trials, 4826 participants; low-certainty evidence). They may have little or no effect on the risk of falling (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.01; I² = 55%; 38 trials, 12,774 participants; low-certainty evidence)." Guirguis-Blake 2024: "Multifactorial interventions were associated with a statistically significant reduction in falls (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.84 [95% CI, 0.74-0.95]) but not a statistically significant reduction in individual risk of 1 or more falls (relative risk [RR], 0.96 [95% CI, 0.91-1.02])"
location: Swarnalatha 2026 Abstract, Main results; Guirguis-Blake 2024 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: The gap can be bigger. In the 2026 Cochrane review of multifactorial programmes (an individual falls assessment followed by treatments matched to each person's risks), compared with usual care the programmes may lower the rate of falls by about a quarter but may make little or no difference to the number of people who fall at all. The evidence is low certainty. A 2024 review for the US Preventive Services Task Force found the same pattern.
qualifications: Low-certainty evidence, high heterogeneity. Keep 'may' wording. This is a sharper illustration of the post's point than exercise.

claim: The same pattern appears in care homes: vitamin D probably reduces the rate of falls but not the number of residents who fall (in residents with low vitamin D).
supporting_passage: "Vitamin D supplementation (with or without calcium supplementation, alone or within a multivitamin) probably reduces the rate of falls (RaR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.86; I² = 72%; 5 trials; 4603 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) but probably makes little or no difference to the risk of falling (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.08; I² = 12%; 6 trials; 5186 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The population in these trials had low vitamin D levels."
safe_wording: The same split shows up elsewhere: in care homes, vitamin D for residents with low vitamin D levels probably lowers the rate of falls but probably makes little or no difference to how many residents fall (Cochrane 2025).
qualifications: Optional supporting example; different population (care homes, low vitamin D). Not needed for the core post.

claim: Major falls reviews report the rate of falls and the number of people who fall as separate critical outcomes.
supporting_passage: Swarnalatha 2026: "Our critical outcomes were falls rate (falls per person-year), risk of falling (number of people sustaining one or more falls), and risk of recurrent falls (number of people sustaining two or more falls)." McLennan 2026: "Critical outcomes were rate of falls (number of falls per unit time) and risk of falling (number of fallers)."
safe_wording: Cochrane falls reviews report the rate of falls and the number of people who fall as two separate main outcomes. Anyone quoting a falls result can say which one they mean (judgement).
qualifications: The candidate's ProFaNE consensus claim (Lamb 2005) could not be verified: only the abstract was available and it does not state the reporting recommendation. Use Cochrane methods instead, or drop the ProFaNE reference.

claim: About half of older people who fell without serious injury were unable to get up without help after at least one fall (Tinetti 1993).
supporting_passage: "1103 New Haven, Conn, residents aged 72 years and older who were able to follow simple commands and walk unassisted." ... "Inability to get up without help was reported after 220 of 596 non-injurious falls. Of 313 non-injured fallers, 148 (47%) reported inability to get up after at least one fall."
safe_wording: In a US study that followed 1103 people aged 72 and over living at home, almost half of those who fell without serious injury (148 of 313) said that at least once they could not get up without help.
qualifications: Old (1993), US, self-reported. Say 'a US study published in 1993' rather than implying current UK figures.

claim: Inability to get up was linked with later decline in daily activities; links with hospital admission and death were not statistically significant, and nursing-home placement was not more common (Tinetti 1993).
supporting_passage: "Compared with fallers who were able to get up, fallers who were unable to get up were more likely to suffer lasting decline in activities of daily living (35% vs 26%). Fallers who were unable to get up were more likely to die, to be hospitalized, and to suffer a decline in activities of daily living for at least 3 days, and were less likely to be placed in a nursing home than were fallers who were able to get up, but these trends were not statistically significant."
safe_wording: In that study, people who could not get up were more likely to have a lasting decline in everyday activities afterwards (35 in 100, against 26 in 100 of those who could get up). Differences in hospital admission and death pointed the same way but could have been chance.
qualifications: The candidate claimed Tinetti showed links with hospital admission and moves into long-term care: the hospital link was not statistically significant and nursing-home placement was, if anything, less common. Attribute the long-term care link to Fleming 2008 only, with its caveat (C01-03-c). Association, not cause.

claim: Among people over 90, most who fell could not get up after at least one fall, nearly a third lay on the floor for an hour or more, and long lies were linked with serious injury and hospital admission.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "In one year's intensive follow-up, 54% (144/265) of fall reports described the participant as being found on the floor and 82% (217/265) of falls occurred when the person was alone. Of the 60% who fell, 80% (53/66) were unable to get up after at least one fall and 30% (20/66) had lain on the floor for an hour or more." ... "Lying on the floor for a long time was strongly associated with serious injuries, admission to hospital, and subsequent moves into long term care." Results: "giving a threefold increased odds of admission to a care home, though the risk estimate did not reach significance in this smaller sample (n=51 not living in care who fell) until the censoring, conducted when everyone had completed their year since interview (crude hazard ratio 3.4 (1.2 to 9.5), adjusted 2.3 (0.8 to 7.0))." Conclusions: "People need training in strategies to get up from the floor."
location: Abstract; Results (Factors associated with inability to get up and lying on the floor for a long time); Conclusions
safe_wording: In a Cambridge study of 110 people aged over 90, followed for a year, 66 fell. Of those, 53 (80%) could not get up on their own after at least one fall and 20 (30%) lay on the floor for an hour or more. Most falls (82 in 100) happened when the person was alone. Lying on the floor for a long time was linked with serious injury and hospital admission; the link with later moving into a care home was uncertain once other factors were allowed for.
qualifications: Very old, frail population; small numbers; associations. The abstract's 'strongly associated' with long-term care is not borne out after adjustment (adjusted HR 2.3, 0.8 to 7.0).

claim: The World Falls Guidelines 2022 treat lying on the floor unable to get up for at least an hour as a marker of high falls risk that should lead to a multifactorial falls risk assessment.
supporting_passage: "An adult who sustains an injury requiring medical (including surgical) treatment, reports recurrent falls (≥2) in the previous 12 months, was laying on the floor unable to rise independently for at least one hour, is considered frail or is suspected to have experienced a transient loss of consciousness should be regarded as at high risk of future falls.." ... "(iv) inability to get up after the fall without help for at least an hour and (v) accompanied by (suspected) transient loss of consciousness. These high-risk older adults should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment."
safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines count being unable to get up for an hour or more after a fall as a sign of high risk of further falls. People at high risk should be offered a full falls assessment.
qualifications: The criterion is 'for at least one hour'; the candidate's wording ('lying on the floor and being unable to get up') must add the hour.

claim: Long lies are linked with serious complications, and the skill of getting up is best relearnt by practising each movement (backward chaining).
supporting_passage: "An important aspect to consider is avoiding 'long-lies' and harm from being unable to get up from the floor. One in 8 older adults who fall report lying on the floor for more than 1 hour [] and in those over the age of 90, up to 80% cannot rise from the floor after a fall []. Lying on the floor for more than an hour is associated with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, renal failure, hypothermia, pneumonia and urinary tract infections, skin damage and pain [,], and declines in mobility and restrictions in activity, probably due to fear of a repeat fall." ... "Regaining the skill to rise from the floor is most successfully re-learnt through practice of each of the specific movements required (often called backward-chaining) where the last step in the chain is taught first []. Some falls prevention exercise programmes also have a specific focus on this skill and have shown success in regaining this function []." Also: "It may also be useful to assess rising from the floor and dual task activity performance."
location: Full text, Exercise and physical activity interventions (Recommendation details and justification); Gait and balance assessment
safe_wording: The World Falls Guidelines say lying on the floor for more than an hour is linked with dehydration, kidney problems, low body temperature, pneumonia, skin damage and pain. They say the skill of getting up is best relearnt by practising each movement in turn, often starting with the last step first (called backward chaining).
qualifications: The 'one in 8' and 'up to 80%' figures are background citations within the guideline; if used, attribute them to the guideline citing other studies. The complications are associations.

claim: Getting up from the floor can be learnt: in a 2026 pilot trial, brief practice sessions improved older people's ability and speed at getting up.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Intervention: 5 weekly 20-minute FRT sessions utilising backward-chaining. Controls viewed a FRT demonstration video followed by discussion (20-minutes total), without physical practise." ... "Primary outcome (FES-I), FoF and activity avoidance showed no significant differences." Results: "At baseline, 77% of the FRT group could rise independently from supine, increasing to 100% post-intervention. In contrast, independent supine floor-rise in the control group remained unchanged at 63% (seefor more data on floor-rise ability). After adjusting for age, Otago duration and baseline ability, the intervention significantly increased the probability of rising from the supine position by 27% compared with controls (adjusted RD = 27%, 95% CI 7% to 47%,= .007)."
safe_wording: In a small Scottish pilot trial published in 2026, older people from community exercise classes practised getting up from the floor in five weekly 20-minute sessions. Afterwards, all of them could get up from lying on their back (77 in 100 could before). In the comparison group, who watched a video instead, it stayed at 63 in 100. Fear of falling did not change.
qualifications: Pilot; only 49 analysed; unblinded assessor; fitter participants already in exercise classes (BMI under 30, no frame indoors); groups differed in age; outcomes measured one week after; falls and long lies not measured. Say practice builds the skill and confidence to get up; do not say it prevents long lies (judge's concern).

claim: Earlier evidence on floor-rise training is small and mixed, and no study has shown it prevents long lies.
supporting_passage: Leonhardt 2020: "Seven studies with a total of 446 participants (mean age 82.4 ± 5.3 years) were identified. Emerging evidence shows that BCM significantly improves the ability to get up unassisted from the floor, as well as mobility with reduced fall incidence in older people. Furthermore, it can potentially reduce fear of falling. Reporting on feasibility and acceptance of BCM was limited. Study quality varied widely." Burton 2018: "meta-analyses of all RCT interventions indicated no significant change in time for older people to get up off the floor independently with intervention (MD: -0.43[-1.38, 0.51])." ... "Heterogeneity between studies was high, therefore results should be viewed with some caution." Swancutt 2020: "However, future research is required to establish whether undertaking 'getting up' training is effective and cost-effective at, for example, reducing the consequences of a long lie or ambulance callouts."
location: Leonhardt 2020 Abstract; Burton 2018 Abstract; Swancutt 2020 Discussion (Implications)
safe_wording: The earlier research is small and mixed. One review of 7 studies (446 people) found backward chaining improved people's ability to get up unaided; another review that pooled trials did not find a clear change in the time taken to get up. No study has yet shown that practising prevents long lies.
qualifications: Evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.

claim: Getting-up techniques are rarely taught by therapists or ambulance staff.
supporting_passage: Swancutt 2020: "Neither therapists nor ambulance service staff routinely teach strategies on how to get up, meaning that healthcare professionals largely have a reactive role in managing falls." Seeley 2026 (Introduction): "Floor-rise ability is an important functional skill, recognised in international guidelines [], which is rarely taught to fallers by physiotherapists or ambulance crews [] and is frequently omitted from fall prevention programmes []."
safe_wording: It is often not taught. In a study in Devon, neither therapists nor ambulance staff routinely showed people how to get up after a fall. That is why it is worth asking.
qualifications: Qualitative, one region; Seeley's statement is background citing other work.

claim: FaME (Falls Management Exercise) classes include practice at getting up from the floor.
supporting_passage: "The Falls Management Exercise (FaME) programme is the only evidence-based exercise intervention for high-risk fallers that includes floor-rise training (FRT) [,] but usually only after 12 weeks of the 24-week programme."
safe_wording: Some falls prevention classes, such as FaME (Falls Management Exercise), include practice at getting up from the floor, usually from about halfway through the 24-week programme.
qualifications: Background statement in a paper co-authored by FaME's developer (Skelton); the FaME trial (Skelton 2005, PMID 16267192) has no abstract in PubMed and was not opened. Do not quote the '31% fewer falls' figure from this background sentence.

claim: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film ('Upwards and Onwards') on getting up after a fall.
supporting_passage: Seeley 2026: "Controls viewed the NHS Inform video 'Upwards and Onwards' [], divided into segments over five 20-minute sessions including facilitated discussion." Swancutt 2020: "resources for older people and their families to enable them to practice getting up, such as the film produced by NHS Inform in Scotland [], could be a valuable supplement to face-to-face training or as a self-management resource." Seeley 2026 Discussion: "However, this did not translate to increased functional success (binary ability to rise), suggesting that while videos improve awareness, supervised practice is necessary for skill acquisition."
location: Seeley 2026 Methods and Discussion; Swancutt 2020 Discussion
safe_wording: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film called 'Upwards and Onwards' about getting up after a fall. In the 2026 trial, watching it without practising did not change whether people could get up, so use it alongside practice with a physiotherapist or trained instructor.
qualifications: The NHS Inform page itself could not be opened; Alasdair must check the current link before it goes in source_reply.

claim: People who are hurt or in pain after a fall should not try to get up and should call for help (safety line the judge requires).
supporting_passage: No supporting passage found in any opened source.
safe_wording: Not verified. Until a source is opened, frame it as a question for the reader to ask: 'Ask the physiotherapist how to tell when to try to get up and when to stay put and call for help.'
qualifications: The instruction is standard advice but no opened guideline or paper states it; NHS and CSP pages could not be opened.

claim: A step-by-step sequence for getting up (roll onto your side, hands and knees, crawl to a sturdy chair, stronger leg forward, push up, turn and sit) copied from a verified physiotherapy guide, for the carousel.
supporting_passage: No step-by-step guide was opened. Nearest verified description, Seeley 2026: "Participants were instructed to rise from half-kneeling (one knee down), side-sitting (weight on one hip) and supine (lying flat on the back) positions using a sturdy chair for support".
safe_wording: Do not publish a step-by-step carousel from unverified steps. A visual may show the three positions practised in the trial (half-kneeling, side-sitting on one hip, lying on the back, each with a sturdy chair for support), labelled as positions practised in a 2026 trial, with 'Practise this with a physiotherapist first'.
qualifications: A verified guide (for example the NHS Inform film or a CSP leaflet) must be opened before any step list is drawn.

claim: Exercise programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises reduce falls; programmes that are mainly strength training, dance or walking have uncertain effects.
supporting_passage: "Compared with control, balance and functional exercises reduce the rate of falls by 24% (RaR 0.76, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.81; 7920 participants, 39 studies; high-certainty evidence) and the number of people experiencing one or more falls by 13% (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.91; 8288 participants, 37 studies; high-certainty evidence). Multiple types of exercise (most commonly balance and functional exercises plus resistance exercises) probably reduce the rate of falls by 34% (RaR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; 1374 participants, 11 studies; moderate-certainty evidence)" ... "Tai Chi may reduce the rate of falls by 19% (RaR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.99; 2655 participants, 7 studies; low-certainty evidence)" ... "We are uncertain of the effects of programmes that are primarily resistance training, or dance or walking programmes on the rate of falls and the number of people who experience falls."
location: Abstract, Main results (Different exercise types versus control)
safe_wording: In the 2019 Cochrane review, programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises, such as standing up from a chair and stepping, cut falls by about a quarter. Programmes that mix several types, usually balance plus strength, probably cut falls too, and Tai Chi may. For programmes that are mainly strength training, dancing or walking, the effect on falls is uncertain.
qualifications: 'Uncertain' is an evidence gap, not proof of no effect. Examples of functional exercise come from the World Falls Guidelines ('e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping').

claim: The balance exercises that prevented falls best were challenging exercises done standing.
supporting_passage: "The greatest relative effects of exercise on fall rates (RR=0.58, 95% CI=0.48-0.69, 68% of between-study variability explained) were seen in programs that included a combination of a higher total dose of exercise (>50 hours over the trial period) and challenging balance exercises (exercises conducted while standing in which people aimed to stand with their feet closer together or on one leg, minimize use of their hands to assist, and practice controlled movements of the center of mass) and did not include a walking program."
safe_wording: In the trials, the balance exercises that challenged people most were done standing: feet closer together or on one leg, using the hands less for support, and practising controlled shifts of body weight.
qualifications: The 'larger effects' part is a between-trial comparison (meta-regression). The definition is what the post needs.

claim: Programmes that challenged balance and involved more than about 3 hours a week had larger effects (between-trial comparison).
supporting_passage: Sherrington 2017: "Overall, exercise reduced the rate of falls in community-dwelling older people by 21% (pooled rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.85, p<0.001, I47%, 69 comparisons) with greater effects seen from exercise programmes that challenged balance and involved more than 3 hours/week of exercise. These variables explained 76% of the between-trial heterogeneity and in combination led to a 39% reduction in falls (incident rate ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.72, p<0.001)." Sherrington 2020: "Interventions with a total weekly dose of 3+ h that included balance and functional exercises were particularly effective with a 42% reduction in rate of falls compared to control (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76)."
safe_wording: Across trials, programmes that challenged balance and added up to 3 hours or more a week had the biggest effects. This comes from comparing different trials, not from a trial that tested different amounts, so treat 3 hours as a guide rather than a rule.
qualifications: Meta-regression across trials, not a dose trial (judge's concern). Participants in higher-dose trials may differ in other ways.

claim: The World Falls Guidelines recommend balance-challenging and functional exercise, three or more times a week, individualised and progressed for at least 12 weeks and continued longer; benefits are lost when people stop.
supporting_passage: "We recommend exercise programmes for fall prevention for community-dwelling older adults which include balance challenging and functional exercises (e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping), with sessions three times or more weekly which are individualised, progressed in intensity for at least 12 weeks and continued longer for greater effect." (1A) "We recommend inclusion, when feasible, of Tai Chi and/or additional individualised progressive resistance strength training." (1B) "Exercise needs to be progressive initially and maintained once a plateau is reached." "Benefits of exercise are lost on cessation so opportunities to continue with appropriate activity at the end of the programme are important."
location: Full text, WG4 Exercise interventions table; Component interventions, Exercise and physical activity interventions
safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines recommend exercise that challenges balance and practises everyday movements such as standing up from a chair and stepping, three or more times a week, tailored to the person and made harder over time, for at least 12 weeks and kept up for longer. Strength training or Tai Chi can be added where possible. The benefits are lost when people stop.
qualifications: The candidate's wording 'with resistance training' should read 'with strength training added where feasible' (separate 1B recommendation).

claim: WHO 2020 guidelines advise older adults to do varied multicomponent activity emphasising balance and strength on 3 or more days a week to prevent falls (replaces the UK CMO claim, which could not be opened).
supporting_passage: "As such it is recommended that as part of their weekly physical activity, older adults should do varied multicomponent physical activity at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week in order to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls." ... "Third, with respect to older adults, the recommendation regarding multicomponent physical activity that emphasises functional balance and strength training to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls now applies to all older adults rather than specifically those with poor mobility."
location: Full text, Older adults section; Discussion (differences from 2010 guidelines)
safe_wording: The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines advise all older adults to do varied activity that focuses on balance and strength, at moderate effort or more, on 3 or more days a week, to keep up everyday abilities and prevent falls.
