qualifications: The candidate's UK Chief Medical Officers' claim (strength and balance on at least two days a week) was not verified: the CMO document was not in Drive and gov.uk could not be opened. Use WHO 2020 instead, or drop the CMO line.

claim: Seated (chair-based) exercise has other benefits but has not been tested well as a way to prevent falls, and did not clearly improve balance.
supporting_passage: Klempel 2021 (Abstract): "In this systematic review including 1388 participants, results demonstrated that chair-based exercise programmes improve upper extremity (handgrip strength: MD = 2.10; 95% CI = 0.76, 3.43 and 30 s arm curl test: MD = 2.82; 95% CI = 1.34, 4.31) and lower extremity function (30 s chair stand: MD 2.25; 95% CI = 0.64, 3.86)." Results: "No significant differences between groups were observed in the Berg balance scale, timed up and go test or gait speed between the intervention and control groups." Discussion: "The findings of a lack of effect on balance are in keeping with a previous review of chair-based exercise []." Anthony 2013: "The quality of the evidence base for CBEs is low with inconclusive findings to clearly inform practice."
location: Klempel 2021 Abstract, Results 3.5, Discussion; Anthony 2013 Abstract
safe_wording: Seated exercise has real benefits: a 2021 review of 25 studies found chair-based classes improved arm and leg strength. But in those studies it did not clearly improve balance or walking, and none measured falls. A seated class can be a good start if you can't yet stand for long; on its own it has not been tested as a way to prevent falls.
qualifications: The candidate's wording 'Seated exercise has not been shown to reduce falls (Sherrington reviews)' does not match any Sherrington review. Supportable form: an evidence gap from chair-based exercise reviews plus the standing definition of challenging balance exercise (C01-25-b). Meets the judge's values concern.

claim: For people who are frail or at higher risk, guidelines recommend more supervision or smaller groups, and exercise adapted to their abilities.
supporting_passage: "Exercise programmes that need to be of sufficient intensity and duration should be delivered in a way that ensures safety and considers functional abilities." ... "Higher supervision levels or smaller group numbers are recommended for those at higher risk of a fall including those who are frail [,]."
location: Full text, Exercise and physical activity interventions (Recommendation details and justification)
safe_wording: If you are frail or have fallen before, the guidelines recommend classes with more supervision or smaller groups, run in a way that keeps you safe and suits what you can do.
qualifications: None.

claim: If no suitable class exists, exercise can be taught as an individual home programme; the Otago home programme reduced falls.
supporting_passage: WFG: "Exercise programmes can be delivered in a group or taught and supported as an individualised home exercise programme or a mix of both in order to achieve an effective dose [,]." Thomas 2010: "seven trials, involving 1503 participants were included. The mean age of participants was 81.6 (±3.9) years." ... "and significantly reduced fall rates (incidence rate ratio = 0.68, 95% CI = 0.56-0.79)." ... "Of the 747 participants who remained in the studies at 12 months, 274 (36.7%) were still exercising three or more times per week."
location: WFG full text, Exercise section; Thomas 2010 Abstract
safe_wording: If there is no suitable class near you, ask about a home programme. The guidelines say exercise can be taught as an individual home programme, or a mix of home and group sessions. A review of 7 trials of the Otago home programme (1503 people, average age 82) found it cut the rate of falls by about a third.
qualifications: 2010 review; do not use its mortality finding. Adherence fell over time (about 37 in 100 still exercising 3 times a week at 12 months).

claim: Hospital falls are commonly reported as falls per 1000 occupied bed days.
supporting_passage: NAIF 2015: "Falls per 1,000 OBDs We report, for the first time, current falls rates across most hospitals in England and Wales. The average number of falls per 1,000 OBDs is 6.63" and "Clinical staff and hospital managers should review the total number of falls and the number of falls with an outcome of harm per 1,000 OBDs." Healey 2008: "Falls rates were standardised as number of falls per 1,000 occupied bed days." Pu 2025: "[95 %, one-tailed, non-inferiority confidence limit of 2.00 falls/1000 occupied bed days (OBDs) increase]"
location: NAIF 2015 Key findings and Recommendations; Healey 2008 Abstract; Pu 2025 Abstract
safe_wording: Hospitals usually count falls as falls per 1000 occupied bed days. The Royal College of Physicians' national audit used this measure (2015 report, average 6.63 falls per 1000 bed days in England and Wales), and trials still use it.
qualifications: The NAIF report opened is from 2015; current NAIF metrics were not verified. Use present tense only for 'commonly used', not for current national figures.

claim: The national audit itself warned that a low falls rate does not necessarily mean good care.
supporting_passage: "A low number of falls per 1,000 OBDs does not necessarily mean the trust or LHB performed well in the clinical audit." ... "Therefore comparisons need to be made with caution, as hospitals with higher than average reported rates of falls may have better reporting, or better falls prevention care for more vulnerable patients. Conversely, organisations with very low rates may have a poor culture of defining or reporting falls rather than having robust approaches for prevention of falls."
location: NAIF 2015, Falls reporting (Falls per 1,000 OBDs caveats)
safe_wording: The national audit itself warned that a low falls rate does not necessarily mean a hospital is doing well, because a very low rate can reflect poor reporting.
qualifications: The audit's stated reason is under-reporting, not immobility. Do not imply the audit said wards keep patients in bed.

claim: Older people in hospital spend most of their time lying in bed, including many who can walk.
supporting_passage: Brown 2009: "Forty-five male patients (mean age 74.2) with a mean length of stay of 5.1 days generated 2,592 one-hour periods of data. A baseline functional assessment indicated that 35 (77.8%) study patients were willing and able to walk a short distance independently. No patient remained in bed the entire measured hospital stay, but on average, 83% of the measured hospital stay was spent lying in bed. The average amount of time that any one individual spent standing or walking ranged from a low of 0.2% to a high of 21%, with a median of 3%, or 43 minutes per day." Pedersen 2013: "The ambulatory patients were lying median 17 hours, (interquartile range [IQR]: 14.4-19.1), sitting 5.1 hours (IQR: 2.9-7.1), and standing and/or walking 1.1 hours (IQR: 0.6-1.7) per day."
location: Brown 2009 Abstract, Results; Pedersen 2013 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: Older people in hospital spend most of the day in bed, including many who can walk. In a US veterans' hospital, 45 men aged 65 and over spent on average 83% of their measured time lying in bed, and the typical time standing or walking was 43 minutes a day. In a Danish study of 43 older medical patients who could walk, the typical time lying down was 17 hours a day.
qualifications: Small cohorts, one US hospital (men only, 2009) and one Danish hospital (2013). Give Brown 2009 as one US hospital cohort (judge's concern). Do not use Growdon's '95% of their time in bed' figure (background estimate).

claim: Low mobility in hospital is associated with loss of function, new institutionalisation and death, and much bed rest has no documented medical reason.
supporting_passage: "When compared with the high mobility group, the low and intermediate groups were associated with the adverse outcomes in a graded fashion, even after controlling for multiple confounders." ... "Bedrest was ordered at some point during hospitalization in 165 (33%) patients. For most patients, mobility was limited involuntarily (bedrest orders), and almost 60% of bedrest episodes in the lowest mobility group had no documented medical indication."
safe_wording: Low mobility in hospital is linked with worse outcomes. In a US study of 498 medical patients aged 70 and over, those who moved least were more likely to lose everyday abilities, move into a care home or die, even after allowing for how ill they were. That link does not prove the lack of movement caused the harm. A third had bed rest ordered, and almost 60% of bed rest episodes in the least mobile group had no recorded medical reason.
qualifications: Observational; sicker patients move less (reverse causation possible). Do not convert the adjusted odds ratios. Covinsky 2011 (PMID 22028354) is a review that puts hospital-associated disability at about one third of patients over 70; not needed.

claim: Pressure to prevent falls has been linked with restricting patients' movement.
supporting_passage: King 2018: "Intense messaging from hospital administration to achieve zero falls resulted in nurses developing a fear of falls, protecting self and unit, and restricting fall risk patients as a way to stop messages and meet the hospital goal." Capo-Lugo 2023: "Non-ambulatory status, the primary outcome, was defined as a median Johns Hopkins Highest Level of Mobility <6 (i.e., patient walks less than 10 steps) throughout hospitalization." ... "8% of patients at low risk for falls were non-ambulatory, compared to 25% and 54% of patients at moderate and high risk for falls, respectively." ... "Patients categorized into higher fall risk groups had decreased mobility throughout their hospitalization, even when they had the functional capacity to ambulate." Growdon 2017: "Our current system of “keeping score” of falls has created a strong disincentive for mobilizing patients."
location: King 2018 Abstract (Results); Capo-Lugo 2023 Abstract; Growdon 2017 full text
safe_wording: There is evidence that pressure to prevent falls can restrict movement. In interviews with 27 US hospital nurses and nursing assistants, 'zero falls' messages from managers led staff to restrict patients at risk of falling. In a US hospital study of 48,271 adult patients, 54% of those labelled high falls risk were recorded as mostly not walking (fewer than 10 steps), against 8% of those labelled low risk, and the gap remained among patients who were able to walk.
qualifications: US evidence under a 'never event' payment context; UK practice may differ. Capo-Lugo is observational and includes adults of all ages. Keep criticism on the metric and the incentive, not on nurses (judge's values concern).

claim: Patients who stay at bed level fall less than those starting to move, but patients who walk fall least of all.
supporting_passage: "Interestingly, the relationship between mobility performance using JH‐HLM and fall incidence followed an inverse U‐shaped curve (Figure, Panel C). Patients with JH‐HLM scores of 1 or 2, which indicate limited mobility performance at bed level, experienced fewer falls compared to those with moderate mobility performance, who move in the transition zone between bed level and walking. Conversely, patients with high mobility performance, as reflected by JH‐HLM scores of 6 or higher—which represent increasing walking distances—had the lowest incidence of falls." Discussion: "Patients who stay in bed and perform extremely low levels of activity (e.g., bed‐level activity) have lower fall incidence, but importantly, their fall rates are still higher than those of patients who were ambulatory early in their hospitalisation."
safe_wording: In a study of 54,206 adult patients in three US hospitals, patients who stayed at bed level had fewer falls than patients who were starting to move between bed and walking. Patients who were walking had the fewest falls of all.
qualifications: Exploratory, unadjusted, all adult ages (mean about 61). This supports the logic that a ward could see fewer falls if fewer people start to move, but it does not show that any ward lowered its rate this way.

claim: Wards lower their falls rates by keeping people in bed (direct evidence).
supporting_passage: No opened source shows a ward or hospital lowering its falls rate by immobilising patients.
safe_wording: Present this as a limitation of the measure, marked as judgement: 'A falls rate on its own can't show whether falls went down because care improved or because people moved less.'
qualifications: Judge's accuracy concern confirmed. The opening line 'A ward can lower its falls rate by keeping people in bed, and the falls figure will record that as an improvement' should be reworded as a statement about what the measure can and can't show.

claim: A mobility measure already exists and is recorded routinely in some hospitals; a project that raised mobility did not increase injurious falls.
supporting_passage: Hoyer 2025 (Methods): "The JH‐HLM is an 8‐point scale documented based on the patient's observedmobility (ranging from 1 = lying in bed to 8 = walking 250+ feet). It is also required to be recorded at least once per shift by nursing staff and after every therapy session." Hoyer 2016: "Comparing the ramp-up versus post-QI phases, patients reaching JH-HLM's ambulation status increased from 43% to 70% (P < 0.001)" ... "Increased mobility was not associated with an increase in injurious falls compared to 12 months prior on the QI units (P = 0.73)."
safe_wording: Some hospitals already record mobility next to falls. In Johns Hopkins hospitals in the US, nurses record each patient's highest level of mobility at least once a shift on an 8-point scale, from lying in bed to walking 250 feet or more. A quality improvement project there raised the share of patients who walked from 43% to 70%, with no rise in falls causing injury.
qualifications: Before-after design, not a trial; injurious falls only; US general medicine, adults of all ages. Meets the judge's request for a named service that already reports a mobility measure; no UK example was found in opened sources.

claim: Experts have proposed that hospitals measure mobility (for example times out of bed or walks per shift) alongside falls, and adjust falls metrics for the benefits of mobility.
supporting_passage: "The CMS should develop quality measures that promote mobility as part of routine clinical care, such as early mobilization protocols for hospital staff, mobility aides, and trained volunteers. Associated process measures might focus on documentation of number of times patients are out of bed or episodes of ambulation per nursing shift." ... "As more data regarding mobility are systematically collected, it will be important to ensure that current fall prevention metrics are adjusted to reflect the counterbalancing benefits of increased mobility."
safe_wording: Geriatricians writing in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2017 proposed counting how often patients get out of bed or walk in each nursing shift, and argued that falls measures should be adjusted for the benefits of moving. We think a falls rate should be reported next to a measure like this (judgement).
qualifications: Expert opinion, not a formal guideline; US context. Mark the post's position as judgement.

claim: Measures that restrict movement, such as bed alarms and restraints, lack good evidence for preventing hospital falls.
supporting_passage: Shorr 2012: "An intervention designed to increase bed alarm use in an urban hospital increased alarm use but had no statistically or clinically significant effect on fall-related events or physical restraint use." WFG: "There is currently no robust research evidence to recommend the use of (i) bed/chair alarms, (ii) grip socks/non-slip socks for the purpose of falls prevention and (iii) the use of physical restraints when the sole purpose is falls prevention in hospitals."
location: Shorr 2012 Abstract, Conclusion; WFG full text, Falls in hospitals
safe_wording: Measures that limit movement have weak evidence for preventing falls: a US trial that increased bed alarm use did not reduce falls, and the World Falls Guidelines found no strong research evidence for bed or chair alarms or physical restraints to prevent falls in hospital.
qualifications: Earlier posts (E166) covered alarms; use this only as supporting context, not as the argument.

claim: In a Sydney cohort of 500 older people living at home, combining concern about falling with measured physical risk gave four groups, and about a third had a mismatch between the two.
supporting_passage: Methods: "A total of 500 people aged 70–90 years participated in the prospective cohort study with a one year follow-up for falls. They were randomly recruited from a cohort of 1037 men and women living in the community in eastern Sydney and participating in the first stage of the Sydney Memory and Ageing Study (January 2006 to October 2007)." ... "Falls frequency during the one year follow-up was monitored with monthly falls diaries." Results: "Most people had an accurate perception of their fall risk: 144 (29%) comprised a “vigorous” group who had both low physiological and perceived fall risks, and 202 (40%) comprised an “aware” group who had both high physiological and perceived fall risks. About a third of our population, however, had disparities between their perceived and physiological fall risk: 54 (11%) had low physiological fall risk but a high perceived risk and were classified as “anxious,” and 100 (20%) had a high physiological risk but low perceived risk and were classified as “stoic.”"
location: Full text, Methods (Participants; Falls follow-up); Results (Classification tree); Abstract
safe_wording: A Sydney study of 500 people aged 70 to 90 living at home measured two things: how worried each person was about falling, and their physical risk (vision, sensation in the legs, leg strength, reaction time and balance). Most people's worry matched their risk. But about 1 in 3 did not: 11 in 100 were very worried despite a low physical risk, and 20 in 100 were unworried despite a high one.
qualifications: One Australian cohort, published 2010, of fairly healthy volunteers recruited from the electoral roll; people with dementia or Parkinson's disease were excluded. 'Physical risk' is the Physiological Profile Assessment score, not a clinical judgement. Group labels are the authors' (vigorous, aware, anxious, stoic).

claim: Both concern about falling and physical risk predicted injurious or repeated falls over the next year, each independently of the other.
supporting_passage: Delbaere 2010: "Fallers were defined as people who had at least one injurious fall or at least two non-injurious falls during the 12 month follow-up period." ... "Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified both risk factors as independent of each other and of similar importance (χ=13.32, df=2, P=0.001) (table 2)." Abstract: "Multivariate logistic regression analyses showed that perceived and physiological fall risk were both independent predictors of future falls." Results: "In all, 149 (30%) of participants reported one or more falls in the previous year, and 214 (43%) reported one or more falls during the one year follow-up (six participants were lost during follow-up for falls)." WFG 2022: "Concerns about falling—or the closely related notion of fear of falling—shows heterogeneous results in predicting future falls in the community."
location: Delbaere: Methods (Statistical analyses), Results (Predicting injurious or multiple falls, Table 2), Abstract. WFG: Concerns about falling and falls, Recommendation details and justification
safe_wording: In that study, both worry about falling and physical risk were linked with having an injurious fall or repeated falls over the next year, and each still counted after allowing for the other.
qualifications: Association in one cohort; the outcome is 'injurious or multiple falls', not any fall. Do not convert the odds ratios (1.29 and 1.23 in Table 2; the scaling unit is not stated in the extracted text) into 'times more likely'. Across other studies, concern predicts falls inconsistently (WFG).

claim: The 'anxious' group (low physical risk, high concern) had more depressive symptoms, more neurotic personality traits and poorer executive function; almost 40% of them had injurious or repeated falls, and they were not less active.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "The anxious group (54 (11%)) had a low physiological risk but high perceived fall risk, which was related to depressive symptoms (P=0.029), neurotic personality traits (P=0.026), and decreased executive functioning (P=0.010)." Discussion: "About 10% of the study population showed excessive levels of perceived fall risk and were classified as anxious. Despite their low physiological fall risk, almost 40% of the anxious group experienced multiple or injurious falls during the one year follow-up. In keeping with previous studies, we anticipated that self imposed restriction on levels of physical activity would contribute to overall risk in this group.However, there was no indication of lower levels of activity, so other reasons need to be explored as to why “anxious” participants fell more than “vigorous” participants during follow-up." Results: "the people who rated their fall risk inappropriately high (“anxious”) were more likely to be female, showed higher levels of self rated disability, had a lower quality of life, had more symptoms of depression, showed higher levels of neuroticism, scored poorly on executive functioning, and performed badly on the coordinated stability test compared with the group with an accurate perception of their low fall risk (“vigorous”)."
location: Abstract; Results (Differences between groups, Table 1); Discussion (Comparison with other studies)
safe_wording: The very worried people with a low physical risk were more likely to have low mood, a more anxious temperament and slower thinking on a planning test. Almost 4 in 10 of them had an injurious fall or repeated falls during the year. They were no less active than people with a matching low risk and low worry.
qualifications: Group differences are associations measured at baseline. The authors suggest poorer dynamic balance (coordinated stability test) and fear-induced stiffening as possible reasons; these are hypotheses.

claim: The 'stoic' group (high physical risk, low concern) were younger, stronger, more active and more positive; about 1 in 3 had injurious or repeated falls, fewer than the 'aware' group, and most who fell stayed unconcerned.
supporting_passage: Results: "People who rated their fall risk inappropriately low (“stoic”) were younger, took fewer medications in total and fewer psychotropic medications, had lower levels of self rated disability, had a better reported quality of life, did more planned exercise, had fewer symptoms of depression, showed lower levels of neuroticism, were stronger, and performed better on the coordinated stability test compared with the group with an accurate perception of their high fall risk (“aware”)." ... "Only six of the 34 stoics who fell during the follow-up year increased their concern about fall risk after an injurious or multiple fall, while the remainder stayed unconcerned about falls." Discussion: "About one in three stoics fell in the follow-up year—a rate intermediate between those of the vigorous group and the aware group." ... "However, the psychological profile of stoics did not indicate excessive risk taking behaviour but rather a positive attitude to life, emotional stability, and low reactivity to stress."
location: Results (Differences between groups); Discussion (Comparison with other studies)
safe_wording: The unworried people with a high physical risk tended to be younger, stronger, more active and more positive. About 1 in 3 of them had an injurious fall or repeated falls during the year: fewer than the worried high-risk group, more than the unworried low-risk group. Of the 34 who fell, only 6 became more concerned afterwards.
qualifications: Being unworried went with fewer falls than in the 'aware' group, probably through staying active; the authors found no sign of risk-taking. So do not present stoics as reckless or as the most endangered group; the point is that a worry-only check would call them low risk when 1 in 3 had serious or repeated falls.

claim: The authors suggested matching help to the group: psychological therapy (CBT) for the anxious, balance-challenging exercise for the stoic, both for the aware; guideline and trial evidence support exercise and CBT for reducing concerns.
supporting_passage: Delbaere 2010: "People equivalent to our anxious group should be guided towards cognitive behavioural therapy with the aim of improving self efficacy and sense of control over falling,reducing symptoms of depression,and promoting an active and healthy lifestyle.Stoics should be motivated to participate in exercise programmes specifically designed to reduce fall risk, comprising high intensity balance training,in addition to their own exercise regimen. For the aware, a combination of both exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy is likely to be most effective." WFG 2022: "We recommend exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and/or occupational therapy (as part of a multidisciplinary approach) to reduce concerns about falling in community-dwelling older adults" Liu 2018: "Our analysis suggests that CBT interventions have significant immediate and retention effects up to 12 months on reducing fear of falling, and 6 months post-intervention effect on enhancing balance." Kendrick 2014: "Exercise interventions in community-dwelling older people probably reduce fear of falling to a limited extent immediately after the intervention, without increasing the risk or frequency of falls."
location: Delbaere: Discussion (Clinical and future research implications). WFG: Concerns about falling and falls interventions. Liu 2018 and Kendrick 2014: Abstracts
safe_wording: The researchers suggested different help for each mismatch: for people who are very worried but physically at low risk, a talking therapy (cognitive behavioural therapy) to rebuild confidence; for people at high physical risk who are not worried, challenging balance exercise; for people who are both, both. International guidelines recommend exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy or occupational therapy to reduce concerns about falling.
qualifications: The per-group matching is the authors' proposal, not a tested strategy; say 'the researchers suggested'. The paper gives no specific advice for the 'vigorous' group; if the grid needs a line there, use the WFG advice for low-risk people (advice on staying safely active) and label it as general advice. Exercise evidence for reducing fear is low certainty and effects fade after programmes end.

claim: Guidelines recommend assessing concern about falling together with balance or gait, to put the concern in context.
supporting_passage: WFG 2022: "We recommend clinicians adopt a holistic approach, combining concern about falling with balance and/or gait assessment as this will help to put the degree of concern in context, when assessing older adults in the community." ... "an older adult inappropriately very fearful of falling may be reluctant to increase their physical activity and follow an exercise programme if this is not dealt with" Delbaere 2010 Conclusion: "Measures of both physiological and perceived fall risk should be included in fall risk assessments and the proposed disparity categorisation may assist in designing tailored interventions for preventing falls in elderly people."
location: WFG: Concerns about falling and falls, Recommendation details and justification. Delbaere: Conclusion
safe_wording: The World Falls Guidelines advise checking worry about falling alongside a test of balance or walking, so the worry can be read in context. The Sydney researchers reached the same conclusion: measure both.
qualifications: None beyond attributing it to the guideline.

claim: The four groups are approximate: the cut-points were derived in this sample, did not separate four distinct groups, and have not been confirmed elsewhere.
supporting_passage: "Although dichotomising the physiological profile assessment and the falls efficacy scale international provided a parsimonious way of assessing disparities between perceived and physiological fall risk, the cut-points we derived for these measures should be considered estimates only, as it can be seen from fig 2that the cut-points did not identify four distinct groups. Further studies are therefore necessary to confirm the cut-points in external samples, and to investigate whether the same disparity categorisation can also be found in elderly people at increased risk of falls, including those with cognitive impairment and Parkinson’s disease." Also: "Our sample largely consists of healthy, community dwelling, elderly adults"
safe_wording: The four groups are a way of thinking, not a validated test: the researchers said their dividing lines were estimates and needed checking in other groups of people, including people with dementia or Parkinson's disease.
qualifications: PubMed and Consensus searches (25 Sep 2026) found no replication of the four-group classification; that is an absence of evidence, not a failed replication.

claim: Wild, Nayak and Isaacs (BMJ 1981) studied 125 people aged 65 and over who fell at home, found through six general practices; 20 lay on the floor for more than an hour, and half of those 20 died within six months of the fall.
supporting_passage: Wild 1981 abstract: "From a survey in six general practices information was obtained on 125 people aged 65 and over who fell in their own homes. Three fractured their femurs and 15 had other fractures; most of the rest suffered only trivial injuries. Twenty lay on the floor for more than one hour; none were known to have suffered hypothermia. One-quarter of these patients died within one year of the fall, five times as many as in an age- and sex-matched control group; while of those who lay on the floor for more than one hour, half died within six months of the fall." Fleming 2008 (Discussion): "In a UK survey in general practice 16% of those aged over 65 who fell in their own homes lay on the floor for more than an hour."
location: Wild 1981 Abstract (full text not available as text); Fleming 2008 Discussion (Key findings in context)
safe_wording: The line 'half of people who lie on the floor for more than an hour die within six months' comes from a 1981 BMJ study. Researchers followed 125 people aged 65 and over who had fallen at home, found through six general practices. Twenty of them lay on the floor for more than an hour, and half of those 20 died within six months.
qualifications: The finding rests on 20 people; say 'half of 20 people', not a percentage of a large group. Do not say how many practices' patients were screened or give an exact number of deaths beyond 'half of the 20'; the full text was not read. Do not claim the figure is 'often quoted' (not verified; see C01-08-h). Do not imply the figure is wrong: it is small, old and describes an association.

claim: In the same 1981 study, fallers as a whole had high mortality, and the authors themselves concluded that falls at home often signal severe ill health.
supporting_passage: "One-quarter of these patients died within one year of the fall, five times as many as in an age- and sex-matched control group" ... "Factors associated with mortality from falls were impaired mobility, abnormal balance, and a disturbed pattern of gait. Falls at home in old age are often indicative of the presence of severe ill health."
safe_wording: The same study found that a quarter of all the people who fell died within a year, five times as many as in a comparison group of the same age and sex. The authors' own conclusion was that falls at home often point to severe ill health. So the deaths after long lies cannot all be put down to the time on the floor.
qualifications: The last sentence is an inference that follows from the design (no adjustment for illness in a series of 20); present it as a reading of the study, not a finding.

claim: People who cannot get up after a fall differ from those who can: they are older, have poorer balance, gait and mobility, and more depression or cognitive impairment.
supporting_passage: Tinetti 1993: "Compared with non-fallers, the risk factors independently associated with inability to get up included the following: an age of at least 80 years (adjusted relative risk [RR], 1.6; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2 to 2.1); depression (RR, 1.5; CI, 1.1 to 2.0); and poor balance and gait (RR, 2.0; CI, 1.5 to 2.7)." Fleming 2008 abstract: "Difficulty in getting up was consistently associated with age, reported mobility, and severe cognitive impairment. Cognition was the only characteristic that predicted lying on the floor for a long time." Kubitza 2023: "Older adults suffered falls [–,–,,–], but it has been the frailty of the individuals that affected their inability to get up after the fall [–,,–,]."
location: Tinetti Abstract (Results); Fleming Abstract; Kubitza Findings (Causes and associated factors)
safe_wording: People who can't get up after a fall are, on average, older, with weaker balance and walking, and more often have low mood or memory problems. Those same things are linked with dying sooner.
qualifications: The second sentence is general background; if used, keep it as a reason the link is hard to interpret, not as a new statistic.

claim: In a larger 1993 US cohort, fallers who could not get up were more likely to have a lasting decline in daily activities; differences in death and hospital admission pointed the same way but were not statistically significant.
supporting_passage: "Inability to get up without help was reported after 220 of 596 non-injurious falls. Of 313 non-injured fallers, 148 (47%) reported inability to get up after at least one fall." ... "Compared with fallers who were able to get up, fallers who were unable to get up were more likely to suffer lasting decline in activities of daily living (35% vs 26%). Fallers who were unable to get up were more likely to die, to be hospitalized, and to suffer a decline in activities of daily living for at least 3 days, and were less likely to be placed in a nursing home than were fallers who were able to get up, but these trends were not statistically significant."
safe_wording: A larger US study published in 1993 followed 1103 people aged 72 and over. Among those who fell without serious injury, almost half (148 of 313) could not get up at least once. They were more likely to lose everyday abilities for good (35 in 100, against 26 in 100 of those who could get up). They were also more likely to die, but that difference could have been chance.
qualifications: Exposure is 'unable to get up without help', not a timed long lie. Self-reported. Old US cohort.

claim: A 2008 UK cohort of people over 90 linked lying on the floor for an hour or more with serious injury and fall-related hospital admission; the link with moving into a care home was uncertain after adjustment, and death was not reported.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Of the 60% who fell, 80% (53/66) were unable to get up after at least one fall and 30% (20/66) had lain on the floor for an hour or more." Results: "Serious injury, however, was consistently associated with lying on the floor for a long time, regardless of adjustment. Of the 20 people who were reported to be on the floor over an hour after falling, 60% (12) had a fall related hospital admission during the follow-up year (4.0, 1.3 to 12.3)." ... "giving a threefold increased odds of admission to a care home, though the risk estimate did not reach significance in this smaller sample (n=51 not living in care who fell) until the censoring, conducted when everyone had completed their year since interview (crude hazard ratio 3.4 (1.2 to 9.5), adjusted 2.3 (0.8 to 7.0))." Limitations: "Some caution is warranted in interpreting the analyses of association between risk factors and these consequences of falling; lack of association might indicate only the limited power of the small sample size."
location: Abstract; Results (Factors associated with inability to get up and lying on the floor for a long time; Table 4); Discussion (Limitations)
safe_wording: A 2008 Cambridge study of people over 90 found that 20 of the 66 who fell lay on the floor for an hour or more at least once in a year. Twelve of those 20 had a hospital admission for a fall. Long lies were linked with serious injury. A link with moving into a care home was uncertain once other factors were allowed for.
qualifications: Small, very old population; associations; injuries can be a cause as well as a result of a long lie (the authors say so). The abstract's 'strongly associated' with long-term care is not borne out after adjustment. The study did not report deaths by long-lie status, so it does not update the 1981 six-month death figure.

claim: Current guidelines treat an hour or more on the floor as a sign of high falls risk that should lead to a full falls assessment, and list harms linked with long lies.
supporting_passage: "An adult who sustains an injury requiring medical (including surgical) treatment, reports recurrent falls (≥2) in the previous 12 months, was laying on the floor unable to rise independently for at least one hour, is considered frail or is suspected to have experienced a transient loss of consciousness should be regarded as at high risk of future falls" ... "These high-risk older adults should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment." ... "Lying on the floor for more than an hour is associated with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, renal failure, hypothermia, pneumonia and urinary tract infections, skin damage and pain [,], and declines in mobility and restrictions in activity, probably due to fear of a repeat fall. ‘Lift and assist’ call outs should trigger falls prevention interventions []."
location: Full text: Older adults presenting with falls or related injuries; Assessment and algorithm flow; Exercise and physical activity interventions (Recommendation details and justification)
safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines count being unable to get up for an hour or more as a sign of high risk of further falls, and say it should lead to a full falls assessment. They link long lies with dehydration, kidney problems, low body temperature, pneumonia, skin damage and pain. They also say that a call-out just to help someone up should trigger falls prevention.
qualifications: Harms are listed as associations. The guideline does not cite or repeat the 'half die within six months' figure.

claim: There is no agreed definition of a 'long lie'; studies have used thresholds from five minutes to an hour or more.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "The results show that a standard concept of a long lie is lacking. The duration of lying and the location alone are not relevant criteria." Findings: "In eight studies, a specific time was also used to determine long lie, ranging from five minutes [], ten minutes [], and fifteen minutes [] to one hour or more [,,,,]. While seven studies were more unspecific in this aspect and used the terms longer time [,,–,] or several hours to days [], five studies did not use time restrictions at all [,,,,]." Discussion: "The consequences significantly improve with increasing lying time, but they can already occur in less than one hour"
safe_wording: There is no agreed definition of a 'long lie'. Studies have used anything from 5 minutes to an hour or more, so figures from different studies are not directly comparable.
qualifications: The review's sentence about consequences 'improving' with lying time is ambiguous wording in the source (it appears to mean worsening); do not quote it.

claim: The 1981 figure is often quoted in falls teaching.
supporting_passage: No opened source measures or states how often the figure is quoted. The WFG 2022 long-lie section does not quote it; Swancutt 2020 and Fleming 2008 mention death as a possible consequence of long lies without giving the figure.
safe_wording: Do not say the figure is 'often quoted'. Open with the quoted line itself and its source, for example: 'Half of people who lie on the floor for more than an hour die within six months.' That line comes from a 1981 study of 20 people.
qualifications: Frequency of use in teaching is an unverified assumption.

claim: The World Falls Guidelines 2022 advise asking older people whether concerns about falling limit their usual activities, both in routine contacts and after a fall.
supporting_passage: "Clinicians should routinely ask about falls in their interactions with older adults, as they often will not be spontaneously reported." ... "If resources and time are available, we conditionally recommend to additionally ask (iii) if they have experienced dizziness, loss of consciousness or any disturbance of gait or balance and (iv) if they experience any concerns about falling causing limitation of usual activities" ... "Older adults presenting with a fall or related injury should be asked about the details of the event and its consequences, previous falls, transient loss of consciousness or dizziness and any pre-existing impairment of mobility or concerns about falling causing limitation of usual activities."
location: Full text: Opportunistic case-finding; Older adults presenting with falls or related injuries
safe_wording: International falls guidelines advise asking older people whether worry about falling is limiting what they usually do. After a fall, this question is part of the recommended history; in routine contacts it is a conditional recommendation where time allows.
qualifications: The candidate's 'in every conversation about falls' is stronger than the guideline; say 'whenever falls come up' or 'after any fall' and mark it as advice.

claim: The guidelines recommend including concern about falling in a full falls assessment, using the FES-I or Short FES-I, and using the word 'concern' rather than 'fear'.
supporting_passage: "We recommend including an evaluation of concern about falling in a multifactorial falls risk assessment of older adults" (1B) ... "We recommend using a standardized instrument to evaluate concerns about falling such as the Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I) or Short FES-I in community-dwelling older adults." (1A) ... "The older adult panel we consulted about the recommendations preferred the term concern over fear. Based on this, we recommend that clinicians use the term concerns about falling when making enquiries."
location: Full text: Table of recommendations (WG 12 Concerns about Falling and Falls); Concerns about falling and falls (Recommendation details and justification)
safe_wording: The guidelines recommend that a full falls assessment includes a check on worry about falling, ideally with a short standard questionnaire (the Falls Efficacy Scale International, or its 7-question short form). The older people who advised the guideline panel preferred the word 'concern' to 'fear'.
qualifications: Grades: 1B for including concern; 1A for using FES-I/Short FES-I in the community.

claim: Worry about falling is common in older people, including people who have never fallen, although estimates vary widely with how it is measured.
supporting_passage: Scheffer 2008: "fear of falling (FOF) is a major health problem among the elderly living in communities, present in older people who have fallen but also in older people who have never experienced a fall." ... "Due to the many different kinds of measurements used, the reported prevalence of FOF varied between 3 and 85%." ... "The main consequences were identified as a decline in physical and mental performance, an increased risk of falling and progressive loss of health-related quality of life." Xiong 2024: "A total of the 153 studies with 200,033 participants from 38 countries worldwide were identified. The global prevalence of fear of falling was 49.60%, ranging from 6.96-90.34%."
safe_wording: Worry about falling is common in later life, and it affects people who have never fallen as well as those who have. How common depends on how it is measured: studies range from fewer than 1 in 10 to 9 in 10 older people.
qualifications: Avoid a single headline figure; if the pooled 49.6% is used, say 'about half, in a review whose studies ranged from 7 to 90 in 100'. Consequences in Scheffer are associations.

claim: Among older people who report fear of falling, most have cut back at least one activity, and cutting back three or more activities is linked with faster loss of physical function over three years.
supporting_passage: "Six hundred seventy-three community-living elderly (≥65) participants in the Invecchiare in Chianti Study who reported FF." ... "One-quarter (25.5%) of participants did not report any activity restriction, 59.6% reported moderate activity restriction (restriction or avoidance of <3 activities), and 14.9% reported severe activity restriction (restriction or avoidance of ≥3 activities)." ... "Severe activity restriction was a significant independent predictor of worsening ADL disability and accelerated decline in lower extremity performance on SPPB over the 3-year follow-up. Severe and moderate activity restriction were independent predictors of worsening IADL disability. Results were consistent even after adjusting for multiple potential confounders."
safe_wording: In an Italian study of 673 people aged 65 and over who said they were afraid of falling, 3 in 4 had cut back or avoided at least one activity because of it. People who had given up three or more activities lost everyday abilities and leg function faster over the next 3 years, even after allowing for other health differences.
qualifications: Association, not proof that restriction caused the decline. '3 in 4' = 59.6% + 14.9% = 74.5%. Population is people who already reported fear of falling, not all older people.

claim: The standard questionnaires ask about concern during specific everyday activities, inside and outside the home, physical and social.
supporting_passage: Yardley 2005: "Factor analysis suggested a unitary underlying factor, with two dimensions assessing concern about less demanding physical activities mainly in the home, and concern about more demanding physical activities mainly outside the home." ... "The FES-I has close continuity with the best existing measure of fear of falling, excellent psychometric properties, and assesses concerns relating to basic and more demanding activities, both physical and social." Kempen 2008: "the Short FES-I is a good and feasible measure to assess fear of falling in older persons." Delbaere 2010: "Using the falls efficacy scale international (FES-I), we assessed participants’ perceived fall risk by asking about concern about falling across a wide range of activities of daily living (such as cleaning the house, shopping, walking on uneven surfaces)."
location: Yardley Abstract; Kempen Abstract; Delbaere Methods (Neuropsychological assessment)
safe_wording: The standard questionnaire (FES-I) asks how concerned a person is about falling during specific everyday activities, such as cleaning the house, shopping or walking on uneven ground, covering things done at home, outside and socially.
qualifications: Individual item wording was not read; use only the example activities quoted (cleaning the house, shopping, walking on uneven surfaces). The drawn icons (walk, bus, bath, visiting friends) must be labelled as examples, not as FES-I items.

claim: What to do with the answer: exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and occupational therapy are recommended to reduce concerns about falling, though the evidence on restoring the activities people have given up is thin.
supporting_passage: WFG 2022: "We recommend exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and/or occupational therapy (as part of a multidisciplinary approach) to reduce concerns about falling in community-dwelling older adults" ... "Existing fall prevention strategies, i.e. exercise interventions, can reduce concerns about falling in older adults." Kendrick 2014: "Exercise interventions in community-dwelling older people probably reduce fear of falling to a limited extent immediately after the intervention, without increasing the risk or frequency of falls. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether exercise interventions reduce fear of falling beyond the end of the intervention or their effect on other outcomes." ... "No studies reported the effects of exercise interventions on activity avoidance or costs." Liu 2018: "Our analysis suggests that CBT interventions have significant immediate and retention effects up to 12 months on reducing fear of falling, and 6 months post-intervention effect on enhancing balance."
location: WFG: Concerns about falling and falls interventions; Kendrick Abstract (Results, Authors' conclusions); Liu Abstract
safe_wording: If the answer is yes, tell the GP or physiotherapist what has stopped. Guidelines recommend strength and balance exercise, a talking therapy called cognitive behavioural therapy, or help from an occupational therapist with the activity itself. Exercise reduces worry a little; the talking therapy has shown benefit lasting up to a year.
qualifications: The instruction 'tell the GP or physiotherapist' is practical advice, not a tested intervention. No exercise trial in the Cochrane review measured activity avoidance, so do not promise that the lost activities will come back.

claim: Concern about falling can be sensible caution or excessive; either way, high concern is a signal for clinical attention, and a 'no' does not prove low risk.
supporting_passage: Ellmers 2023: "On the one hand, high CaF can lead to overly cautious or hypervigilant behaviours that increase the risk of falling, and may also cause undue activity restriction ('maladaptive CaF'). But concerns can also encourage individuals to make appropriate modifications to their behaviour to maximise safety ('adaptive CaF'). We discuss this paradox and argue that high CaF-irrespective of whether 'adaptive' or 'maladaptive'-should be considered an indication that 'something is not right', and that is represents an opportunity for clinical engagement. We also highlight how CaF can be maladaptive in terms of inappropriately high confidence about one's balance." Delbaere 2010: "100 (20%) had a high physiological risk but low perceived risk and were classified as “stoic.”"
safe_wording: Some caution after a fall is sensible, and some is more than the risk warrants. Either way, falls specialists treat high concern as a sign that something needs looking at. A 'no' is not an all-clear: in one study, 1 in 5 people with a high physical risk were not worried at all.
qualifications: Ellmers is expert opinion. '1 in 5' is from the Sydney cohort (100 of 500).

claim: In a 1988 US study, between 13% and 32% of people who had a confirmed fall did not remember falling when asked at the end of the year, depending on the period asked about.
supporting_passage: "we studied 304 ambulatory men and women over the age of 60 years who completed a 12-month prospective study of risk factors for falling. We developed a system of weekly follow-up and home visits to record and confirm all falls. During the study, 179 participants suffered at least one fall that was confirmed by home visit. At the end of the study, all subjects were interviewed by telephone about whether they had suffered a fall during the preceding 3, 6, or 12 months. Depending on the time period of recall, 13% to 32% of those with confirmed falls did not recall falling during the specific period of time. Recall was better for the preceding 12 months than for 3 or 6 months." ... "Those with lower scores on the Mini-Mental State Examination were more likely to forget falls."
safe_wording: In a US study, researchers checked on 304 people over 60 every week for a year and visited to confirm each fall. At the end of the year, between 13 and 32 in 100 of the people who had a confirmed fall did not remember falling in the period they were asked about. People with poorer memory test scores forgot more often.
qualifications: The figures are for people, not falls (judge's correction). The abstract does not say which figure applies to 12 months, so do not write 'a third forgot a year later'; use the range, or 'up to 1 in 3'. Recall of the whole 12 months was better than of the last 3 or 6 months, so the problem is partly misplacing falls in time.

claim: A systematic review found that asking people about falls over the past year misses about 1 or 2 in 10 people who fell; injurious falls are remembered better.
supporting_passage: "Six studies met the inclusion criteria. Recall of falls in the previous year was specific (specificity 91-95%) but less sensitive (sensitivity 80-89%) than the criterion standard of ongoing prospective collection of fall data using fall calendars or postcards. Patients with injurious falls were more likely to recall their falls. Lower Mini-Mental State Examination score was associated with poorer recall of falls in the one study addressing this issue."
safe_wording: A review of six studies found that when people were asked about the past year, 80 to 89 in 100 of those who had fallen remembered it. Falls that caused an injury were remembered better.
qualifications: 'Misses 1 or 2 in 10' is 100 minus sensitivity (11 to 20 in 100), a simple restatement.

claim: Even over three months, telephone recall missed a quarter of people whose daily falls calendar showed a fall.
supporting_passage: "Falls were tracked prospectively on daily calendars (mailed back monthly)." ... "However, while the 3-month recall correctly classified persons who did not fall (164 persons by both methods), it missed 25% of participants who fell (of 36 participants with a calendar-reported fall, 9 did not report a fall by telephone recall)." ... "Calendars should be considered the preferred method of ascertaining falls in longitudinal studies."
safe_wording: In a Boston study, 9 of 36 people whose daily calendar recorded a fall did not mention it when phoned three months later.
qualifications: Small number of fallers.

claim: In people with dementia, about half of those who recorded a fall did not recall it a year later, GPs knew of few falls, and information from carers improved accuracy.
supporting_passage: "GPs knew of only 14% of falls and 19% of fallers. In addition, 49% of subjects who documented a fall prospectively did not recall a fall after 12 months." ... "If feasible, recall periods should be as short as one week; additional information by care-givers increases accuracy of reports. Retrospective recall of falling with long recall periods is not recommended."
safe_wording: In a German study of 110 people with dementia, about half of those who had recorded a fall did not remember falling when asked a year later. Their GPs knew about only 14 in 100 of the falls. Information from carers made the record more accurate.
qualifications: Dementia-specific and research setting; GP awareness figure is for this study only.

claim: Falls research records falls as they happen, on daily calendars or diaries returned weekly or monthly, because recall over months is unreliable.
supporting_passage: Ganz 2005: "Whenever accurate data on all falls are critical, such as with interventions to decrease the rate of falls, researchers should gather information on falls every week or every month from study participants. The optimal method of fall monitoring--postcard, calendar, diary, telephone, or some combination of these--remains unknown." Hannan 2010: "Calendars should be considered the preferred method of ascertaining falls in longitudinal studies." Delbaere 2010: "Falls frequency during the one year follow-up was monitored with monthly falls diaries." Fleming 2008 abstract: "1 year follow-up of participants in a prospective cohort study of ageing, using fall calendars, phone calls, and visits."
location: Ganz Abstract (Conclusion); Hannan Abstract; Delbaere Methods; Fleming Abstract
safe_wording: Falls researchers don't rely on memory: they ask people to mark each fall on a calendar or diary as it happens and send it in every week or month.
qualifications: Lamb 2005 (ProFaNE consensus, PMID 16137297) was checked but its abstract does not state the calendar recommendation, and the full text was not available, so it is not cited for this claim. Ganz notes the best method is unknown.

claim: Guidelines ask clinicians to take a detailed history of each fall: how often, the circumstances, dizziness or blackout, consequences, and whether the person could get up; recollection of falls is unreliable, and many people do not mention falls unless asked.
supporting_passage: "Older adults in contact with healthcare for any reason should be asked, at least once yearly, if they have (i) experienced one or more falls in the last 12 months, and (ii) about the frequency, characteristics, context, severity and consequences of any fall/s." ... "Older adults presenting with a fall or related injury should be asked about the details of the event and its consequences, previous falls, transient loss of consciousness or dizziness and any pre-existing impairment of mobility or concerns about falling causing limitation of usual activities." ... "Furthermore, recollection of the occurrence or date (e.g., how many months ago) of previous falls is unreliable []" ... "Studies indicate that older adults, particularly men, are reluctant to report falls with less than a third mentioning them to their clinician if not directly asked []." ... "was laying on the floor unable to rise independently for at least one hour"
location: Full text: Opportunistic case-finding; Older adults presenting with falls or related injuries; Assessment and algorithm flow; Multifactorial falls risk assessment (Recommendation details)
safe_wording: Falls guidelines ask doctors to find out, for each fall, what the person was doing, where, whether they felt dizzy or blacked out, what happened afterwards and whether they could get up. The guidelines also say people's memory of when falls happened is unreliable, and that fewer than 1 in 3 older men mention a fall unless asked.
qualifications: The 'fewer than a third' statement is the guideline's summary of other studies and refers to older adults, 'particularly men'; keep that wording. The diary columns in the visual (date and time, where, what you were doing, how you felt just before, could you get up and how long on the floor) map onto these items; 'how long on the floor' matters because an hour or more marks high risk.

claim: Keeping a written note of each fall at home, and taking it to appointments, helps the clinician.
supporting_passage: No study was found that tested patient- or family-held falls diaries in clinical care. Indirect support: Cummings 1988 "Researchers and clinicians should consider using methods besides long-term recall for ascertaining and counting falls over specific periods of time." Zieschang 2011 "additional information by care-givers increases accuracy of reports."
safe_wording: Present it as practical advice: 'Write each fall down on the day, and take the note to appointments. Memory of falls fades, and the details are what the doctor needs.' Do not claim that keeping a diary has been shown to reduce falls or improve care.
qualifications: Evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit. Cummings's recommendation to consider methods other than recall is addressed to researchers and clinicians.

claim: A structured check (new head, neck or back pain; can't move a limb; unconscious at any point; chest pain or breathing difficulty; head knock while on a blood thinner) decides whether to call an ambulance or help the person up, taken word for word from one current opened source (ISTUMBLE, NHS inform, NHS website or St John Ambulance).
supporting_passage: No opened source gives the checklist. Search-engine summary only (not verbatim from an opened page): "ISTUMBLE is a free interactive post-falls assessment tool devised by the West Midlands Ambulance Service to help carers and care assistants assess fallen residents and make informed decisions whether they can lift the fallen person themselves safely and with the appropriate lifting equipment." ... "The free ISTUMBLE App takes carers through a series of questions, such as 'Does the person who has fallen have new neck or back pain?,' to help distinguish whether the carer can safely lift the resident themselves with lifting equipment or if they need to call an ambulance immediately." Gunson 2025 systematic review of ambulance responses to older fallers (PDF read via Undermind): no mention of ISTUMBLE or of a care-home lifting checklist.
location: WebSearch result summary (winncare.uk, thiis.co.uk, attoday.co.uk, mangarhealth.com, apps.apple.com pages listed; none opened); Gunson 2025 full text
safe_wording: Not verified. Do not publish a checklist. The only information on ISTUMBLE came from search-engine summaries of manufacturer and app-store pages, which also show the tool is promoted by a lifting-equipment company.
qualifications: Safety-critical advice (when not to move someone) must come verbatim from an opened, current official source. NHS inform, NHS website, St John Ambulance and West Midlands Ambulance Service pages could not be opened (WebFetch blocked); PubMed, Consensus and Undermind searches found no published description of ISTUMBLE's items; Google Drive holds no copy.

claim: Moving and handling guidance advises against manually lifting a fallen person from the floor because of the risk of injury to carers.
supporting_passage: Swancutt 2020 (Introduction, background citing other work): "It is not only the person who has fallen who suffers; carers suffer distress due to the person fallen not being able to get up, or not being able to help them. They may be unsure how best to assist, which may result in their own injury or the need for additional assistance [,]."
safe_wording: Not verified as guidance. At most: 'Helping someone up can injure the helper as well' (background statement in a 2020 study), which is too thin for a safety instruction.
qualifications: HSE moving and handling pages could not be opened. The Swancutt sentence is an introduction citation, not a finding or a recommendation.

claim: An uninjured person can often get up with coaching, using a sturdy chair, following a published physiotherapy method.
supporting_passage: No opened source gives a step-by-step method (the same gap was recorded in C01-B2, claim C01-03-l). NHS inform, Chartered Society of Physiotherapy and Age UK pages could not be opened.
safe_wording: Not verified. Do not give getting-up steps.
qualifications: See C01-B2 C01-03-f to C01-03-l for what is verified about floor-rise training.

claim: Guidelines recommend a post-fall assessment for care home residents, partly to avoid unnecessary transfer to hospital.
supporting_passage: "We recommend conducting a post-fall assessment in care home residents following a fall in order to reassess fall risk factors, adjust the intervention strategy for the resident and avoid unnecessary transfer to acute care." and "We recommend conducting a post-fall assessment in care home residents following a fall in order to identify the mechanism of the fall, any resulting injuries, to reassess the resident's fall risk factors, adjust the intervention strategy for the resident and avoid unnecessary transfer to hospital."
location: Full text: Table of recommendations (Care homes assessment, grade E); Care homes section
safe_wording: International falls guidelines recommend that care home residents are assessed after every fall, to find any injury, work out why it happened, and avoid sending people to hospital when they don't need to go.
qualifications: Grade E (expert opinion). The guideline does not specify what the on-the-floor assessment should contain, so it cannot supply the candidate's checklist.

claim: Under the 2019 European definition (EWGSOP2), low muscle strength is the primary parameter: low strength means probable sarcopenia, low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and low physical performance marks it as severe.
supporting_passage: "In its 2018 definition, EWGSOP2 uses low muscle strength as the primary parameter of sarcopenia; muscle strength is presently the most reliable measure of muscle function (Table). Specifically, sarcopenia is probable when low muscle strength is detected. A sarcopenia diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of low muscle quantity or quality. When low muscle strength, low muscle quantity/quality and low physical performance are all detected, sarcopenia is considered severe." Also: "In these revised guidelines, muscle strength comes to the forefront, as it is recognised that strength is better than mass in predicting adverse outcomes"
safe_wording: Since 2019, the main European definition puts muscle strength first. Low strength (weak grip or slow chair rises) means sarcopenia is 'probable'. A measure of muscle quantity confirms it, and slow walking or other poor performance marks it as severe.
qualifications: European consensus; other regions (for example Asia) use their own criteria. Published in Age Ageing 2019 (the group met in 2018).

claim: EWGSOP2 cut-offs: grip strength below 27 kg in men and 16 kg in women, or more than 15 seconds for five chair rises, indicate low strength; a usual gait speed of 0.8 m/s or less indicates severe sarcopenia.
supporting_passage: EWGSOP2 Figure 2 caption: "Cut-off points based on T-score of ≤ -2.5 are shown for males and females (≤ 27 kg and 16 kg, respectively)." EWGSOP2 text: "The chair stand test measures the amount of time needed for a patient to rise five times from a seated position without using his or her arms" and "For simplicity, a single cut-off speed ≤0.8 m/s is advised by EWGSOP2 as an indicator of severe sarcopenia." Habboub 2026 abstract: "Sarcopenia was defined using EWGSOP2 criteria: probable sarcopenia as handgrip strength < 27 kg (men) or < 16 kg (women) and/or chair stand test > 15 s." Brennan-Olsen 2019: "the EWGSOP2 cut-points [11] of < 27 kg for men and < 16 kg for women as indicative of low grip strength"
location: EWGSOP2 full text (Figure 2 caption; 'Muscle strength' and 'Physical performance' sections); Habboub 2026 Abstract, Methods; Brennan-Olsen 2019 full-text excerpt
safe_wording: In the European definition, grip strength below about 27 kg in men or 16 kg in women, or needing more than 15 seconds to stand up from a chair five times without using the arms, counts as low strength. A usual walking speed of 0.8 metres per second or slower marks severe sarcopenia.
qualifications: The chair-stand cut-off (>15 s) was confirmed from secondary sources quoting EWGSOP2 because Table 3 of the consensus was not readable; the Figure 2 caption writes the grip cut-off as '<= 27 kg and 16 kg' whereas secondary sources quote '< 27 kg and < 16 kg'. Say 'below about 27 kg / 16 kg'. EWGSOP2 says its cut-offs focus on European populations and advises regional norms where available. Grip needs a calibrated dynamometer under standard conditions.

claim: EWGSOP2 states that in clinical practice low muscle strength (probable sarcopenia) is enough to trigger assessment of causes and to start intervention, without waiting for a muscle-mass measurement.
supporting_passage: Brennan-Olsen 2019 (full-text excerpt): "The revised EWGSOP2 consensus regarding sarcopenia identified that, in clinical practice, low grip strength is enough to trigger assessment of causes and start intervention for sarcopenia [11], which is indicative of an increasing focus on muscle strength rather than muscle mass as a key determinant of sarcopenia". EWGSOP2 Figure 1 note (PMC text): "Consider other reasons for low muscle strength (e.g. depression, sroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders)."
location: Brennan-Olsen 2019 Discussion (Scite full-text excerpt); EWGSOP2 Figure 1 legend
safe_wording: In everyday practice, the European group says weak grip or slow chair rises are enough to start looking for causes and to start treatment. A scan to measure muscle can come later, if it will change what you do.
qualifications: The exact EWGSOP2 wording sits in its algorithm figure, which could not be read directly; it is verified through a peer-reviewed paper quoting it (and a second, conference abstract found in Scite with the same wording). Low strength has other causes (EWGSOP2 lists depression, stroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders), so 'look for causes' must stay in the wording. Do not say imaging is unnecessary: EWGSOP2 still confirms sarcopenia with a muscle-quantity measure.

claim: The 2018 international (ICFSR) guideline strongly recommends resistance-based physical activity to treat sarcopenia, conditionally recommends protein supplementation or a protein-rich diet, and gives no recommendation for vitamin D or anabolic hormones.
supporting_passage: Dent 2018: "To treat sarcopenia, we strongly recommend the prescription of resistance-based physical activity, and conditionally recommend protein supplementation/a protein-rich diet. No recommendation is given for Vitamin D supplementation or for anabolic hormone prescription. There is a lack of robust evidence to assess the strength of other treatment options." Sayer 2024: "Resistance exercise is currently the mainstay of treatment; however, it is not suitable for all."
safe_wording: The international sarcopenia guideline strongly recommends strength (resistance) exercise as treatment and gives a weaker recommendation for more protein. It makes no recommendation for vitamin D or hormone treatment. A 2024 review calls resistance exercise the mainstay of treatment, while noting it does not suit everyone.
qualifications: Guideline dated 2018; 'strong' and 'conditional' are GRADE strengths of recommendation, not effect sizes.

claim: EWGSOP2 recommends the SARC-F questionnaire for case-finding, but SARC-F has low-to-moderate sensitivity and mainly detects severe cases.
supporting_passage: EWGSOP2: "EWGSOP2 recommends use of the SARC-F questionnaire as a way to elicit self-reports from patients on signs that are characteristic of sarcopenia." and "SARC-F has a low-to-moderate sensitivity and a very high specificity to predict low muscle strength []. As such, SARC-F will mostly detect severe cases." Also: "case-finding may start when a patient reports symptoms or signs of sarcopenia (i.e. falling, feeling weak, slow walking speed, difficulty rising from a chair or weight loss/muscle wasting)." Dent 2018: "advocate for rapid screening using gait speed or the SARC-F."
location: EWGSOP2 full text, 'Finding sarcopenia cases'; Dent 2018 Abstract
safe_wording: A five-question checklist (SARC-F: strength, walking, rising from a chair, climbing stairs, falls) is recommended to pick out people to test. It misses milder cases, so falls, feeling weak, slow walking or trouble getting out of a chair are reasons to test strength anyway.
qualifications: SARC-F is a screen, not a diagnosis.

claim: The 2024 GLIS global definition is conceptual: muscle mass, muscle strength and muscle-specific strength are components and impaired physical performance is an outcome; an operational definition with cut-offs had not been published by early 2026.
supporting_passage: Kirk 2024: "A key finding of the Delphi survey was that muscle mass, muscle strength and muscle-specific strength were all accepted as 'components of sarcopenia', whereas impaired physical performance was accepted as an 'outcome' rather than a 'component' of sarcopenia." and "The GLIS has created the first global conceptual definition of sarcopenia, which will now serve to develop an operational definition for clinical and research settings." Yin 2026: "While the Global Leadership Initiative on Sarcopenia (GLIS) is promising to standardize sarcopenia diagnosis, its operational implementation remains largely undefined."
safe_wording: A 2024 global consensus agreed what sarcopenia is in concept (muscle mass, strength and strength per unit of muscle), but has not yet set bedside tests or cut-offs. For now the European pathway is the practical one.
qualifications: Keep GLIS out of the pathway diagram (judge's concern); mention in one line at most. The absence of an operational GLIS definition is based on a PubMed search to September 2026 and one 2026 paper's statement.

claim: No medicine is licensed for sarcopenia.
supporting_passage: "Progress in developing effective drug treatments has been slow [,] and there are no licenced drugs for sarcopenia because initially promising avenues to date have not been supported by findings from well conducted randomised controlled trials []."
safe_wording: There is no medicine licensed to treat sarcopenia; exercise, above all strength training, is the treatment.
qualifications: Statement from a 2022 expert review, not a check of the BNF or MHRA (not accessible here). Say 'no licensed medicine' without adding 'in the UK' unless the BNF is checked.

claim: A practical starting dose of resistance exercise for sarcopenia is two sessions a week of upper- and lower-body exercises, 1-3 sets of 6-12 repetitions, with a relatively high degree of effort.
supporting_passage: "For example, a recent review on the prescription and delivery of resistance exercise for sarcopenia proposed a programme that consisted of two exercise sessions per week involving a combination of upper- and lower-body exercises performed with a relatively high degree of effort for 1–3 sets of 6–12 repetitions []." Also: "The consensus on the benefit of resistance exercise for the treatment of sarcopenia within the research world has yet to translate into consistent provision of resistance exercise in clinical practice"
safe_wording: One proposed starting point: strength exercises for arms and legs twice a week, one to three sets of 6 to 12 repetitions, hard enough that the last few feel like real effort.
qualifications: This is a proposal from a review, not a tested standard; frame as 'one proposed programme'. Adapt for pain, heart disease and frailty (judgement: suggest a physiotherapist for people with complex needs).

claim: In a randomised trial, 100 frail nursing home residents (mean age 87.1, range 72 to 98) received progressive resistance training, a nutritional supplement, both or neither for 10 weeks.
supporting_passage: "We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial comparing progressive resistance exercise training, multinutrient supplementation, both interventions, and neither in 100 frail nursing home residents over a 10-week period." and "The mean (+/- SE) age of the 63 women and 37 men enrolled in the study was 87.1 +/- 0.6 years (range, 72 to 98); 94 percent of the subjects completed the study."
safe_wording: In a 1994 US trial, 100 frail care home residents with an average age of 87 (the oldest was 98) were randomly given strength training or not for 10 weeks.
qualifications: Single trial, 1994, in residents well enough to consent and take part.

claim: Muscle strength increased by 113% with training versus 3% without; gait velocity rose 11.8% with training and fell 1.0% without; stair-climbing power improved 28.4% versus 3.6%. The supplement alone had no effect.
supporting_passage: "Muscle strength increased by 113 +/- 8 percent in the subjects who underwent exercise training, as compared with 3 +/- 9 percent in the nonexercising subjects (P < 0.001). Gait velocity increased by 11.8 +/- 3.8 percent in the exercisers but declined by 1.0 +/- 3.8 percent in the nonexercisers (P = 0.02). Stair-climbing power also improved in the exercisers as compared with the nonexercisers (by 28.4 +/- 6.6 percent vs. 3.6 +/- 6.7 percent, P = 0.01), as did the level of spontaneous physical activity." and "The nutritional supplement had no effect on any primary outcome measure."
safe_wording: Residents who did the strength training more than doubled their muscle strength on average (up 113%, against 3% in those who did not). Their walking speed rose by about 12%, while it fell slightly in the others. The supplement drink on its own made no difference.
qualifications: These are average percentage changes from each person's own starting level (relative, not absolute); starting strength was low. 'More than doubled' is accurate for a 113% increase. The training was high-intensity progressive resistance training (abstract conclusion); the full text was not accessible, so do not describe equipment or supervision as fact, and treat the proposed drawing of machines as unverified.

claim: An earlier small study found high-intensity strength training in frail care home residents aged about 90 increased strength by 174% over 8 weeks.
supporting_passage: "Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers aged 90 +/- 1 years undertook 8 weeks of high-intensity resistance training." and "Strength gains averaged 174% +/- 31% (mean +/- SEM) in the 9 subjects who completed training." and "high-resistance weight training leads to significant gains in muscle strength, size, and functional mobility among frail residents of nursing homes up to 96 years of age."
safe_wording: Even earlier, in 1990, a small study of 10 care home residents aged around 90 found their strength rose substantially after 8 weeks of strength training.
qualifications: Tiny, uncontrolled pilot; use only as background, not as the headline figure.

claim: A Cochrane review of physical rehabilitation for older people in long-term care found small improvements in daily activities, did not show a clear effect on walking speed, found no increase in deaths, and warned that bias may have overestimated benefits.
supporting_passage: "We included 67 trials, involving 6300 participants." "The estimated effects of physical rehabilitation at the end of the intervention were an improvement in Barthel Index (0 to 100) scores of six points (95% confidence interval (CI) 2 to 11, P = 0.008, seven studies) ... and walking speed of 0.03 m/s (95% CI -0.01 to 0.07, P = 0.1, nine studies)." "Synthesis of secondary outcomes suggested there is a beneficial effect on strength, flexibility, and balance" "rehabilitation does not increase risk of mortality in this population (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13). However, it is possible bias has resulted in overestimation of the positive effects of physical rehabilitation." "Physical rehabilitation for long-term care residents may be effective, reducing disability with few adverse events, but effects appear quite small and may not be applicable to all residents."
safe_wording: A Cochrane review of 67 trials in care homes found that exercise and rehabilitation probably help a little with everyday activities and with strength and balance, without increasing deaths. The effects were small, may not apply to every resident, and may be overstated by weaknesses in the trials.
qualifications: Covers all physical rehabilitation, not only strength training. Searches ran to about 2012.

claim: A 2022 meta-analysis found resistance training and multicomponent training improved physical performance tests in nursing home residents compared with usual care.
supporting_passage: "A total of 30 studies were included in the qualitative review (n = 1887, mean age 82.68 years and 70% female)."
