"Multicomponent training and resistance training showed statistically significant difference (P <= .05) in the physical performance of institutionalized older adults compared with the control groups (usual care); this was evaluated with the Short Physical Performance Battery (+1.2 points; +2 points), 30-second chair-stand (approximately +3 repetitions; both), and Timed Up and Go (-4 seconds on mean; both) tests." "Further studies with more representative sample numbers, an improvement in methodological quality, and a more specified prescription of the training used are necessary."
safe_wording: More recent pooled trials in care homes found that strength training improved simple tests such as standing up from a chair and getting up and walking, compared with usual care.
qualifications: Physical-performance outcomes, not daily-living independence; study quality limited.

claim: Care home residents in the UK have limited access to physiotherapy and progressive strength exercise.
supporting_passage: No UK care-home-specific source found. Closest general statement (Sayer 2022): "The consensus on the benefit of resistance exercise for the treatment of sarcopenia within the research world has yet to translate into consistent provision of resistance exercise in clinical practice"
safe_wording: Do not state that UK care home residents lack access to physiotherapy. Supportable: 'Experts note that agreement on the value of strength exercise has not yet turned into consistent provision in practice.' Anything about care homes specifically should be phrased as judgement ('We should offer...').
qualifications: PubMed searches and a Drive search found no UK survey or audit of physiotherapy or strength-exercise access in care homes.

claim: A single-centre, single-blind randomised trial in an acute care of the elderly unit in Navarra, Spain, randomised 370 patients (mean age 87.3) to exercise or usual care.
supporting_passage: "A single-center, single-blind randomized clinical trial was conducted from February 1, 2015, to August 30, 2017, in an acute care unit in a tertiary public hospital in Navarra, Spain. A total of 370 very elderly patients undergoing acute-care hospitalization were randomly assigned to an exercise or control (usual-care) intervention." "Of the 370 patients included in the analyses, 209 were women (56.5%); mean (SD) age was 87.3 (4.9) years."
safe_wording: In a Spanish hospital trial, 370 medical patients with an average age of 87 were randomly given an exercise programme or usual care.
qualifications: Single centre; usual care included physiotherapy focused on walking when needed.

claim: The programme was two 20-minute sessions a day (morning and evening) for 5 to 7 consecutive days including weekends: a supervised morning session of individualised progressive resistance (machines, 30-60% of one-repetition maximum), balance and walking exercise, and an unsupervised evening session with light ankle weights, a grip ball and corridor walking. Median intervention length was 5 days.
supporting_passage: "The intervention was programmed in 2 daily sessions (morning and evening) of 20 minutes’ duration during 5 to 7 consecutive days (including weekends). An experienced fitness specialist with in-depth training on safe patient handling techniques (F.Z.-F.) supervised each patient’s session" "The morning sessions included individualized supervised progressive resistance, balance, and walking training exercises. The resistance exercises were tailored to the individual's functional capacity using variable resistance training machines ... aiming at 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 repetitions with a load equivalent to 30% to 60% of the 1-repetition maximum." "The evening session consisted of functional unsupervised exercises using light loads (ie, 0.5- to 1-kg anklets and handgrip ball), such as knee extension and flexion, hip abduction, and daily walking in the corridor" Abstract: "Median duration of the intervention was 5 days (interquartile range, 0)"
safe_wording: Each patient had two 20-minute sessions a day, including weekends. Mornings were supervised strength training (sit-to-stand, leg press, knee extension and chest press, at a moderate load), plus balance and walking practice. Evenings were simple exercises with light ankle weights and a walk along the ward corridor.
qualifications: Abstract calls intensity 'moderate'; the discussion calls the resistance training 'low-intensity'. Use 'moderate'.

claim: Delivering the programme required one physiotherapist hired for the project plus an exercise-physiology researcher, seven days a week, and about 4,000 euros of equipment.
supporting_passage: "The costs derived from the intervention were basically those generated by hiring 1 physiotherapist (M.L.S.deA.) ad hoc for the project and the collaboration of a researcher (with a PhD background in exercise physiology) (F.Z.-F.) who shared the work during 7 days a week for the duration of the study. An initial investment of €4000 (US $4645) was made to buy the weight-training equipment"
safe_wording: It needed dedicated staff: a physiotherapist and an exercise specialist sharing the work seven days a week, and about 4,000 euros of equipment.
qualifications: Trial-run staffing; real-world staffing may differ.

claim: At discharge, function fell with usual care (Barthel -5.0 points from baseline) and rose slightly with exercise (+1.9); the between-group differences were 6.9 Barthel points and 2.2 SPPB points in favour of exercise.
supporting_passage: "At discharge, the exercise group showed a mean increase of 2.2 points (95% CI, 1.7-2.6 points) on the SPPB scale and 6.9 points (95% CI, 4.4-9.5 points) on the Barthel Index over the usual-care group. Hospitalization led to an impairment in functional capacity (mean change from baseline to discharge in the Barthel Index of -5.0 points (95% CI, -6.8 to -3.2 points) in the usual-care group, whereas the exercise intervention reversed this trend (1.9 points; 95% CI, 0.2-3.7 points). The intervention also improved the SPPB score (2.4 points; 95% CI, 2.1-2.7 points) vs 0.2 points; 95% CI, -0.1 to 0.5 points in controls)."
safe_wording: By the time they went home, people on usual care had lost ground in everyday activities (down 5 points on a 100-point scale), while those who exercised had gained a little (up 2 points). The difference between the groups was about 7 points on everyday activities and 2 points on a 12-point test of balance, walking and standing up.
qualifications: Keep within-group changes (-5.0, +1.9) separate from between-group differences (6.9, 2.2). Outcomes at discharge only. The trial pre-set a meaningful change as 5 Barthel points and 1 SPPB point; the Cochrane review uses 11 Barthel points as the minimal important difference, so the 6.9-point gain is modest by that yardstick.

claim: No adverse effects of the exercise were recorded, and there were no differences in length of stay, in-hospital falls, or 3-month readmission or mortality.
supporting_passage: "No adverse effects associated with the prescribed exercises were recorded and no patient had to interrupt the intervention or had their hospital stay modified because of it." "There were, however, no significant differences between groups in the remainder of secondary outcomes, including incident delirium (P > .10) (Table 2), length of hospitalization, proportion of patients having 1 or more falls during hospitalization, 3-month hospital readmission rate/mortality, or patient transfer (all P > .10)"
safe_wording: No harms from the exercise were recorded. It did not change length of stay, falls in hospital, or readmissions and deaths over the next three months.
qualifications: 'Did not show a difference' rather than 'no effect' for secondary outcomes. The post will not discuss delirium (topic exclusion).

claim: Participants had to be aged 75 or over, have a Barthel Index of 60 or more, be able to walk (with or without help) and be able to communicate and cooperate; people expected to stay under 6 days, with very severe dementia or terminal illness were excluded.
supporting_passage: "inclusion criteria: age 75 years or older, Barthel Index score of 60 or more ..., being able to ambulate (with/without assistance), and being able to communicate and collaborate with the research team. Exclusion criteria included expected length of stay less than 6 days, very severe cognitive decline (ie, Global Deterioration Scale score, 7), terminal illness, uncontrolled arrhythmias, acute pulmonary embolism, recent myocardial infarction, recent major surgery, or extremity bone fracture in the past 3 months."
safe_wording: The trial included people who could walk, with or without help, and who could take part; the most dependent patients and those expected to stay less than 6 days were not included.
qualifications: Findings apply to relatively able very old medical patients, not to the most dependent.

claim: A three-hospital replication with 3 days of the same kind of exercise found a smaller SPPB benefit (0.93 points) and no clear Barthel benefit; the authors link the smaller effect to fewer training days and more illness.
supporting_passage: "We performed a multicenter randomized clinical trial (RCT) within departments of geriatric medicine in 3 tertiary hospitals in Spain" "The intervention group received 2 daily 20-minute sessions of exercise over 3 consecutive days." "200 patients were randomly assigned ... mean [SD] age, 86.5 [4.4] years" "At discharge, the exercise group had a mean increase of 0.93 points (95% CI, 0.39-1.48 points) on the SPPB scale over the usual care group (Table 2). There was a worsening over hospitalization in the Barthel Index over time of -11.0 points (95% CI, -14.6 to -7.44 points), with a trend for attenuated declines in the intervention group: -6.49 points; 95% CI, -10.20 to -2.73; P = .09." "Factors that could have reduced the efficacy of the intervention include the reduction of the number of training days (from 5 days to 3), and a greater complexity and number of baseline diseases (11 vs 9) per person."
location: Methods, Results, Discussion (full text of research letter)
safe_wording: When the same team repeated the programme in three hospitals with only three days of exercise, the benefit was smaller: under 1 point on the 12-point test, and no clear difference in everyday activities. The authors think the shorter programme and sicker patients explain this.
qualifications: The authors' explanation (dose) is their interpretation, not tested.

claim: Across 24 trials (Cochrane 2022), in-hospital exercise for older medical patients may make little difference to independence in daily activities at discharge, the effect on mobility is uncertain, and it probably does not increase falls.
supporting_passage: "We included 24 studies ... with 7511 participants." "Exercise may have no clinically important effect on independence in activities of daily living at discharge from hospital compared to controls (16 studies, 5174 participants; low-certainty evidence)." "independence in activities of daily living was 1.8 points better (0.43 worse to 4.12 better) with exercise compared to controls. The minimally clinical important difference (MCID) is estimated to be 11 points." "We are uncertain regarding the effect of exercise on functional mobility at discharge" "Exercise interventions did not affect the risk of falls during hospitalisation (moderate-certainty evidence)." "Exercise may make little difference to independence in activities of daily living or QoL, but probably does not result in more falls in older medical inpatients."
safe_wording: When all 24 trials are pooled, in-hospital exercise did not show a clear, meaningful gain in everyday independence at discharge, and the effect on walking and moving is uncertain. It did not lead to more falls.
qualifications: Low to very low certainty evidence for function; the review mixes very different programmes (walking promotion to progressive resistance), and subgroup analysis by type did not differ meaningfully.

claim: In a pooled analysis of 9 cohorts (34,485 community-dwelling adults aged 65+), faster usual gait speed was associated with longer survival: hazard ratio 0.88 per 0.1 m/s faster.
supporting_passage: "Pooled analysis of 9 cohort studies (collected between 1986 and 2000), using individual data from 34 485 community-dwelling older adults aged 65 years or older with baseline gait speed data, followed up for 6 to 21 years." "Gait speed was associated with survival in all studies (pooled hazard ratio per 0.1 m/s, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.87-0.90; P < .001)."
safe_wording: Across 34,000 older people in nine studies, those who walked faster at their usual pace tended to live longer, at every speed measured.
qualifications: Association, not cause. Do not convert the hazard ratio into 'X% less likely to die'.

claim: At age 75, predicted 10-year survival across the range of gait speeds ranged from 19% to 87% in men and from 35% to 91% in women.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "At age 75, predicted 10-year survival across the range of gait speeds ranged from 19% to 87% in men and from 35% to 91% in women." Results text: "the probability of 10-year survival at age 75 years ranged from 0.18 to 0.86 (eFigure 4A). In women ... 10-year survival at age 75 years ranged from 0.34 to 0.92"
safe_wording: At age 75, the predicted chance of being alive 10 years later ranged from about 1 in 5 for the slowest-walking men to nearly 9 in 10 for the fastest. For women the range was about 1 in 3 to 9 in 10.
qualifications: Group predictions spanning the extremes of walking speed, not a forecast for one person. Abstract and results text differ by one point (19-87% vs 18-86% men; 35-91% vs 34-92% women); cite the abstract figures and label them 'predicted'.

claim: Prediction from age, sex and gait speed was about as accurate as models using chronic conditions, smoking, blood pressure, BMI and hospitalisation, with moderate discrimination (C statistics about 0.72-0.74).
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Predicted survival based on age, sex, and gait speed was as accurate as predicted based on age, sex, use of mobility aids, and self-reported function or as age, sex, chronic conditions, smoking history, blood pressure, body mass index, and hospitalization." Comment: "the reported values are in the range found in the present study (published area under the curve range, 0.66-0.82 vs this study, 0.717 and 0.737)."
safe_wording: A simple walking test predicted survival across groups about as well as a long list of medical facts. But no model like this can tell one person how long they will live.
qualifications: The second sentence is judgement, supported by moderate discrimination (C statistics about 0.72-0.74). Note that the authors themselves suggest gait speed 'may offer the clinician tools for assessing expected survival'; present the caution as the post's view.

claim: The cohorts were collected between 1986 and 2000 and were about 80% white; only one of nine was based in clinical practice.
supporting_passage: "Participants were a mean (SD) age of 73.5 (5.9) years; 59.6%, women; and 79.8%, white" "This study has the limitations of observational research; it cannot establish causal relationships and is vulnerable to various forms of healthy volunteer bias." "Only 1 of the 9 studies was based in clinical practice, and advanced dementia is rare in populations who are competent to consent for research."
safe_wording: The data came from research volunteers in the 1980s and 1990s, mostly white and mostly not recruited from clinics.
qualifications: None.

claim: A usual gait speed of 0.8 m/s or less indicates severe sarcopenia in EWGSOP2, and 0.8 m/s was about the speed matching median life expectancy in Studenski's data.
supporting_passage: EWGSOP2: "For simplicity, a single cut-off speed ≤0.8 m/s is advised by EWGSOP2 as an indicator of severe sarcopenia." Studenski: "Predicted years of remaining life for each sex and age increased as gait speed increased, with a gait speed of about 0.8 m/s at the median life expectancy at most ages for both sexes" "Gait speeds of 1.0 m/s or higher consistently demonstrated survival that was longer than expected by age and sex alone."
safe_wording: A usual walking speed of 0.8 metres per second or slower is a common warning threshold; it is roughly the speed at which predicted survival matched the average for age and sex.
qualifications: Thresholds are conventions; Studenski found the gait-survival relationship continuous.

claim: Common causes of slow gait include joint pain, parkinsonism, neuropathy, heart and lung disease, low mood and medicines.
supporting_passage: Studenski: "Walking requires energy, movement control, and support and places demands on multiple organ systems, including the heart, lungs, circulatory, nervous, and musculoskeletal systems. Slowing gait may reflect both damaged systems and a high-energy cost of walking." and "A recommended evaluation and management of slow walking includes cardiopulmonary, neurological and musculoskeletal systems." Snijders: "gait disorders are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing, but implicate the presence of underlying diseases that warrant specific diagnostic tests." EWGSOP2: "Consider other reasons for low muscle strength (e.g. depression, sroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders)."
location: Studenski Comment; Snijders Abstract; EWGSOP2 Figure 1 legend
safe_wording: Walking depends on the heart, lungs, circulation, nerves, muscles and joints, so slow walking can come from a problem in any of them. A slow walk is a reason to look for a cause, not a diagnosis of 'old age'.
qualifications: The specific list (joint pain, parkinsonism, neuropathy, low mood, medicines) was not verified in an opened source; use the organ-system wording above. Depression is listed by EWGSOP2 as a cause of low muscle strength, not specifically of slow gait.

claim: Gait speed is most useful when repeated: a small meaningful change is about 0.05 m/s and a substantial change about 0.10 m/s; a decline suggests a new problem to evaluate, and improvement over a year was linked with better survival.
supporting_passage: Perera 2006: "Best initial estimates of small meaningful change are near 0.05 m/s for gait speed ... and of substantial change are near 0.10 m/s for gait speed" "For clinical use, substantial change in these measures and small change in gait speed and 6MWD, but not SPPB, are detectable." Studenski: "Fourth, gait speed might be monitored overtime, with a decline indicating a new health problem that requires evaluation." Hardy 2007: "Mortality after 8 years was 31.6%, 41.2%, and 49.3% for those with improved, transiently improved, and never improved gait speed, respectively. The survival benefit for improvement at 1 year persisted after adjustment for covariates (hazard ratio=0.42, 95% confidence interval=0.29-0.61, P<.001)" "Further research is needed to determine whether interventions to improve gait speed affect survival."
location: Perera Abstract; Studenski Comment; Hardy Abstract
safe_wording: Measure usual walking speed the same way each time and repeat it. A drop of about 0.1 metres per second is a substantial change and a reason to look for a new problem. In one study, people whose walking speed improved over a year were less likely to die over the next 8 years, though that does not prove that speeding up caused it.
qualifications: Hardy is observational; say 'linked with', not 'improving speed extends life'. Change thresholds are estimates.

claim: UK pedestrian crossing timings assume a walking speed of 1.2 m/s.
supporting_passage: Asher 2012 abstract: "to compare walking speed in the UK older population with the speed required to utilise pedestrian crossings (≥1.2 m/s)" and "An assumed normal walking speed for pedestrian crossings of 1.2 m/s is inappropriate for older adults and revision of these timings should be considered." Asher 2012 introduction (Scite excerpt): "UK pedestrian crossing timings assume a minimum walking speed of 1.2m/s (2.7miles/hr)." Webb 2017 introduction: "Pedestrian crossings in the UK and US require people to walk at 1.2 m/s to cross in time ( Pedestrian Facilities at Signal-Controlled Junctions, 2005 ; Fitzpatrick et al., 2006 )"
location: Asher Abstract and Introduction; Webb Introduction
safe_wording: UK researchers reported in 2012 and 2017 that pedestrian crossing times in the UK are based on an assumed walking speed of 1.2 metres per second (about 2.7 miles per hour).
qualifications: Attribute it to the researchers and their cited guidance (DfT 2005). Current DfT guidance (Traffic Signs Manual Chapter 6, 2019) could not be opened, so do not say 'crossings are timed for 1.2 m/s today' as a bare fact. This figure is background in both papers' introductions.

claim: In Health Survey for England 2005 data on 3,145 adults aged 65+, mean usual walking speed was 0.9 m/s in men and 0.8 m/s in women; 84% of men and 93% of women either walked slower than 1.2 m/s or could not do the test.
supporting_passage: "random population sample of 3,145 adults (1,444 men) aged ≥65 years." "walking speed was assessed by timing a walk of 8 feet at normal pace. Walking impairment was defined as walking speed <1.2 m/s or non-participation in the test due to being unsafe or unable." "the mean walking speed was 0.9 m/s in men and 0.8 m/s in women; 84% of men and 93% of women ≥65 years had walking impairment." Full-text excerpt: "76% men and 85% women had a walking speed <1.2m/s; 93% of woman and 84% of men had walking impairment" and "90% of men and 87% of women took the walking speed test; 5.7% of men and 7.2% of women were unable to walk short distances or felt unsafe"
safe_wording: In a 2005 national survey in England, older people's average walking speed was 0.9 metres per second for men and 0.8 for women. More than 8 in 10 women (85%) and about 3 in 4 men (76%) walked slower than 1.2 metres per second; counting those who could not safely do the walk, it was over 9 in 10 women (93%) and more than 8 in 10 men (84%).
qualifications: Survey from 2005, private households only. Speed was timed over a short 8-foot (2.4 m) walk at normal pace, which may not match speed on a real crossing. Put the test method and year on the chart. The 84%/93% figures include people who could not do the test; the 76%/85% figures are walking speed alone.

claim: Female sex, older age, lower socioeconomic status, poorer health and lower grip strength were associated with walking impairment.
supporting_passage: Asher: "Female gender, increasing age, lower socio-economic status, poorer health and lower grip strength were predictors of walking impairment." Webb: "Female, less wealthy and less healthy older people had slower walking speeds. For instance, predicted probability of crossing the road in time at age 60 was 14.8% (10.1, 18.5) and 2.7% (1.5, 3.8) for the richest and poorest men"
safe_wording: Women, the oldest, the poorest and people in worse health were the most likely to walk too slowly to cross in time.
qualifications: Associations; do not say poverty 'causes' slow walking.

claim: The study authors recommended that crossing timings be reconsidered.
supporting_passage: Asher: "An assumed normal walking speed for pedestrian crossings of 1.2 m/s is inappropriate for older adults and revision of these timings should be considered." Webb: "Crossing times should be increased to allow for older peoples' slower walking speeds or other policies considered to improve walkability, and to help avoid injuries and social isolation."
safe_wording: The researchers concluded that crossing times should be reconsidered to allow for older people's slower walking.
qualifications: Report as the researchers' recommendation, not as Alasdair's policy position (values_concern).

claim: In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2002-2014), only 10% of measured walking speeds among people aged 60+ were fast enough to cross in the allotted time.
supporting_passage: "31,015 walking speed measurements were taken from 10,249 men and women aged 60+ years in waves 1-7 of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2002-2014)." "10% of measured walking speeds were fast enough to cross the road in time." Methods: "Participants walked eight feet (2.44 m) and back at their usual walking pace, using walking aids if required." Limitations: "our analyses only included the 74% of potential walking speeds which were measured"
location: Abstract; Methods and Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts)
safe_wording: A second, larger English study (2002 to 2014) found only 1 in 10 walking-speed measurements in people over 60 was fast enough.
qualifications: Unit is measurements, not people. Same short-walk method.

claim: UK crossing guidance has or has not changed since 2012.
supporting_passage: Not verified: the DfT Traffic Signs Manual Chapter 6 (2019) was located by web search but could not be opened; no passage was read.
safe_wording: Do not state whether current guidance still uses 1.2 m/s. If needed: 'Researchers in 2012 and 2017 reported...'.
qualifications: Recheck against the DfT document before publication if the editor wants a present-tense claim.

claim: Some UK crossings (Puffin crossings) can extend the crossing time for people who take longer to cross.
supporting_passage: "In the UK, the Puffin crossing has provision to extend pedestrian green time for those who take longer to cross."
location: Abstract (first sentence; rest of abstract not available)
safe_wording: Some newer UK crossings, called Puffin crossings, can hold the traffic for longer when someone is still crossing.
qualifications: Only the first sentence of a traffic-engineering abstract was read. How many crossings have this, and whether the extra time is enough, are unknown. Keep to 'some crossings'.

claim: About 3 in 10 older people admitted to an acute hospital leave less able to do basic daily activities (washing, dressing, using the toilet, eating, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking) than they were before they became ill.
supporting_passage: "Random effects meta-analysis showed the combined prevalence across studies was 30% (95% CI: 24%, 36%; p<0.001). Sensitivity analysis of only studies assessing ADL decline from 2 weeks prior to admission to discharge or within a month of discharge showed a combined prevalence of 33% (95% CI: 26%, 41%;)." ... "Prevalence among all hospital-based studies ranged from 17% to 61%" ... "The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) describes functional impairments in activities as having a limitation in independent execution of daily tasks including self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)."
location: Full text, Results (Prevalence of Hospital-Associated Disability) and Introduction; abstract Results
safe_wording: About 3 in 10 older people who go into an acute hospital come out less able to wash, dress, use the toilet, eat, or get in and out of bed or a chair than they were before they became ill. When only studies that asked about the person's abilities 2 weeks before admission were counted, the figure was about 1 in 3.
qualifications: Pooled estimate from studies that varied widely (17% to 61%); mostly US; data from 1983 to 2013. Measures basic self-care, not tasks such as making tea or using a key. Some of the loss starts with the illness before admission, not only in hospital; do not say the hospital stay caused it. Quote the percentage, not the confidence interval (abstract and full text give different upper limits).

claim: Loss of daily abilities after a hospital stay is more common the older the person.
supporting_passage: "Thirty-five percent of patients declined in ADL function between baseline and discharge." ... "The frequency of ADL decline between baseline and discharge varied markedly with age (23%, 28%, 38%, 50%, and 63% in patients aged 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, and > or =90, respectively, P <.001)."
safe_wording: In one large US study of people aged 70 and over admitted with a medical illness, about 1 in 4 of those aged 70 to 74 left hospital less able to manage basic self-care than 2 weeks before admission, rising to about 6 in 10 of those aged 90 or over.
qualifications: One cohort, 1990s US data; crude age-band percentages; outcome measured at discharge only.

claim: The first-hour tasks (door key, front step, toilet, chair, kettle, bed) make a practical pre-discharge check; the toilet, chair and bed are the kinds of task the hospital-disability studies measured, while the key, step and kettle go beyond them.
supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)". Covinsky 2003: "interviewed about their independence in five ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, and toileting)".
location: Loyd full text, Introduction; Covinsky abstract, Methods
safe_wording: Present the six tasks as a practical checklist to ask about, not as a tested tool. Getting to and using the toilet, getting up from a chair and getting into bed are basic daily activities that studies of hospital-associated disability count; the key, the front step and the kettle are extra, everyday tasks the post suggests adding.
qualifications: The first-hour framing and the checklist are judgement. No study tested this checklist. Do not claim that asking these questions prevents readmission or harm.

claim: Occupational therapists can assess how a person manages at home, including by a home visit before discharge; families can ask whether this has happened.
supporting_passage: "To determine the effectiveness of pre-discharge home assessment visits by occupational therapists in assisting hospitalized patients from a range of settings to return to community living." ... "There is low-to-moderate quality evidence that pre-discharge home assessment visits reduce patients' risk of falling and increase participation. The risk of readmission to hospital is also reduced, but not for patients following stroke." ... "There was no effect on activity or quality of life."
safe_wording: Ask the ward therapist whether they have seen your relative do each of these tasks. If something has not been tried, ask whether it can be practised before discharge, whether equipment is needed, and whether an occupational therapist should look at the home.
qualifications: A home visit is not needed or offered for everyone; do not say every hospital provides one or that NICE requires one (NICE NG27 could not be opened). If the evidence is mentioned, say 'low to moderate quality evidence' and that it did not improve daily activity or quality of life.

claim: Of older people who leave hospital after a medical illness less able to look after themselves than before, about 3 in 10 are back to their usual level a year later, about 3 in 10 are alive but have not recovered, and about 4 in 10 have died.
supporting_passage: "By 12 months after discharge, among those discharged with new or additional ADL disability, 41.3% died, 28.6% were alive but had not recovered to baseline function, and 30.1% were at their baseline function. Among those discharged with baseline function, 17.8% died, 15.2% were alive but with worse than baseline function, and 67% were at their baseline function(p<.001)." Full text: "Out of 2,279 patients who were eligible for this analysis, 1,480 patients were discharged with similar or better functional status compared to 2 weeks prior to admission while 799 patients were discharged with worse functional status".
location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Setting and Participants)
safe_wording: In a US study of people aged 70 and over admitted in an emergency with a medical illness (1993 to 1998), 799 of 2,279 left hospital needing more help with washing, dressing, eating, the toilet or moving from bed to chair than 2 weeks before admission. A year later, about 30 in 100 of them were back to their usual level, about 29 in 100 were alive but still needed more help, and about 41 in 100 had died. Among people who left hospital at their usual level, 67 in 100 were still at that level a year later.
qualifications: Old US data; lengths of stay have shortened since (authors' limitation). Deaths reflect how ill this group was; present them plainly and without drama, and say that for some people this decline marks the end of life (the authors recommend considering palliative care alongside rehabilitation).

claim: Among people discharged with new loss of self-care, being back to their usual level one month after discharge is linked with a much better outlook at a year.
supporting_passage: "Among patients discharged with a new or additional disability in self-care ADL, the presence or absence of recovery by one month was associated with long-term outcomes. Among those who had recovered by one month after discharge, 56.2% remained at baseline function 1 year after discharge, 20.7% died, and 23.1% declined again in self-care ADL function (). In contrast, among those who did not recover by one month after hospital discharge, only 17.1% recovered baseline function at 1 year after discharge, 44.4% died, and 38.4% were alive but not recovered (p<.001)."
location: Full text, Results (Role of One-Month Outcomes in Predicting Long-term Outcomes); analysis sample n=651
safe_wording: In that study, people who were back to their usual self-care one month after leaving hospital did much better over the year: 56 in 100 were still at their usual level at 12 months. Of those not back to their usual level at one month, 17 in 100 had recovered by 12 months.
qualifications: The study measured being back to the usual level by one month, not whether recovery had 'started'; do not say 'started to recover'. Prognostic association only; it does not show that a review at one month improves outcomes. Nearly a quarter of those recovered at one month later declined again.

claim: Not being back to normal at one month does not rule out recovery: many recoveries happen later.
supporting_passage: "Among those who had a new or additional disability in self-care ADL at hospital discharge, 30% recovered and were at their baseline level of functioning at 1 year. Of these patients, 62% recovered by 1 month with the remainder recovering over the next 11 months. Thus, most recovery, when it happens, occurs in the first month after hospitalization. However, 38% of patients who recovered in the year following discharge do so after the first month after hospitalization." Conclusion: "Since outcomes in the first month seem to predict long-term outcomes, particularly aggressive interventions may be indicated in the first month. However, as a large number of patients may recover after one month, and many who recover by one month decline again, there may also be a need for sustained long-term interventions."
location: Full text, Results (Timing of Functional Recovery) and Conclusion
safe_wording: Of the people who were back to their usual level a year after discharge, about 6 in 10 had got there within the first month and about 4 in 10 got there later. So the one-month point is a useful time to check progress, not a final verdict.
qualifications: Same cohort limitations (US, 1990s). The one-month review is the post's judgement, informed by the authors' conclusion; mark it as a suggestion.

claim: Among community-living people aged 70 and over who became newly disabled (any cause), most regained independence within a year, but recovery was often short-lived; frail, cognitively impaired or severely disabled people recovered less often, although most still did.
supporting_passage: "A total of 420 participants (56%) experienced disability during a median follow-up of 51 months. Of these participants, 399 (81%) recovered (ie, regained independence in all 4 ADLs) within 12 months of their initial disability episode, and a majority (57%) of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Among participants who experienced 3 or more consecutive months of disability, a majority (60%) recovered, but only a third of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Persons who were cognitively impaired, physically frail, or severely disabled (ie, in 3-4 ADLs) at onset were less likely to recover than those who were cognitively intact, nonfrail, or mildly disabled, respectively. Nonetheless, a majority of participants within each subgroup recovered."
safe_wording: In a US community study, 81 in 100 older people who became newly dependent (from any cause) regained independence within a year, but only 57 in 100 of those who recovered stayed independent for at least 6 months.
qualifications: Not a post-hospital cohort; do not place its 81% beside Boyd's 30% as if they were the same group. If used at all, label it as disability arising in the community from any cause. Recommend leaving it out of a post about discharge.

claim: Older people in hospital spend most of the day lying in bed, including many who can walk.
supporting_passage: Brown 2009: "Forty-five male patients (mean age 74.2) with a mean length of stay of 5.1 days generated 2,592 one-hour periods of data. A baseline functional assessment indicated that 35 (77.8%) study patients were willing and able to walk a short distance independently. No patient remained in bed the entire measured hospital stay, but on average, 83% of the measured hospital stay was spent lying in bed. The average amount of time that any one individual spent standing or walking ranged from a low of 0.2% to a high of 21%, with a median of 3%, or 43 minutes per day." Pedersen 2013: "The ambulatory patients were lying median 17 hours, (interquartile range [IQR]: 14.4-19.1), sitting 5.1 hours (IQR: 2.9-7.1), and standing and/or walking 1.1 hours (IQR: 0.6-1.7) per day."
location: Brown 2009 Abstract, Results; Pedersen 2013 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: Older people in hospital spend most of the day in bed, even many who can walk. In a US veterans' hospital, 45 men aged 65 and over spent on average 83% of their measured time lying in bed; the typical time standing or walking was 43 minutes a day, although 35 of the 45 were able to walk a short distance on their own. In a Danish hospital, 43 older medical patients who could walk spent a typical 17 hours a day lying down and about 1 hour standing or walking.
qualifications: Two small single-hospital studies; Brown 2009 is men only. Always name the setting with the figure. Pick one headline figure for the visual (judge's advice).

claim: Low mobility in hospital is linked with worse daily functioning at discharge and a month later.
supporting_passage: "Low versus high in-hospital mobility was associated with worse basic functional status at discharge (adjusted odds ratio (AOR)=18.03, 95% confidence interval (CI)=7.68-42.28) and at follow-up (AOR=4.72, 95% CI=1.98-11.28) and worse IADLs at follow-up (AOR=2.00, 95% CI=1.05-3.78)." ... "Forty-six percent of participants had declined in ADLs at discharge and 49% at follow-up; 57% had declined in IADLs at follow-up."
safe_wording: In an Israeli study of 525 people aged 70 and over, those who moved least in hospital were more likely to have lost everyday abilities at discharge and a month later, even after allowing for how unwell they were. This link does not prove that lying in bed caused the loss.
qualifications: Observational; do not quote or convert the odds ratios for the public. Reverse causation possible.

claim: In a randomised trial, a hospital walking programme helped older patients keep how far they got around their community a month after discharge, but made no difference to basic daily activities.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Patients in the MP group were assisted with ambulation up to twice daily, and a behavioral strategy was used to encourage mobility. Patients in the UC group received twice-daily visits." ... "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "The MP patients were seen up to twice a day for 15 to 20 minutes each session 7 days a week." ... "The MP group completed 122 of the potential 238 walks (51.3%)." ... "Although this is a small study that needs replication".
location: Abstract, Interventions and Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment, Hospital MP), Results and Discussion
safe_wording: In one small US trial of 100 older veterans, helping people walk up to twice a day in hospital, with daily goals for time out of bed, did not change their basic daily activities. A month after going home, those who had the walking programme were getting about as far beyond their front door as before admission, while the usual-care group had lost about 10 points on a 120-point scale of how far and how often they went out.
qualifications: 97% men, one veterans' hospital, cognitively intact, median stay 3 days; the originally registered main outcome (time out of bed) could not be measured, so these results come from other planned aims; only about half of offered walks happened; needs replication. Frame the family question around 'What is the walking plan for today?', not pressure to walk: some patients should not walk without help (the programme told patients not to walk without nursing help where needed).

claim: The Life-Space Assessment asks how far a person has moved from their bedroom out to beyond their town in the past 4 weeks, how often, and with what help.
supporting_passage: Brown 2009 (Ann Intern Med) full text: "The LSA measures mobility during the four weeks preceding the assessment by asking about movement to specific life-space levels ranging from within one’s dwelling to beyond one’s town (–). Frequency of movement and use of assistance, either from equipment or another person, were assessed. Specifically, participants were asked: “During the past 4 weeks, have you: 1) been to other rooms in your home besides the room where you sleep; 2) been to an area outside your home such as your porch, deck, or patio, hallway of an apartment building, or garage; 3) been to places in your neighborhood other than your own yard or apartment building; 4) been to places outside your neighborhood, but within your town; and 5) been to places outside your town?”" ... "Life-Space composite scores ranged from 0 to 120 with higher scores representing greater mobility." Baker 2003: "The LSA assessed the range, independence, and frequency of movement over the 4 weeks preceding assessments." Brown 2016: "Life-space levels range from within one’s bedroom to beyond one’s town."
location: Brown 2009 full text, Methods (Life-Space Mobility); Baker 2003 abstract, Measurements; Brown 2016 full text, Methods
safe_wording: A life-space assessment asks about the past 4 weeks: have you been to other rooms of your home, outside your door (porch, garden, garage or landing), around your neighbourhood, elsewhere in your town, and beyond your town? It also asks how often and whether you needed a stick, frame or another person. Scores run from 0 to 120.
qualifications: UK wording of the zones ('garden', 'landing') is a plain translation of the US questions; keep the five levels in the same order. Self-reported.

claim: Standard daily-living scales count self-care tasks done in and around the home (washing, dressing, eating, toilet, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking across a room).
supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "Included studies used the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living or Barthel Index to measure ADL." ... "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)." Brown 2016: "Participants were asked at baseline to rate their ability to perform basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, feeding, toileting, grooming, transferring, and walking)".
location: Loyd full text, Methods and Introduction; Brown 2016 full text, Methods (Functional Outcome Assessment)
safe_wording: The usual daily-living scores count whether you can wash, dress, eat, use the toilet, get in and out of bed or a chair, and walk across a room. They do not ask whether you get to the shop, the bus stop or a friend's house.
qualifications: Some versions add walking or grooming; describe the items, not every version.

claim: In a small randomised trial, a hospital walking programme showed no difference on a daily-living scale but a difference in life-space a month after discharge.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "For all periods, groups were similar in their ability to perform ADL (= .62); furthermore, ability to perform ADL did not significantly change over time (= .77), and there were no significant group-time interactions (= .76)." ... "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "In addition, the study was not powered to see significant ADL changes." ... "An example of a 10-point decrease would be an older person who previously reported no assistance to go into town 1 to 3 times a week (LSA score, 64) but who now requires a cane to go into town and goes less than once a week (LSA score, 54)."
location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment), Results and Discussion
safe_wording: In a small US trial of 100 older veterans, a hospital walking programme made no difference to daily-living scores, which barely changed in either group. The life-space measure did pick up a difference: a month after discharge, people who had usual care had lost about 10 points, for example going from getting into town unaided 1 to 3 times a week to needing a stick and going less than once a week, while the walking group stayed close to where they started.
qualifications: Do not say 'the choice of measure decided whether the programme looked useful' as a finding. Life-space was not the trial's registered primary outcome (time out of bed, which failed technically), so present this as one small trial that needs replication. The daily-living scale did not change in either group, so it could not show a difference; the trial was not powered for it. 97% men, cognitively intact, one veterans' hospital. For practitioner versions, name the registered-outcome issue.

claim: After an emergency medical admission, older people's life-space falls and, on average, does not recover over up to two years.
supporting_passage: "Immediately after hospitalization, covariate-adjusted LSA scores decreased in non-surgical patients by 10.31 points (95% CI −14.30 to −6.32) and in surgical patients by 22.45 points (95% CI −29.91 to −14.99)." ... "Indeed, LSA score recovery after non-surgical hospitalizations was non-significantly different from the null (average recovery of 0.66 points [95% CI −0.60 to 1.91] per log week). For example, at 12 weeks post-discharge, life-space recovered by an average of 1.69 points in non-surgical patients and by 13.80 points in surgical patients. As illustrated in, on average, within up to two years of the incident non-surgical hospitalization, these patients did not recover to their pre-hospital levels of life-space."
safe_wording: In a US study that followed older people living at home, those admitted to hospital for a medical (non-surgical) reason lost about 10 points of life-space on average and, as a group, had not got back to their earlier level up to two years later. People admitted for surgery lost more at first but recovered within about a year.
qualifications: Observational; averages hide individual variation; life-space was reported every 6 months, so the before and after values are model estimates; 'non-surgical' was self-reported and broad. Not 'caused by' hospital: say 'after' or 'linked with'.

claim: A smaller life-space is linked with a higher risk of death and of moving into a care home.
supporting_passage: Boyle 2010: "In a proportional hazards model adjusted for age, sex, race, and education, a more-constricted life space was associated with a greater risk of death (hazard ratio=1.18, 95% confidence interval=1.09-1.27, P<.001)" ... "This association persisted after the addition of terms for several potential confounders, including physical activity, performance-based physical function, disability, depressive symptoms, social networks, body mass index, and number of chronic medical conditions." Mackey 2014: "In multivariable-adjusted models, there was a strong linear trend between decreasing life-space and increasing risk of noncancer mortality (P = .005)." Watanabe 2022: "We found a negative association between LSM score and overall mortality even after adjusting for confounders". Sheppard 2013: "Over 6 years, the odds of NH admission increased 2% for every one point lower baseline life-space score independent of previously recognized risk factors."
safe_wording: In studies in the US and Japan, older people whose life-space was smaller were more likely to die in the following years, and in an Alabama study more likely to move into a nursing home, even after allowing for other health problems. These links do not show that shrinking life-space itself causes these outcomes; it may be a sign of declining health.
qualifications: Associations only. Do not convert the hazard or odds ratios into 'times more likely' or absolute risks. Do not use Mackey's crude 41.2% vs 2.4% (only 34 men in the lowest group).

claim: People with Alzheimer's disease can still improve a movement skill through repeated practice (implicit or procedural learning), even without being aware of learning it, though their performance stays below that of people without dementia.
supporting_passage: "The present review discusses 23 experimental studies on implicit motor-skill learning in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). All studies found intact implicit motor-learning capacities." (Abstract) ... "In implicit learning, skills are mastered without awareness, often simply by repeated exposure, and can be unconsciously revived from implicit memory" (Introduction) ... "All the studies found preserved motor-skill learning in AD patients although their overall performance levels in terms of reaction and movement time were always inferior to those of the controls." ... "Patients are capable of acquiring motor skills without awareness simply by repeated exposure, although their performances will not reach normal levels." (Conclusions)
location: Abstract; full text Introduction, Performance and Amount of Learning, Conclusions and Recommendations
safe_wording: A person with Alzheimer's disease who does not remember yesterday's practice may still have learned from it. A 2007 review of 23 laboratory studies found that people with Alzheimer's disease still got better at movement tasks with repeated practice, even though they stayed slower than people without dementia.
qualifications: Laboratory tasks, not real rehabilitation tasks; mainly mild Alzheimer's disease; people who could not do a task were removed from the analyses; learning did not reach normal levels and transferred little to other skills. Say 'often relatively preserved', not 'intact' or 'normal'. Do not extend to other dementias.

claim: The review recommends frequent, consistent practice of the same movement, in a setting and with equipment like those the person uses in daily life, avoiding doing two things at once, and good vision; it found no Alzheimer's studies testing demonstration.
supporting_passage: "The studies we reviewed showed that in (re)learning motor skills, constant, or rather frequent and consistent practice is important in AD patients. This way of learning draws less on episodic memory and other cognitive functions compromised in AD patients. These data also suggest that practice under dual-task conditions should also be avoided." ... "Because AD patients have difficulty in generalizing the motor skills learned during the sessions, training has to take place in an environment that closely resembles the one in which the skill is going to be used and presumably with tools used by the AD patient in his or her daily life." ... "Patients with AD appear to remain dependent upon visual feedback throughout training and performance. Screening and subsequent correction of visual problems or the use of visual aids can be effective in the training process in this group" ... On guidance, observation and mental practice: "Our automated computer search and an extra search combining the three keywords with Alzheimer dementia both failed to generate any relevant studies that employed one of these training methods." ... On verbal feedback: "it may be hypothesized that both forms of feedback knowledge probably place too much weight on the cognitive abilities in AD patients and therefore contribute little to successful performance."
location: Full text: Conclusions and Recommendations; Practice; Feedback
safe_wording: Practise the same movement the same way each time, in the place and with the chair, frame or bed the person will actually use, one task at a time, with glasses on. A review of the research recommends consistent practice of this kind for people with Alzheimer's disease because it relies less on remembering the session.
qualifications: These are the review authors' recommendations drawn from laboratory studies, not tested rehabilitation trials. 'Show rather than tell' and 'use few words' were not tested in Alzheimer's disease (the review found no studies of demonstration and only hypothesised that verbal feedback helps little); present them as practical suggestions, not findings. The judge's 'same sit-to-stand sequence with one cue each time' fits the consistent-practice recommendation; 'one cue' is judgement.

claim: In a randomised trial, dementia-adapted strength and function training improved strength and chair-stand performance in people with mild to moderate dementia, and the degree of cognitive impairment did not predict who benefited.
supporting_passage: "Individuals with confirmed mild to moderate dementia, no severe somatic or psychological disease, and ability to walk 10 m." ... "Supervised, progressive resistance and functional group training for 3 months specifically developed for people with dementia (intervention, n = 62) compared with a low-intensity motor placebo activity (control, n = 60)." ... "Training significantly improved both primary outcomes" ... "Training gains were partly sustained during follow-up. Low baseline performance on motor tasks but not cognitive impairment predicted positive training response." ... "The intensive, dementia-adjusted training was feasible and substantially improved motor performance in frail, older people with dementia"
safe_wording: In a German trial of 122 people with mild to moderate dementia, 3 months of supervised strength and balance training designed for people with dementia made them stronger and quicker at standing up from a chair than gentle placebo exercise. How much their memory and thinking were affected did not predict who improved; people who started weakest gained most.
qualifications: Participants could walk 10 m and had no severe illness; gains were only partly kept 3 months after training stopped. Do not quote the strength percentages (the abstract's units are inconsistent).

claim: Many people with dementia receive no rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery.
supporting_passage: "Of 11,200 individuals with dementia who experienced a hip fracture during the study period, 4,494 (40.1%) received no rehabilitation, 2,474 (22.1%) were admitted to CCC, 1,157 (10.3%) received HCR, and 3,075 (27.4%) received IPR." ... "Postfracture rehabilitation for older adults with dementia is associated with lower risk of LTC placement and mortality. Improving access to rehabilitation services for this vulnerable population may improve postfracture outcomes."
safe_wording: In Ontario, Canada, about 4 in 10 people with dementia living at home who had surgery for a hip fracture between 2003 and 2011 got no rehabilitation afterwards.
qualifications: Canadian data from 2003 to 2011. The abstract gives no figure for people without dementia and no reasons, so do not say they were 'excluded because of dementia'. The lower care home placement and death rates with rehabilitation are associations; fitter people may have been chosen for rehabilitation.

claim: The evidence on preserved motor learning comes mainly from laboratory tasks in Alzheimer's disease; transfer to everyday tasks and to other dementias is less certain, and some studies find learning is impaired.
supporting_passage: van Halteren 2007: "It should be noted that in all studies the patients that could not perform the task were eliminated from the analyses." ... "Clearly, AD patients show preserved implicit learning abilities that can be utilized in teaching (motor) skills, yet transfer to other skills is minimal." Palma 2023: "we selected 15 studies describing cognitive assessment tools, experimental designs, and the severity of cognitive impairment. Although seven studies reported that cognitive impairment impaired motor learning, most studies included a high risk of bias."
location: van Halteren full text (Implicit Learning Ability; Conclusions); Palma abstract
safe_wording: Most of this research used laboratory tasks with people with Alzheimer's disease. Some studies find learning is weaker, and it is less clear for other types of dementia.
qualifications: State the limitation once, plainly.

claim: Observational research by Baltes and colleagues described a pattern in which dependent behaviour of older people was met with help while independent behaviour was ignored or met with more help, in institutions and at home.
supporting_passage: Baltes 1994: "Research has attested to the prevalence of a "dependency-support" and "independence-ignore" script characterizing the interactions between staff and elderly residents in long-term care institutions." Baltes and Wahl 1992: "This study tested the generalizability of the dependency-support script, a behavioral system describing and explaining dependent behaviors of the institutionalized elderly. A comparative study with 22 community-dwelling elderly was conducted, which identified typical interaction patterns between the elderly and family members or home health nurses. The dominant interaction pattern in the community setting, too, was the dependency-support script." ... "Independent behaviors were followed about twice as often by an incongruent (dependence-supportive) than by a congruent (independence-supportive) response."
safe_wording: Researchers in Berlin, publishing in the early 1990s, watched how staff responded to older people in long-term care. When a resident needed help, staff paid attention and helped. When a resident managed alone, it tended to go unnoticed. A 1992 study of 22 older people at home found the same: when they did something for themselves, family or nurses were about twice as likely to step in and help as to encourage them.
qualifications: Small, old German studies; observational; describe responses, not long-term loss of ability. The 1994 abstract cites the institutional research without dates, so say 'published in the early 1990s' rather than naming a decade of fieldwork.

claim: A staff training programme in 3 institutions reduced dependence-supportive staff behaviour, increased independence-supportive behaviour and increased residents' independent self-care behaviour.
supporting_passage: "To examine whether the scripts could be modified, a staff training program (focusing on communication skills, knowledge about aging, and basic behavior principles) was implemented in 3 different institutions. Observational data on staff-resident interactions in the context of self-care were collected pre- and postintervention. Findings revealed significant changes for the experimental group. Specifically, a decrease in dependence-supportive behavior of staff and an increase in their independence-supportive behavior, an increase in independent behavior of residents, and an increase in independence-related interaction patterns were demonstrated."
safe_wording: In a 1994 German study, staff in 3 care institutions were trained in communication, ageing and simple behaviour principles. Afterwards, staff did less for residents and encouraged them more, and residents did more of their own self-care.
qualifications: Sample size, how groups were formed and how long the change lasted are not in the abstract; the outcome was observed behaviour during self-care, not a measured gain in function. Date and place the study.

claim: Function-focused (restorative) care has been tested in randomised trials in nursing homes; in a 12-home US trial it improved mobility, walking, bathing and stair climbing.
supporting_passage: "A randomized controlled repeated-measure design was used, and generalized estimating equations were used to evaluate status at baseline and 4 and 12 months after initiation of the Res-Care intervention." ... "Twelve nursing homes in Maryland." ... "Four hundred eighty-seven residents consented and were eligible" ... "Res-Care was a two-tiered self-efficacy-based intervention focused on motivating nursing assistants and residents to engage in functional and physical activities." ... "Significant treatment-by-time interactions (P<.05) were found for the Tinetti Mobility Score and its gait and balance subscores and for walking, bathing, and stair climbing." ... "The findings provide some evidence for the utility and safety of a Res-Care intervention in terms of improving function in NH residents."
safe_wording: In a US trial in 12 nursing homes, training care assistants to encourage residents to do what they could for themselves improved residents' walking, balance, bathing and stair climbing over a year, compared with homes without the programme.
qualifications: The abstract gives no effect sizes; authors call it 'some evidence'. US nursing homes, 2009.

claim: A recent Dutch cluster-randomised trial of a staff programme improved nurses' encouragement of residents' independence but did not show a statistically significant change in residents' self-reliance.
supporting_passage: "Twenty-eight nursing home wards, with 287 nurses and 241 residents participated in the study. A statistically significant treatment by time interaction effect was observed in nurses' activity encouragement behavior at three months (d = 0.53; p = .003; 95 % CI 1.88-8.02) and at nine months (d = 0.38; p = .02; 95 % CI 0.67-7.27). No statistically significant treatment by time interaction effects were observed in residents' self-reliance in activities of daily living. However, a trend was observed towards a less pronounced decrease in self-reliance in those residents allocated to wards that exposed nurses to the SELF-program"
safe_wording: In a Dutch trial in 28 nursing home wards, training helped nurses encourage residents to do more for themselves. Residents' independence in daily activities did not change clearly over 6 months, though it declined a little less on trained wards.
qualifications: State both halves. 'Did not change clearly' is the correct reading of p = .07, not 'no effect'.

claim: Time pressure and staff shortages are reasons staff give for still taking over tasks residents could do themselves.
supporting_passage: "Still, time constraints, staffing shortages and lack of motivation were put forwards as factors leading some nurses to still take over tasks." ... "Contextual barriers to program implementation and outcomes included staffing shortages, low program attendance, time constraints, lack of manager support, and delivery of the program during the COVID-19 pandemic."
safe_wording: In the Dutch trial, nurses named time pressure and staff shortages among the reasons some of them still took over tasks that residents could do themselves.
qualifications: Staff-reported barriers from one Dutch trial, not a measurement of how much extra time supported care takes. The position that time and training must be built into the rota is judgement and should be written as such ('Care homes should...').

claim: Reablement aims to maximise independence rather than doing tasks for people; trial evidence on its effects was very low certainty.
supporting_passage: "Unlike traditional home-care services, reablement is frequently time-limited (usually six to 12 weeks) and aims to maximise independence by offering an intensive multidisciplinary, person-centred and goal-directed intervention." ... "We are very uncertain as to the effects of reablement compared with usual care as the evidence was of very low quality for all of the outcomes reported."
safe_wording: Home care 'reablement' services aim to help people do things for themselves again. A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials and was very uncertain about their effects.
qualifications: Optional context; home care, not care homes; searches from 2015 and no update checked.

claim: Doing a task for someone saves time today and can cost them ability later.
supporting_passage: Vluggen 2024 (background, not a finding): "However, nurses often take over tasks unnecessarily, which can deprive resident's remaining abilities."
safe_wording: Present as reasoning, not a finding: 'If staff always do it, residents get less practice. Trials that trained staff to encourage residents found gains in some homes and not in others.'
qualifications: A background sentence in a paper's introduction is not that paper's finding. Do not say doing tasks for people 'causes' or 'leads to' loss of ability.

claim: The top of a walking stick should be level with the crease of the wrist when the person stands upright with arms relaxed by their sides.
supporting_passage: "The top of a cane or walker should be the same height as the wrist crease when the patient is standing upright with arms relaxed at his or her sides."
safe_wording: Stand up straight in your usual shoes with your arms hanging loosely. The top of the stick should be level with the crease on the inside of your wrist.
qualifications: Professional advice from a clinical review, not a trial. 'In your usual shoes' is a practical addition, not from the source; keep or drop.

claim: A stick is held in the hand opposite the weak or painful leg and moved forward at the same time as that leg.
supporting_passage: "A cane should be held contralateral to a weak or painful lower extremity and advanced simultaneously with the contralateral leg."
safe_wording: Hold the stick in the hand on the opposite side to the painful or weak leg, and move the stick forward at the same time as that leg.
qualifications: Applies to pain or weakness on one side. Someone with problems in both legs or poor balance may need a different aid (see C02-01-e).

claim: Among people who use walking sticks, wrong height, poor condition, use in the wrong hand and lack of professional advice are common.
supporting_passage: Sheehan 2008: "Fifty randomly selected patients attending a rheumatology department were surveyed to determine whether their stick was appropriate to their needs and whether they were using it correctly." ... "Of the 50 patients, 38% used their stick incorrectly, usually in the wrong hand. Forty-four per cent of sticks were of the wrong length and 54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." Liu 2011: "Five major problems from data analysis were identified: lack of medical consultation for device selection/use, incorrect cane height/maintenance, placement of cane in improper hand, inability to maintain the proper reciprocal gait pattern, and improper posture during ambulation." Bradley 2011: "Most patients with assistive devices have never been instructed on the proper use and often have devices that are inappropriate, damaged, or are of the incorrect height." George 1988: "Many of the aids that the elderly had were faulty, including half of the walking aids and 15% of hearing aids, reading spectacles, and dentures"
safe_wording: In a survey of 50 stick users at an English hospital arthritis clinic, 44 in 100 sticks were the wrong length and 54 in 100 were in poor condition, most often because the rubber tip was worn. About 4 in 10 people were using their stick wrongly, usually in the wrong hand. A US study of 93 stick users aged over 65 found the same problems, and many had never had professional advice when choosing the stick.
qualifications: Small surveys; Sheehan's clinic patients were not all older people. Liu gives no percentages in the abstract, so quote only Sheehan's figures. George 1988 ('half of the walking aids' faulty, 140 people over 75) is dated and 'walking aids' includes frames; use only with the year.

claim: A worn rubber tip (ferrule) is a common defect and should be checked and replaced.
supporting_passage: "Walking sticks are used widely by people with arthritis, principally to reduce pain and improve stability and balance. However, they are frequently used incorrectly and can be dangerous if not properly maintained." ... "54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." ... "These findings highlight the importance of educating patients on how to obtain greatest benefit from their walking stick and of the necessity to check it regularly for defects to ensure safe usage."
safe_wording: Turn the stick over and look at the rubber tip. A worn tip was the most common defect in one English clinic survey, and the authors advise checking sticks regularly for faults. If the tread is worn smooth, replace the tip.
qualifications: The source says poorly maintained sticks 'can be dangerous' and names the worn ferrule as the main defect; it does not measure grip. Do not claim a worn tip 'grips less well' as a finding. 'Replace it' is practical advice.

claim: The right aid depends on strength, balance and cognition; people with weakness or poor balance may need a frame rather than a stick, and clinicians should check height, fit and maintenance.
supporting_passage: "Selection of a suitable device depends on the patient's strength, endurance, balance, cognitive function, and environmental demands." ... "Walkers improve stability in those with lower extremity weakness or poor balance and facilitate improved mobility by increasing the patient's base of support and supporting the patient's weight. Walkers require greater attentional demands than canes and make using stairs difficult." ... "Clinicians should routinely evaluate their patients' assistive devices to ensure proper height, fit, and maintenance, and also counsel patients on correct use of the device."
safe_wording: A stick is the wrong aid for some people. If both legs are weak or balance is poor, a walking frame may be safer; ask a physiotherapist or GP to check which aid suits you and that it fits.
qualifications: Clinical review advice. Frames have downsides too (more attention needed, harder on stairs).

claim: In a randomised trial of 110 frail patients aged 65+ (mean 78) having colorectal cancer surgery within an enhanced recovery pathway, a multimodal programme started before surgery did not reduce 30-day complications compared with the same programme started after surgery.
supporting_passage: "A total of 418 patients 65 years or older were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 298 patients were excluded (not frail [n = 290], unable to exercise [n = 3], and planned neoadjuvant treatment [n = 5]), and 120 frail patients (Fried Frailty Index,≥2) were randomized." ... "Hence, 110 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (55 in the prehabilitation [Prehab] and 55 in the rehabilitation [Rehab] groups)." ... "Multimodal program involving exercise, nutritional, and psychological interventions initiated before (Prehab group) or after (Rehab group) surgery. All patients were treated within a standardized enhanced recovery pathway." ... "Of 110 patients randomized, mean (SD) age was 78 (7) years" ... "There was no between-group difference in the primary outcome measure, 30-day Comprehensive Complications Index (adjusted mean difference, -3.2; 95% CI, -11.8 to 5.3; P = .45)." Discussion (via Scite, the article's own text): "The low adherence of patients to the rehabilitation program (14%), however, supports that this control intervention was closer to a sham condition than to an active comparator." ... "Although our sample size was relatively small (n = 110), the lower bounds of the 95% CI observed for between-group differences in CCI (11.8) suggest that we were unlikely to miss a meaningful benefit of the intervention due to type II error (when accounting for the reported minimal important difference of 10)."
location: Abstract; Discussion (verbatim sentences retrieved through Scite)
safe_wording: In a Montreal trial, 110 frail people aged 65 and over (average age 78) having bowel cancer surgery were given a 4-week programme of exercise, nutrition and psychological support. Half started it before the operation; the other half were offered the same programme after it. Complications in the 30 days after surgery did not differ clearly between the two groups. Only about 1 in 7 people in the after-surgery group kept to that programme, so in practice the comparison was close to no programme.
qualifications: Follow the editor: state the comparison with the same programme after surgery; do not write a bare 'gave no fewer complications'. Bowel cancer surgery within a well-run enhanced recovery pathway; the authors note complication rates were similar to unselected patients, so benefit may be smaller where perioperative care is already optimised. The judge's underpowering concern is partly answered by the authors' confidence-interval argument, but 110 is small.

claim: Secondary outcomes, including recovery of walking capacity, length of stay and readmissions, did not differ between groups.
supporting_passage: "Secondary outcomes were 30-day overall and severe complications, primary and total length of hospital stay, 30-day emergency department visits and hospital readmissions, recovery of walking capacity, and patient-reported outcome measures." ... "Secondary outcome measures were also not different between groups." Discussion (via Scite): "We also did not observe between-group differences in primary and total LOS, rates of readmission and emergency department visits, postoperative walking capacity, and PROMs."
safe_wording: Walking ability 4 weeks after the operation, time in hospital and readmissions were also similar in the two groups.
qualifications: Say 'did not differ clearly' or 'were similar', not 'had no effect'.

claim: The prehabilitation programme lasted about 4 weeks before surgery.
supporting_passage: (via Scite, the article's own text) "Eligible patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 4-week prehabilitation program (Prehab group) or a 4-week postoperative rehabilitation program (Rehab group)." ... "The program started after the baseline visit and continued for 4 weeks before surgery, as recommended by the Canadian Oncological Society." ... "Patients were asked to attend training sessions supervised by a trained kinesiologist at the hospital prehabilitation unit once a week for 4 weeks." ... "In addition to the supervised exercise sessions, participants were prescribed a personalized home-based program of aerobic activities (walk daily for a total of 30 minutes as moderate-intensity aerobic activity) and resistance training (elastic band routine 3 times per week)" ... Discussion: "Third, a prehabilitation program lasting 4 to 5 weeks may not be sufficient to increase physiological reserve preoperatively and reduce postoperative complications."
location: Methods (Study procedures; Prehabilitation; Exercise intervention) and Discussion, verbatim via Scite
safe_wording: The programme ran for 4 weeks before surgery: one supervised exercise session a week plus daily walking and home strength exercises, with nutrition and psychological support.
qualifications: The authors themselves suggest 4 to 5 weeks may be too short; a longer programme was not tested.

claim: An umbrella review found low to very low certainty evidence that prehabilitation reduces complications, and moderate certainty evidence that any prehabilitation improves functional recovery after cancer surgery.
supporting_passage: "From 1412 titles, 55 systematic reviews were included. For patients with cancer undergoing surgery who participate in any prehabilitation, moderate certainty evidence supports improvements in functional recovery. Low to very low certainty evidence supports reductions in complications (mixed, cardiovascular, and cancer surgery), non-home discharge (orthopaedic surgery), and length of stay (mixed, cardiovascular, and cancer surgery). There was low to very low certainty evidence that exercise prehabilitation reduces the risk of complications, non-home discharge, and length of stay." ... "Low certainty evidence suggests that prehabilitation may improve postoperative outcomes."
safe_wording: A 2022 review of 55 earlier reviews rated the evidence that prehabilitation reduces complications as low or very low certainty. It found moderate certainty that prehabilitation helps people with cancer recover their physical function after surgery.
qualifications: All adults, not frail older people specifically. The moderate-certainty finding is for any prehabilitation in cancer surgery, not exercise alone. Searches end 2020.

claim: A home-based exercise prehabilitation trial in older people with frailty having cancer surgery did not significantly improve its primary outcome (walking distance).
supporting_passage: "This double blind randomised trial enrolled people ≥60 yr having elective cancer surgery and ≥3 weeks from enrolment to surgery as eligible. Participation in a remotely supported, home-based exercise prehabilitation program plus nutritional guidance was compared with standard care plus written advice on age-appropriate activity and nutrition. The primary outcome was 6-min walk test (6MWT) distance at the first postoperative clinic visit." ... "Of 543 patients assessed, 254 were eligible and 204 (80%) were randomised (102 per arm); 182 (94 intervention and 88 control) had surgery and were analysed. Mean age was 74 yr and 57% were female. Mean duration of participation was 5 weeks, mean adherence was 61% (range 0%-100%). We found no significant difference in 6MWT at follow-up (+14 m, 95% confidence interval -26-55 m, P=0.486), or for secondary outcomes.
