Analyses using a prespecified adherence definition of ≥80% supported improvements in 6MWT distance, complication count, and disability."
safe_wording: A Canadian trial of home exercise before cancer surgery in 182 older people with frailty found no clear difference in walking distance after surgery. People kept to about 6 in 10 of the planned exercise on average.
qualifications: Published in Br J Anaesth 2022 (not JAMA Surg). The better results in people with 80% or more adherence come from a secondary analysis and may reflect who adheres; do not present as the main finding.

claim: Recent pooled analyses of prehabilitation in older and frail surgical patients disagree, and frail patients remain understudied.
supporting_passage: Liu 2026: "Nine randomized controlled trials involving 1027 patients were included. The meta-analysis showed that prehabilitation significantly reduced the risk of postoperative complications (risk ratio [RR] = 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.46 to 0.99, p = 0.04), with low heterogeneity among studies (I² = 24%). Subgroup analyses indicated a greater trend towards risk reduction in frail patients (RR = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.24 to 1.16)" ... "the trend suggesting potentially greater benefit in specifically frail patients requires confirmation in future larger, specifically designed trials." Lopez-Gonzalez 2025: "Five studies involving 400 participants were included. The p-MD for the 6MWT showed no significant improvement at any time point" ... "The LOS was also not significantly reduced" ... "Prehabilitation did not significantly improve aerobic capacity or reduce hospital stay." Buckinx 2026: "Nine studies (n = 36–182; mean/median age 68–82) were included." ... "Vascular surgery studies showed modest reductions in complications and hospital stay, whereas abdominal surgery studies generally reported no significant improvements, except for isolated reductions in severe complications or gains in functional reserve." ... "Prehabilitation in older adults remains understudied, especially in frail patients, the oldest old, and cardiac surgery."
safe_wording: Newer reviews disagree. One pooled 9 trials in people aged 60 and over having bowel or stomach cancer surgery and found about a third fewer complications with prehabilitation (a relative figure), but the result for frail patients on their own was uncertain. Another pooled 5 trials in frail older people and found no clear improvement in walking or length of stay. A third concluded that prehabilitation for frail and very old people is still understudied.
qualifications: Relative risk only; no absolute numbers are available from these abstracts, so do not give 'N in 100'. Liu's search began in 2020 and the overall result only just reached significance. Do not cite the retracted Xie 2025 meta-analysis (PMID 41518969).

claim: In the HIP ATTACK trial (2970 people with hip fracture, 69 hospitals, 17 countries), surgery at a median of 6 hours after diagnosis did not reduce deaths or major complications at 90 days compared with standard care at a median of 24 hours.
supporting_passage: "HIP ATTACK was an international, randomised, controlled trial done at 69 hospitals in 17 countries. Patients with a hip fracture that required surgery and were aged 45 years or older were eligible." ... "2970 of these were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive accelerated surgery (n=1487) or standard care (n=1483). The median time from hip fracture diagnosis to surgery was 6 h (IQR 4-9) in the accelerated-surgery group and 24 h (10-42) in the standard-care group (p<0·0001). 140 (9%) patients assigned to accelerated surgery and 154 (10%) assigned to standard care died, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0·91 (95% CI 0·72 to 1·14) and absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 1% (-1 to 3; p=0·40). Major complications occurred in 321 (22%) patients assigned to accelerated surgery and 331 (22%) assigned to standard care, with an HR of 0·97 (0·83 to 1·13) and an ARR of 1% (-2 to 4; p=0·71)." Interpretation: "Among patients with a hip fracture, accelerated surgery did not significantly lower the risk of mortality or a composite of major complications compared with standard care."
safe_wording: In a trial of about 3,000 people with a broken hip in 17 countries, operating within about 6 hours of diagnosis did not clearly reduce deaths or serious complications compared with usual care, where half had surgery within about 24 hours. At 90 days, about 9 in 100 had died in the fast group and 10 in 100 in the usual-care group; serious complications affected about 22 in 100 in both.
qualifications: Did not show a clear difference; the uncertainty range runs from about 1 fewer to 3 more deaths per 100 prevented, so a small benefit or none is possible. Times are from diagnosis, not from admission. Say 'did not clearly reduce', not 'no benefit'.

claim: In HIP ATTACK, accelerated surgery did not harm patients, and it was linked with faster mobilisation after surgery, a shorter hospital stay and less postoperative confusion (secondary outcomes).
supporting_passage: "This study found that accelerated surgery (within a goal of 6 h after diagnosis) did not improve either mortality or non-fatal major complications (myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, sepsis, pneumonia, life-threatening bleeding and major bleeding) 90 days later among 1487 people with hip fracture, compared with a similar number (n = 1483) who received standard care (median time from diagnosis to surgery of 24 h (IQR 10–42). Accelerated surgery did not harm patients, even for those with acute medical conditions. Interestingly, accelerated surgery significantly reduced both the prevalence of postoperative delirium (9% vs. 12%, HR 0.72 (95%CI 0.58–0.92), p = 0.0089) and length of inpatient stay, and improved the speed of postoperative mobilisation. The Working Party considers these data re-assuring and clinically important for patients but acknowledge that the resource implications of accelerated surgery need to be calculated before recommending its adoption into current UK practice."
location: Griffiths 2021 guideline, full text, Controversies section (surgical delay); passage spanned two retrieved text chunks at '0.58–0' / '.92'
safe_wording: The fast-surgery group did get up and about sooner after the operation and left hospital sooner, and the trial found no sign that operating that fast caused harm.
qualifications: Verified through the Association of Anaesthetists guideline's summary, not the trial paper itself (Lancet full text not accessible). Secondary outcomes, so treat as supportive rather than definitive. Less pain was claimed by the judge but was NOT verified; do not state it. Delirium is excluded as a topic: the post can say 'less confusion after surgery' at most, and need not mention it.

claim: In a large Ontario cohort, waiting more than 24 hours for hip fracture surgery was linked with a small increase in 30-day deaths (association, not proof of cause).
supporting_passage: "Among 42 230 patients with hip fracture (mean [SD] age, 80.1 years [10.7], 70.5% women) who met study entry criteria, overall mortality at 30 days was 7.0%. The risk of complications increased when wait times were greater than 24 hours, irrespective of the complication considered. Compared with 13 731 propensity-score matched patients who received surgery earlier, 13 731 patients who received surgery after 24 hours had a significantly higher risk of 30-day mortality (898 [6.5%] vs 790 [5.8%]; % absolute RD, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.23-1.35) and the composite outcome (1680 [12.2%]) vs 1383 [10.1%]; % absolute RD, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.43-2.89)." Conclusion: "Among adults undergoing hip fracture surgery, increased wait time was associated with a greater risk of 30-day mortality and other complications. A wait time of 24 hours may represent a threshold defining higher risk."
safe_wording: In a study of over 40,000 people in Ontario, those who waited more than 24 hours for surgery were slightly more likely to die within 30 days: about 6.5 in 100 compared with 5.8 in 100 among similar people operated on sooner. This is a link, and it does not prove that the wait caused the deaths.
qualifications: Observational; adjusted and propensity matched but residual confounding possible (people who wait may be sicker). Absolute difference under 1 percentage point. Timing from hospital arrival (HIP ATTACK timed from diagnosis). Use 'linked with', not 'causes' or 'leads to'.

claim: UK guidance sets the target: NICE recommends surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission; the Association of Anaesthetists recommends a 36-hour limit from fracture to surgery; the Scottish standard is surgery within 36 hours of admission.
supporting_passage: NICE full guideline 4.2.2 Timing of surgery: "➢ Perform surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission." Ong 2023 abstract: "The scope of this recent update focussed on surgical implants for hip fracture. ... Other recommendations such as the importance of multidisciplinary orthogeriatric care, early surgery and prompt mobilisation remain." Griffiths 2021: "The Working Party continues to recommend a 36-h limit from fracture to surgery in the UK." Scottish standards: "Standard 6: Surgical repair of the hip fracture is performed within 36 hours of admission".
location: NICE full guideline section 4.2.2; Ong 2023 abstract; Griffiths 2021 Controversies; Scottish standards, Standard 6
safe_wording: UK guidance asks for surgery on the day of admission or the day after (NICE), and within 36 hours (Association of Anaesthetists; Scottish standard).
qualifications: NICE wording taken from the 2011 full guideline in Drive; the 2023 update kept early-surgery recommendations per the Age and Ageing commentary, but the live NICE page was not opened. Cite the Scottish standard as a published standard, never with audit results.

claim: HIP ATTACK compared very fast surgery with surgery that was already fairly fast: half the standard-care group had surgery within 24 hours of diagnosis (the candidate's wording 'faster than many hospitals achieve' is not supported).
supporting_passage: HIP ATTACK abstract: "The median time from hip fracture diagnosis to surgery was 6 h (IQR 4-9) in the accelerated-surgery group and 24 h (10-42) in the standard-care group (p<0·0001)." Griffiths 2021: "...compared with a similar number (n = 1483) who received standard care (median time from diagnosis to surgery of 24 h (IQR 10–42)."
location: HIP ATTACK abstract, Findings; Griffiths 2021 Controversies
safe_wording: The comparison group was not left waiting days: half of them had their operation within about 24 hours of diagnosis, and three quarters within about 42 hours. So the trial tested very fast against fairly fast, not fast against slow.
qualifications: No source opened compares the 24 h median with what hospitals typically achieve; do not say 'faster than many hospitals achieve'. The interquartile range (10 to 42 h) means a quarter of the standard group waited longer than 42 h.

claim: NICE lists correctable problems to identify and treat immediately so that they do not delay surgery: anaemia, anticoagulation, volume depletion, electrolyte imbalance, uncontrolled diabetes, uncontrolled heart failure, correctable cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemia, acute chest infection, and exacerbation of chronic chest conditions.
supporting_passage: "4.2.2 Timing of surgery ➢ Perform surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission. ➢ Identify and treat correctable comorbidities immediately so that surgery is not delayed by: • anaemia • anticoagulation • volume depletion • electrolyte imbalance • uncontrolled diabetes • uncontrolled heart failure • correctable cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemia • acute chest infection • exacerbation of chronic chest conditions."
location: NICE full guideline (2011, 2017 update), section 4.2.2; repeated in the timing-of-surgery chapter recommendation table
safe_wording: NICE lists nine problems to find and treat straight away so that they do not delay surgery: anaemia, blood thinners (anticoagulation), dehydration, salt and potassium problems, uncontrolled diabetes, uncontrolled heart failure, a correctable heart rhythm problem or ischaemia, a chest infection, and a flare of a long-term chest condition.
qualifications: Keep NICE's framing: treat immediately so surgery is not delayed. Do NOT present the list as 'reasons that justify delay'. NICE wording from the Drive copy of the 2011 full guideline; the 2023 update did not cover this section per the Age and Ageing commentary, but the live page was not opened.

claim: NICE's evidence review states that patients should not be delayed for routine tests that will not affect the surgical or anaesthetic procedure.
supporting_passage: "Trade off between clinical benefits and harms: Patients should not be delayed for routine tests which will not affect the surgical or anaesthetic procedure. It has been shown in the majority of patients that longer delay leads to an increase in complications and length of stay in those medically fit."
location: NICE full guideline, chapter on timing of surgery, evidence-to-recommendations table for the correctable comorbidities recommendation
safe_wording: NICE's guideline developers wrote that people should not be kept waiting for routine tests that will not change the operation or the anaesthetic.
qualifications: This sentence is in the guideline's evidence-to-recommendations text, not a numbered recommendation; attribute it as 'the NICE guideline says' or 'NICE's guideline developers', not as a formal recommendation.

claim: The Association of Anaesthetists does not recommend delaying hip fracture surgery to wait for an echocardiogram.
supporting_passage: "Valvular heart disease occurs in approximately 10% hip fracture patients in the UK [19]. However, delay to hip fracture surgery for diagnostic echocardiography also increases postoperative mortality." ... "However, the treatment of any valvular disease is very unlikely to precede surgery in the surgical population with hip fracture, and it remains unlikely that the results of echocardiography will inform a change in the anaesthetic management of patients with suspected valvular heart disease. The Working Party does not recommend delaying surgery pending echocardiography. Instead, management should continue to involve carefully administered, (invasively) monitored general or spinal anaesthesia, which aims to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion pressures, with possible short-term admission to a higher-level care unit postoperatively."
safe_wording: UK anaesthetic guidance says not to delay surgery while waiting for a heart scan (echocardiogram); the result rarely changes how the anaesthetic is given, and the heart valve problem is very unlikely to be treated before the hip.
qualifications: The guideline acknowledges echocardiography can quantify disease, and notes conflicting studies and a possible future RCT. The guidance still expects careful, monitored anaesthesia and possible higher-level care after surgery.

claim: Antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin and clopidogrel are not, on their own, a reason to delay hip fracture surgery.
supporting_passage: Griffiths 2021: "Approximately 30–40% of people with hip fracture in the UK are taking anticoagulant/antiplatelet medications pre-operatively." ... "The 2011 guidance advised that surgery should not be delayed in patients taking aspirin, clopidogrel or warfarin, provided vitamin K-assisted reversal of the latter reduced the international normalised ratio below 2 for surgery and 1.5 for spinal anaesthesia." ... "Data suggest that the use of anticoagulants/antiplatelet therapies is associated with a slightly increased risk of peri-operative transfusion in hip fracture patients but no increase in mortality [60–62]." ... "Abrupt cessation of such medication and failure to restart it postoperatively can expose the person to increased risks of cardiac ischaemia and stent occlusion, cerebrovascular accident [65] and limb ischaemia." Doleman 2015 abstract: "For patients taking clopidogrel undergoing early surgery, there was no associated increase in overall mortality (OR 0.89; 95% CI: 0.58-1.38) or 30-day mortality (OR 1.10 95% CI: 0.48-2.54). However, there was an associated increase in blood transfusion (OR 1.41 95% CI: 1.00-1.99)." ... "Early surgery appears safe for patients with hip fracture though there may be a small increase in the rate of blood transfusion. However, larger prospective trials are required to confirm these findings."
location: Griffiths 2021 full text, Controversies (anticoagulant and antiplatelet management); Doleman 2015 abstract
safe_wording: Association of Anaesthetists guidance has advised since 2011 that surgery should not be delayed because someone takes aspirin or clopidogrel. Studies of people on clopidogrel who had early surgery found slightly more blood transfusions but no rise in deaths.
qualifications: The 2020 guideline's main text restates the 2011 advice and moves detailed antiplatelet/anticoagulant recommendations to Appendix S1, which was not opened; attribute to 'Association of Anaesthetists guidance (2011, restated in the 2020 update)'. Meta-analysis evidence is observational. Stopping antiplatelets abruptly carries its own risks (stents, stroke). Warfarin is an anticoagulant and needs reversal; do not group it with antiplatelets. Spinal anaesthesia decisions in people on antiplatelets are the anaesthetist's call.

claim: People on direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are a separate case with specific guidance; in England and Wales in 2018 about 3% of hip fracture patients were delayed more than 36 hours by DOAC therapy or warfarin reversal, and almost all DOAC users were delayed beyond 36 hours.
supporting_passage: "Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC), such as rivaroxaban, apixaban and dabigatran, were introduced into the UK in 2008, but their prescription increased more markedly after 2012 and so were not considered in the 2011 guidance. Approximately 2% of UK hip fracture patients currently take DOACs." ... "There are significant and progressive mortality and morbidity risks associated with delay to surgery beyond 24(–48) h in hip fracture patients [68, 69]. In 2018, approximately 3% of hip fracture patients in England and Wales were delayed > 36 h before surgery as a result of their DOAC therapy or for warfarin reversal; virtually all patients taking DOACs were delayed > 36 h before surgery [6]. Mindful of these risks and in recognition of other Association of Anaesthetists' guidance, the Working Party has developed comprehensive recommendations for the management of patients with hip fracture who are taking antiplatelet/anticoagulant medication pre-operatively. These can be found in online Supporting Information, Appendix S1, together with a one-page summary..."
location: Griffiths 2021 full text, Controversies (anticoagulant and antiplatelet management)
safe_wording: Blood thinners of the DOAC type (such as apixaban or rivaroxaban) are handled differently: the Association of Anaesthetists publishes specific advice on timing. In 2018, almost everyone in England and Wales taking a DOAC waited more than 36 hours for hip fracture surgery. Ask the anaesthetist or orthogeriatrician what the plan is and when surgery can go ahead.
qualifications: The candidate's claim that DOAC timing 'depends on the drug, dose and kidney function' was NOT verified (Appendix S1 not opened); do not state it. The 3% figure is a national figure cited by the guideline (ref 6), not a trial result; it is 2018 data. The 2020 text says DOAC users were about 2% of UK hip fracture patients.

claim: Guidance expects medical problems to be corrected proactively within the 36-hour window, with the team told what needs to happen and decisions documented, rather than surgery cancelled on the day for a single abnormal value.
supporting_passage: Griffiths 2021: "In many cases, the risks of delay associated with pain and immobility contribute to poor outcomes to a far greater extent than correction of an abnormality to a particular numerical value. Rather than cancelling surgery on the day of operation in reaction to one of the seven abnormalities listed, the Working Party considers that 36 h (or less) provides sufficient time for the proactive involvement of anaesthetists in correcting medical obstacles to surgery. In the (rare) event of cancellation for medical reasons, patients should be kept under 12-hourly assessment by anaesthetic teams. Anaesthetists should work with orthogeriatricians to optimise the person for surgery as soon as possible, communicate with the hip fracture care team what needs to happen to avoid repeated cancellation and delay, and document any decisions clearly in the person's medical notes." Scottish standards, Standard 6: "Hip fracture patients are likely to have multiple co-morbidities, however in general surgery should not be delayed unless 'the benefits of additional medical treatment outweigh the risks of delaying surgery'. [23] Thirty-six hours (or less) is a sufficient period to allow for correction or reduction of medical obstacles to surgery, provided this is instigated immediately at presentation. [24]"
location: Griffiths 2021 Controversies (surgical delay); Scottish standards Standard 6 rationale
safe_wording: UK guidance says surgery should be delayed only if the benefit of more medical treatment outweighs the risk of waiting, that 36 hours is enough time to correct most problems if work starts at once, and that the team should say what needs to happen and write the decision down.
qualifications: The candidate's position that 'any delay should name the specific correctable problem and when it will be corrected' is a reasonable reading of this guidance ('communicate ... what needs to happen', 'document any decisions') but the time-by-when element is an editorial judgement; mark it as 'we should' rather than as a guideline quotation. The angle's claim that delays 'often turn out' to be waits for tests or drugs to wear off is NOT supported by any opened source; drop it or replace with the DOAC figure (C03-21-e).

claim: The Association of Anaesthetists' 2011 guidance listed seven 'acceptable' reasons for delaying surgery, each with a threshold (for example haemoglobin below 80 g/L, heart rate above 120 with a correctable arrhythmia).
supporting_passage: "The 2011 guidelines list seven 'acceptable' reasons for delaying surgery: 1Haemoglobin < 80 g.l−1 2Plasma sodium concentration < 120 or > 150 mmol.l−1 and potassium concentration < 2.8 or > 6.0 mmol−1 3Uncontrolled diabetes 4Uncontrolled or acute onset left ventricular failure. 5Correctable cardiac arrhythmia with a ventricular rate > 120.min−1 6Chest infection with sepsis 7Reversible coagulopathy The Fragility Fracture Network guidance states “surgery should be delayed only if the benefits of additional medical treatment outweigh the risks of delaying surgery”."
safe_wording: The 2011 anaesthetic guidance gave seven reasons that could justify a delay, each with a cut-off, such as haemoglobin below 80 g/L or a correctable fast heart rhythm above 120 beats a minute. The 2020 update says these should be corrected within the 36 hours rather than used to cancel on the day.
qualifications: Optional detail for a practitioner post; if used, pair it with the 2020 update's reframing (C03-21-f).

claim: In England and Wales, being next of kin does not by itself give legal power to consent to an operation for an adult who lacks capacity: the decision-maker is someone the person appointed through a lasting power of attorney (health and welfare), or a court-appointed deputy; otherwise it is usually the responsible clinician, who decides in the person's best interests.
supporting_passage: Wade and Kitzinger 2019 abstract: "Context: The legal framework is the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) 2005, which applies to England and Wales. Theory: Unless there is a valid and applicable Advance Decision, an appointed decision-maker needs to decide for those without capacity. This may be someone appointed by the patient through a Lasting Power of Attorney, or a Deputy appointed by the court. Otherwise the decision-maker is usually the responsible clinician." Orr and Baruah 2018: "If a patient is unable to consent, treatment is carried out in their best interests." ... "A patient may have an advanced decision, lasting power of attorney for health and welfare (LPA) or a court-appointed deputy." Zalmay 2021: "The Consent Form Four (CF) is filled out when treatment is offered to a patient who is deemed to lack the capacity to be involved in this decision-making. Within it, a section entitled 'Involvement of those close to the patient' outlines that the clinician taking consent should seek the views of those close to the patient, and requires them to document this discussion (Appendix 1]. This is part of the best-interests decision-making process as outlined by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 []."
location: Wade 2019 abstract (Context, Theory); Orr 2018 full text, 'The Mental Capacity Act 2005'; Zalmay 2021 full text, Introduction
safe_wording: In England and Wales, being next of kin does not give you the legal right to consent to an operation for your mother. If she can't decide for herself, the decision is made by someone she appointed under a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare, or a court-appointed deputy. If there is no one like that, the doctor responsible makes the decision in her best interests.
qualifications: Say 'usually the responsible clinician' or 'the doctor responsible'. An LPA must be registered to be used (Orr 2018). None of these can compel treatment that is not in the person's best interests. Do not describe the Northern Ireland process (editor's instruction). Do not claim how often relatives are wrongly asked to sign: no opened source measures it.

claim: Under the Mental Capacity Act, family and close friends must be consulted (if time permits) and the person's own wishes and values inform the best-interests decision.
supporting_passage: Orr and Baruah 2018: "If a patient is unable to consent, treatment is carried out in their best interests. Assessment of best interests must include social, psychological, and medical factors and should be informed by the patient's attitudes and opinions. If time permits, family or close friends must be consulted. If this is not possible, and the course of action proposed may have serious consequences or the risks and benefits are finely balanced, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate should be consulted." Wade and Kitzinger 2019: "Once persistent lack of capacity is confirmed, an early meeting should be arranged with family and friends, to start a process of sharing information about the patient's medical condition and their values, wishes, feelings and beliefs with a view to making timely treatment decisions in the patient's best interests." Zalmay 2021: "When a patient is judged to lack the capacity to consent to a procedure, the Mental Capacity Act outlines that where appropriate, the clinician should seek the views of those interested in their welfare, usually referring to their NoK or lasting power of attorney []."
location: Orr 2018 full text ('The Mental Capacity Act 2005'); Wade 2019 abstract (Solution); Zalmay 2021 full text (Intervention design)
safe_wording: The team must still ask you about her. The law expects the decision to take account of what she would want, her values and her beliefs, and family or close friends should be consulted if there is time.
qualifications: 'If time permits': in an emergency the consultation may be brief or not possible. The Wade 2019 'early meeting' is a recommendation from that review, not a legal requirement.

claim: In Scotland, the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 gives doctors general authority to treat an adult who can't consent once a certificate of incapacity is completed; but if the person has a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must seek that attorney's consent where reasonable and practicable.
supporting_passage: "The Act gives a 'general authority' to healthcare practitioners to treat a patient who is incapable of consenting to treatment provided that a certificate of incapacity has been completed (Fig. 1), and provided that the treatment falls within the general principles of the Act. Medical treatment is defined as 'any procedure or treatment designed to safeguard or promote physical or mental health'. If the patient is known to have appointed a proxy decision maker who has been granted power of attorney to make decisions regarding welfare, this general authority does not apply and the practitioner issuing the certificate must seek the consent of the welfare power of attorney before commencing treatment, where it is reasonable and practicable to do so. In an emergency, common law authority to provide treatment for the emergency preservation of life remains in place and completion of a certificate is not required to render this emergency treatment lawful."
location: Edwardson and Baruah 2018, full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
safe_wording: In Scotland the law is different. If she can't decide, a doctor completes a certificate of incapacity, which allows treatment. But if she has appointed a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must ask for that attorney's consent where it is reasonable and practicable.
qualifications: Welfare attorney consent is verified. The editor's wording that a court-appointed guardian with medical treatment powers can also consent was NOT verified in an opened source (the opened text lists guardians only among people to be consulted); either omit guardians or phrase as 'a welfare attorney (or a guardian with powers over medical treatment)' only after the editor accepts that it rests on the statute, which was not opened. Emergency life-saving treatment does not need a certificate. Do not describe Northern Ireland.

claim: In Scotland, any treatment under the Act must take account of the person's past and present wishes and feelings, and involve consultation with specified people, including any guardian or welfare attorney; there is a presumption of capacity.
supporting_passage: "In Scots law, there is a presumption that adults are legally capable of making decisions for themselves [presumption of capacity also applies to the Mental Capacity Act (2005) in England and Wales]." ... "The general principles of the Act are laid out in Section 1. This states that an intervention carried out under the Act: (i) should achieve a benefit not otherwise achievable; (ii) is the least restrictive option (i.e. the action made or decision taken should be the minimum necessary to achieve the intended purpose); (iii) account is taken of past and present expressed wishes and feelings as far as this is practicable; (iv) there is consultation with another specified person as far as is reasonable and practicable. Specified persons include a guardian or welfare attorney."
location: Edwardson and Baruah 2018, full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
safe_wording: In Scotland too, the law says her past and present wishes and feelings must be taken into account, and certain people must be consulted.
qualifications: The opened text says specified persons 'include' a guardian or welfare attorney; it does not list the nearest relative or carer explicitly, so the post should not say the law names relatives in Scotland.

claim: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; a person who can communicate with help is not incapable for that reason alone, so it is fair to ask whether she could decide with help and time.
supporting_passage: Orr and Baruah 2018: "A patient may lack capacity to make decisions about some aspects of their care but retain the capacity to make decisions about more straightforward aspects." ... "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Edwardson and Baruah 2018: "If this inability to communicate can be overcome with human or mechanical aids, it does not constitute incapacity for the purposes of the Act."
location: Orr 2018 full text ('Consent: ethical principles'; 'Capacity: evolution of case law'); Edwardson 2018 full text
safe_wording: Capacity is about one decision at one time. A person may be able to make some decisions but not others, and it can change from hour to hour. You can ask whether she could decide for herself with help, or later in the day.
qualifications: Hip fracture surgery is time-critical; waiting for capacity to return has to be weighed against the harm of delay. Do not imply surgery should wait indefinitely.

claim: At one English hospital, before a feedback intervention, only 80% of people with hip fracture who lacked capacity had a documented attempt to contact their next of kin before surgery, and the next-of-kin section of Consent Form Four was completed in 30%.
supporting_passage: "Pre-intervention, 80% (24/30) were noted to have had documented attempts at contacting their NoK prior to surgery. The section of Consent Form Four regarding the NoK discussion was completed in 30% (10/30). Following the intervention, all 28 patients had documented attempts at contacting their NoK prior to going for hip surgery, a significant improvement (p <0.05). The Consent Form Four NoK section was appropriately completed in 64.3% (18/28) (p <0.05)." Limitations: "A major limitation of this project was that we measured the documentation of attempts to contact next of kin; the actual rates of clinicians contacting next of kin may have been higher."
location: Zalmay 2021, full text, Results and Limitations
safe_wording: At one English hospital, notes showed an attempt to contact the family before surgery for 24 of 30 people who couldn't consent, and the family section of the consent form was filled in for 10 of 30. After the team was given feedback, contact attempts were recorded for all 28 people in the next group.
qualifications: One hospital, small numbers, documentation rather than actual conversations; not generalisable. Optional detail; the post does not depend on it.

claim: In a Cochrane review, peripheral nerve blocks reduced pain on movement within 30 minutes of being placed, by the equivalent of about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale (high-certainty evidence).
supporting_passage: "We included 49 trials (3061 participants; 1553 randomized to PNBs and 1508 to no nerve block (or sham block))." ... "Results of 11 trials with 503 participants show that PNBs reduced pain on movement within 30 minutes of block placement (standardized mean difference (SMD) -1.05, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.25 to -0.86; equivalent to -2.5 on a scale from 0 to 10; high-certainty evidence)." Authors' conclusions: "PNBs reduce pain on movement within 30 minutes after block placement..."
safe_wording: A Cochrane review of the trials found that a nerve block (an injection of local anaesthetic near the nerves to the hip) reduced pain on movement within half an hour by about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale, compared with no block.
qualifications: The 30-minute result comes from 11 of the 49 trials (503 people). Everyone could have other pain relief as well.

claim: Nerve blocks probably reduce chest infection and shorten the time to first getting out of bed by about 11 hours (moderate certainty, small numbers of trials); effects on death are uncertain.
supporting_passage: "From three trials with 131 participants, PNBs probably reduce the risk for chest infection (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.89; NNTB 7, 95% CI 5 to 72; moderate-certainty evidence). Based on 11 trials with 617 participants, the effects of PNBs on mortality within six months are uncertain due to very serious imprecision (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.60; low-certainty evidence). From three trials with 208 participants, PNBs likely reduce time to first mobilization (mean difference (MD) -10.80 hours, 95% CI -12.83 to -8.77 hours; moderate-certainty evidence)."
safe_wording: The same review found that blocks probably mean fewer chest infections and getting out of bed about 11 hours sooner, though these results come from only a few small trials. Whether blocks affect survival is uncertain.
qualifications: Chest infection: 3 trials, 131 people; mobilisation: 3 trials, 208 people. Do not give the relative risk as 'times less likely'; if a number is needed use the NNT with its wide range (about 1 fewer infection for every 7 people treated, range 5 to 72) or avoid it. The review also reports fewer cases of acute confusion; delirium is an excluded topic, so leave it out.

claim: People with dementia were often excluded from the nerve block trials.
supporting_passage: "The average age of participants ranged from 59 to 89 years. People with dementia were often excluded from the included trials. Additional analgesia was available for all participants."
safe_wording: People with dementia were often left out of these trials, so the evidence is thinner for the people who may find it hardest to say they are in pain.
qualifications: The second half of the safe wording is a reasonable inference; keep it modest or omit.

claim: UK anaesthetic guidance recommends single-shot nerve blocks in the emergency department and again at the time of surgery, and notes that blocks reduce pain at rest and on movement, reduce time to getting moving and are not contraindicated in people on anticoagulants.
supporting_passage: "Randomised controlled trials [25, 26], observational studies [19], consensus opinion [2], national audit initiatives [8] and systematic review [27] all support the widespread use of peripheral nerve blocks for analgesia on admission to hospital and in the early postoperative period. These are effective at reducing pain and quadriceps spasm at rest and on movement; reduce time to remobilisation; reduce opioid administration (to a patient population 40% of who have renal dysfunction and are at greater risk of postoperative delirium); and are not contra-indicated in anticoagulated patients [28]. The Working Party recommends that: 1Single shot nerve blocks should be provided in the Emergency Department and at the time of surgery (provided 6 h has passed between blocks) [27]. There is some evidence for their efficacy in providing pre-hospital analgesia [29]; 2Femoral or fascia iliaca blocks should be used, the latter possibly providing better incisional analgesia after surgery."
location: Griffiths 2021 full text, 'Specific changes to the 2011 guidance' (analgesia)
safe_wording: The Association of Anaesthetists recommends a single-injection nerve block in the emergency department and another at the time of surgery.
qualifications: The guideline says 'in the Emergency Department', not 'before X-ray'; the drawn sequence must not show the block before imaging unless labelled as one possible order. A second block needs at least 6 hours after the first.

claim: NICE recommends considering nerve blocks if paracetamol and opioids are not enough before surgery, or to limit opioid dose, and asks that pain relief be enough to allow the movements needed for investigations, nursing care and rehabilitation.
supporting_passage: "4.2.3 Analgesia ➢ Assess the patient's pain: • immediately upon presentation at hospital and • within 30 minutes of administering initial analgesia and • hourly until settled on the ward and • regularly as part of routine nursing observations throughout admission. ➢ Offer immediate analgesia to patients presenting at hospital with suspected hip fracture, including people with cognitive impairment. ➢ Ensure analgesia is sufficient to allow movements necessary for investigations (as indicated by the ability to tolerate passive external rotation of the leg), and for nursing care and rehabilitation." ... "➢ Consider adding nerve blocks if paracetamol and opioids do not provide sufficient preoperative pain relief, or to limit opioid dosage. Nerve blocks should be administered by trained personnel. Do not use nerve blocks as a substitute for early surgery."
safe_wording: NICE asks that pain relief be good enough for the person to be moved for X-rays, nursing care and rehabilitation, and says a nerve block should be considered when paracetamol and morphine-type drugs are not enough, or to reduce how much of them is needed.
qualifications: NICE's nerve block recommendation is conditional ('consider'), not 'offer'. It was not changed in the 2023 update per the Age and Ageing commentary (live page not opened). NICE also says blocks are not a substitute for early surgery.

claim: The Scottish standards note that people with hip fracture often have little pain at rest but severe pain on movement, and make a fascia iliaca block the first-line choice in the emergency department.
supporting_passage: "Standard 2: The 'big six' bundle is carried out in the emergency department (ED)" ... "4. Provide pain relief: all patients who sustain this painful injury must be offered analgesia. It is important to recognise that patients often have little pain on rest but severe pain on movement and for this reason a fascia iliaca block is the first-line choice."
location: Scottish standards of care for hip fracture patients (v1.2, Sep 2025), Standard 2 rationale
safe_wording: Scotland's national hip fracture standards point out that people often have little pain lying still but severe pain when moved, and name a nerve block (fascia iliaca block) as the first choice for pain relief in the emergency department.
qualifications: Cite as a published standard; do not mention or imply audit results (Alasdair chairs the audit).

claim: A single-injection block lasts hours, not the whole wait for surgery: a review puts a single-shot fascia iliaca block with bupivacaine at about 8 hours of pain relief, and trial evidence in the emergency department measured benefit up to 4 hours.
supporting_passage: Verbeek 2021 abstract: "Single-shot FICB is faster to place, yet providing about 8 h of analgesia when bupivacaine is used. Continuous FICB provides prolonged titratable analgesia..." Makkar 2021 abstract: "A significant difference in pain relief at rest and on movement started within 30 min and lasted till 4 h of the block." ... "However, the quality of evidence is low and additional trials are necessary." Griffiths 2021: "Single shot nerve blocks should be provided in the Emergency Department and at the time of surgery (provided 6 h has passed between blocks)".
location: Verbeek 2021 abstract; Makkar 2021 abstract (Results, Conclusions); Griffiths 2021 analgesia section
safe_wording: A single injection does not last until the operation. It usually gives several hours of relief (one review suggests about 8 hours with a long-acting local anaesthetic), which is why UK guidance also advises another block at the time of surgery. Giving it early in the emergency department covers the X-ray, the move to the ward and the first hours of nursing care.
qualifications: The 8-hour figure comes from a narrative review and depends on drug and dose; trial evidence (low certainty) measured benefit only to 4 hours. Do not say it 'spares pain at every later move' (judge's concern). The link between the ED block and the second block at surgery is guideline structure, not a stated rationale; phrase as 'UK guidance also advises', not 'because'.

claim: A person with a hip fracture typically goes through several transfers (floor, ambulance trolley, emergency department trolley, X-ray table, ward bed), each of which moves the fracture.
supporting_passage: No source found or opened that describes or counts the transfers. NICE (DRIVE:1pftOMXMI_OAkTBofH11t6ayryZ2F-YXb) supports the related point that analgesia must allow 'movements necessary for investigations ... and for nursing care'.
safe_wording: On the way from home to a ward bed, a person with a broken hip is usually lifted or slid several times: onto an ambulance trolley, onto a hospital trolley, for the X-ray and into bed.
qualifications: Present as a generic, typical description, not a measured count; no numbers. The visual must not place the ED block before the X-ray as fact (in UK practice the block is given in the ED, often after the fracture is confirmed); show it as 'in the emergency department'. Prehospital blocks exist in some services ('some evidence for their efficacy', Griffiths 2021) but are not routine; do not imply they are.

claim: In the REGAIN trial (1600 previously walking adults aged 50 and over, 46 US and Canadian hospitals), death or inability to walk about 3 metres at 60 days occurred in 18.5% with spinal and 18.0% with general anaesthesia.
supporting_passage: "We conducted a pragmatic, randomized superiority trial to evaluate spinal anesthesia as compared with general anesthesia in previously ambulatory patients 50 years of age or older who were undergoing surgery for hip fracture at 46 U.S. and Canadian hospitals. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive spinal or general anesthesia. The primary outcome was a composite of death or an inability to walk approximately 10 ft (3 m) independently or with a walker or cane at 60 days after randomization." ... "Among patients in the modified intention-to-treat population for whom data were available, the composite primary outcome occurred in 132 of 712 patients (18.5%) in the spinal anesthesia group and 132 of 733 (18.0%) in the general anesthesia group (relative risk, 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.84 to 1.27; P = 0.83)."
safe_wording: In a trial of 1,600 people who could walk before their hip fracture, about 18 in 100 had died or could not walk across a small room (about 3 metres) two months later, whether they had a spinal or a general anaesthetic.
qualifications: Composite outcome; say what it combines. US and Canadian hospitals; only people who could walk before the fracture. Did not show a clear difference (not 'proved equal').

claim: Deaths within 60 days (3.9% vs 4.1%) and inability to walk independently at 60 days (15.2% vs 14.4%) were similar; about 1 in 6 people assigned to spinal did not receive spinal only.
supporting_passage: REGAIN abstract: "A total of 666 patients (83.8%) assigned to spinal anesthesia and 769 patients (95.5%) assigned to general anesthesia received their assigned anesthesia." ... "An inability to walk independently at 60 days was reported in 104 of 684 patients (15.2%) and 101 of 702 patients (14.4%), respectively (relative risk, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.82 to 1.36), and death within 60 days occurred in 30 of 768 (3.9%) and 32 of 784 (4.1%), respectively (relative risk, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.59 to 1.57)." Vail 2024 (full-text passage quoted in Scite): "As reported previously, 12 666 of 795 patients assigned to spinal anesthesia (84%) received spinal anesthesia only. Of the remaining patients in the spinal anesthesia arm, 119 (15%) received general anesthesia, with or without an initial attempt to place a spinal block."
location: REGAIN abstract (Results); Vail 2024 Results (via Scite citation snippet)
safe_wording: About 4 in 100 had died within two months in each group. About 1 in 6 people meant to have a spinal ended up with a general anaesthetic or something other than a spinal alone, which blurs the comparison a little.
qualifications: Crossover: 16% of the spinal arm did not receive spinal only (15% received general). Deaths were few, so the death comparison alone is imprecise.

claim: At one year, survival and recovery of walking were also similar between spinal and general anaesthesia in REGAIN.
supporting_passage: "Survival did not differ by treatment arm; at 365 days after randomization, there were 98 deaths in patients assigned to spinal anesthesia versus 92 deaths in patients assigned to general anesthesia (hazard ratio, 1.08; 95% CI, 0.81 to 1.44, P = 0.59). Recovery of ambulation among patients who survived a year did not differ by type of anesthesia (adjusted odds ratio for spinal vs. general, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.67 to 1.14; P = 0.31). Other outcomes did not differ by treatment arm." Conclusions: "Long-term outcomes were similar with spinal versus general anesthesia." Discussion (Scite snippet): "While the CI reported here argue against large effects of anesthesia type on long-term outcomes, the available sample does not permit us to fully exclude the potential for more subtle effects."
location: Vail 2024 abstract (Results, Conclusions); Discussion via Scite snippet
safe_wording: A year later, survival and getting back to walking were still similar with either anaesthetic.
qualifications: Vital status known for 89.2%; one-year mortality lower than in unselected hip fracture populations (authors' note), so the trial may under-represent the frailest. Subtle differences cannot be excluded. This replaces the judge's 'longer-term outcomes not settled' point: one-year outcomes are now reported.

claim: In REGAIN, people given spinal anaesthesia reported slightly worse pain in the first 24 hours after surgery and were more likely to be using prescription pain medicines at 60 days.
supporting_passage: "A total of 73.5% (1050 of 1428) of patients reported severe pain during the first 24 hours after surgery. Worst pain over the first 24 hours after surgery was greater with spinal anesthesia (rated from 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain imaginable]; mean difference, 0.40 [95% CI, 0.12 to 0.68]). Pain did not differ across groups at other time points. Prescription analgesic use at 60 days occurred in 25% (141 of 563) and 18.8% (108 of 574) of patients assigned to spinal and general anesthesia, respectively (relative risk, 1.33 [CI, 1.06 to 1.65]). Satisfaction was similar across groups." Limitations: "Missing outcome data and multiple outcomes assessed."
safe_wording: One result went the other way: people who had a spinal reported slightly worse pain in the first day after surgery (less than half a point on a 0 to 10 scale), and at two months 25 in 100 were still taking prescription painkillers compared with 19 in 100 after a general anaesthetic. Most people in both groups had severe pain in the first 24 hours.
qualifications: Secondary outcomes with missing data and multiple comparisons. The pain difference is small. Satisfaction was similar.

claim: NICE recommends offering people a choice of spinal or general anaesthesia after discussing the risks and benefits.
supporting_passage: "4.2.4 Anaesthesia ➢ Offer patients a choice of spinal or general anaesthesia after discussing the risks and benefits. ➢ Consider intraoperative nerve blocks for all patients undergoing surgery."
safe_wording: NICE says people should be offered a choice of spinal or general anaesthetic after the risks and benefits have been discussed.
qualifications: The person (or their legal decision-maker) chooses; families inform the discussion. The anaesthetist's assessment of individual risks still applies. Live NICE page not opened (see NICE source note).

claim: After a hip fracture, different abilities reach their best at different times: about 4 months for mood, arm function and thinking, and almost a year for leg function.
supporting_passage: Community-residing hip fracture patients (n = 674) admitted to eight hospitals in Baltimore, Maryland, 1990-1991 were followed prospectively for 2 years from the time of hospitalization. ... Recuperation times were specific to area of function, ranging from approximately 4 months for depressive symptoms (3.9 months), upper extremity function (4.3 months), and cognition (4.4 months) to almost a year for lower extremity function (11.2 months).
safe_wording: In a large US study, leg function kept improving for close to a year after a hip fracture on average; mood, arm function and thinking reached their best at about 4 months.
qualifications: Group averages from people who lived at home before the fracture, studied in 1990-91 in Baltimore. The time to reach a maximum is not the same as recovering fully; many never regain earlier function (see C03-12-b). Say 'on average' and 'one large US study'.

claim: Most recovery of walking and daily activities happens in the first 6 months, and only about half of people regain their previous mobility.
supporting_passage: The bulk of recovery of walking ability and activities for daily living occurred within 6 months after fracture. Between 40 and 60 % of study participants recovered their pre-fracture level of mobility and ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living, while 40-70 % regained their level of independence for basic activities of daily living.
safe_wording: Across many studies, most of the recovery in walking and daily activities came in the first 6 months, and roughly 4 to 6 in 10 people got back to the mobility they had before the fracture.
qualifications: Ranges across studies of usual care, not predictions for one person. Fewer people from care homes recovered their earlier function.

claim: Rehabilitation in hospital by a specialist multidisciplinary team probably means fewer people die or have to move to a care home in the following 6 to 12 months.
supporting_passage: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation probably results in fewer cases of 'poor outcome' (death or deterioration in residential status, generally requiring institutional care) at 6 to 12 months' follow-up (risk ratio (RR) 0.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 0.98; 13 studies, 3036 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Based on an illustrative risk of 347 people with hip fracture with poor outcome in 1000 people followed up between 6 and 12 months, this equates to 41 (95% CI 7 to 69) fewer people with poor outcome after multidisciplinary rehabilitation.
safe_wording: In trials, rehabilitation in hospital led by a specialist team probably meant fewer people died or needed a move to a care home over the next 6 to 12 months: about 31 in 100 compared with 35 in 100.
qualifications: The outcome combines death and moving to a higher level of care; do not present it as care home moves alone. Moderate certainty. Trials of supported discharge and rehabilitation at home gave very low-certainty evidence, so do not claim that a 'supported trial at home' is proven to help.

claim: UK health policy in England and Scotland has advised against moving people into a care home directly from an acute hospital.
supporting_passage: Both NHS England and the Scottish Government policy argue that care home admission from acute hospitals should be avoided
location: Harrison 2017, full text, Background (secondary statement citing the policy documents); abstract: 'with policy documents advising against this transition'
safe_wording: Policy in both England and Scotland has said that moving into a care home straight from an acute hospital ward should be avoided where possible.
qualifications: Supported only through a 2017 peer-reviewed paper's summary of policy; the official documents themselves could not be opened, so do not quote their wording, do not say 'guidance says decisions must not be made in hospital', and do not name a specific document or year. The candidate's original wording ('decisions about long-term care are not normally made in an acute hospital') is not verified.

claim: (Optional context) In one Scottish hospital, just over half of decisions for a new care home move were made while the person was still on the acute hospital.
supporting_passage: About 55% were in the acute hospital when the decision for a care home was made and 44% of that group were discharged directly from the acute hospital.
location: Abstract, Results; full text, Discharge planning
safe_wording: In one Scottish hospital study of 100 people who moved into a care home after an emergency admission, just over half had the decision made while still on the acute hospital.
qualifications: Not hip-fracture specific (most were medical admissions; 10% had fractures). Single centre. Alasdair MacLullich is a co-author. Optional; the post does not need it.

claim: FRAIL-HIP studied 172 very frail care home residents aged 70 and over with limited life expectancy who broke a hip; after shared decision-making, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. It was not randomised.
supporting_passage: Eligible patients were aged 70 years or older, frail, and institutionalized and sustained a femoral neck or pertrochanteric fracture. The term frail implied at least 1 of the following characteristics was present: malnutrition (body mass index ... <18.5) or cachexia, severe comorbidities (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status class of IV or V), or severe mobility issues (Functional Ambulation Category ≤2). ... Of the 172 enrolled patients with proximal femoral fractures (median [25th and 75th percentile] age, 88 [85-92] years; 135 women [78%]), 88 opted for nonoperative management and 84 opted for operative management.
location: Abstract, Design/Setting/Participants and Results; full-text excerpt: 'Only a randomized clinical trial would have avoided selection bias through the SDM process but was considered unfeasible and unethical.'
safe_wording: A Dutch study followed 172 very frail care home residents (median age 88) who broke a hip and whose life expectancy was already short. After talking it through, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. People chose; they were not allocated at random.
qualifications: Say near the top that it was a small, selected, non-randomised group who chose. Very frail and institutionalised; not applicable to most people with hip fracture.

claim: In the weeks after the fracture, quality of life (rated by relatives and carers) in people who chose no operation was not worse than in those who had an operation, within the study's preset margin.
supporting_passage: The EQ-5D utility scores by proxies and caregivers in the nonoperative management group remained within the set 0.15 noninferiority limit of the operative management group (week 1 ... week 2 ... and week 4 ...). ... Although the short-term mortality in the nonoperative management group was higher than in the operative management group, there was no loss of QOL and HRQoL, and there was high treatment satisfaction and humane quality of dying.
location: Abstract, Results; full-text excerpt (Discussion) via Scite
safe_wording: Relatives and care staff rated the person's quality of life in the following weeks as no worse, by the study's own test, when there was no operation.
qualifications: Proxy-rated, not self-rated. Non-inferiority within a 0.15 margin, not 'the same'. Comparisons after about 30 days are unreliable because most of the non-operative group had died (authors' own limitation). Do not quote EQ-5D numbers (abstract confidence intervals look inconsistent).

claim: Most people who chose no operation died within 30 days, but this reflects who chose it, not the effect of not operating.
supporting_passage: The 30-day mortality rate was 83% (n = 73) in the nonoperative management group and 25% (n = 21) in the operative management group ... The high mortality rate was as expected given that we hypothesized that the frailest patients would opt for nonoperative management and that the explicit choice for nonoperative management would most likely result in an earlier palliative care approach compared with patients who opted for operative management.
location: Abstract, Results; full-text excerpt (Discussion) via Scite. Also full text: 'Six months after the injury, 83 patients (94%) in the nonoperative management group and 40 patients (48%) in the operative management group had died'
safe_wording: About 8 in 10 of those who chose no operation died within a month, compared with 1 in 4 of those who had surgery. The frailest people, closest to death, were the ones who chose not to have surgery, so this gap does not show what the operation itself did.
qualifications: Must not be read or presented as the effect of not operating. Even with surgery, about half had died by 6 months.

claim: Relatives of about half of those who died without an operation rated the quality of dying as good to almost perfect.
supporting_passage: The dying process in both groups was judged as humane (eTable 13 in Supplement 1). The quality of dying was rated as good-almost perfect by 26 proxies (51%) in the nonoperative management group, with only 2 proxies (4%) rating the process as terrible-poor. The quality of dying in the operative management group was scored as intermediate by most proxies (13 [62%]).
location: Full-text excerpt (Results) via Scite; abstract gives the 26 (51%) figure
safe_wording: Among relatives who answered about a death without an operation, about half rated the dying as good to almost perfect; 2 rated it terrible or poor.
qualifications: Denominator is proxies who completed the questionnaire (26 is 51%, so about 51 respondents), not all 88 people. Proxy judgement.

claim: Care without an operation still needs active pain relief; in FRAIL-HIP the authors judged pain in the non-operative group to have been undertreated, and 2 people switched to surgery because of increasing pain.
supporting_passage: The study results do suggest that pain in the nonoperative management group was undertreated and was a factor in end-of-life care that should be improved. ... After initially opting for nonoperative management, 2 patients were treated surgically within the index admission because of progressive pain.
safe_wording: Even in this study, the researchers judged that pain was undertreated in the group without an operation, and 2 people changed to surgery because their pain grew worse. Care without an operation has to include good, regular pain relief.
qualifications: This belongs in the post: it makes the 'care without an operation is active care' point honest.

claim: UK guidance treats surgery as the best pain relief for a broken hip and says surgery should still be considered even when the fracture comes with a terminal illness, as part of palliative care.
supporting_passage: It is recognized surgery is the best form of analgesia and as over 30% present with cognitive impairment, it can be otherwise difficult to assess patients suffering. ... If a hip fracture complicates or precipitates a terminal illness, the multidisciplinary team should still consider the role of surgery, as part of a palliative care approach that: • minimises pain and other symptoms and • establishes patients' own priorities for rehabilitation and • considers patients' wishes about their end-of-life care.
location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011: Timing of surgery, guideline group discussion (page 65); Guideline summary recommendations (page 38)
safe_wording: UK guidance (NICE) describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip, and says that even when a hip fracture comes with a terminal illness, the team should still consider surgery as part of palliative care that eases pain and respects the person's wishes.
qualifications: 'Best form of analgesia' is from the guideline group's discussion, not a numbered recommendation; attribute it as 'NICE's guideline group'. NICE does not set out when non-operative care is appropriate.

claim: Scottish hip fracture standards allow for a decision not to operate, provided a management or palliative care plan is recorded and the decision is reviewed if the person improves.
supporting_passage: Should conservative treatment be agreed, the management plan or palliative care plan, should be clearly recorded in the patient records. Best practice is to evaluate this decision should the patient's medical condition improve.
safe_wording: Scotland's hip fracture standards expect that, if a decision not to operate is agreed, a clear care or palliative care plan is written down and the decision is looked at again if the person gets better.
qualifications: Quote the standard only; do not state or imply Scottish Hip Fracture Audit results or Alasdair's role.

claim: In a gait study with pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 people aged 75 and over after hip fracture surgery kept to a partial weight-bearing limit of 20 kg; 11 of 16 put more than twice that weight through the leg.
supporting_passage: Both groups were instructed to maintain partial weight-bearing on the affected limb (≤20 kg) postoperatively. Following standardized physiotherapy training, gait analysis was performed. None of the patients in the elderly test group were able to comply with the weight-bearing restriction as recommended. We found that 69% (11 of 16) of the patients exceeded the specified load by more than twofold, whereas significantly more patients in the younger control group (>75% [14 of 18]) achieved almost the entire weight-bearing restriction (p < 0.001). Only 1 of the elderly patients was able to comply with the predetermined weight-bearing restriction, and only for a short period of time.
safe_wording: In a German study using pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 older people after hip fracture surgery kept to a 'partial weight-bearing' limit when they walked (one managed it briefly); 11 of the 16 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. Most young adults with ankle fractures could keep to it.
qualifications: Very small single-centre study, one walking session. Say 'none kept to it throughout; one managed briefly'.

claim: Told to partial weight-bear, older people after hip fracture walked less well and more slowly, yet put the same load through the leg as those allowed full weight-bearing.
supporting_passage: The postoperative Parker Mobility Score in the PWB group compared to the FWB group was significantly reduced (3.21 vs. 4.73, p < 0.001). Accordingly, a significantly lower gait speed in the PWB group of 0.16 m/s vs. 0.28 m/s was seen (p = 0.003). No difference in weight bearing was observed in between the groups (average peak force 350.25 N vs. 353.08 N, p = 0.918), nor any differences in the demographic characteristics, ASA Score, Barthel Index or EQ5D.
safe_wording: In a second small German study, older people told to limit weight on the leg after hip fracture surgery walked more slowly and had lower mobility scores on day 5 than those allowed full weight, but pressed just as hard through the leg.
qualifications: Small, non-randomised (before-and-after groups), same research group as C03-19-a.

claim: NICE recommends that hip fracture surgery should aim to let the person bear full weight without restriction straight after the operation.
supporting_passage: 4.2.6 Surgical procedures ➢ Operate on patients with the aim to allow them to fully weight bear (without restriction) in the immediate postoperative period.
location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011, Guideline summary, section 4.2.6 Surgical procedures
safe_wording: NICE guidance says surgeons should operate with the aim of letting the person put full weight on the leg, without restriction, straight after surgery.
qualifications: Wording verified in the 2011 full guideline (not among the 2017 replaced recommendations); the current web version was not opened. BOAST wording not checked; do not cite BOAST.

claim: Restricted weight-bearing after hip fracture surgery is linked with more complications and deaths.
supporting_passage: Ottesen 2018: 'Controlling for patient and procedural factors, multivariate odds of any adverse event, major adverse event, delirium, infection, transfusion, length of stay ≥ 75th percentile (six days) and mortality within 30 days were all higher in patients with weight-bearing restrictions.' Tarrant 2022: 'In adjusted analysis, RWB did not influence 30-day mortality (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.15-01.13, p = 0.293) ... RWB was significantly related to increased DVT (OR 7.81, 95% CI: 1.81-33.71 p = 0.002) but no other secondary outcomes.' Xu 2026: 'Unrestricted weight-bearing was significantly associated with lower long-term mortality compared with restricted weight-bearing (RR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.51-0.88 ...). Short-term mortality did not differ significantly in the primary analysis ... No significant differences were observed for short-term complications, long-term complications, reoperation risk, or LOS between the two groups (all> 0.05). GRADE assessment showed low certainty of evidence for long-term mortality and short-term complications, and very low certainty of evidence for the remaining outcomes.'
safe_wording: Studies disagree about harm. A large US database study linked restrictions with more complications and deaths within 30 days; an Australian study did not find more deaths; a 2026 review found restriction was linked with more deaths in the longer term, but the evidence was weak, and found no clear difference in complications or repeat operations.
qualifications: Observational only: 'linked with', never 'causes'. Restriction is usually prescribed for harder fractures or fixations, so these links may reflect the injury, not the instruction. Do not give the Ottesen percentages (arithmetic inconsistency in abstract). Better to rest the post on the compliance and mobility findings plus NICE, and mention harm evidence as mixed.

claim: In a Norwegian randomised trial, people on the fourth day after hip fracture surgery spent under an hour of the whole day upright (standing or walking): 58 minutes on average with comprehensive geriatric care and 45 minutes with orthopaedic ward care.
supporting_passage: Primary outcome was measurement of upright time (standing and walking) recorded for 24 hours the fourth day postsurgery by a body-worn accelerometer-based activity monitor. ... A total of 317 (CGC n = 175, OC n = 142) participants wore the activity monitor for a 24-hour period. CGC participants had significantly more upright time (mean 57.6 vs 45.1 min, p = .016)
safe_wording: In a Norwegian trial, people wore a small activity monitor for the whole of the fourth day after hip fracture surgery. On average they spent 58 minutes of the 24 hours standing or walking if cared for on a geriatric ward, and 45 minutes on an orthopaedic ward.
qualifications: Averages on one day; people who lived at home and could walk before; 80 of 397 did not wear the monitor. The difference between wards comes from randomisation, so the geriatric care model can be said to increase upright time in this trial.

claim: Geriatric ward care also gave more separate times upright and better leg function on day 5, although the need for help to walk did not differ.
supporting_passage: CGC participants had significantly more upright time (mean 57.6 vs 45.1 min, p = .016), higher number of upright events (p = .005) and better Short Physical Performance Battery scores (p = .002), than the OC participants. Cumulated Ambulation score did not differ between groups (p = .234).
safe_wording: The geriatric ward group also got up more often during the day and had better leg function on day 5; the help they needed to walk in the first 3 days did not differ.
qualifications: The number of upright events per day is not in the abstract; do not give a figure.

claim: National hip fracture measures count whether mobilisation started by the day after surgery, and the Scottish standard counts getting out of bed to the toilet or into a chair as mobilisation.
supporting_passage: Griffiths 2021: 'Based on National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance [20], the National Hip Fracture Database has adopted patient remobilisation on the day of or day after surgery as a Key Performance Indicator.' Scottish standards 2025: 'Standard 9a: Mobilisation is commenced by the end of the first day after surgery' ... 'ix Mobilisation can include getting out of bed to use the toilet or transferring onto a chair as well as more formal mobilisation with nursing or physiotherapy staff.' ... '9.4.1 The number of patients who had a surgical repair of their hip fracture who were mobilised by the end of the first day after surgery.'
location: Griffiths 2021, Remobilisation section (two-column PDF text reassembled from one column); Scottish standards, Standard 9a, pages 27-28
safe_wording: UK hip fracture measures record whether a person was got up by the day after surgery. Scotland's standard counts getting out of bed to the toilet or into a chair as a start. These measures record whether mobilisation started, not how long the person spends on their feet each day.
qualifications: The final sentence is an accurate description of what the audit measure counts (a start of mobilisation by a deadline), based on the published definitions read; do not claim that wards 'rarely measure' upright time, which was not sourced. Do not state or imply Scottish Hip Fracture Audit results, and do not frame the post as Alasdair criticising the audit he chairs; NHFD indicator wording is as described in the 2020 guideline, current NHFD wording not opened.

claim: Across studies using activity monitors, older people with hip fracture spend very little time upright in hospital (16 to 52 minutes a day) and remain inactive during recovery.
supporting_passage: Older adults had excessive sedentary time (>10 hours/day) and low physical activity. Participants' average upright time differed across settings. During hospital stay, it ranged 16-52 minutes/day, while in the community, it ranged 51-261 minutes/day.
safe_wording: Studies that fitted activity monitors found older people in hospital after a hip fracture spent on average between 16 and 52 minutes a day upright, and most of their waking day sitting or lying during recovery.
qualifications: Ranges from small, varied studies. This replaces the candidate's uncertain 'Fleig 2016' claim on activity after discharge; community upright time ranged 51 to 261 minutes a day.

claim: In an Australian orthogeriatric unit, 34% of older people had swallowing difficulty after hip fracture surgery.
supporting_passage: one hundred and eighty-one patients with a mean age of 83 years (range: 65-103) admitted to a specialised orthogeriatric unit were assessed for OD post-surgery for hip fracture. ... OD was found to be present post-operatively in 34% (n = 61) of the current population.
safe_wording: In one Australian hospital unit, about 1 in 3 older people (61 of 181) had trouble swallowing after hip fracture surgery.
qualifications: Single unit with formal assessment; name it as one study.

claim: Across studies, around a third of older people have swallowing problems after hip fracture surgery, with estimates ranging widely depending on how and when swallowing is tested.
supporting_passage: Suzuki 2024: 'The estimated dysphagia prevalence rates [95 % confidence interval] of cervical spine disease, hip fractures, and others were 16 % [8-27], 32 % [15-54], and 6 % [4-8], respectively.' Mateos-Nozal 2021: 'a total of 320 patients (mean age 86.2 years, 73.4% women) were assessed for dysphagia within 72 hours post-surgery using the Volume-Viscosity Swallow Test. ... dysphagia was present in 176 (55%) patients.'
safe_wording: Studies that checked swallowing after hip fracture surgery found problems in roughly 1 in 3 older people on average, and more than half in one Spanish study that tested everyone with a bedside test.
qualifications: Pooled estimate has wide uncertainty (15% to 54%). Say 'roughly a third' or 'between 1 in 3 and 1 in 2 in different studies'.

claim: Swallowing problems after hip fracture surgery were more likely in people who were older, lived in a care home, or already had neurological or lung conditions.
supporting_passage: Multivariate logistic regression analyses revealed the presence of pre-existing neurological and respiratory medical co-morbidities, presence of post-operative delirium, age and living in a residential aged care facility prior to hospital admission to be associated with the post-operative OD.
safe_wording: Trouble swallowing was more common in people who were older, came from a care home, or already had a neurological or lung condition.
qualifications: Associations only. The study also lists postoperative delirium; the post can leave this out (delirium excluded as a topic) without misrepresenting the finding.

claim: Swallowing problems after hip fracture are linked with aspiration pneumonia and higher death rates.
supporting_passage: Two groups were identified and compared: those with a coded diagnosis of dysphagia (n = 165) in addition to hip/femur fracture (HF + D), and a group with hip fracture alone (HF-D) (n = 2,288) ... For those in the HF + D group, mean age was 85 years compared to 78 years in the HF-D group (P < .05) ... Mortality within 30 days of admission was significantly higher (18% vs. 4%,respectively) ... Rate of aspiration pneumonia was 14 times greater in HF + D (9.7%) compared with HF-D (0.7%).
safe_wording: In a New Zealand hospital, people with hip fracture who had a recorded swallowing problem had aspiration pneumonia (chest infection from food or drink going the wrong way) far more often: about 1 in 10 compared with fewer than 1 in 100. They were also more likely to die within 30 days (18 in 100 vs 4 in 100). They were older, and this link does not show that the swallowing problem caused the deaths.
qualifications: Observational, unadjusted in the abstract; the dysphagia group was 7 years older on average. Say 'linked with'. Do not say that watching the first drink prevents pneumonia; that has not been tested.

claim: Signs of a swallowing problem include coughing or choking on drinks, a change in the voice after swallowing, throat clearing, swallowing several times per mouthful and food left in the mouth; many older people do not notice their own swallowing problem.
supporting_passage: Prominent among the main symptoms are aspiration, residue, excessive throat clearing, coughing, hoarse voice, atypical ventilation periods, and repetitive swallowing. An added risk is that many older people are unaware of their swallowing dysfunction. ... bedside clinical tests with water or other liquids together with oximetry, to look for coughing, choking, voice changes, and desaturation ... Clinical signs of impaired safety include cough, fall in oxygen saturation ≥3%, and voice changes; and signs of impaired efficacy include impaired labial seal, piecemeal deglutition, and oral and pharyngeal residue.
location: Full text: 'Combination of symptoms' and 'Screening and clinical assessment of dysphagia' sections
safe_wording: Signs to watch for at a drink or meal: coughing or choking, a hoarse or changed voice after swallowing, lots of throat clearing, swallowing several times for one mouthful, or food left in the mouth. Many older people do not notice these problems themselves.
qualifications: Source is a European consensus paper, not a UK (RCSLT or NICE) document; 'wet' or 'gurgly' voice is not the source's wording, use 'hoarse or changed voice'. 'Very slow eating' is not in the source; leave it out or use 'swallowing several times per mouthful'.

claim: People with swallowing difficulty are advised to eat and drink sitting fully upright and to stay upright for at least 30 minutes after meals.
supporting_passage: A general directive is to swallow in an upright position (90° seated)and to maintain this posture after the meal for at least 30 minutes.
safe_wording: Sitting fully upright to eat and drink, and staying upright for about half an hour after a meal, is standard advice for people with swallowing difficulty.
qualifications: Consensus advice for people with dysphagia, not trial evidence after hip fracture. Sitting upright after hip surgery may need help and good pain relief.

claim: Who can carry out a bedside swallow screen on an orthopaedic ward (judge's sharpen request).
safe_wording: Ask the ward team whether swallowing has been checked, and ask for a swallowing assessment if you see these signs.
