"We evaluated only one vitamin D dose, and the trial was not designed to test the effects of vitamin D supplementation in those who are vitamin D deficient. Only a small percentage of participants (2.4%) had vitamin D levels of less than 12 ng per milliliter." ... "In addition, results may not be generalizable to adults with osteoporosis or osteomalacia or older institutionalized persons."
location: Full text: Results (Trial participants; Fracture incidence); Discussion (limitations)
safe_wording: Most VITAL volunteers already had normal vitamin D levels; only about 2 in 100 were very low. The trial was not designed to test people who are deficient, and in that small very-low group there was no sign of benefit either. The authors say the results may not apply to people with osteoporosis or to older people living in care homes. So the evidence for deficient people is thin, not absent.
qualifications: The very-low subgroup (401) is post hoc and small; 'no benefit found' in it is weak evidence, but it must be stated. Do not say deficient people were 'untested'.

claim: D-Health: in 21,315 Australians aged 60 to 84, 60,000 IU vitamin D monthly for up to 5 years did not reduce fractures.
supporting_passage: "We did a population-based, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of oral vitamin D supplementation (60 000 IU per month) for up to 5 years in adults aged 60-84 years living in Australia." ... "Over a median follow-up of 5·1 years (IQR 5·1-5·1), 568 (5·6%) participants in the vitamin D group and 603 (5·9%) in the placebo group had one or more fractures. There was no effect on fracture risk overall (HR 0·94 [95% CI 0·84-1·06]), and the interaction between randomisation group and time was not significant (p=0·14). However, the HR for total fractures appeared to decrease with increasing follow-up time."
safe_wording: In D-Health, over 20,000 Australians aged 60 to 84 took a monthly dose of vitamin D or a dummy for about 5 years. 5.6 in 100 broke a bone with vitamin D and 5.9 in 100 with the dummy, not a clear difference.
qualifications: Fractures were a tertiary outcome; monthly bolus dosing; baseline vitamin D status not in abstract, so do not describe D-Health participants as 'having enough' without qualification.

claim: An older French trial in 3,270 ambulatory women with an average age of 84 found that vitamin D3 plus calcium reduced hip and other non-spinal fractures over 18 months.
supporting_passage: "We studied the effects of supplementation with vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and calcium on the frequency of hip fractures and other nonvertebral fractures, identified radiologically, in 3270 healthy ambulatory women (mean [+/- SD] age, 84 +/- 6 years). Each day for 18 months, 1634 women received tricalcium phosphate (containing 1.2 g of elemental calcium) and 20 micrograms (800 IU) of vitamin D3, and 1636 women received a double placebo." ... "Among the women who completed the 18-month study, the number of hip fractures was 43 percent lower (P = 0.043) and the total number of nonvertebral fractures was 32 percent lower (P = 0.015) among the women treated with vitamin D3 and calcium than among those who received placebo. The results of analyses according to active treatment and according to intention to treat were similar."
safe_wording: An older French trial in women with an average age of 84 found fewer hip fractures (43% fewer) with daily vitamin D and calcium together over 18 months. It tested the two together, so it cannot show vitamin D alone works.
qualifications: Care home or sheltered-housing setting NOT verified from the opened abstract: do not describe the participants as care home residents on the strength of this source. Relative reduction only (absolute numbers not in abstract); completers analysis headline; published 1992.

claim: Meta-analyses find vitamin D alone does not prevent fractures, while vitamin D with calcium gives a small reduction in hip fractures, larger in absolute terms for people living in institutions.
supporting_passage: Bolland 2018: "In pooled analyses, vitamin D had no effect on total fracture (36 trials; n=44 790, relative risk 1·00, 95% CI 0·93-1·07), hip fracture (20 trials; n=36 655, 1·11, 0·97-1·26), or falls". Avenell 2014: "There is high quality evidence that vitamin D alone, in the formats and doses tested, is unlikely to be effective in preventing hip fracture" ... "There is high quality evidence that vitamin D plus calcium results in a small reduction in hip fracture risk (nine trials, 49,853 participants; RR 0.84, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.74 to 0.96; P value 0.01). In low-risk populations (residents in the community: with an estimated eight hip fractures per 1000 per year), this equates to one fewer hip fracture per 1000 older adults per year (95% CI 0 to 2). In high risk populations (residents in institutions: with an estimated 54 hip fractures per 1000 per year), this equates to nine fewer hip fractures per 1000 older adults per year (95% CI 2 to 14)." Yao 2019: "a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (49 282 participants, 5449 fractures, 730 hip fractures) of combined supplementation with vitamin D ... and calcium ... found a 6% reduced risk of any fracture (RR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89-0.99) and a 16% reduced risk of hip fracture (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.72-0.97)."
safe_wording: Reviews of many trials agree that vitamin D on its own does not prevent fractures. Vitamin D with calcium cut hip fractures slightly: about 1 fewer per 1000 older people a year living at home, and about 9 fewer per 1000 a year in care homes, where hip fractures are far more common.
qualifications: The per-1000 figures apply the pooled relative risk to assumed baseline risks (8 and 54 per 1000 per year); they are estimates, not separate results in each setting. Reviews predate VITAL and D-Health.

claim: UK guidance says people taking osteoporosis drugs should be vitamin D replete, and that calcium with vitamin D supplements should be targeted to those at risk who do not get enough calcium in their diet.
supporting_passage: "Overall, there is little evidence that vitamin D supplementation alone reduces fracture incidence, although it may reduce falls risk [,]; (). However, it is important for patients taking antiresorptive and anabolic osteoporosis drug therapies to be vitamin D replete. In clinical practice, dietary sources of calcium are the preferred option and calcium (combined with vitamin D) supplementation should be targeted to those who do not get sufficient calcium from their diet and who are at risk of osteoporosis and/"
location: NOGG full text, calcium and vitamin D section
safe_wording: UK guidance still says people on bone medicines should have enough vitamin D, and that calcium with vitamin D should go to those at risk whose diet is short of calcium.
qualifications: Guideline statement, not a trial result. The passage is truncated in the extracted text after 'and/'.

claim: VERO: in women with severe osteoporosis and existing spinal fractures, 24 months of daily teriparatide injections led to fewer new spinal fractures than weekly risedronate tablets (5.4% v 12.0%).
supporting_passage: "we enrolled post-menopausal women with at least two moderate or one severe vertebral fracture and a bone mineral density T score of less than or equal to -1·50. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 20 μg of teriparatide once daily plus oral weekly placebo or 35 mg of oral risedronate once weekly plus daily injections of placebo for 24 months." ... "At 24 months, new vertebral fractures occurred in 28 (5·4%) of 680 patients in the teriparatide group and 64 (12·0%) of 680 patients in the risedronate group (risk ratio 0·44, 95% CI 0·29-0·68; p<0·0001). Clinical fractures occurred in 30 (4·8%) of 680 patients in the teriparatide group compared with 61 (9·8%) of 680 in the risedronate group (hazard ratio 0·48, 95% CI 0·32-0·74; p=0·0009). Non-vertebral fragility fractures occurred in 25 (4·0%) patients in the teriparatide group and 38 (6·1%) in the risedronate group (hazard ratio 0·66; 95% CI 0·39-1·10; p=0·10)."
safe_wording: In VERO, 1,360 women with severe osteoporosis and spinal fractures took daily teriparatide injections (a bone-building drug) or weekly risedronate tablets for two years. New spinal fractures on X-ray: about 5 in 100 with teriparatide, 12 in 100 with risedronate. Fractures that caused symptoms: about 5 in 100 against 10 in 100. Fractures away from the spine did not clearly differ.
qualifications: Two drugs compared over 24 months, not a sequence. Women only. Lilly-funded. Percentages do not match 28/680 and 64/680 (denominators appear to be women with follow-up X-rays), so quote the percentages only. Errata listed (content not checked).

claim: ARCH: 12 months of romosozumab followed by alendronate prevented more fractures over 24 months than alendronate throughout, with more serious cardiovascular events on romosozumab in year one.
supporting_passage: "We enrolled 4093 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture and randomly assigned them in a 1:1 ratio to receive monthly subcutaneous romosozumab (210 mg) or weekly oral alendronate (70 mg) in a blinded fashion for 12 months, followed by open-label alendronate in both groups." ... "Over a period of 24 months, a 48% lower risk of new vertebral fractures was observed in the romosozumab-to-alendronate group (6.2% [127 of 2046 patients]) than in the alendronate-to-alendronate group (11.9% [243 of 2047 patients]) (P<0.001). Clinical fractures occurred in 198 of 2046 patients (9.7%) in the romosozumab-to-alendronate group versus 266 of 2047 patients (13.0%)" ... "the risk of hip fracture was lower by 38% (41 of 2046 patients [2.0%] vs. 66 of 2047 patients [3.2%]; P=0.02)." ... "During year 1, positively adjudicated serious cardiovascular adverse events were observed more often with romosozumab than with alendronate (50 of 2040 patients [2.5%] vs. 38 of 2014 patients [1.9%])."
safe_wording: In ARCH, about 4,100 women who had already broken a bone took romosozumab (a bone-building injection) for a year and then alendronate, or alendronate throughout. Over two years, new spinal fractures on X-ray: 6 in 100 against 12 in 100. Hip fractures: 2.0 in 100 against 3.2 in 100. Serious heart and circulation events in the first year: 2.5 in 100 with romosozumab against 1.9 in 100 with alendronate.
qualifications: Women only; industry-funded; clinical and hip fracture figures are at the primary analysis rather than exactly 24 months.

claim: Some sequences work less well: switching from denosumab to teriparatide led to progressive or transient bone loss, with smaller hip density gains than switching the other way.
supporting_passage: DATA-Switch: "total hip bone mineral density increased more in the teriparatide to denosumab group (6·6% [95% CI 5·3-7·9]) than in the denosumab to teriparatide group (2·8% [1·3-4·2], p=0·0002)" ... "In postmenopausal osteoporotic women switching from teriparatide to denosumab, bone mineral density continued to increase, whereas switching from denosumab to teriparatide results in progressive or transient bone loss." NOGG: "In women previously treated with denosumab, switching to teriparatide is associated with transient bone loss in the spine and greater and longer-lasting bone loss in the hip [] ... The impact of these effects, if any, on fracture risk is unknown."
location: DATA-Switch abstract (Findings; Interpretation); NOGG full text, 'Treatment sequence'
safe_wording: Order also affects bone density: in a small trial, women who went from teriparatide to denosumab kept gaining hip density (6.6% over four years), while those who went from denosumab to teriparatide gained much less (2.8%) and lost bone for a time.
qualifications: Small (77 women); density only; NOGG says the effect on fractures is unknown.

claim: UK guidance defines very high fracture risk (for example a spinal fracture in the last 2 years, two or more spinal fractures, T-score -3.5 or lower, or high-dose steroids) and advises considering specialist referral and a bone-building drug first, particularly with spinal fractures.
supporting_passage: "Consider referral of very high-risk patients to an osteoporosis specialist in secondary care, for assessment and consideration of parenteral treatment (some may need first-line anabolic drug treatment, especially those with multiple vertebral fractures)." ... "Indications for referral to an osteoporosis specialist may arise through several routes, for example in the presence of single but important clinical risk factors, such as a recent vertebral fracture (within the last 2 years), ≥ 2 vertebral fractures (whenever they have occurred), a BMD T-score ≤  − 3.5, high-dose glucocorticoids use (≥ 7.5 mg/day of prednisolone or equivalent over 3 months)" ... "Consider teriparatide or romosozumab as first-line treatment options in postmenopausal women at very high fracture risk, particularly in those with vertebral fractures" ... "Consider teriparatide as a first-line treatment option in men age 50 years and older who are at very high fracture risk, particularly in those with vertebral fractures" ... "Comparator studies of anti-resorptive and anabolic agents have not been reported in men." ... "very high risk is identified as a FRAX-based fracture probability that exceeds the intervention threshold by 60%"
location: NOGG full text: 'Indications for specialist referral in those at very high-fracture risk'; 'Anabolic drug treatment' recommendations 9 and 10; 'Treatment sequence'
safe_wording: UK guidance counts as very high risk, for example: a spinal fracture in the last 2 years, two or more spinal fractures at any time, very low bone density (T-score -3.5 or lower), or steroid tablets at 7.5 mg prednisolone a day or more for 3 months. For these people it says consider referral to a specialist and consider a bone-building drug first, especially after spinal fractures.
qualifications: 'Consider', not 'must'. Head-to-head trials were in women only; for men, NOGG suggests teriparatide but no comparator trials exist.

claim: Romosozumab must not be used after a heart attack or stroke, is licensed only for postmenopausal women, and is given for 12 months.
supporting_passage: "Romosozumab is contraindicated in patients with hypocalcaemia, hypersensitivity to any of the constituents of the formulation, or a history of myocardial infarction or stroke. When determining whether to use romosozumab for an individual patient, both fracture and cardiovascular risk (based on risk factors) over the next year need to be considered." ... "is approved for the treatment of severe osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at very high risk of fracture. It is currently not approved for use in men." ... "The duration of treatment is limited to 12 months."
safe_wording: Romosozumab is not an option for anyone who has had a heart attack or stroke, which rules it out for many older people; it is licensed only for women after the menopause and given for 12 months. Teriparatide is the other bone-building option.
qualifications: Licensing summarised by a guideline, not the SmPC itself; check current licence before stating specifics beyond these.

claim: Bone-building drugs are once-only courses and must be followed without delay by an antiresorptive, so the sequence needs planning from the start.
supporting_passage: "the sequence in which they are used is important; for example, the two available anabolic agents (teriparatide and romosozumab) are licensed for once only treatment courses." ... "Following the approved duration of treatment with teriparatide or romosozumab (24 or 12 months respectively), initiate treatment with alendronate, zoledronate or denosumab without delay" ... "Any patient stopping denosumab, romosozumab or teriparatide requires a sequential therapy strategy usually involving an anti-resorptive drug, which should be planned at the time the initial therapy is instigated to avoid a gap in treatment."
location: NOGG full text, specialist referral section; recommendation 12; 'Treatment sequence'
safe_wording: Teriparatide (24 months) and romosozumab (12 months) are each given once. Afterwards a drug such as alendronate, zoledronate or denosumab should start straight away, and that plan should be made at the outset.
qualifications: Guideline recommendation.

claim: NICE TA791 recommends romosozumab for severe osteoporosis after menopause only after a major osteoporotic fracture within 24 months.
supporting_passage: Search-engine extract (not opened): "Romosozumab is recommended as an option for treating severe osteoporosis in people after menopause who are at high risk of fracture, only if they have had a major osteoporotic fracture (spine, hip, forearm or humerus fracture) within 24 months (so are at imminent risk of another fracture) and the company provides romosozumab according to the commercial arrangement."
safe_wording: Not for use as an essential claim. If mentioned at all: 'In England, NICE restricts romosozumab to women after the menopause with a major fracture in the past two years' (search extract; confirm on the live page first).
qualifications: Search extract only; NOGG 2022 predates the final NICE decision.

claim: In FIT (2,027 women with existing spinal fractures, 36 months), alendronate cut spinal fractures found on scheduled X-rays from 15.0% to 8.0%, spinal fractures that came to clinical attention from 5.0% to 2.3%, and any clinical fracture from 18.2% to 13.6%.
supporting_passage: "2027 women were randomly assigned placebo (1005) or alendronate (1022) and followed up for 36 months." ... "New vertebral fractures, the primary endpoint, were defined by morphometry as a decrease of 20% (and at least 4 mm) in at least one vertebral height between the baseline and latest follow-up radiograph." ... "New symptomatic vertebral fractures were based on self-report and confirmed by radiography." ... "78 (8.0%) of women in the alendronate group had one or more new morphometric vertebral fractures compared with 145 (15.0%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.53 [95% Cl 0.41-0.68]). For clinically apparent vertebral fractures, the corresponding numbers were 23 (2.3%) alendronate and 50 (5.0%) placebo (relative hazard 0.45 [0.27-0.72]). The risk of any clinical fracture, the main secondary endpoint, was lower in the alendronate than in the placebo group (139 [13.6%] vs 183 [18.2%]; relative hazard 0.72 [0.58-0.90]). The relative hazards for hip fracture and wrist fracture for alendronate versus placebo were 0.49 (0.23-0.99) and 0.52 (0.31-0.87)."
safe_wording: Per 100 women over 3 years in the alendronate trial: spinal fractures seen on scheduled X-rays, 15 with placebo and 8 with alendronate; spinal fractures diagnosed because of symptoms, 5 and 2.3; any fracture that came to medical attention, 18 and 14.
qualifications: Women with existing spinal fractures and low hip density; absolute hip-fracture numbers are not in the abstract (only relative hazard 0.49), so do not chart hip bars from this source.

claim: In FREEDOM, denosumab reduced new X-ray spinal fractures from 7.2% to 2.3% and hip fractures from 1.2% to 0.7% over 3 years.
supporting_passage: "We enrolled 7868 women between the ages of 60 and 90 years who had a bone mineral density T score of less than -2.5 but not less than -4.0 at the lumbar spine or total hip." ... "As compared with placebo, denosumab reduced the risk of new radiographic vertebral fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 2.3% in the denosumab group, versus 7.2% in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.32 ...)--a relative decrease of 68%. Denosumab reduced the risk of hip fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 0.7% in the denosumab group, versus 1.2% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.60 ...)--a relative decrease of 40%. Denosumab also reduced the risk of nonvertebral fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 6.5% in the denosumab group, versus 8.0% in the placebo group"
safe_wording: In the denosumab trial, a 68% cut in X-ray spinal fractures meant 7 in 100 falling to 2 in 100 over 3 years; the 40% cut in hip fractures meant about 12 in 1000 falling to 7 in 1000.
qualifications: Different drug and population from FIT; do not mix into one chart without labelling.

claim: Only about a quarter of new spinal fractures found on scheduled X-rays in FIT were diagnosed clinically at the time.
supporting_passage: "Of incident radiograpic vertebral deformities, 22.6% were also clinically diagnosed as incident vertebral fractures, with clinical diagnoses made for 28.4% of the deformities that exceeded 30% and 4 mm height loss (severe deformity) compared with 14.3% for deformities that involved > or = 20% and 4 mm but < 30% height loss (milder deformity)." ... "Approximately one-fourth of incident radiographic vertebral deformities were clinically diagnosed as new vertebral fractures"
safe_wording: In the same trial, only about 1 in 4 of the new spinal fractures seen on the scheduled X-rays had been diagnosed at the time (about 1 in 7 of the milder ones, closer to 3 in 10 of the severe ones).
qualifications: 'Not diagnosed' is not the same as 'not felt' (see C04-30-d).

claim: New spinal fractures that were not recognised clinically were still linked with more back pain and limitation of activity.
supporting_passage: "New vertebral fractures that did not come to medical attention were associated with increased back pain and functional limitation." Conclusion: "New vertebral fractures, even those not recognized clinically, are associated with substantial increases in back pain and functional limitation due to back pain in older white women."
safe_wording: Spinal fractures found only on X-ray are not harmless: in a large study of older women, new fractures that never reached a doctor were still linked with more back pain and more days of limited activity.
qualifications: Observational association; white women only. Use 'not diagnosed at the time', never 'never felt'.

claim: Women who had a new spinal fracture on X-ray had about a 1 in 5 chance of another within the next year.
supporting_passage: "Among the 381 participants who developed an incident vertebral fracture, the incidence of a new vertebral fracture in the subsequent year was 19.2% (95% CI, 13.6%-24.8%)." ... "Our data indicate that women who develop a vertebral fracture are at substantial risk for additional fracture within the next year."
safe_wording: X-ray-detected spinal fractures also signal risk: in trial placebo groups, about 1 in 5 women with a new one had another within a year.
qualifications: Placebo arms of risedronate trials (women on calcium); radiographically identified fractures.

claim: UK guidance says to take alendronic acid after an overnight fast, swallowed whole with a glass of plain water (about 200 mL) while sitting or standing, at least 30 minutes before the first food or drink (other than water), other medicines or supplements including calcium, and not to lie down for 30 minutes afterwards.
supporting_passage: "Alendronate should be taken after an overnight fast and at least 30 min before the first food or drink (other than water) of the day or any other oral medicinal products or supplementation (including calcium). Tablets should be swallowed whole with a glass of plain water (~ 200 ml) whilst the patient is sitting or standing in an upright position. Patients should not lie down for 30 min after taking the tablet."
location: NOGG full text, 'Specific drug options: Anti-resorptive drugs: bisphosphonates' (alendronate)
safe_wording: Take the weekly tablet first thing, before breakfast, with a full glass of plain water (about 200 mL), sitting or standing. Then wait at least 30 minutes before any food, any drink other than water, or any other tablets, including calcium. Do not lie down for those 30 minutes.
qualifications: Instructions are the same for the daily and weekly forms; effervescent or soluble forms are dissolved in at least 120 mL of plain water. Say 'plain water' (not tea, coffee, juice); 'tap water', 'mineral water' and 'not at bedtime' were not verified from an opened source.

claim: Even when taken correctly, less than 1 in 100 of the alendronate dose is absorbed (0.76% in women, 0.59% in men, fasting with water and food 2 hours later).
supporting_passage: "In women, oral bioavailability of alendronate was independent of dose (5 to 80 mg) and averaged (90% confidence interval) 0.76% (0.58, 0.98) when taken with water in the fasting state, followed by a meal 2 hours later. Bioavailability was similar in men [0.59%, (0.43, 0.81)]."
safe_wording: Only a tiny fraction of each tablet is absorbed, less than 1 part in 100, even when it is taken with water on an empty stomach. That figure comes from absorption studies in volunteers.
qualifications: Measured with a 2-hour wait before breakfast, longer than the usual 30 minutes. It is an absorption measure, not a fracture outcome.

claim: In volunteer absorption studies, black coffee or orange juice taken with the tablet cut absorption by about 60%, and taking it with or up to 2 hours after breakfast cut absorption by more than 85%.
supporting_passage: "Taking alendronate either concurrently with or 2 hours after breakfast drastically (> 85%) impaired availability. Black coffee or orange juice alone, when taken with the drug, also reduced bioavailability (approximately 60%)."
safe_wording: In absorption studies in volunteers, taking the tablet with black coffee or orange juice instead of water cut the amount absorbed by about 60 per cent. Taking it with breakfast, or within 2 hours after breakfast, cut it by more than 85 per cent.
qualifications: Relative reductions of an already tiny absorbed amount; measured in volunteers, not in fracture trials. Say it is an absorption finding. Do not claim a specific loss of fracture protection.

claim: Waiting 30 or 60 minutes before breakfast gave about 40% less absorption than waiting 2 hours; the authors set at least 30 minutes as a practical minimum for long-term use.
supporting_passage: "Taking alendronate either 60 or 30 minutes before a standardized breakfast reduced bioavailability by 40% relative to the 2-hour wait." ... "A practical dosing recommendation, derived from these findings and reflective of the long-term nature of therapy for a disease such as osteoporosis, is that patients take the drug with water after an overnight fast and at least 30 minutes before any other food or beverage."
safe_wording: Thirty minutes is the minimum wait, set as a practical compromise; in the absorption studies, waiting 2 hours let more of the tablet be absorbed than waiting 30 minutes.
qualifications: Optional nuance; do not advise a 2-hour wait, since guidance says at least 30 minutes.

claim: Alendronate can irritate the gullet (oesophagus); reported cases were linked with taking it with little or no water, lying down during or after the dose, or carrying on after symptoms began.
supporting_passage: de Groen: "In patients for whom adequate information was available, esophagitis seemed to be associated with swallowing alendronate with little or no water, lying down during or after ingestion of the tablet, ... continuing to take alendronate after the onset of symptoms, and having preexisting esophageal disorders." ... "Recommendations to reduce the risk of esophagitis include swallowing alendronate with 180 to 240 ml (6 to 8 oz) of water on arising in the morning, remaining upright for at least 30 minutes after swallowing the tablet and until the first food of the day has been ingested, and discontinuing the drug promptly if esophageal symptoms develop." NOGG: "Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated in people with abnormalities of the oesophagus that delay oesophageal emptying such as stricture or achalasia, and inability to stand or sit upright for at least 30–60 min."
location: de Groen abstract (Results; Conclusions); NOGG full text, bisphosphonate contraindications
safe_wording: The full glass of water and staying upright help the tablet pass quickly into the stomach. Reports of gullet irritation from alendronic acid were mostly linked with taking it with little water or lying down afterwards. If swallowing becomes painful or you get new heartburn, stop taking it and ask your doctor or pharmacist.
qualifications: Case reports and spontaneous reports only; gives no rate. Do not state how common oesophagitis is. The 'stop if symptoms' advice comes from de Groen's recommendations ('discontinuing the drug promptly if esophageal symptoms develop'); 'painful swallowing' and 'new heartburn' are a plain-English gloss of 'esophageal symptoms', not quoted examples.

claim: If a weekly dose is missed, take one tablet on the morning after remembering, do not take two on the same day, then return to the usual day.
supporting_passage: Search-engine summary of the emc leaflet: "If you miss a dose, just take one tablet on the morning after you remember. Do not take two tablets on the same day. Return to taking one tablet once a week, as originally scheduled on your chosen day."
location: Search extract of patient information leaflet (page not opened)
safe_wording: Leave out, or say: 'If you miss a week, the leaflet in the box says what to do.'
qualifications: Search extract only; not enough for a stated instruction in the post.

claim: UK guidance says a fracture risk assessment (FRAX) should be done for any postmenopausal woman or man aged 50 or over who has a clinical risk factor for fracture; people found to be at low risk without a previous fracture are reassured and given lifestyle advice rather than drug treatment.
supporting_passage: "A FRAX assessment should be performed in any postmenopausal woman, or man age ≥ 50 years, with a clinical risk factor for fragility fracture, to guide BMD measurement and prompt timely referral and/or drug treatment, where indicated" ... "Men and women with, without a prior fragility fracture, can be reassured that their fracture risk is low and offered lifestyle advice as appropriate" ... "An initial FRAX assessment, which provides the ten-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture (MOF; clinical spine, hip, forearm or humerus) and/or hip fracture, can be used to identify patients at low, intermediate, high or very high risk of fracture"
location: NOGG full text, 'Fracture risk assessment and case finding' and 'Intervention thresholds and strategy' recommendations (the risk category after 'Men and women with' is missing from the PMC text extraction)
safe_wording: A decision that you do not need bone medicine yet is based on your risk factors at the time, which a doctor turns into a 10-year fracture risk. UK guidance says a new risk factor is a reason for that risk to be worked out.
qualifications: The 'decision for now' framing is a reasonable reading of the guideline, not a quotation. No opened source sets a routine recheck date for untreated people at low risk (searches of the NOGG text found set intervals only for people near the treatment threshold who are on steroids or cancer hormone treatment, and after pausing treatment). Do not claim anything about GP recall systems.

claim: A new broken bone after a minor fall or strain is a risk factor for further fractures: in pooled data from 11 cohorts, a previous fracture was linked with nearly twice the risk of another fracture, and UK guidance says the risk is highest just after the fracture, falls over the next 2 years, and stays above average after that.
supporting_passage: Kanis: "A previous fracture history was associated with a significantly increased risk of any fracture compared with individuals without a prior fracture (RR = 1.86; 95% CI = 1.75-1.98). The risk ratio was similar for the outcome of osteoporotic fracture or for hip fracture. There was no significant difference in risk ratio between men and women." NOGG: "Prior fragility fracture is a well-established risk factor for a future fracture. This risk of subsequent osteoporotic fracture is particularly acute immediately after an index fracture and wanes progressively over the next 2 years, but thereafter remains higher than that of the general population"
location: Kanis abstract; NOGG full text, 'Indications for specialist referral in those at very high-fracture risk'
safe_wording: A broken bone after a minor fall or bump is the clearest reason to have your fracture risk looked at again. People who have had one fracture have nearly twice the risk of another. The risk is highest soon after the fracture, eases over the next 2 years, and stays above average after that.
qualifications: Relative risk from observational cohorts (association). 'Nearly twice' is the plain reading of RR 1.86; do not convert to an absolute number. 'Fragility fracture' means a fracture from a fall from standing height or less.

claim: Steroid tablets taken for 3 months or more (any dose) count as a fracture risk factor; bone loss starts early after they begin, and UK guidance says some people should start bone protection at the same time as the steroids.
supporting_passage: "The input into FRAX includes, with age and sex, BMD independent clinical risk factors including the following: Body mass index (calculated from weight and height in kg/m), previous fragility fracture (including morphometric vertebral fracture), parental history of hip fracture, current glucocorticoid treatment (any dose, by mouth for 3 months or more), current smoking, alcohol intake 3 or more units daily, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary causes of osteoporosis" ... "Because bone loss and increased fracture risk occur early after initiation of oral glucocorticoids, bone-protective treatment should be started in the following people, at the same time as glucocorticoid therapy without waiting for bone density assessment, which should follow later" ... "Bone loss and increased fracture risk occur rapidly after initiation of oral glucocorticoid therapy and increase with the dose of glucocorticoids"
location: NOGG full text, 'Fracture risk assessment tools' (FRAX inputs) and 'Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis' recommendation 16 and text
safe_wording: Starting steroid tablets such as prednisolone that you are likely to take for 3 months or more. Bone loss begins soon after they start, so ask about your bones when they are started, not months later.
qualifications: The list of people who should start bone protection with the steroids is missing from the extracted text, so do not state who they are. Oral (tablet) steroids only; inhalers and joint injections are not covered by this wording.

claim: Losing 4 cm or more in height, or a new stoop (kyphosis), is a reason for spine imaging to look for spinal fractures and for fracture risk assessment.
supporting_passage: "Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) is indicated in postmenopausal women, and men age ≥ 50 years, if there is a history of ≥ 4 cm height loss, kyphosis, recent or current long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy, a BMD T-score ≤  − 2.5 at either the spine or hip, or in cases of acute onset back pain with risk factors for osteoporosis" ... "There are many clinical risk factors for fracture in addition to those included in FRAX which can be used to trigger fracture risk assessment (Table), including thoracic kyphosis and height loss (> 4 cm), either in comparison with recalled young adult height or a documented loss on serial measurements"
location: NOGG full text, 'Fracture risk assessment and case finding' recommendations; 'Screening and case finding'
safe_wording: Losing 4 cm (about an inch and a half) or more in height compared with your height as a young adult, or developing a stoop. UK guidance says this should prompt a check of the spine for fractures.
qualifications: The guideline uses '≥ 4 cm' in the recommendation and '> 4 cm' in the text; '4 cm or more' is safe. Height loss can be compared with remembered young adult height.

claim: Sudden new back pain, especially in the upper back, in someone with osteoporosis risk factors should raise the possibility of a spinal fracture.
supporting_passage: "Primary care clinicians should always have in mind the possibility of vertebral fracture in postmenopausal women and men age ≥ 50 years who present with acute onset back pain, especially thoracic pain if they have risk factors for osteoporosis" ... "Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) is indicated ... in cases of acute onset back pain with risk factors for osteoporosis"
location: NOGG full text, primary care and case-finding sections
safe_wording: Sudden new back pain, especially between the shoulder blades, if you have other risk factors for weak bones. It can be a broken bone in the spine.
qualifications: The guideline says 'acute onset back pain', not 'after a minor strain'; do not require a strain. Applies to people with osteoporosis risk factors.

claim: Repeated falls (two or more in the last year) raise fracture probability; UK guidance adjusts the FRAX result upward by 30% for recurrent falls, and most fractures other than spinal fractures follow a fall.
supporting_passage: "Arithmetic adjustments to FRAX probabilities of major osteoporotic fracture (MOF: clinical spine, hip, forearm or humerus) and hip fracture (Table) can be used in clinical practice, to take account of additional clinical risk factors, such as glucocorticoid use, discordantly low lumbar spine BMD, type II diabetes, and a history of falls" ... Table 1: "Falls history" "Increase MOF and hip fracture probability by 30% for a history of recurrent falls (≥ 2 falls in the last year)" ... "The majority of non-vertebral fractures are preceded by a fall."
location: NOGG full text, 'Fracture risk assessment and case finding' recommendations; Table 1; 'Falls interventions'
safe_wording: Falling twice or more in a year. Falls raise the chance of a broken bone, and UK guidance adds them to the fracture risk calculation.
qualifications: The trigger is recurrent falls (two or more in the last year), not a single fall. The 30% is a relative uplift of the calculated probability, not 30 extra fractures in 100; practitioner version only. A falls assessment is also appropriate, which is a separate point.

claim: In US registry and Medicare records of 50,613 men with prostate cancer, among men who survived at least 5 years, 19.4% of those given androgen deprivation therapy had a fracture compared with 12.6% of those not given it; the study is observational.
supporting_passage: "We studied the records of 50,613 men who were listed in the linked database of the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program and Medicare as having received a diagnosis of prostate cancer in the period from 1992 through 1997." ... "Of men surviving at least five years after diagnosis, 19.4 percent of those who received androgen-deprivation therapy had a fracture, as compared with 12.6 percent of those not receiving androgen-deprivation therapy (P<0.001). In the Cox proportional-hazards analyses, adjusted for characteristics of the patient and the tumor, there was a statistically significant relation between the number of doses of gonadotropin-releasing hormone received during the 12 months after diagnosis and the subsequent risk of fracture."
safe_wording: In US records of men with prostate cancer, among men who lived at least 5 years after diagnosis, about 19 in 100 who had hormone treatment had broken a bone, compared with about 13 in 100 who did not. The study was observational, so it shows a link; men who had more doses of treatment had more fractures.
qualifications: Crude percentages in the subgroup who survived at least 5 years; difference is about 7 percentage points. Say 'linked with', not 'causes', despite the paper's own wording. Treatments and bone care have changed since the 1990s.

claim: A 2021 meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies (519,168 men) found androgen deprivation therapy was linked with higher fracture risk (odds ratio 1.39), with moderate-certainty evidence.
supporting_passage: "Sixteen eligible studies were included, and total population was 519,168 men. ADT use is associated with increasing fracture risk (OR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.26-1.52) and fracture requiring hospitalization (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.29-1.88)." ... "The GRADE level of evidence was moderate for any fracture and low for fracture requiring hospitalization."
safe_wording: Across 16 studies of more than half a million men, hormone treatment for prostate cancer was consistently linked with more broken bones.
qualifications: Odds ratio from observational studies; do not turn it into 'X times more likely' or an absolute figure. Use for consistency, not for a number in public posts.

claim: UK guidance says bone loss from androgen deprivation therapy is rapid in the first 6 to 12 months, fracture risk is raised in the 5 years after starting, and aromatase inhibitors and androgen deprivation are among medicines known to increase hip fracture risk.
supporting_passage: "Osteoporosis caused by ADT is associated with rapid loss of BMD within 6–12 months of initiation of ADT []; (). There is a significant increase in fracture risk in men with prostate cancer in the 5 years following the initiation of ADT when compared to those not receiving ADT" ... "In addition to glucocorticoids, several medications are known to increase hip fracture risk including thyroid hormone excess, aromatase inhibitors for the treatment of breast cancer and androgen deprivation for the treatment of prostate cancer"
location: NOGG full text, 'Men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy'; 'Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis' section
safe_wording: Hormone treatment that lowers testosterone thins bone fastest in the first 6 to 12 months, which is why the start of treatment is the time to ask about bones.
qualifications: Guideline summary statement citing observational studies.

claim: Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) speed up bone loss (on average 1 to 3% a year in postmenopausal women) and are linked with more fractures; the excess risk is seen mainly during treatment.
supporting_passage: NOGG: "The use of aromatase inhibitors (AI) in postmenopausal women induces bone loss at an average rate of 1–3% per year at sites rich in trabecular bone." Hadji 2025: "AI, which are now more commonly prescribed due to improved anticancer efficacy, are associated with a higher fracture risk than tamoxifen due to their ability to almost completely suppress circulating and tissue estrogen levels, and are known to accelerate bone loss and increase fracture risk in this population beyond that seen with natural menopause" ... "A meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including 117,974 breast cancer patients found a significantly higher incidence of osteoporotic fractures, in AI users versus those not treated with AI (controls), particularly for vertebral fractures []. The relative risk (RR) for hip fractures and non-vertebral fractures was 1.18 (p < 0.001 in each case) versus controls, while the RR for vertebral fractures was 1.84 (p < 0.001)." Tseng: "Compared with the tamoxifen group, aromatase inhibitor-associated fracture risk increased by 33% (pooled RR 1.33; 95% CI 1.21-1.47) during the tamoxifen/aromatase inhibitor treatment period, but did not increase (pooled RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.72-1.37) during the post-tamoxifen/aromatase inhibitor treatment period."
location: NOGG full text, 'Women receiving aromatase inhibitor therapy'; Hadji 2025 full text section 3.1; Tseng abstract
safe_wording: Aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) work by removing almost all oestrogen, and they speed up bone loss. Women taking them lose on average 1 to 3 per cent of bone density a year and have more fractures than women not taking them.
qualifications: Relative risks quoted by Hadji 2025 come from a meta-analysis not opened here; keep them out of public posts. Tseng is limited to women aged 65 and under. Longer (extended) AI treatment adds to the risk (Hadji 2025).

claim: Tamoxifen, the other common hormone tablet for breast cancer, has not been found to harm bone or raise fracture risk in postmenopausal women.
supporting_passage: Hadji 2025: "In contrast to the case in premenopausal women, tamoxifen has not been found to have a negative impact on BMD or fracture risk in postmenopausal women []. Indeed, results of a systematic review and meta-analysis suggest it may potentially preserve bone mass in postmenopausal women" Tseng: "Similar fracture risk was observed in women treated and not treated with tamoxifen [pooled risk ratio (RR) 0.95; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84-1.07]."
location: Hadji 2025 full text section 3.1; Tseng abstract
safe_wording: The bone warning applies to aromatase inhibitors; tamoxifen has not been found to thin bone after the menopause.
qualifications: Tamoxifen can reduce bone density in premenopausal women; keep the statement to women after the menopause.

claim: UK guidance says all women starting an aromatase inhibitor should have their fracture risk assessed (FRAX, counting the AI as a cause of osteoporosis, with a bone density scan where practical), and international position statements say every woman starting or on an AI should be told of the risk and have it assessed.
supporting_passage: NOGG recommendation 24: "All women starting aromatase inhibitor (AI) therapy should have their fracture risk assessed using FRAX, considering AI use as a secondary cause of osteoporosis, including BMD measurement where practical" Hadji 2017: "In all patients initiating AI treatment, fracture risk should be assessed and recommendation with regard to exercise and calcium/vitamin D supplementation given." Hadji 2025: "All women receiving AI treatment should be informed of this significantly increased risk and its consequences and have their individual fracture risk evaluated to determine an appropriate management strategy."
location: NOGG full text, recommendation 24; Hadji 2017 abstract (Conclusions); Hadji 2025 full text, Conclusions
safe_wording: UK guidance says every woman starting an aromatase inhibitor should have her fracture risk checked, with a bone density scan where practical. If you are starting one and nobody has mentioned your bones, ask.
qualifications: NOGG also advises a repeat assessment after 12 to 24 months for women near the treatment threshold or starting other treatments such as steroids.

claim: UK consensus guidance, supported by NOGG, says all men starting or continuing long-term androgen deprivation therapy should get bone health advice and have fracture risk calculated with FRAX (with a bone density scan where feasible), repeated after 12 to 18 months if near the treatment threshold.
supporting_passage: Brown 2020: "All men starting or continuing long-term ADT should receive lifestyle advice regarding bone health. Calcium/vitamin D supplementation should be offered if required. Fracture risk should be calculated (using the FRAX® tool), with BMD assessment included where feasible." ... "Those near to, but below an intervention threshold, and patients going on to additional systemic therapies (particularly those requiring glucocorticoids), should have FRAX® (including BMD) repeated after 12-18 months." NOGG: "The NOGG supports the recent guideline published by Brown et al. 2020" ... "A recent UK consensus statement on prostate cancer treatment-induced bone loss concluded that fracture risk should be calculated using FRAX, considering ADT use as a secondary cause of osteoporosis, and including BMD where available and practical."
location: Brown 2020 abstract (Results/recommendations); NOGG full text, 'Men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy'
safe_wording: UK bone and cancer specialists advise that every man starting long-term hormone treatment for prostate cancer should have his fracture risk worked out, with a bone scan where possible. Ask for this when treatment starts.
qualifications: Consensus guidance endorsed by the UK osteoporosis guideline; applies to long-term ADT.

claim: UK expert guidance in 2020 judged that fracture risk from prostate cancer treatment was not well managed and that prostate cancer guidelines lacked specific bone health recommendations.
supporting_passage: "In this context, careful consideration of skeletal health is required to reduce the risk of treatment-related fragility fractures and their associated morbidity and mortality. This risk is currently not well-managed." ... "Current PC guidelines lack specific recommendations for optimising bone health."
safe_wording: UK specialists writing in 2020 said bone health was often not well managed in men on hormone treatment for prostate cancer.
qualifications: Expert judgement from 2020, not an audit figure; do not state how often assessment is missed today.

claim: If fracture risk is high, treatment helps: bisphosphonates and denosumab prevent bone loss in men on androgen deprivation therapy (fracture reduction shown for denosumab in one trial, not clearly for bisphosphonates), and in women on aromatase inhibitors denosumab and risedronate have been shown to reduce fracture risk.
supporting_passage: NOGG: "Bisphosphonates and denosumab are effective drug treatments for preventing BMD loss in men with prostate cancer taking ADT, although effects on fracture risk have not been demonstrated." ... "Denosumab and zoledronate both lead to significant gains in BMD at the spine and hip in postmenopausal women with breast cancer receiving AI, and both denosumab and risedronate have been shown to reduce fracture risk" Bassatne 2026: "Oral bisphosphonates had no effect on fracture incidence at 12-months (RR = 0.57; 95%CI[0.10, 3.23]; very low certainty). Intravenous bisphosphonates had no effect on the risk of morphometric vertebral fractures at 36-months (RR = 1.06; 95%CI[0.57,1.98]; very low certainty). One trial showed that denosumab probably results in a large reduction in new morphometric vertebral fracture risk at 12 (RR = 0.15), 24 (RR = 0.31) and 36-months (RR = 0.38; 95%CI[0.19-0.78]). Treatment with bisphosphonates or denosumab for 12-months increased BMD at the hip (+1.5 to +3.9%) and lumbar spine (+4.0 to +6.8%)"
location: NOGG full text, ADT and AI sections; Bassatne abstract (Results)
safe_wording: If the check shows a high risk, bone medicines can stop the thinning. In women on aromatase inhibitors, some have been shown to prevent fractures; in men on hormone treatment for prostate cancer, the fracture evidence is thinner but the bone loss can be prevented.
qualifications: For ADT, bisphosphonate 'no effect' results are very low certainty (evidence gap, not proof of no benefit); denosumab fracture evidence rests on one trial of spinal fractures seen on X-ray.

claim: NICE early breast cancer guidance recommends a baseline bone density (DXA) scan when aromatase inhibitor treatment starts (as reported by NOGG 2022).
supporting_passage: "NICE guidance on the management of early breast cancer, which recognises the excess risk of osteoporosis with the use of AIs, recommends a baseline DXA scan to assess BMD at the time of initiation of AI therapy"
location: NOGG full text, 'Women receiving aromatase inhibitor therapy'
safe_wording: Optional: 'NICE breast cancer guidance also recommends a bone density scan when these tablets start.' Cite NOGG as the source, not the NICE page.
qualifications: Second-hand report from 2022; the NICE NG101 page itself was not opened and may have been updated. Exact NICE wording (for example 'offer' and which women) not verified.

claim: NICE prostate cancer guidance (NG131) includes a recommendation on fracture risk or bone density assessment for men on androgen deprivation therapy.
location: Not found: the NICE NG131 page could not be opened and no opened source reports its wording.
safe_wording: Leave out. Use the UK consensus guidance supported by NOGG (C04-22-g) instead.
qualifications: Do not cite NICE NG131 wording.

claim: CFS version 2.0 defines level 7 (living with severe frailty) as completely dependent for personal care from whatever cause, physical or cognitive.
supporting_passage: Figure 1 (CFS version 2.0): "7 | LIVING WITH SEVERE FRAILTY Completely dependent for personal care, from whatever cause (physical or cognitive). Even so, they seem stable and not at high risk of dying (within ~6 months)."
location: Figure 1 (CFS version 2.0), page 2 of the PDF; transcribed via Undermind read_pdfs
safe_wording: On the Clinical Frailty Scale, level 7 means a person is completely dependent on others for personal care, whether the cause is physical or cognitive.
qualifications: Paraphrase the scale in plain words; the scale is copyright (all rights reserved), so do not reproduce the full level text or pictograms on a visual without permission.

claim: CFS scoring guidance says that in people with dementia the degree of frailty generally corresponds to the degree of dementia; in moderate dementia people can do personal care with prompting.
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "SCORING FRAILTY IN PEOPLE WITH DEMENTIA The degree of frailty generally corresponds to the degree of dementia. Common symptoms in mild dementia include forgetting the details of a recent event, though still remembering the event itself, repeating the same question/story and social withdrawal. In moderate dementia, recent memory is very impaired, even though they seemingly can remember their past life events well. They can do personal care with prompting. In severe dementia, they cannot do personal care without help. In very severe dementia they are often bedfast. Many are virtually mute." Body text: "The degree of dementia generally corresponds to the degree of frailty."
location: Figure 1 (dementia scoring box); body text section 'Scoring the Clinical Frailty Scale in People with Cognitive Impairment'
safe_wording: The scale's own guidance says that for people with dementia the frailty level generally matches the stage of dementia: mild dementia goes with mild frailty (level 5), moderate dementia with moderate frailty (level 6), severe dementia with severe frailty (level 7).
qualifications: The guidance says 'generally', so it is a scoring guide, not a fixed rule. The mild-to-5, moderate-to-6, severe-to-7 pairing is stated in the body text (mild dementia 'would go with mild frailty'; moderate dementia 'as with moderate frailty'; severe 'as in severe frailty').

claim: CFS 6 (living with moderate frailty) describes needing help with all outside activities and keeping house, often problems with stairs, help with bathing, and possibly minimal help (cuing, standby) with dressing.
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "6 | LIVING WITH MODERATE FRAILTY People who need help with all outside activities and with keeping house. Inside, they often have problems with stairs and need help with bathing and might need minimal assistance (cuing, standby) with dressing."
safe_wording: Level 6 on the scale describes someone who needs help with all activities outside the home and with housework, often has trouble with stairs, needs help to bathe, and may need prompting or someone standing by while dressing.
qualifications: Paraphrase; copyright applies to the scale text.

claim: The same CFS level can be reached by a cognitive route or a physical route: the developers state that the level-6 pattern applies both to moderate dementia and to cognitively intact people whose physical disability means they need someone nearby.
supporting_passage: "With [Level 6 - Living with Moderate Frailty] (previously 'Moderately Frail'), dependence now extends past instrumental ADLs to intermediate ones, notably including dependence in bathing. Often at this level minimal assistance with personal care might be needed. Moderate dementia is the case when people who are dependent in their performance of instrumental ADLs can still do their basic or personal ADLs with prompting. This can also be the case in people who are cognitively intact, but whose disability obliges them to have someone nearby (so-called 'standby assistance' or 'set-up')." Also for level 7: "Still, people living with severe frailty can be mobile."
location: Body text, section 'Using the Clinical Frailty Scale to Grade Clinically Meaningfully Increased Risk' (level name stripped from PMC text; restored in brackets from Figure 1)
safe_wording: The scale's developers say the same level can describe two different people: someone with moderate dementia who can wash and dress only with prompting, and someone whose thinking is fine but whose physical disability means they need a person standing by. The number alone does not tell you which.
qualifications: The two-person comparison in the post must be labelled 'Illustrative example'. 'Walks well' for the dementia example is consistent with the guidance (people with severe frailty 'can be mobile'), but the scale does not say mobility is normal in moderate dementia; keep it as an illustration.

claim: The CFS is a judgement-based summary that requires clinical judgement; prognosis needs both baseline frailty and the severity of the acute illness; the score is no substitute for a patient-centred care plan.
supporting_passage: "It is not a questionnaire. Grading the degree of frailty requires clinical judgement that is based in part on screening criteria..." ... "Still, as discussed below, their prognosis requires information about both their baseline degree of frailty, and the severity of their acute illness." ... "In geriatric medicine, the goal of grading the degree of frailty is both to ease communication through a shared language, and also as the foundation for a care plan. The care plan needs to address the gap between the current level of function, cognition, mobility, and social relationships (especially with the primary carer) and how those have changed with the acute illness (when present)." ... "It should not be confused with the more instrumental purpose to which the Clinical Frailty Scale is now being put, which is no substitute for a patient-centred care plan."
location: Body text: 'What is the Clinical Frailty Scale?'; 'Summary'
safe_wording: The developers describe the score as a clinical judgement that summarises function, cognition and mobility; they say predicting outcome also needs the severity of the current illness, and that the score is the start of a care plan, not a substitute for one.
qualifications: This is developer guidance, not a trial result.

claim: In routine practice, both dementia and mobility independently relate to the CFS score given.
supporting_passage: "The CFS was scored on 658 (89%) (median 4, range 1-8; mean age 81 years, 61% women). Independent predictors of higher CFS were older age (p<0.001), history of dementia (p<0.001), mobility (p≤0.007), disability (p<0.001), and higher acuity of illness (p=0.009). Disability and mobility were the main classifiers in the CRT."
safe_wording: In one Dublin emergency department, higher CFS scores were linked with a history of dementia and, separately, with poorer mobility and more disability.
qualifications: One service, association only; the study did not look at what happened afterwards to people who reached the same score by different routes. Optional supporting point, not needed for the post.

claim: Position: record what drove the CFS score (physical, cognitive or both) beside the number, and do not use the number alone to judge how someone will tolerate surgery, rehabilitation or exercise.
supporting_passage: See C05-16-d and C05-16-e: "This can also be the case in people who are cognitively intact, but whose disability obliges them to have someone nearby"; "requires clinical judgement"; "no substitute for a patient-centred care plan".
safe_wording: Mark this as a practice suggestion: 'Write the reason next to the number', for example 'CFS 6 (moderate dementia; walks independently)'. It follows from how the scale is built; it is not a published recommendation and no outcome study of this habit was found.
qualifications: Present as clinical judgement ('We should write...'), not as evidence that outcomes differ by route. Do not claim that people with a cognitive route to CFS 6 do better or worse after surgery or rehabilitation: no study comparing outcomes by route was found in this batch's searches (searching was limited).

claim: CFS version 2.0 has 9 levels: very fit, fit, managing well, living with very mild frailty, living with mild frailty, living with moderate frailty, living with severe frailty, living with very severe frailty, terminally ill.
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "1 | VERY FIT ... 2 | FIT ... 3 | MANAGING WELL ... 4 | LIVING WITH VERY MILD FRAILTY ... 5 | LIVING WITH MILD FRAILTY ... 6 | LIVING WITH MODERATE FRAILTY ... 7 | LIVING WITH SEVERE FRAILTY ... 8 | LIVING WITH VERY SEVERE FRAILTY ... 9 | TERMINALLY ILL". Abstract: "It also introduces an updated version (CFS version 2.0), with revised level names (e.g., 'vulnerable' becomes 'living with very mild frailty') and minor edits to level descriptions."
safe_wording: The Clinical Frailty Scale has 9 levels, from 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Levels 4 to 8 are called living with very mild, mild, moderate, severe and very severe frailty.
qualifications: Older letters may use the earlier names (for example 'vulnerable' for level 4, 'moderately frail' for level 6). Copyright applies to the scale; paraphrase on visuals.

claim: Levels 5 to 8 describe increasing need for help from others; level 4 (living with very mild frailty) means symptoms limit activities but the person does not depend on others for daily help (editor's guidance).
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "4 | LIVING WITH VERY MILD FRAILTY Previously 'vulnerable,' this category marks early transition from complete independence. While not dependent on others for daily help, often symptoms limit activities. A common complaint is being 'slowed up' and/or being tired during the day. 5 | LIVING WITH MILD FRAILTY People who often have more evident slowing, and need help with high order instrumental activities of daily living (finances, transportation, heavy housework)... 6 | ... People who need help with all outside activities and with keeping house... 7 | ... Completely dependent for personal care, from whatever cause (physical or cognitive)... 8 | LIVING WITH VERY SEVERE FRAILTY Completely dependent for personal care and approaching end of life. Typically, they could not recover even from a minor illness." Body text: "Levels 5 to 7 relate to changes in function."
safe_wording: Levels 5 to 8 describe increasing need for help: at 5, help with things like money, transport and heavy housework; at 6, help with everything outside the home, housework and bathing; at 7, complete dependence for personal care; at 8, complete dependence and approaching the end of life. Level 4 (very mild frailty) means symptoms slow a person down, but they do not need help from others day to day.
qualifications: Levels 7 and 8 both mean complete dependence for personal care; 8 differs mainly in being near the end of life and unlikely to recover even from a minor illness. Do not say 'levels 4 to 8 describe increasing need for help' (level 4 needs no daily help).

claim: The CFS is meant to describe the person's usual (baseline) state, for example how they were about two weeks before an acute illness, not how they seem while ill.
supporting_passage: "The key to scoring the Clinical Frailty Scale is to determine the person's baseline health state. This is especially needed in clinical settings where health can change quickly. For example, many older patients in the Emergency Department who were fit two weeks ago (their baseline state), may appear to be frail while ill; a prospect that becomes more likely the longer they wait there." ... "We then ask about four features: how the person moved, functioned, thought, and felt about their health over the last two weeks." Abstract: "the Clinical Frailty Scale assays the baseline state".
location: Body text, 'What is the Clinical Frailty Scale?'; Abstract
safe_wording: The score is meant to describe how you usually are, not how you seem while ill. The scale's developers give the example of how someone was two weeks before coming into hospital.
qualifications: In this paper 'two weeks' appears as an example of the baseline, not a strict rule; say 'about two weeks before the illness' or 'your usual self before this illness'.

claim: Level 9 (terminally ill) applies to people with a life expectancy under about 6 months who are not otherwise living with severe frailty, and is the one level scored on the current rather than baseline state.
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "9 | TERMINALLY ILL Approaching the end of life. This category applies to people with a life expectancy <6 months, who are not otherwise living with severe frailty. (Many terminally ill people can still exercise until very close to death.)" Body text: "[Level 9] is notable for being the only level in which the current state trumps the baseline state, in that the terminally ill person might have been operating at any frailty level at baseline." ... "Even so, if a terminally ill person was completely dependent for personal care at baseline, they would be scored as Level 8."
location: Figure 1; body text, 'Using the Clinical Frailty Scale in People Towards the End of Life'
safe_wording: Level 9 is used for people expected to live less than about 6 months who are not otherwise severely frail; many are still active. It is the one level based on the current illness rather than the usual state.
qualifications: None beyond paraphrase.

claim: What the score is used for and its limits: prognosis and setting care goals (and, during COVID-19, triage for scarce resources); it requires clinical judgement; it is not widely validated in younger people or people with stable single-system disabilities.
supporting_passage: "In ordinary time (i.e., with no pandemic), the Clinical Frailty Scale is used both in prognosis and to set care goals." Abstract: "The key points discussed are that the Clinical Frailty Scale assays the baseline state, it is not widely validated in younger people or those with stable single-system disabilities, and it requires clinical judgement. The Clinical Frailty Scale is now commonly used as a triage tool to make important clinical decisions such as allocating scarce health care resources for COVID-19 management". Body text: "In geriatric medicine, the goal of grading the degree of frailty is both to ease communication through a shared language, and also as the foundation for a care plan."
safe_wording: Doctors use the score to help judge how someone may cope with illness and treatment and to plan care. It depends on a clinician's judgement, so you can ask what it was based on. It was designed for older people and is not well tested in younger people or in people with a long-standing single disability.
qualifications: Do not imply that the score alone decides treatment; describe it as one input.

claim: The CFS is copyright (Rockwood, 2005 to 2020; all rights reserved; permission via geriatricmedicineresearch.ca).
supporting_passage: Figure 1: "Clinical Frailty Scale ©2005–2020 Rockwood. Version 2.0 (EN). All rights reserved. For permission: www.geriatricmedicineresearch.ca"
safe_wording: (For the visual, not the caption.) Describe the 9 levels in your own plain words as a simple drawn ladder; do not copy the official pictograms or full level text.
qualifications: Short level names in plain words are a description, not a reproduction; seek permission before reproducing the scale itself.

claim: In pooled community studies (average follow-up about 4 years), about 14 in 100 older people became less frail, about 29 in 100 became more frail and about 57 in 100 stayed the same.
supporting_passage: "Among 42,775 community-dwelling older people from 16 studies with a mean follow-up of 3.9 years (range: 1-10 years), 13.7% (95%CI = 11.7-15.8%) improved, 29.1% (95%CI = 25.9-32.5%) worsened and 56.5% (95%CI = 54.2-58.8%) maintained the same frailty status."
safe_wording: In 16 studies of 42,775 older people living at home, followed for about 4 years on average, about 14 in 100 became less frail. About twice as many, 29 in 100, became more frail, and 57 in 100 stayed the same.
qualifications: Worsening must appear next to improvement, in the first two lines. Figures use one definition (the frailty phenotype) and people living at home; follow-up ranged from 1 to 10 years. Describe as 'of people reassessed' (handling of deaths not stated in the abstract).

claim: Improvement to meeting no frailty criteria was much more common among prefrail people (about 23 in 100) than frail people (about 3 in 100); among frail people, about 40 in 100 moved to prefrail and about 55 in 100 stayed frail.
supporting_passage: "Among those who were prefrail at baseline, corresponding rates to robust, prefrail and frail were 23.1% (95%CI = 18.8-27.6%), 58.2% (95%CI = 55.6-60.7%) and 18.2% (95%CI = 14.9-21.7%), respectively. Among those who were frail at baseline, pooled rates of transitioning to robust, prefrail and remaining frail were 3.3% (95%CI = 1.6-5.5%), 40.3% (95%CI = 34.6-46.1%) and 54.5% (95%CI = 47.6-61.3%), respectively." ... "Given that while one quarter of prefrail older people improved to robust only 3% of frail older people did, early interventions should be considered."
safe_wording: Among people in the early stage (prefrail), about 23 in 100 later met none of the frailty criteria, while about 18 in 100 became frail. Among people who were frail, only about 3 in 100 later met none of the criteria, but about 40 in 100 moved to the milder, prefrail stage; about 55 in 100 stayed frail.
qualifications: 'Robust' is the paper's term for meeting none of the 5 phenotype criteria. Most improvement among frail people was to prefrail, not to 'not frail at all'. Pooled percentages within a group need not add to exactly 100 because each was pooled separately.

claim: In a US cohort assessed every 18 months, moving from frail to not frail was very rare (0% to 0.9%), and moves to greater frailty were more common than moves to lesser frailty.
supporting_passage: "Of the 754 participants, 434 (57.6%) had at least 1 transition between any 2 of the 3 frailty states during 54 months." ... "During the 18-month intervals, transitions to states of greater frailty were more common (rates up to 43.3%) than transitions to states of lesser frailty (rates up to 23.0%), and the probability of transitioning from being frail to nonfrail was very low (rates, 0%-0.9%), even during an extended period."
safe_wording: A US study of 754 people aged 70 and over found that more than half moved between frailty stages over 4.5 years, but going straight from frail to not frail at all was very rare (under 1 in 100 per 18 months).
qualifications: Single US cohort from the 1990s to 2000s. Consistent with the pooled review: improvement is real but mostly by one step.

claim: International guidelines recommend a physical activity programme with a resistance (strength) training component as first-line management of frailty (strong recommendation), with protein or calorie supplements when weight loss or undernutrition is present (conditional recommendation).
supporting_passage: "First-line therapy for the management of frailty should include a multi-component physical activity programme with a resistance-based training component (strong recommendation). Protein/caloric supplementation is recommended when weight loss or undernutrition are present (conditional recommendation)." Also: "For individuals screened as positive for frailty, a more comprehensive clinical assessment should be performed to identify signs and underlying mechanisms of frailty (strong recommendation)."
location: Abstract, Recommendations for Management; Recommendations for Screening and Assessment
safe_wording: International frailty guidelines recommend, as the first step, an exercise programme that includes strength training. They recommend protein or calorie supplements when someone is losing weight or undernourished. They also recommend a fuller assessment for anyone found to be frail.
qualifications: Replace the candidate's 'strength exercise combined with enough protein has the most consistent evidence' with this guideline wording. Protein supplements are recommended conditionally and for people losing weight or undernourished, not for everyone.

claim: A systematic review of 46 primary care studies ranked strength training combined with protein supplementation highest for relative effectiveness and ease of implementation.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "A total of 925 studies satisfied search criteria and 46 were included. There were 15 690 participants (median study size was 160 participants). Studies reflected a broad heterogeneity." ... "Interventions with both muscle strength training and protein supplementation were consistently placed highest for effectiveness and ease of implementation." Full text (Scite excerpt): "Of the 46 studies, 30% (n = 14) reported the outcome of an intervention on frailty status, 71% (n = 10) of which demonstrated significant improvement."
safe_wording: A review of 46 studies in general practice ranked strength training combined with protein supplements as the most effective of the approaches studied and among the easiest to deliver. The studies were varied and the ranking was a comparison, not a pooled measure of effect.
qualifications: Only 14 of the 46 studies measured change in frailty status. Do not say 'most consistent evidence' or 'enough protein'; the studies tested protein supplements, and the ranking is relative.

claim: In a Singapore RCT of prefrail and frail adults (mean age 70), 6-month physical, nutritional, cognitive and combined interventions each reduced frailty more than usual care, though frailty also fell in 15% of controls.
supporting_passage: "The participants' mean age was 70.0 years, and 61.4% (n = 151) were female. Five different 6-month interventions included nutritional supplementation (n = 49), cognitive training (n = 50), physical training (n = 48), combination treatment (n = 49), and usual care control (n = 50)." ... "Frailty score and status over 12 months were reduced in all groups, including control (15%), but were significantly higher (35.6% to 47.8%) in the nutritional (odds ratio [OR] 2.98), cognition (OR 2.89), and physical (OR 4.05) and combination (OR 5.00) intervention groups."
safe_wording: In a Singapore trial of 246 people (average age 70) who were prefrail or frail, about 36 to 48 in 100 of those given 6 months of exercise, nutrition, memory training or all three became less frail over a year, compared with about 15 in 100 of those given usual care.
qualifications: Small arms (about 50 each), mostly prefrail and relatively young; improvement happened in controls too. Optional supporting point; the guideline (C05-07-d) and Kojima are enough for the post.

claim: Pooled prevalence of frailty in community-dwelling people aged 65 and over was 10.7% (21 studies, 61,500 participants), 9.9% with physical definitions and 13.6% with broad definitions.
supporting_passage: "Reported prevalence in the community varies enormously (range 4.0-59.1%). The overall weighted prevalence of frailty was 10.7% (95% confidence interval (CI) = 10.5-10.9; 21 studies; 61,500 participants). The weighted prevalence was 9.9% for physical frailty (95% CI = 9.6-10.2; 15 studies; 44,894 participants) and 13.6% for the broad phenotype of frailty (95% CI = 13.2-14.0; 8 studies; 24,072 participants)"
safe_wording: Across 21 studies of 61,500 people aged 65 and over living at home, about 1 in 10 met criteria for frailty.
qualifications: 2012 review; figures depend on definition.

claim: Prevalence rose with age to about a quarter of people aged 85 and over, so most people aged 85 and over living at home are not frail.
supporting_passage: Collard abstract only: "Prevalence increased with age (χ(2) = 6067, df = 1, P < .001)" (no age-band values in the abstract; full text not accessible). Gale 2015 Results: "The overall weighted prevalence of frailty was 14% (12% in men, 16% in women). Prevalence rose exponentially with increasing age, increasing from 6.5% in those aged 60–69 years to 65% in those aged 90 or over (Figure 1)."
location: Collard: Abstract. Gale: Results and Figure 1 (via Undermind read_pdfs).
safe_wording: None for the headline. The age-band figure (about 1 in 4 at 85+) could not be checked, and in England's national ageing study about 65 in 100 people aged 90 and over met frailty criteria, so 'most people over 85 living at home are not frail' is not safe.
qualifications: If any age statement is used elsewhere, the only verified one is Gale 2015: 6.5% at 60 to 69 rising to 65% at 90+ (Fried criteria; only 64 people aged 90+).

claim: Prevalence was higher in women than men (Collard: 9.6% vs 5.2%).
supporting_passage: Collard: "Prevalence increased with age (χ(2) = 6067, df = 1, P < .001) and was higher in women (9.6%, 95% CI = 9.2-10.0%) than in men (5.2%, 95% CI = 4.9-5.5%; χ(2) = 298.9 df = 1, P < .001)." Gale: "Frailty occurred more frequently in women than in men (16 versus 12%)."
safe_wording: Frailty was more common in women than in men.
qualifications: Collard's sex-specific figures are both lower than its overall 10.7% (different subset of studies), so do not quote them next to the overall figure.

claim: Reported community prevalence varied from 4.0% to 59.1% depending on definition.
supporting_passage: "Reported prevalence in the community varies enormously (range 4.0-59.1%)." ... "Frailty is common in later life, but different operationalization of frailty status results in widely differing prevalence between studies."
safe_wording: Studies of older people living at home have reported frailty in anywhere from 4 in 100 to 59 in 100, partly because they defined frailty differently and partly because they studied different people.
qualifications: Do not attribute the range to definition alone (judge's note). Give the range in only one post (C05-04 carries it).

claim: When 35 published frailty scores were applied to the same 5,377 people aged 60+ in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, they often disagreed about which individuals were frail (Cohen's kappa 0.10 to 0.83; only about 1 in 9 pairs reached kappa 0.6 or more).
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Data from 5,377 participants (ages ≥60 years) were analyzed (44.7% men, 55.3% women). FS showed widely differing degrees of agreement with the mean of all scores and between each pair of scores. Frailty classification also showed a very wide range of agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.10-0.83)." Results: "κ values ranged from 0.10 to 0.83 and were ≥0.80 for 0.8% of pairs, ≥0.60 and <0.80 for 10.4% of pairs, ≥0.40 and <0.60 for 35.3% of pairs, ≥0.20 and <0.40 for 45.9% of pairs, and <0.20 for 7.6% of pairs". Discussion: "Out of 595 pairs of scores, almost 90% had a κ value under 0.6." ... "We found that in some cases agreement was as low as 0.1 (10%), which, with a prevalence of 0.2, means that approximately 30% of individuals would be classified differently. The highest agreement (0.83 or 83%) translates to about 6% of individuals being classified differently, at the predefined prevalence of 0.2."
location: Abstract; Results; Discussion (full text via Undermind read_pdfs)
safe_wording: Researchers applied 35 published frailty tools to the same 5,377 people aged 60 and over in England. The tools often disagreed about who was frail. For almost 9 in 10 pairs of tools, agreement was only weak to moderate; in the worst pairs, about 3 in 10 people would be labelled differently by the two tools.
