"A total of 460 MRH events (74%) were attributable to medicines prescribed at hospital discharge"
location: Full text, Methods (severity); Results (Severity; Health service utilization)
safe_wording: About 29 in 100 of everyone followed up needed NHS care because of harm from a medicine within 8 weeks, mostly a GP visit. About 8 in 100 were readmitted to hospital because of it. Three quarters of the harm came from medicines prescribed at discharge.
qualifications: 29 in 100 (328 of 1116) and 8 in 100 (87 of 1116) are calculated here from the reported counts; the paper reports 328 as 79% of those with harm. 'Serious' is the study's own grade (needs a change of treatment or treatment by a health professional), not necessarily dangerous.

claim: Discharging doctors' predictions of which patients would have medication-related harm needing healthcare in the next 8 weeks showed no relationship with who actually did.
supporting_passage: "Doctors discharging patients (aged ≥65 years) from medical wards predicted the likelihood of their patient experiencing MRH requiring healthcare (hospital readmission or community healthcare) in the initial 8‐week period post‐discharge. Patients were followed up by senior pharmacists to determine MRH occurrence." "Data of 1066 patients (83%) with completed predictions and follow‐up, out of 1280 recruited patients, were analysed." "There was no relationship between doctors' predictions and patient MRH (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.82–1.46,= 0.53), irrespective of years of clinical experience." "Clinical judgement of doctors is not a reliable tool to predict MRH in older adults post‐discharge." Full-text excerpt: "Doctors correctly predicted the outcome (MRH or no MRH) in 469 out of 1066 patients (44%)."
location: Abstract (Methods, Results, Conclusions); full-text Results excerpt via Scite
safe_wording: When doctors discharging older patients were asked who would be harmed by their medicines in the next 8 weeks, their predictions showed no link with who actually was.
qualifications: An observational study of mostly junior doctors' single-question predictions; say 'showed no clear link', not 'worse than chance'. Do not use the 44% accuracy figure without explaining how predictions were dichotomised (not available here).

claim: Most predictions (85%) were made by doctors with less than 5 years' experience; predictive ability did not differ significantly by experience, but only 126 predictions (11.8%) were by registrars or consultants.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Most predictions (85%) were made by junior doctors with less than 5 years' clinical experience." Full-text excerpts: "Over half of MRH predictions (n = 595, 55.8%) were by doctors with less than one full year of clinical experience post-medical qualification, i.e. foundation year one, 306 (28.7%) predictions by doctors with years clinical experience, i.e. senior house officer level, and 126 (11.8%) predictions by senior doctors of five or more year's clinical experience, i.e. registrar or consultant grade." "We found no significant difference in predictive ability between doctors with varying years of clinical experience (<1 year, 1-4 year, >4 years) (Table 2)."
location: Abstract; full-text Results excerpts via Scite
safe_wording: Most of the predictions were made by doctors in their first few years after qualifying, who usually write the discharge. The study found no clear difference by experience, but few predictions came from senior doctors.
qualifications: The candidate's 'whatever their experience' is weakly supported (judge's concern confirmed): with 126 senior predictions the study could miss a difference. Prefer 'mostly junior doctors, who write most discharges'.

claim: Doctors' predictions were more likely to be accurate when they reported higher confidence, especially for harm leading to readmission.
supporting_passage: "Doctors' predictions were more likely to be accurate when they reported higher confidence in their prediction, especially in predicting MRH‐associated hospital readmissions (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.42–1.76,< 0.001)."
safe_wording: Doctors did better when they felt confident about a prediction, particularly for harm serious enough to bring someone back into hospital.
qualifications: This is the result that goes the other way and must be stated if the post argues that judgement is unreliable. Do not turn the odds ratio into 'times more likely'.

claim: It remains unclear from trials whether medication review alone reduces harm after discharge; multicomponent interventions with patient education have shown success at transitions of care (authors' summary).
supporting_passage: "While it remains unclear from randomized trials if medication review on its own reduces MRH in older adults, multicomponent interventions incorporating patient education have demonstrated success during transitions of care,."
location: Full text, Discussion (Implications for practitioners and policy makers)
safe_wording: Whether a medicines check after discharge prevents harm is not settled; approaches that include explaining medicines to patients have had better results.
qualifications: Background statement in the Discussion, citing other studies not opened here. The post's call for routine follow-up (for example a community pharmacy check) is a judgement drawn from the prediction finding, not a tested intervention; mark it as 'we should'. No specific named NHS service is verified in this batch.

claim: In 2017 interviews, 13 GPs and 10 pharmacists in England and Scotland said that, because of workload, most medication reviews were done remotely without involving the patient; several called them a 'tick box' exercise.
supporting_passage: "In total, 13 GPs and 10 pharmacists were interviewed." "Analysis of semi-structured interviews with GPs and pharmacists working in the South West of England, Northern England, and Scotland, sampled for heterogeneity. Interviews took place between January and October 2017." "Due to high workload pressures and time constraints, interviewees reported that most medication reviews were conducted remotely, without involving the patient. Several GPs and pharmacists described the medication reviews as a ‘tick box’ exercise, which they did in the quickest way possible without involving the patient. Two GPs and most pharmacists argued that a ‘proper’ medication review required patient involvement and could not be done remotely"
location: Abstract (Design and setting; Results); full text Results (Patient-centredness: Involving patients versus being time efficient)
safe_wording: When researchers interviewed 23 GPs and pharmacists in England and Scotland in 2017, they said most medication reviews were done from the notes, without the patient, because of workload. Several called it a 'tick box' exercise.
qualifications: Report as what these professionals said, not as how often it happens. Frame as workload and systems, not individual GPs (judge's note). Data are from 2017, before structured medication reviews began in England (C06-29-f).

claim: When a repeat prescription came up with a review overdue, GPs could sign it anyway, do a remote review from the notes, or book a review appointment.
supporting_passage: "For requests where the medication review was out of date, GPs could then either ignore this and sign the prescription, carry out a remote medication review using the patient’s notes, or arrange a medication review appointment over the phone, face-to-face, or in the patient’s home"
location: Full text, Results (The role of others in medication reviews)
safe_wording: Interviewees described how a review can be done from the notes when a repeat prescription is due, without a conversation with the person.
qualifications: Describes the options interviewees reported, not what the record shows. Do not claim the GP record displays 'Medication review: done'; the visual should be labelled illustrative.

claim: Interviewees said it was easier to continue medicines than to stop them, because stopping required involving the patient and created extra work; the authors concluded medicines were rarely stopped or reduced.
supporting_passage: "Interviewees argued that it was easier to continue medicines than it was to stop them, particularly because stopping medicines required involving the patient and this generated extra work." "Practices tended to prioritise being efficient (getting the work done) rather than being thorough (doing it well), so that most medication reviews were carried out with little or no patient involvement, and medicines were rarely stopped or reduced."
safe_wording: The same professionals said it was easier to carry on a medicine than to stop it, because stopping needs a conversation with the person, and that takes time.
qualifications: Interview accounts; 'rarely stopped' is the authors' conclusion from interviews, not a measured rate.

claim: This is a qualitative study of professionals' views from practices in a trial; it did not interview patients or measure how often reviews exclude them.
supporting_passage: "One limitation was that interviewees were recruited from practices involved in a trial; practices, the GPs, and pharmacists who take part in clinical trials may not be representative of all practices." "It was outside the scope of this study to interview other health professionals involved in medication reviews, such as nurses, and to interview patients about their experiences of medication review."
safe_wording: This was a small interview study of what GPs and pharmacists said. It did not count how often reviews leave the person out, and patients were not asked.
qualifications: Must appear in the post (judge's concern).

claim: NICE guidance emphasises involving the person in medication review; NICE defines a medication review as a structured examination of a person's medicines aiming to reach agreement with the person about treatment.
supporting_passage: Duncan 2019 (peer-reviewed description of NICE): "The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends that patients with frailty, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy should undergo regular medication review, and emphasises the importance of involving them in this process." "This does not align with NICE guidance, which puts a strong emphasis on involving patients and their families in decisions about their medicines, and on reducing medicine waste." NICE NG5 (search-engine extract only, page not opened): Medication review is defined as "a structured, critical examination of a person's medicines with the objective of reaching an agreement with the person about treatment, optimising the impact of medicines, minimising the number of medication‑related problems and reducing waste". Search summary also states: "During a structured medication review, healthcare professionals should take into account the person's, and their family members or carers where appropriate, views and understanding about their medicines, as well as their concerns, questions or problems with the medicines."
location: Duncan 2019 full text (How this fits in; Discussion); NICE NG5 via search extract
safe_wording: National guidance in England says a medication review should involve the person taking the medicines, with the aim of agreeing what to do.
qualifications: NG5 itself could not be opened; rely on Duncan's peer-reviewed description and phrase generally ('national guidance in England says reviews should involve the person'). Do not quote NICE wording verbatim in the post or give a recommendation number.

claim: Since September 2020 England has had structured medication reviews (SMRs), distinct from re-authorising repeat prescriptions; in a survey of 120 clinical pharmacists doing them, most were by telephone, and only 26% said they gave patients information in advance.
supporting_passage: Introduction: "SMRs were formally introduced via NHS England (NHSE) in September 2020,8 as distinct from the act of re-authorising repeat prescriptions or a review of specific medicines during a long-term condition review. However, full implementation was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic 9". Abstract: "Patient selection was largely driven by the primary care contract specification: care home residents, patients with polypharmacy, patients on medicines commonly associated with medication errors, patients with severe frailty and/or patients using potentially addictive pain management medication. Only 26% (n=36) of respondents reported providing patients with information in advance. The majority of SMRs were undertaken remotely by telephone and were 21–30 min in length." Introduction: "A qualitative interview study with clinical pharmacists delivering SMRs remotely in primary care in England between 2020–2022 reported that early implementation, without the opportunity for adequate clinical knowledge development, consultation training provision and skills acquisition, fell short of policy aspirations for holistic, personalised reviews."
safe_wording: Since 2020, practices in England have offered a longer 'structured medication review' for some people, such as care home residents and people on many medicines. In a survey of pharmacists who do them, most were by phone, and only about 1 in 4 pharmacists said they sent people information beforehand.
qualifications: The 2020 start date is background from the paper's introduction (citing NHS England). Survey of pharmacists who chose to reply; no response rate. England only; Scotland's arrangements not checked. '26% (n=36)' as printed (denominator unclear).

claim: Some structured medication reviews start from a request by patients, carers or family members, or from patients self-referring.
supporting_passage: Table footnotes: "*120 respondents were asked to tick all that apply.†Ardens/EMIS searches, medicines manager, administrative team, care coordinator, patients self-referring.‡People with incentivised medicines-related indicators listed by NHS England,16 people with frequent hospital admissions, people with mental health problems, people who are housebound, people using medication compliance aids or with compliance issues, people with complex discharge needs, people on 4–9 medicines, people with a clinical need as requested by other health professionals, patients, carers or family members."
location: Full text, Results (table footnotes on patient identification and selection) via Scite
safe_wording: It is reasonable to ask your practice for a review of your medicines that includes a conversation with you; some pharmacists reported reviews started this way.
qualifications: Shows only that some respondents listed patient or family requests among routes; it does not establish an entitlement. Phrase the close as a suggestion ('you can ask'), not a right.

claim: GPs and pharmacists described the ideal review as finding out what the person actually takes, sharing concerns and discussing pros and cons of continuing or stopping; there is no clear evidence that reviews as practised improve clinical outcomes.
supporting_passage: "Both the pharmacists and GPs described the ‘ideal’ scenario of a patient-centred medication review, whereby the clinician finds out what the patient is actually taking, shares concerns, and has an informative discussion about the pros and cons of continuing or stopping certain higher-risk medicines." "Although a patient-centred model of medication review appears to be a reasonable approach to reducing harmful polypharmacy, there is a lack of evidence that medication review, as currently practised, or in the ‘ideal’ form described, actually improves clinical outcomes."
location: Full text, Discussion (Implications for research and practice)
safe_wording: A good review starts with what you actually take, what worries you, and the pros and cons of carrying on or stopping each medicine.
qualifications: Supports the three questions on the visual as a description of good practice. Do not claim that a patient-involving review improves outcomes; the argument for involvement is a matter of respect and agreement (mark as judgement).

claim: Of 1,981 US Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 or over, 92.0% (weighted) agreed they would be willing to stop one or more regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible; 66.6% wanted to reduce the number of medicines they take.
supporting_passage: "Responses to 2 statements ("If my doctor said it was possible, I would be willing to stop one or more of my regular medicines" and "I would like to reduce the number of medicines I am taking") were the main outcomes of interest." "Of the 1981 Medicare beneficiaries included in the study, 1149 (55.2%, weighted) were women, and the majority (n = 715 [54.6%, weighted]) were 65 to 74 years old. A total of 1752 (92.0%, weighted) older adults reported being willing to stop taking 1 or more of their medicines if their physician said it was possible, and 1241 (66.6%, weighted) older adults wanted to reduce the number of medicines that they were taking."
safe_wording: In a national US survey of about 2,000 people aged 65 or over, 92 in 100 said they would be willing to stop one or more of their regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible. Two in three said they would like to take fewer medicines.
qualifications: Stated, hypothetical willingness, conditional on the doctor saying it is possible (judge's note: make the conditional the point). US population; most respondents were 65 to 74. Not what people did later.

claim: People taking 6 or more medicines had higher odds of being willing to stop one (adjusted odds ratio 2.90) and of wanting fewer medicines (adjusted odds ratio 2.31).
supporting_passage: "Older adults taking 6 or more medications had greater odds than those taking fewer than 6 medications of being willing to stop taking 1 or more of their medicines (adjusted odds ratio, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.74-4.82) and wanting to reduce the number of medicines that they were taking (adjusted odds ratio, 2.31; 95% CI, 1.71-3.13)."
safe_wording: People on 6 or more medicines were more likely than people on fewer to say they would be willing to stop one.
qualifications: Adjusted odds ratio; do not convert to 'times more likely' or to an absolute difference (no valid inputs). Optional claim.

claim: Prescribers report that patients may be reluctant to stop medicines, and cite this among barriers to deprescribing.
supporting_passage: Duncan 2019 (UK interviews, Results): "For many interviewees the key perceived barriers to stopping medicines included: fear of causing problems; not wanting to stop medicines that had been started by hospital specialists; and a lack of clear evidence and guidelines around stopping medicines. Interviewees felt that patients might be reluctant or have no incentive to stop medicines, particularly those that they had taken for a long time and medicines for long-term pain". Anderson 2014 (abstract): "The first three themes are intrinsic to the prescriber (eg, beliefs, attitudes, knowledge, skills, behaviour) and the fourth is extrinsic (eg, patient, work setting, health system and cultural factors)." Reeve 2018 (background only): "Primary care physicians report that patient resistance to discontinuing medication use is a significant barrier to deprescribing."
location: Duncan full text Results (Reducing and stopping inappropriate medicines); Anderson abstract; Reeve abstract Importance (background)
safe_wording: GPs and pharmacists interviewed in the UK said patients might be reluctant to stop medicines, especially ones they had taken for a long time.
qualifications: Primary support is Duncan 2019 (a UK primary source); Reeve's sentence is background and must not be cited as its finding; Anderson's abstract names patient factors only generally. Patient reluctance was one of several barriers, alongside fear of causing problems, specialists' prescriptions and unclear guidance.

claim: Across 29 studies (11,049 participants), 87.6% of patients said they were willing to deprescribe based on their doctor's suggestion; caregivers were less willing (74.8%); willingness did not vary with location, population or number of medicines.
supporting_passage: "Twenty-nine unique studies involving 11,049 participants were included." "Overall, 87.6% (95% CI: 83.3 to 91.4%) patients were willing to deprescribe their medication, based upon the doctors' suggestions. This was lower among caregivers, with only 74.8% (49.8% to 93.8%) willing to deprescribe their care recipients' medications. Patients' or caregivers' willingness to deprescribe were not influenced by study location, study population, or the number of medications they took."
safe_wording: Across 29 studies in different countries, about 88 in 100 patients said they would be willing to stop a medicine if their doctor suggested it. Family carers were somewhat less willing, about 75 in 100.
qualifications: Stated willingness; pooled across heterogeneous surveys. Caregiver estimate is imprecise (50% to 94%).

claim: Attitude questionnaires predict actual deprescribing poorly, so stated willingness in a survey is different from agreement in a consultation.
supporting_passage: "Most patients and their caregivers were willing to deprescribe their medications, whenever possible and thus should be offered a trial of deprescribing. Nevertheless, as these tools have a poor predictive ability, patients and their caregivers should be engaged during the deprescribing process to ensure that the values and opinions are heard, which would ultimately improve patient safety."
safe_wording: What people say in a survey does not reliably predict what they decide when a doctor actually suggests stopping a medicine. The survey answers are a reason to raise the question, not a prediction of the answer.
qualifications: Authors' statement in the conclusion; the underlying evidence on predictive ability was not opened.

claim: STOPP/START, the European checklist for prescribing in older people, covers both medicines that may be inappropriate (STOPP) and potential prescribing omissions, meaning indicated medicines that are missing (START); version 3 (2023) has 133 STOPP and 57 START criteria.
supporting_passage: "STOPP/START criteria are designed to help identify and support deprescribing of adverse medication and introduction of beneficial medication (where inappropriately unprescribed) as part of routine medication review in multimorbid older people with polypharmacy." "START criteria are designed to detect potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) which represent another critically important aspect of inappropriate prescribing, i.e., undertreatment or failure to prescribe appropriate medications despite clear and valid indications." "Over the course of four rounds of Delphi validation, the panel achieved consensus on 133 STOPP criteria and 57 START criteria, i.e., 190 STOPP/START criteria in total" "These criteria cannot replace clinical judgment in individual cases"
safe_wording: The main European checklist for medicines in older people has two halves: one lists medicines to consider stopping, the other lists medicines that may be missing. The 2023 version has 133 items of the first kind and 57 of the second.
qualifications: Consensus criteria; the authors say they cannot replace clinical judgement.

claim: An example of an omission: starting an anticoagulant for an older person with untreated persistent atrial fibrillation, while the same checklist also flags caution where bleeding risk is high.
supporting_passage: "Similarly, avoidance of PPOs (START criteria) should reduce preventable morbidity such as major ischemic stroke through initiation of anticoagulants when untreated older patients have persistent atrial fibrillation." "The updated criteria continue to focus on situations that require caution in multimorbid older people, such as the prescribing of anticoagulants in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation and concurrent increased risk of bleeding (c.f. STOPP criteria C10, C12, C14)."
safe_wording: One medicine that is often worth looking for is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) for someone with long-standing atrial fibrillation who is not on one, because it lowers the risk of stroke. The same checklist also asks for caution where the risk of bleeding is high.
qualifications: Exact START v3 criterion wording not seen (Appendix 1 not accessible); paraphrase from the main text. Must carry 'when indicated and wanted' and the bleeding caution; the decision depends on the person's goals and risks.

claim: STOPP/START flags a regular opioid prescribed without a laxative.
supporting_passage: te Winkel 2023 (STOPP/START Netherlands version 2; full-text excerpt): "The most frequently observed PIM was "stop benzodiazepines" (15.7% of all PIMs) and the most frequently observed PPO was "start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly" (14.7% of all PPOs)." Szoszkiewicz 2024 (STOPP/START version 3 study; full-text excerpt): "The most frequent PIMs were the use of regular opioids without concomitant laxatives (7.8%), drugs causing constipation in patients with constipation (7.3%), long-term opioids for osteoarthritis (6.2%), aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (6.2%), long-term aspirin at doses greater than 100 mg per day (5.6%), and the use of benzodiazepines for more than four weeks (5.6%)."
location: te Winkel full text Results (via Scite); Szoszkiewicz full text Results (via Scite)
safe_wording: The checklist flags a regular opioid painkiller taken without a laxative.
qualifications: The candidate's claim that START version 3 contains 'laxative with regular opioids' is NOT verified: the v3 criteria appendix could not be opened, and the v3 study lists 'regular opioids without concomitant laxatives' among potentially inappropriate medicines (the STOPP side), not omissions. In version 2 (Netherlands) it appears as a START item. Word it as 'the checklist flags', without naming the version or side.

claim: Potential prescribing omissions are about as common as potentially inappropriate medicines: in 25,854 Dutch primary care patients aged 65 or over, 74.3% had at least one omission and 72.2% at least one potentially inappropriate medicine over 6 years; the most common omission was a laxative for someone on regular opioids.
supporting_passage: "All 25,854 patients aged 65 years and older having at least 5 contacts with their practice in 6 years were included." "In our population, 72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively; 30.9% and 34.2% had at least 3 PIMs and PPOs, respectively." Full-text excerpt: "the most frequently observed PPO was "start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly" (14.7% of all PPOs)."
location: Abstract (Methods, Results); full-text Results excerpt via Scite
safe_wording: In a Dutch study of almost 26,000 people aged 65 or over, about 3 in 4 were missing at least one medicine the checklist says may be indicated at some point over 6 years; a similar share had at least one medicine it says may be inappropriate. The most common gap was a laxative for someone on a regular opioid.
qualifications: Automated checklist applied to records over 6 years; 'potential' omissions, not confirmed after clinical review. Netherlands, not UK.

claim: Underprescribing is linked with polypharmacy: in 150 geriatric patients, 42.9% of those on 5 or more drugs were undertreated vs 13.5% of those on 4 or fewer.
supporting_passage: "Underprescription was defined as lack of an indicated drug, while no reason could be found for not prescribing it. Polypharmacy was defined as five or more drugs." "Polypharmacy was present in 61% of 150 patients. Underprescription was found in 47 (31%). Of patients with polypharmacy 42.9% were undertreated, in contrast to 13.5% of patients using four medicines or less (OR 4.8, 95% CI 2.0, 11.2). The estimated probability of underprescription increased significantly with the number of drugs."
safe_wording: In a Dutch study of 150 older patients, people taking 5 or more medicines were more often missing an indicated medicine than people taking fewer: about 43 in 100 compared with about 14 in 100.
qualifications: Small, older (2008), single-setting, cross-sectional association. Do not convert OR 4.8 to 'times more likely'; give the two percentages instead.

claim: Trials increasingly address prescribing omissions; pharmaceutical care may slightly reduce the number of omissions (low certainty) and it is uncertain whether it reduces the proportion of people with one.
supporting_passage: "Pharmaceutical care may slightly reduce the number of potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) (SMD -0.48, 95% CI -1.05 to 0.09; I= 92%; 3 studies, 691 participants; low-certainty evidence), however it must be noted that this effect estimate is based on only three studies, which had serious limitations in terms of risk of bias. Likewise, it is uncertain whether pharmaceutical care reduces the proportion of patients with one or more PPO (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.91; I= 95%; 7 studies, 2765 participants; very low-certainty evidence)." "Since the last update of this review in 2018, there appears to have been an increase in the number of studies seeking to address potential prescribing omissions and more interventions being delivered by multidisciplinary teams."
safe_wording: Research on medicines reviews has started to measure missing medicines as well as unnecessary ones, but the evidence on whether reviews close these gaps is weak.
qualifications: Low and very low certainty; do not quote the SMD or RR in a post.

claim: Polypharmacy can be appropriate (medicines that improve or prolong life with minimal harm) or problematic (where harm outweighs benefit), a distinction made by Duerden and colleagues (King's Fund).
supporting_passage: "Polypharmacy is not always harmful, however, and Duerdenmake the distinction between appropriate polypharmacy, such as where multiple medicines improve quality of life, prolong life, and cause minimal harm, and problematic polypharmacy, where the balance tips and the potential harm of some medicines outweighs the potential benefit."
safe_wording: Taking many medicines is not always a problem. It depends on whether each one is doing more good than harm for that person.
qualifications: Secondary citation of the King's Fund report (not opened). Attribute to 'experts' or to the concept, not a verbatim King's Fund quote.

claim: A medication review judged by the number of medicines removed will miss omissions.
supporting_passage: No source states this directly. Supporting facts: omissions are as common as potentially inappropriate medicines (te Winkel: "72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively"); STOPP/START is designed for "deprescribing of adverse medication and introduction of beneficial medication (where inappropriately unprescribed)".
safe_wording: We should judge a medicines review by how well the medicines fit the person, not by how many are stopped, because missing medicines are about as common as unnecessary ones.
qualifications: This is a judgement; present it as the post's position ('we should'), not as a finding. No study found here measured whether reviews targeted at reducing counts miss omissions.

claim: Among adults aged 66 or over with high blood pressure in Ontario, those newly given a calcium channel blocker were more often given a loop diuretic within 90 days than those newly given an ACE inhibitor or ARB or an unrelated drug (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%).
supporting_passage: "The cohort included 41 086 older adults (≥66 years) with hypertension who were newly dispensed a CCB, 66 494 individuals who were newly dispensed another antihypertensive medication, and 231 439 individuals who were newly dispensed an unrelated medication. At index (ie, the dispensing date), the mean (SD) age was 74.5 (6.9) years, and 191 685 (56.5%) were women. Individuals who were newly dispensed a CCB had a higher cumulative incidence at 90 days of being dispensed a loop diuretic than individuals in both control groups (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%, P < .001)."
safe_wording: In Ontario, among people aged 66 or over with high blood pressure, about 14 in every 1,000 people started on a calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine were given a loop diuretic (a strong water tablet such as furosemide) within 3 months. The figure was about 7 in 1,000 for people started on a different blood pressure tablet, and 5 in 1,000 for people started on an unrelated medicine.
qualifications: Dispensing data: shows who was given a diuretic, not whether swelling was the reason. The gap (about 7 extra per 1,000 compared with other blood pressure tablets) is the best estimate of the cascade; it is small per person but large across a population. Association, not proof that each case was a cascade.

claim: The association persisted, slightly weaker, up to 1 year, and in people started on amlodipine alone; relative rates were 1.68 to 2.40 times higher than after an ACE inhibitor or ARB over the first 3 months.
supporting_passage: "After adjustment, individuals who were newly dispensed a CCB had increased relative rates of being dispensed a loop diuretic compared with individuals who were newly dispensed an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker (HR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.38-2.05 in the first 30 days after index [days 1-30]; 2.26; 95% CI, 1.76-2.92 in the subsequent 30 days [days 31-60]; and 2.40; 95% CI, 1.84-3.13 in the third month of follow-up [days 61-90]) ... This association persisted, although slightly attenuated, from 90 days to up to 1 year of follow-up and when restricted to a subgroup of individuals who were newly dispensed amlodipine."
safe_wording: The pattern was still there a year after starting the drug, and it held when the analysis was limited to people started on amlodipine.
qualifications: Hazard ratios are relative; give the absolute figures from C06-18-a first. The 1-year figures are not in the abstract, so give no number for them.

claim: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one drug is taken for a new condition and a second drug is prescribed to treat it; the term was described by Rochon and Gurwitz in the BMJ in 1997.
supporting_passage: McCarthy 2022: "Prescribing cascades occur when a drug is prescribed to manage side effects of another drug, typically when a side effect is misinterpreted as a new condition." Savage 2020: "A prescribing cascade occurs when the edema is misinterpreted as a new medical condition and a diuretic is subsequently prescribed to treat the edema." Rochon 1997 record title: "Optimising drug treatment for elderly people: the prescribing cascade."
location: McCarthy 2022 Abstract; Savage 2020 Abstract (Importance); Rochon 1997 PubMed record (title only)
safe_wording: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one medicine is mistaken for a new illness, and a second medicine is started to treat it.
qualifications: Attribute the term to Rochon and Gurwitz (BMJ 1997) only by citation; no text from that article was read.

claim: Ankle swelling is a common, dose-related side effect of calcium channel blockers of the amlodipine type.
supporting_passage: Makani 2011: "One hundred and six studies with 99 469 participants, mean age 56 ± 6 years, satisfied our inclusion criteria and were included in this analysis. The weighted incidence of peripheral edema was significantly higher in the CCBs group when compared with controls/placebo (10.7 vs. 3.2%, P < 0.0001). Similarly, the withdrawal rate due to edema was higher in patients on CCBs compared with control/placebo (2.1 vs. 0.5%, P < 0.0001). Both the incidence of edema and patient withdrawal rate due to edema increased with the duration of therapy with CCBs reaching 24 and 5%, respectively, after 6 months. ... Incidence of peripheral edema in patients on DHPs was 12.3% compared with 3.1% with non-DHPs (P < 0.0001). Edema with high-dose CCBs (defined as more than half the usual maximal dose) was 2.8 times higher than that with low-dose CCBs (16.1 vs. 5.7%, P < 0.0001)." Woodford 2020: "CCBs have no prognostic benefit in heart failure and have an absolute risk increase for oedema of around 8-18% (number needed to harm 6-13)."
safe_wording: In trials, ankle swelling affected about 11 in 100 people taking a calcium channel blocker, compared with about 3 in 100 on placebo or other treatment. It was about three times as common on higher doses (16 in 100) as on lower doses (6 in 100), and it became more common the longer people took the drug.
qualifications: Trial participants averaged 56 years, so rates in older people may differ. The swelling mechanism in the abstract ('thought to occur secondary to arteriolar dilatation') is background, so say 'is thought to' if used.

claim: For calcium channel blocker ankle swelling the options are to lower the dose, switch to another drug, or reconsider the need for it; adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB also reduces the swelling; a loop diuretic is justified only where these fail.
supporting_passage: Woodford 2020: "The best way to manage the oedema caused by CCBs is to switch to an alternative medication. Only where this is not possible or fails to achieve therapeutic goals would the CCB-loop diuretic combination appear to be justified. In many cases, therapeutic practice could be improved by targeting people on CCB-loop diuretic combinations for medication review." Makani (Am J Med) 2011: "The incidence of peripheral edema with calcium channel blocker/renin-angiotensin system blocker combination was 38% lower than that with calcium channel blocker monotherapy (P<.00001) (relative risk [RR] 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.53-0.74)." Makani (J Hypertens) 2011: "The risk of peripheral edema with lipophilic DHPs was 57% lower than with traditional DHPs (relative risk 0.43; 95% confidence interval 0.34-0.53; P < 0.0001)."
location: Woodford 2020 Abstract; Makani Am J Med 2011 Abstract, Results; Makani J Hypertens 2011 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: If ankle swelling starts after a calcium channel blocker, the first question is whether the drug is the cause. The options include a lower dose, a different blood pressure medicine, or asking whether the drug is still needed. A UK geriatrician's review concluded that switching is the best way to manage it, and that adding a loop diuretic is justified only when other options fail. In trials, adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB cut the rate of swelling by about a third.
qualifications: The switch advice is expert opinion in a narrative review, not a trial result. 'Reconsider the need for it' is a clinical judgement (no study opened tested stopping). Combination-trial participants were middle-aged and followed for about 9 weeks. Present the RAS-blocker option as one of several, since it adds a drug.

claim: Adding a loop diuretic brings its own harms, such as worse kidney function, dizziness or blood pressure drop on standing, abnormal salts in the blood and falls.
supporting_passage: "In the 60 days following LD initiation, 28 patients (23.3%) experienced 37 events potentially attributable to LD initiation. The most common downstream events were worsening kidney function (n = 9 [7.5%]), orthostasis (n = 7 [5.8%]), electrolyte abnormalities (n = 6 [5.0%]), and falls (n = 5 [4.2%]). Six patients (5.0%) were evaluated in the emergency department and/or hospital for potential downstream events." Also: "Gabapentinoids were rarely noted in the differential (n = 4 [3.3%])."
safe_wording: In a US record review of 120 older veterans who were started on a loop diuretic after a nerve-pain medicine caused swelling, about 1 in 4 had a problem within 2 months that may have come from the diuretic: worse kidney function, a drop in blood pressure on standing, abnormal salts in the blood, or a fall.
qualifications: The first drug in this study was gabapentin or pregabalin, not a calcium channel blocker; state that if it is used in a CCB post. Small, mostly male sample; no comparison group; events 'potentially attributable'. The candidate's visual label 'passing urine often' was not checked against a source; the 'possible third drug' step must be labelled 'Illustrative example'.

claim: Calcium channel blocker ankle swelling responds poorly to diuretics.
supporting_passage: No supporting passage found. Makani 2011 gives the mechanism only as background: "It has been thought to occur secondary to arteriolar dilatation causing intracapillary hypertension and fluid extravasation."
safe_wording: Do not say that water tablets do not work for this swelling. Say instead that the swelling is a side effect of the first drug, and the first step is to review that drug.
qualifications: The Sica 2003 lead could not be found in PubMed.

claim: ThinkCascades lists the calcium channel blocker to loop diuretic cascade among nine clinically important cascades in older people.
supporting_passage: "After these exclusions, the final short consensus-based ThinkCascades tool includes nine clinically important cascades that are examples of potentially inappropriate prescribing affecting older people (Table)."
location: Full text, Results (Phase III); the table itself did not render
safe_wording: An international expert panel (ThinkCascades, 2022) agreed a list of nine prescribing cascades that are usually harmful in older people.
qualifications: That the CCB to loop diuretic cascade is on the nine-item list was not confirmed (table not rendered). Do not name it as on the list unless the table is checked.

claim: A separate US study also found excess loop diuretic starts after calcium channel blockers, more so at high doses.
supporting_passage: "Among 1 206 093 DH CCB initiators, 55 818 patients (4.6%) (33 100 [59.3%] aged <65 years; 32 916 [59.0%] women) had a new loop diuretic prescription 360 days before or after DH CCB initiation, resulting in an aSR of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.84-1.90). An estimated 1.44% of DH CCB initiators experienced the prescribing cascade. The aSR was disproportionately higher among DH CCB initiators who were prescribed high doses (aSR, 2.20; 95% CI, 2.13-2.27)..."
safe_wording: A US insurance study of over a million people starting amlodipine-type drugs estimated that about 1 in 70 went on to a loop diuretic because of the cascade, and the pattern was stronger at higher doses.
qualifications: Mostly people under 65; sequence symmetry design estimates excess, not individual cases.

claim: In a UK primary care study of 487,372 people on blood pressure drugs, taking an NSAID together with a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB was linked with a higher rate of acute kidney injury (rate ratio 1.31).
supporting_passage: "A cohort of 487 372 patients using antihypertensive drugs met the study inclusion criteria (fig 1); they were followed for a mean of 5.9 (SD 3.4) years ... current use of a triple therapy combination was associated with a 31% higher rate of acute kidney injury (rate ratio 1.31, 95% confidence interval 1.12 to 1.53)." Table 1: cases mean (SD) age "76.9 (10.9)"; controls "76.9 (10.7)".
location: Full text, Results and Table 1; Table 2
safe_wording: In UK GP records, people taking an anti-inflammatory painkiller on top of both a water tablet and an ACE inhibitor or ARB (such as ramipril or losartan) had about a third more hospital admissions with sudden kidney injury than people taking the two blood pressure medicines without the painkiller.
qualifications: Observational (linked with, not proven to cause). Prescribed NSAIDs only; shop-bought ibuprofen was not captured. The people who developed kidney injury averaged 77 years old. Relative figure: pair it with the absolute context in C06-32-c and C06-32-e.

claim: The risk with the triple combination was highest in the first 30 days of use.
supporting_passage: "With respect to duration of use, an 82% (rate ratio 1.82, 1.35 to 2.46) increased risk of acute kidney injury was observed in the first 30 days of use, whereas the adjusted rate ratio progressively decreased with longer periods of use and was no longer significant after more than 90 days of use (1.01, 0.84 to 1.23; P for interaction<0.001)."
safe_wording: The extra risk was greatest in the first month after the painkiller was added.
qualifications: Secondary analysis. Relative figure only.

claim: Hospital admission with acute kidney injury was uncommon overall (about 7 per 10,000 person-years among users of blood pressure drugs).
supporting_passage: "We identified 2215 cases of acute kidney injury during follow-up, yielding an overall incidence rate of 7/10 000 (95% confidence interval 7/10 000 to 8/10 000) person years."
safe_wording: Hospital admission with sudden kidney injury was uncommon: about 7 per 10,000 people per year among everyone in the study taking blood pressure medicines.
qualifications: This is the rate for the whole cohort, not for people on the triple combination, and it counts only hospital admissions coded as kidney injury. The Tayside study (C06-32-e), which counted blood-test rises, found about 68 per 10,000 per year.

claim: An NSAID with only one of these drugs (a diuretic alone, or an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone) was not linked with extra kidney injury in the UK hospital-admission study, but a Scottish study counting blood-test rises found a similar relative increase with these double combinations.
supporting_passage: Lapi 2013: "Overall, current use of a double therapy combination of a diuretic or an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker with NSAIDs was not associated with an increased rate of acute kidney injury." Dreischulte 2015: "The relative increase in AKI risk was similar for NSAID use in both triple (adjusted rate ratio 1.64 (95% CI 1.25-2.14)) and dual combinations with either renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (1.60 (1.18-2.17)) or diuretics (1.64 (1.17-2.29))."
location: Lapi 2013 Full text, Results; Dreischulte 2015 Abstract
safe_wording: Do not say that ibuprofen with only one of these medicines is safe. A Scottish study found that taking an anti-inflammatory alongside either a water tablet or an ACE inhibitor or ARB was also linked with more kidney injury, though the extra risk in absolute terms was about half that seen with all three together.
qualifications: The two studies used different definitions of kidney injury and reached different conclusions for double combinations; the Scottish study is the more sensitive.

claim: In absolute terms, about 1 extra kidney injury occurs for every 158 people who take an NSAID for a year alongside both a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB, compared with 1 in over 300 for the double combinations; risk was highest in people over 75 and those with reduced kidney function.
supporting_passage: "This nested case-control study characterized the risk of community-acquired AKI associated with NSAID use among 78,379 users of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors and/or diuretics, where AKI was defined as a 50% or greater increase in creatinine from baseline. The AKI incidence was 68/10,000 person-years. ... However, the absolute increase in AKI risk was higher for NSAIDs used in triple versus dual combinations with renin-angiotensin system inhibitors or diuretics alone (numbers needed to harm for 1 year treatment with NSAID of 158 vs. over 300). AKI risk was highest among users of loop diuretic/aldosterone antagonist combinations, in those over 75 years of age, and in those with renal impairment."
safe_wording: In a Scottish study, for every 158 people who took an anti-inflammatory painkiller for a year on top of both a water tablet and an ACE inhibitor or ARB, about 1 extra person had a kidney injury picked up on blood tests (roughly 6 in 1,000). With only one of the two blood pressure medicines, the extra risk was lower (fewer than 1 in 300). People over 75 and people with weaker kidneys were at highest risk.
qualifications: NNH is for a year of NSAID treatment, not a few days of ibuprofen; say so. Kidney injury here means a blood-test rise of creatinine by half or more, which includes milder events than hospital admissions. Observational.

claim: Each of the three drugs affects the kidney differently, so together they reduce the kidney's ability to keep filtering.
supporting_passage: "Use of diuretics can lead to hypovolaemia, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers cause a haemodynamic reduction in glomerular filtration rate due to efferent arteriolar vasodilation, and NSAIDs cause inhibition of prostacyclin synthesis (leading to renal afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction)." and "among users of the triple therapy combination, the decreased inflow to the glomerulus resulting from the diuretic and NSAID cannot be compensated owing to blockade of the renin-angiotensin system"
location: Full text, Introduction and Discussion (Biological mechanisms)
safe_wording: The water tablet lowers the fluid reaching the kidneys, the anti-inflammatory narrows the blood vessel into the kidney's filters, and the ACE inhibitor or ARB stops the kidney from compensating.
qualifications: Authors' explanation, not a finding of the study. Keep it short and literal.

claim: UK prescribing guidance (BNF, NICE CKS) advises caution with NSAIDs in people taking these medicines, and paracetamol is the alternative for most people.
supporting_passage: No passage opened. BNF and NICE CKS pages cannot be opened from this environment, and no published paper opened in this batch recommends paracetamol as the alternative.
safe_wording: Advise the reader to ask a pharmacist or GP which painkiller is suitable before buying an anti-inflammatory. Do not name paracetamol as the safe alternative, and do not cite the BNF or NICE, unless a source is opened.
qualifications: The Lapi authors conclude only that 'vigilance may be warranted' and that 'a more appropriate use and choice among the available anti-inflammatory or analgesic drugs could therefore be applied'.

claim: DQIP was a cluster-randomised stepped-wedge trial in Tayside general practices (34 randomised, 33 completed) of a 48-week intervention combining professional education, informatics to find patients, and financial incentives for practices to review them.
supporting_passage: "In this cluster-randomized, stepped-wedge trial conducted in Tayside, Scotland, we randomly assigned participating primary care practices to various start dates for a 48-week intervention comprising professional education, informatics to facilitate review, and financial incentives for practices to review patients' charts to assess appropriateness. ... A total of 34 practices underwent randomization, 33 of which completed the study."
safe_wording: In Tayside, 33 general practices took part in a trial of a programme with three parts: training for prescribers, a computer search that listed each practice's patients on specific risky prescriptions, and payment for the practice to review each of those patients.
qualifications: Stepped-wedge design: every practice got the intervention, at randomly assigned start dates.

claim: The programme targeted nine named high-risk prescribing measures involving NSAIDs and antiplatelet drugs (six for stomach bleeding, two for kidney harm, one for heart failure), and flags could be cleared by recording that the prescription was appropriate, stopping it, or adding stomach protection.
supporting_passage: "The individual measures were related to three types of adverse drug events: gastrointestinal events (six measures; e.g., aspirin or clopidogrel prescription for a patient taking an oral anticoagulant without coprescription of a gastroprotective drug), renal events (two measures; e.g., NSAID prescription for a patient with chronic kidney disease), and heart failure (NSAID prescription for a patient with heart failure)." and "Physicians could clear the flag by recording an explicit decision that the prescribing was appropriate, by stopping prescription of the offending drugs, or by adding a gastroprotective drug (proton-pump inhibitor or histamine 2 -receptor antagonist) for measures targeting the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding."
safe_wording: It focused on nine specific combinations, for example an anti-inflammatory painkiller in someone with kidney disease or heart failure, or aspirin with a blood thinner and no stomach protection. For each patient flagged, the doctor could stop the drug, add stomach protection, or record why the prescription was right for that person.
qualifications: Review did not mean automatic stopping; the design allowed a documented decision to continue.

claim: Targeted high-risk prescribing fell from 3.7% to 2.2% of patients at risk (adjusted odds ratio 0.63).
supporting_passage: Dreischulte 2016: "Targeted high-risk prescribing was significantly reduced, from a rate of 3.7% (1102 of 29,537 patients at risk) immediately before the intervention to 2.2% (674 of 30,187) at the end of the intervention (adjusted odds ratio, 0.63; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.68; P<0.001)." Dreischulte 2018: "...reduced the primary end point of high-risk prescribing by 37%, where both ongoing and new high-risk prescribing were significantly reduced."
safe_wording: Among patients at risk, the share on one of these risky prescriptions fell from about 37 in 1,000 to about 22 in 1,000 by the end of the programme.
qualifications: Primary outcome. The 37% is a relative reduction in odds; lead with the absolute figures.

claim: Admissions for stomach ulcer or bleeding fell from 55.7 to 37.0 and heart failure admissions from 707.7 to 513.5 per 10,000 person-years; admissions for acute kidney injury did not show a clear difference.
supporting_passage: "The rate of hospital admissions for gastrointestinal ulcer or bleeding was significantly reduced from the preintervention period to the intervention period (from 55.7 to 37.0 admissions per 10,000 person-years; rate ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.86; P=0.002), as was the rate of admissions for heart failure (from 707.7 to 513.5 admissions per 10,000 person-years; rate ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.56 to 0.95; P=0.02), but admissions for acute kidney injury were not (101.9 and 86.0 admissions per 10,000 person-years, respectively; rate ratio, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.68 to 1.09; P=0.19)." Methods excerpt: "The incidence in the intervention period versus the preintervention period was compared with the use of the conditional maximum-likelihood estimate of the rate ratio."
location: Abstract, Results; full text Methods (via Scite excerpt)
safe_wording: Hospital admissions for stomach ulcers or bleeding fell from about 56 to 37 per 10,000 patients per year, and admissions for heart failure also fell. Admissions for kidney injury did not show a clear difference (102 and 86 per 10,000 per year, a gap that could be chance).
qualifications: Secondary outcomes, compared before and during the programme; the authors conclude it 'may have improved clinical outcomes'. Do not say the programme 'cut admissions' as a proven effect. Rates are among patients at risk, per 10,000 person-years.

claim: The fall in high-risk prescribing was sustained in the year after the financial incentives ended.
supporting_passage: "Reductions in the rates of high-risk prescribing were sustained after financial incentives ceased." and "In an analysis of the primary outcome, 674 of 30,187 patients (2.2%) with risk factors for related adverse drug events had prescriptions for NSAIDs, antiplatelet agents, or both at the end of the intervention, and 560 of 28,616 (2.0%) had such prescriptions at 48 weeks after incentives ceased (adjusted odds ratio, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.85 to 1.53; P = 0.38)." Methods: "Finally, in a post hoc analysis, we examined whether the effect of the DQIP intervention was sustained after the end of the intervention."
location: Full text (via Scite excerpts), Methods and Results
safe_wording: A year after the payments stopped, high-risk prescribing had not gone back up: about 20 in 1,000 patients at risk, compared with 22 in 1,000 at the end of the programme.
qualifications: Post hoc analysis. The informatics and newsletter may have continued; the paper excerpt does not say what support remained.

claim: Effectiveness varied widely between practices, and practice staff saw each component as doing a different job: payments helped practices sign up, education started the work, and the informatics tool kept it going.
supporting_passage: Dreischulte 2018: "(3) Effectiveness ranged from a relative increase in high-risk prescribing of 24.1% to a relative reduction of 77.2%." and "(1) Recruited practices had lower performance in the quality and outcomes framework than those declining participation." Grant 2017: "All the primary components of the intervention were perceived as active, but at different stages of implementation: financial incentives primarily supported recruitment; education motivated the GPs to initiate implementation; the informatics tool facilitated sustained implementation."
location: Dreischulte 2018 Abstract, Results; Grant 2017 Abstract, Results
safe_wording: Results varied a great deal between practices. Staff interviewed said the payment mainly got practices to sign up, the training got the work started, and the patient lists kept it going.
qualifications: Perceptions from interviews, not a test of which component caused the effect. The NEJM authors state they 'cannot identify which aspect of the intervention mattered most'.

claim: A later UK trial of a broader approach (structured polypharmacy review with informatics, training, feedback and financial incentives) did not reduce potentially inappropriate prescribing.
supporting_passage: "There was no evidence of a difference in the primary outcome of number of potentially inappropriate prescribing indicators at the 26-week follow-up between the intervention and control groups after adjustment for pre-randomisation baseline (mean 2·3 in each group; difference in means -0·007 [95% CI -0·21 to 0·20]; p=0·95)." and "The complex intervention comprised a structured, collaborative, and patient-centred approach to medication review, supported by informatics, clinician training, performance feedback, and financial incentivisation."
safe_wording: A 2025 UK trial of broad medication reviews for people on five or more medicines, also with computer support, training and payments, found no difference in potentially inappropriate prescribing after 6 months.
qualifications: Different aim and targets from DQIP. Contrasting the two to argue for a narrow focus is a judgement, not a tested finding; mark it as judgement ('We think...').

claim: In US adults aged 65 or over with diabetes (NHANES 2001 to 2010), tight control (HbA1c below 7%) was as common in those in very complex or poor health (56.4%) as in the relatively healthy (62.8%).
supporting_passage: "Overall, 61.5% (95% CI, 57.5%-65.3%), representing 3.8 million (95% CI, 3.4-4.2), had an HbA1c level of less than 7%; this proportion did not differ across health status categories (62.8% [95% CI, 56.9%-68.3%]) were relatively healthy, 63.0% (95% CI, 57.0%-68.6%) had complex/intermediate health, and 56.4% (95% CI, 49.7%-62.9%) had very complex/poor health (P = .26)." Health status definition: "very complex/poor, based on difficulty with 2 or more activities of daily living or dialysis dependence".
safe_wording: In a US national survey (2001 to 2010), more than half of older people with diabetes who needed help with two or more everyday activities, or were on dialysis, had an HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol). That was about as common as in healthy older people.
qualifications: US data, now 15 to 25 years old. The survey did not measure low blood sugars; the authors call this 'potential overtreatment'.

claim: Of older adults with HbA1c below 7%, 54.9% were treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea (60.0% of those in very complex or poor health).
supporting_passage: "Of the older adults with an HbA1c level of less than 7%, 54.9% (95% CI, 50.4%-59.3%) were treated with either insulin or sulfonylureas; this proportion was similar across health status categories (50.8% [95% CI, 45.1%-56.5%] were relatively healthy, 58.7% [95% CI, 49.4%-67.5%] had complex/intermediate health, and 60.0% [95% CI, 51.4%-68.1%] had very complex/poor health; P = .14)."
safe_wording: Of the older people with an HbA1c below 7%, just over half were on insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as gliclazide), the medicines most likely to cause low blood sugar.
qualifications: 'Most likely to cause low blood sugar' is the study's own framing ('diabetes medications likely to result in hypoglycemia (insulin or sulfonylureas)'). Gliclazide as an example is a UK illustration, not from the study.

claim: In 16 Norfolk general practices, about 3 in 10 people aged 70 or over with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea or insulin had an HbA1c below 53 mmol/mol, and this was as common in those with kidney disease or dementia.
supporting_passage: "Sixteen Norfolk general practices participated ... Of these, 1379 (35.7%) people were prescribed sulfonylurea or insulin therapies." "The median age of the study cohort was 78 years." "In total, 400 older people (29.9%) had an HbAconcentration < 53 mmol/mol (7%), of whom 162 (12.1%) had HbA< 48 mmol/mol (6.5%)." "Treatment to an HbAtarget of < 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) was as prevalent in those with chronic kidney disease or dementia as in those without." [The subscript '1c' is lost in the PubMed text rendering.]
safe_wording: In 16 GP practices in Norfolk, about 3 in 10 people aged 70 or over who were taking gliclazide-type tablets or insulin had an HbA1c below 53 mmol/mol, and about 1 in 8 were below 48. This was just as common in people with kidney disease or dementia, who are more prone to low blood sugars.
qualifications: Last recorded HbA1c only; low blood sugars not measured. Percentages appear to use people with a recorded HbA1c as the denominator.

claim: UK consensus says the usual HbA1c targets (53 to 59 mmol/mol, 7 to 7.5%) are too tight for frail older people.
supporting_passage: "Guidelines from organizations such as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, and the American Diabetes Association acknowledge the need for individualized care, but the glycaemic targets that are suggested to constitute good control [HbA 53-59 mmol/mol (7-7.5%)] are too tight for frail older individuals. We present a framework for the assessment of older adults and guidelines for the management of this population according to their frailty status..."
safe_wording: A UK consensus statement (2018, with NHS England and geriatric and diabetes specialists) says the usual HbA1c targets of 53 to 59 mmol/mol are too tight for older people living with frailty, and that targets should be set according to frailty.
qualifications: Specific frailty targets in the body of the paper were not read; do not quote target numbers for frailty from this source.

claim: A deprescribing guideline recommends reducing or stopping glucose-lowering drugs that cause hypoglycaemia in older adults at risk, and individualising targets for people who are frail, have dementia or limited life expectancy.
supporting_passage: "We recommend deprescribing antihyperglycemic medications known to contribute to hypoglycemia in older adults at risk or in situations where antihyperglycemic medications might be causing other adverse effects, and individualizing targets and deprescribing accordingly for those who are frail, have dementia, or have a limited life expectancy."
safe_wording: An evidence-based guideline on stopping diabetes medicines recommends reducing or stopping those that can cause low blood sugar in older people at risk, and setting targets to suit people who are frail, have dementia or have limited life expectancy.
qualifications: Canadian guideline (2017).

claim: Low blood sugar episodes in older people treated for diabetes are linked with falls and fractures.
supporting_passage: "Similarly, our meta-analysis of six studies demonstrated an association between hypoglycemia and falls and fractures, pooled OR 1.78 (95% CI 1.44-2.21) and 1.68 (95% CI 1.37-2.07) respectively." and "Studies assessing mortality signal a time-response relationship with a higher risk of adverse events occurring within the first 90 days after hypoglycemia."
safe_wording: In studies of older people treated for diabetes, those who had episodes of low blood sugar were more likely to have falls and fractures. This link does not prove the low sugars caused them.
qualifications: Association from observational studies; odds ratios cannot be turned into 'X times more likely' in plain terms or into absolute risks. Mostly severe hypoglycaemia.

claim: HbA1c does not reveal low blood sugars: in older adults with high HbA1c (8% or more), most on insulin, two thirds had low glucose on 3 days of monitoring, and almost all episodes went unnoticed.
supporting_passage: "Forty adults (mean [SD] age, 75 [5] years; HbA(1C) value, 9.3% [1.3%]; diabetes duration, 22 [14] years; 28 patients [70%] with type 2 diabetes mellitus; and 37 [93%] using insulin) were evaluated. Twenty-six patients (65%) experienced 1 or more episodes of hypoglycemia (glucose level <70 mg/dL). ... Of the total of 102 hypoglycemic episodes, 95 (93%) were unrecognized by finger-stick glucose measurements performed 4 times a day or by symptoms." Conclusion: "Raising HbA(1C) goals may not be adequate to prevent hypoglycemia in this population."
safe_wording: An HbA1c result does not show whether someone is having low blood sugars. In a small US study of 40 older people on insulin whose HbA1c was high, 26 had low glucose readings over 3 days of continuous monitoring, and 93 in 100 episodes were not picked up by finger-prick tests or symptoms.
qualifications: Very small; high-HbA1c group, mostly insulin users, some with type 1 diabetes. Use it to show HbA1c alone cannot rule low sugars in or out, not to say a low HbA1c causes them.

claim: HbA1c can be misleading in anaemia: non-iron-deficiency anaemia may lower it and iron deficiency may raise it.
supporting_passage: "HbA1c is likely to be affected by iron deficiency and IDA with a spurious increase in HbA1c values; conversely, non-IDA may lead to a decreased HbA1c value."
safe_wording: Some types of anaemia can make HbA1c read lower than the true blood sugar level, and iron deficiency can make it read higher.
qualifications: Evidence is limited and in people without known diabetes; say 'can' not 'does'.

claim: Tight glucose control in older adults reduces some complications but more than doubles severe hypoglycaemia, without a clear difference in deaths.
supporting_passage: "No difference was noted in all-cause mortality with intensive control (pooled hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.90-1.03), but risk of severe hypoglycemia increased (2.45, 2.22-2.72). Intensive control was associated reductions in microvascular (0.73, 0.68-0.79) and macrovascular complications (0.84, 0.79-0.89). Outcome data for risk of hospitalization, cognition, and falls/fractures were limited."
safe_wording: Across 15 studies in people aged 60 or over, aiming for tight control was linked with fewer blood vessel complications, but more than twice the rate of severe low blood sugars, and no clear difference in deaths.
qualifications: Mixed RCT and observational data with significant heterogeneity; population mostly 60 plus rather than frail. Relative figures only.

claim: The American Diabetes Association recommends less stringent targets and deintensifying hypoglycaemia-causing drugs in older adults with complex or poor health.
supporting_passage: Not opened. ADA Standards of Care 2026 Older Adults section (PMID 41358888, PMC12690186): PMC full text returned empty, Scite returned abstract only; 2024 and 2025 editions also not readable.
safe_wording: Do not cite ADA wording. Use the UK consensus (C06-25-d) and the deprescribing guideline (C06-25-e) instead.

claim: In the trials of direct oral anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation, eligibility and dosing were based on creatinine clearance from the Cockcroft-Gault equation.
supporting_passage: MacCallum 2013: "In clinical trials of dabigatran and rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF), drug eligibility and dosing were determined using the Cockcroft-Gault equation to estimate creatine clearance as a measure of renal function." Chan 2022: "Randomized trials of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) adopted the Cockcroft-Gault (CG) formula to calculate estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to determine the dosages of DOACs."
location: MacCallum 2013 Abstract, Objectives; Chan 2022 Abstract, Background
safe_wording: The trials that tested the newer blood thinners (DOACs) worked out doses from creatinine clearance calculated with the Cockcroft-Gault formula, which uses age, weight and sex, not from the eGFR printed on lab reports.
qualifications: Background statement in both abstracts; 'uses age, weight and sex' is general knowledge of the formula not quoted in an opened source (confirm or omit).

claim: Using eGFR instead of Cockcroft-Gault overestimates kidney function mainly in people over 75 and under 50 kg, leading to overdosing of DOACs; only dosing that was correct by Cockcroft-Gault was linked with less major bleeding than warfarin.
supporting_passage: "At the cutoff values of eGFR of <15, 15-50, and >50 mL/min, the agreements were 78% between MDRD and CG and 81% between CKD-EPI and CG. The disagreements among the different equations were largely due to overestimations, especially for patients aged >75 years and with a body weight of <50 kg (58.8% for MDRD and 50.9% for CKD-EPI). Among patients receiving DOACs whose dosages were defined as "on label" based on MDRD or CKD-EPI, only those whose dosages were "truly on label" based on CG were associated with a lower risk of major bleeding (adjusted HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.26-0.45) compared to warfarin."
safe_wording: In a Taiwanese study of 39,239 people with atrial fibrillation, the lab eGFR and the Cockcroft-Gault calculation disagreed for about 1 in 5 people, mostly because eGFR made kidney function look better. The disagreement was most common in people over 75 who weighed under 50 kg.
qualifications: East Asian population with lower body weight; observational. The 58.8% and 50.9% figures are ambiguous in the abstract (proportion overestimated in that subgroup); do not quote them without the full text.

claim: In east London, using MDRD eGFR instead of Cockcroft-Gault would have made about 15% of people aged 80 or over with AF eligible for dabigatran who were ineligible, and led to too-high rivaroxaban doses in 13.5%.
supporting_passage: "Of 4120 patients, 2706 were <80 years and 1414 were ≥80 years of age. Among those ≥80 years, 14.9% were ineligible for dabigatran according to Cockcroft-Gault equation but would have been judged eligible applying MDRD method. For those <80 years, 0.8% would have been incorrectly judged eligible for dabigatran and 5.3% would have received too high a dose. For rivaroxaban, 0.3% would have been incorrectly judged eligible for treatment and 13.5% would have received too high a dose."
safe_wording: In east London GP records, among people aged 80 or over with atrial fibrillation, about 15 in 100 who were too frail in kidney terms for dabigatran by the Cockcroft-Gault calculation would have looked eligible using the lab eGFR.
qualifications: Uses the older MDRD equation, not CKD-EPI; modelled dosing, not outcomes. The rivaroxaban 13.5% and dabigatran '<80 years' figures are ambiguous in the abstract; use only the 14.9% figure for people aged 80 or over.

claim: MHRA advised in 2019 that creatinine clearance by Cockcroft-Gault should be used to dose DOACs and some other drugs.
supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not verbatim from the MHRA page): 'Creatinine clearance should be calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula to determine dosage adjustments for patients taking direct-acting oral anticoagulants, patients taking nephrotoxic drugs (such as vancomycin and amphotericin B), and patients taking medicines that are largely renally excreted and have a narrow therapeutic index (such as digoxin and sotalol).'
safe_wording: Do not state MHRA wording until it is checked in an opened copy. If it cannot be opened, rely on the published studies (C06-19-a to c).
qualifications: Search extract; which body weight and patient groups the MHRA specifies is unverified.

claim: In very old people with AF on DOACs, whether the dose was judged appropriate by Cockcroft-Gault or by eGFR made no difference to the link with deaths, clots or bleeding.
supporting_passage: "A total of 224 patients were included in the analysis (median age 87 years). Using CrCl, 154 (69%) had an appropriate dose of DOACs, 52 (23%) were underdosed and 18 (8%) were overdosed. ... In participants with discrepancies in dose status using CrCland eGFR equations, the occurrence of endpoints did not differ between participants having an appropriate dose using CrClor eGFR." Conclusions: "In older adults with AF, the association of DOAC dose status with adverse events did not differ when using CrClor eGFR. Our results suggest that eGFR equations are not inferior to CrClwithin this context."
safe_wording: A Berlin study of 224 people with a median age of 87 found that outcomes did not differ according to which kidney formula was used to judge the dose.
qualifications: Small study; wide uncertainty. Conflicts with Chan 2022.

claim: eGFR is adjusted to a standard body size (1.73 m2) and creatinine depends on muscle mass, so eGFR can overestimate kidney function in small people with low muscle mass.
supporting_passage: Not found in opened sources (the 1.73 m2 unit appears in Hambling 2017 but without explanation).
safe_wording: Say only what Chan 2022 supports: eGFR tended to overestimate kidney function compared with Cockcroft-Gault, especially in people over 75 and under 50 kg.

claim: The European labelling convention used in UK and EU medicine leaflets defines frequency words as fixed bands: very common 1 in 10 or more; common 1 in 100 up to 1 in 10; uncommon 1 in 1,000 up to 1 in 100; rare 1 in 10,000 up to 1 in 1,000; very rare fewer than 1 in 10,000.
supporting_passage: Buchter 2014, Table 1 'European commission nomenclature for communicating frequency of adverse effects of drugs': "Very common (≥1/10) Common (≥1/100 to <1/10) Uncommon (≥1/1000 to <1/100) Rare (≥1/10000 to <1/1000) Very rare (<1/10000) Not known cannot be estimated from the available data". Knapp 2004 abstract: "verbal descriptors suggested by the European Union (EU) such as \"common\" (1-10% frequency) and \"rare\" (0.01-0.1%)"
location: Buchter 2014 Background, Table 1 (PMC full text); Knapp 2004 Abstract (Objective)
safe_wording: In a medicine leaflet, 'common' means between 1 in 100 and 1 in 10 people: at most 10 in 100, and often fewer. 'Uncommon' means between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 100. 'Rare' means between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 1,000. 'Very rare' means fewer than 1 in 10,000.
qualifications: 'Up to 1 in 10' is only the upper edge of 'common'; say so. The current EU/UK template wording printed in leaflets (for example 'may affect up to 1 in 10 people') was not opened in this project, so quote the bands, not the leaflet phrase.

claim: In a UK randomised study of 120 adults taking statins, those told constipation was 'common' estimated its likelihood at 34.2% on average, against 8.1% for those told the figure 2.5%; for pancreatitis described as 'rare', estimates were 18% with the word and 2.1% with the number 0.04%.
supporting_passage: "120 adults taking simvastatin or atorvastatin after cardiac surgery or myocardial infarction." "Cardiac rehabilitation clinics at two hospitals in Leeds, UK." "Within each side effect condition half the patients were given the information in verbal form and half in numerical form (for constipation, \"common\" or 2.5%; for pancreatitis, \"rare\" or 0.04%)." "The mean likelihood estimate given for the constipation side effect was 34.2% in the verbal group and 8.1% in the numerical group; for pancreatitis it was 18% in the verbal group and 2.1% in the numerical group."
safe_wording: In a UK study, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed about 34 in 100 people would get it. People given the actual figure, 2.5 in 100, guessed about 8 in 100. For a 'rare' side effect (4 in 10,000), the word led to an average guess of 18 in 100.
qualifications: Small study; allocation not concealed; estimates were made immediately after reading one statement, so the study shows how the words are read, not what people later did. Even the group given numbers overestimated (8.1% against 2.5%): say this plainly.

claim: The frequency words were associated with more negative views of the medicine than the equivalent numbers.
supporting_passage: Knapp 2004: "The verbal descriptors were associated with more negative perceptions of the medicine than their equivalent numerical descriptors." Berry 2003: "In all studies it was found that people significantly over-estimated the likelihood of adverse effects occurring, given specific verbal descriptors. This in turn resulted in significantly higher ratings of their perceived risks to health and significantly lower ratings of their likelihood of taking the medicine."
safe_wording: People given the words also rated the medicine more negatively, and in related studies said they were less likely to take it.
qualifications: Stated intentions on a rating scale, measured once; no study measured whether people actually stopped their medicine.

claim: A systematic review of 10 randomised trials found that verbal frequency words consistently led to overestimation of side-effect risk; numbers also led to overestimation but less.
supporting_passage: "Ten trials were included. Participants perceived probabilities presented in verbal terms as higher than in numeric terms: commonly used verbal descriptors systematically led to an overestimation of the absolute risk of adverse effects (Range of means: 3% - 54%). Numbers also led to an overestimation of probabilities, but the overestimation was smaller (2% - 20%)." Results: "MD for common side effects: -35.36 [CI: -39.92 to -30.81]". "Only between 9% and 50% of the participants in the numerical groups gave a correct probability for the adverse effects". Limitations: "Many studies were conducted with healthy volunteers and used fictional scenarios." "All outcomes were measured shortly after distribution of the information leaflets, and none of the studies had a follow-up."
location: Abstract (Results); Results (Estimation of probabilities); Description of studies; Limitations of the included studies
safe_wording: Across 10 trials, people given the leaflet words overestimated the chance of a side effect every time. People given numbers also overestimated, but by less.
qualifications: Mostly volunteers reading made-up leaflets; all trials from two UK research groups; measured immediately; no data on behaviour. For 'common' side effects the average overestimate with words was about 35 percentage points larger than with numbers: if used, call it percentage points.

claim: Current EU guidance on leaflets pairs the frequency word with a number, rather than the word alone.
supporting_passage: Buchter 2014 Discussion: "Different preferences imply that using a combined verbal and numerical format may be the best compromise to suit various needs. This is also reflected in the current European Commission Guideline on readability from 2009 as well as the current EU template for patient leaflets".
