claim: The largest trial since, MIDDEL (1,021 care home residents with dementia and depressive symptoms in 6 countries), found that neither group music therapy nor recreational choir singing reduced depressive symptoms at 6 months compared with standard care.
supporting_passage: "The trial was done in 86 care home units across Australia, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Türkiye, and the UK." ... "have mild depressive symptoms as indicated by a Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) score of at least 8" ... "The primary outcome was MADRS assessed at 6 months in the intention-to-treat population" ... "Between July 18, 2018, and Feb 1, 2023, 86 care home units with 1021 residents were enrolled and randomly assigned to one of the four groups." ... "Intention-to-treat analysis of 751 residents with data at 6 months showed no significant effect on MADRS scores of either recreational choir singing versus no recreational choir singing (β 0·4 [95% CI -1·3 to 2·1]; p=0·68), group music therapy versus no group music therapy (β 0·8 [-1·0 to 2·6]; p=0·37), or the interaction between recreational choir singing and group music therapy (β -0·6 [-3·1 to 1·9], p=0·63; β represents mean difference estimated from ANCOVA). Effects varied between countries." ... "Internationally, active group music interventions as conducted in this study do not reduce depressive symptoms more than standard care in the long term."
safe_wording: Since then, the largest trial so far, in 86 care home units in six countries including the UK, found that neither music therapy groups nor choir singing eased depressive symptoms more than usual care after 6 months.
qualifications: Results varied by country; residents all had at least mild depressive symptoms; 751 of 1,021 had 6-month data. 'Largest trial' is safe in the form 'a large trial of 1,021 residents'; the Cochrane review's biggest pooled comparison was 503 people.

claim: Daily personalised recorded music built into care did not reduce agitation or other neuropsychiatric symptoms in a Norwegian nursing home trial.
supporting_passage: "The 8-week MBC intervention included daily individualised prerecorded music integration." ... "There was no significant difference in changes either comparing the NPI-NH total score (p = 0.396) (confidence interval: CI [–2.6 to 6.6]) between the intervention group (n = 108) and the control group (n = 124) or comparing any of the three NPI subcategories: psychosis (p = 0.203) (CI [–0.5 to 2.3]), agitation (p = 0.830) (CI [–2.3 to 1.8]) or affective symptoms (p = 0.447) (CI [–0.9 to 2.1])."
safe_wording: Optional. A Norwegian trial of daily personal playlists in nursing homes also found no clear change in agitation.
qualifications: Secondary analysis; population selected for pain; one country. Supporting evidence only; not needed for the post.

claim: No serious adverse events were reported with music-based interventions.
supporting_passage: Cochrane: "Adverse effects were inconsistently measured or recorded, but no serious adverse events were reported." MIDDEL: "No related adverse events were reported and acute medical hospital admission rates were similar across groups at 3 months and 6 months."
safe_wording: No serious harms were reported.
qualifications: Harms were inconsistently recorded in the review.

claim: WHELD was a cluster-randomised trial in 69 UK nursing homes; 847 residents with dementia were randomised and 553 completed 9 months, with death the main reason for not completing.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "This was a randomised controlled cluster trial conducted between 1 January 2013 and 30 September 2015 that compared the WHELD intervention with treatment as usual (TAU) in people with dementia living in 69 UK nursing homes, using an intention to treat analysis." ... "In all, 847 people were randomised to WHELD or TAU, of whom 553 completed the 9-month randomised controlled trial." Full text, Results: "The majority of participants had moderately severe or severe dementia, and 71% were female. Follow-up assessments were available for 553 participants. Mortality accounted for the majority of participants who did not complete follow-up assessments."
safe_wording: A trial in 69 UK nursing homes followed 847 residents with dementia for 9 months. About a third did not reach the final assessment, mostly because they had died, which is expected in nursing home research.
qualifications: Primary analysis was of the 553 completers; an imputation sensitivity analysis agreed.

claim: The programme combined staff training in person-centred care, tailored social activities aiming at 60 minutes per resident per week, and a system to trigger antipsychotic review, delivered through two trained care staff champions in each home.
supporting_passage: Full text, Interventions: "The intervention focused on training in PCC for care staff and on promoting tailored person-centred activities and social interactions. The intervention also involved the development of a system for triggering appropriate review of antipsychotic medications by the prescribing physician attached to each home." ... "Two lead care staff members (WHELD champions) were nominated in each care home. These individuals received additional training over a period of 4 months (1 training day per month) with further coaching, supervision, and regular review with the therapist over the 9-month period." Box 1: "Writing strengths-based care plans and providing tailored, structured social activities that recognise people's abilities and interests, with the aim of providing 60 minutes per week per person."
safe_wording: The programme trained staff in person-centred care and built in social activities tailored to each resident's interests, aiming for an hour a week each. It also set up a way to prompt the GP to review antipsychotic medicines. Two care staff in each home were trained as champions to keep it going.
qualifications: Box 1 describes an 8-month delivery phase (months 2 to 9) with 1 off-site training day a month for champions plus 8 hours a month of on-site consultation from a therapist; the Methods text says the champions' extra training ran 'over a period of 4 months'. Keep the description of dose general.

claim: The programme improved residents' quality of life (effect size 0.24), agitation (0.23) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (0.30) by small amounts, with the largest benefits in moderately severe dementia.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "The intervention conferred a statistically significant improvement in QoL (DEMQOL-Proxy Z score 2.82, p = 0.0042; mean difference 2.54, SEM 0.88; 95% CI 0.81, 4.28; Cohen's D effect size 0.24). There were also statistically significant benefits in agitation (CMAI Z score 2.68, p = 0.0076; mean difference 4.27, SEM 1.59; 95% CI -7.39, -1.15; Cohen's D 0.23) and overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH Z score 3.52, p < 0.001; mean difference 4.55, SEM 1.28; 95% CI -7.07,-2.02; Cohen's D 0.30). Benefits were greatest in people with moderately severe dementia." ... Conclusions: "These findings suggest that the WHELD intervention confers benefits in terms of QoL, agitation, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, albeit with relatively small effect sizes". Full text, Outcome measures: "The primary outcome was QoL, measured by the DEMQOL-Proxy [], a 31-item interviewer-administered questionnaire answered by a caregiver, with a score range of 31 to 124". Discussion: "Whilst the effect sizes would be considered marginal in terms of a clinically significant benefit, we believe that the benefits to the broader population of people with dementia in care homes make this a meaningful benefit in the quality of care."
location: Abstract (Methods and findings; Conclusions); Methods (Outcome measures); Discussion
safe_wording: After 9 months, residents in the programme homes had slightly better quality of life and slightly less agitation and distress than residents in usual-care homes. The researchers described the effects as small. The benefit was clearest in people with moderately severe dementia.
qualifications: Quality of life and agitation were rated by care staff, not residents; staff in programme homes may have known their home was taking part (only the champions were excluded as informants). The authors call the effect sizes 'marginal in terms of a clinically significant benefit'. For a concrete figure: quality of life improved by about 2.5 points on a 31 to 124 scale.

claim: Positive care interactions between staff and residents increased more in programme homes.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "There was a statistically significant benefit in positive care interactions as measured by QUIS (19.7% increase, SEM 8.94; 95% CI 2.12, 37.16, p = 0.03; Cohen's D 0.55)." Full text, Results: "The quality of interactions of positive care between care staff and residents with dementia (QUIS) was collected as a care-home-level assessment in 62 of the participating care homes. There was a statistically significant 19.7% greater increase in the proportion of positive care interactions from baseline to 9 months in the WHELD group compared to the TAU group"
safe_wording: Observers also saw more positive, warm contact between staff and residents in the programme homes.
qualifications: Care-home-level measure with a wide confidence interval; the 19.7% figure is ambiguous (relative or percentage points), so avoid quoting it.

claim: Antipsychotic use was already low (under 10%) and was not reduced.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Antipsychotic drug use was at a low stable level in both treatment groups, and the intervention did not reduce use." Full text, Results: "no reduction in antipsychotic use in the WHELD treatment group compared to TAU (change in antipsychotic use: WHELD −0.1%, SEM 0.1; TAU −0.2%, SEM 0.1, [p =] 0.60; antipsychotic use at 9 months: WHELD versus TAU relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.82, [p =] 0.82)". Discussion: "Interestingly, there was a low baseline use of antipsychotic medications (<10%) in this study" ... "This is likely attributable to a combination of the low baseline levels of antipsychotic prescription and the more limited education programme for primary care physicians within the current study than in the previous factorial RCT".
safe_wording: The result that went the other way: antipsychotic use did not fall. But fewer than 1 in 10 residents were taking antipsychotics at the start, and the GPs were given only limited training.
qualifications: Baseline 9.2% (usual care) and 8.9% (WHELD) of the randomised cohort. In the full-text quotation, '[p =]' marks characters lost in the PMC text extraction.

claim: The programme reduced costs compared with usual care.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "The WHELD intervention reduced cost compared to TAU, and the benefits achieved were therefore associated with a cost saving." Full text, Cost analysis: "The direct cost of delivering the intervention compared to TAU was £8,627 more per home." ... "Delivery of the intervention to residents incurred an additional £130 per person per month." ... "Analysis of service use showed higher healthcare costs unrelated to the intervention in the TAU group compared to the WHELD intervention group." Table 5 (9-month follow-up): "Accommodation charges" ... "−4,399" "−5,725 to −2,898"; "Primary care" ... "−320"; "Total health and social care costs" "29,702" ... "34,442" ... "−4,740" "−6,129 to −3,156". Baseline: "Total health and social care costs" ... "−768" "−1,249 to −338".
safe_wording: The researchers reported that overall care costs were lower in the programme homes, even after paying for the programme. Most of that difference came from care home fees, which were already lower in those homes at the start. Treat the cost result with caution and do not lead with it.
qualifications: Of the £4,740 lower 9-month cost, £4,399 was accommodation charges. Baseline costs already differed by £768 (lower in intervention homes). The intervention is unlikely to have changed fees directly, and the authors describe the healthcare cost difference as 'unrelated to the intervention'. Table 5's title says 'unadjusted' but its footnote lists covariates.

claim: The trial tested the programme as a package; the authors thought the structured social activities probably contributed the added benefit; sustaining it with staff turnover is a challenge.
supporting_passage: Discussion: "That study reported a reduction in QoL following antipsychotic review that was mediated by social interaction within the context of an overall PCC training paradigm for care staff []. We would speculate that the added benefit was probably a reflection of the structured approach to promoting pleasant activities involving social interaction." ... "Elements of the WHELD intervention, such as social interaction and pleasant events, have previously been demonstrated to improve agitation in modest-sized RCTs" ... "A key issue for future studies is the sustainability of the intervention, particularly with turnover of staff, including the WHELD champions." ... "In what is, to our knowledge, the largest RCT conducted of a staff training and non-pharmacological intervention for people with dementia living in nursing homes"
safe_wording: The trial tested the whole package, so it cannot say which part did the good. The researchers' own view was that the planned social activities, about an hour a week per resident, probably mattered most; that is a reasonable first step for a home, but it is a judgement, not a tested result.
qualifications: Authors' speculation; label it as such. The first-step suggestion for managers is editorial judgement.

claim: When the lecanemab trial's entry rules were applied to 237 older people with early memory problems and amyloid on a brain scan in a US population study, 112 (47.3%) met the inclusion criteria and 19 (8%) remained after the exclusion criteria.
supporting_passage: Two hundred thirty-seven MCSA participants (mean age [SD] 80.9 [6.3] years, 54.9% male, and 97.5% White) with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild dementia and increased brain amyloid burden by PiB PET comprised the study sample. Lecanemab trial's inclusion criteria reduced the study sample to 112 (47.3% of 237) participants. The trial's exclusion criteria further narrowed the number of potentially eligible participants to 19 (overall 8% of 237).
safe_wording: In a US population study, 237 older people (average age 81) had early memory problems and amyloid on a brain scan. When the lecanemab trial's entry rules were applied, 19 of them, about 8 in 100, would have qualified for the trial.
qualifications: Say 'would have qualified for the trial' or 'met the trial's entry rules', not 'eligible for treatment': trial criteria are stricter than the licence and real-world use recommendations. One US study; 97.5% White. Relaxing the cognitive criteria to include everyone with MCI raised trial eligibility to 17.4% of those with MCI.

claim: The most common reasons people fell outside the trial rules were other long-term health conditions and brain scan findings.
supporting_passage: Pittock 2023: "Common exclusions were related to other chronic conditions and neuroimaging findings." Borgström Bolmsjö 2026: "In total, 180 participants had any comorbidity or ongoing treatments incompatible with ATT, of whom 98 were receiving anticoagulant therapy. Most participants met multiple exclusion criteria (Fig.), with 102 patients (16.8%) fulfilling five or more criteria simultaneously." and "At the same time, MRI abnormalities were common overall, affecting nearly 200 (32.3%) participants, most often in combination with other exclusion criteria. Severe white matter disease (Fazekas score 3) was the most frequent imaging-based exclusion (= 156; 25.7%)."
location: Pittock 2023 Abstract, Results; Borgström Bolmsjö 2026 full text, Results, 'Specific exclusion criteria' and Table 2
safe_wording: People were mostly ruled out by other health problems and by brain scan findings. In a Swedish primary care study of 607 people with memory symptoms, about 1 in 6 were taking a blood thinner (anticoagulant), which rules out lecanemab, and about 1 in 4 had marked changes in the brain's small blood vessels on MRI. Most people who were ruled out had more than one reason.
qualifications: Pittock gives only the broad categories; the specific counts come from the Swedish primary care study, which applied use recommendations rather than trial rules. Anticoagulants rule out lecanemab under the use recommendations quoted (the FDA allows anticoagulants with donanemab). Exclusion reasons overlap, so the proportions must not be added.

claim: In a primary care population (the typical route for older people with memory concerns), about 1 in 7 people presenting with cognitive symptoms met real-world eligibility criteria for lecanemab after a full work-up.
supporting_passage: In a full diagnostic work-up of 607 patients with sequential exclusions, 86 patients (14.2%) and 78 patients (12.8%) ultimately met the eligibility criteria for lecanemab and donanemab, respectively. Due to comorbidities, medication use, and age/BMI, around 1/3 of the original population was excluded. Most ineligible patients met more than one exclusion criterion. The eligible population was 63% female, mean age 77 years. ... Importantly, clinical eligibility does not equate to treatment initiation.
safe_wording: In a Swedish study of 607 people who went to their GP with memory symptoms, 86 (about 1 in 7) met the criteria for lecanemab after full tests. About a third were ruled out early by other illnesses, medicines, age or weight.
qualifications: Denominator is everyone presenting with cognitive symptoms, including people with only subjective complaints and people whose problems were not due to Alzheimer's disease; about half were amyloid negative. Excluding APOE e4 homozygotes, as European guidance requires, reduced eligibility to 75 (12.4%). One Swedish region; research setting. Eligibility is not the same as being offered or choosing treatment.

claim: Frail older people were much less likely to meet the Clarity AD trial criteria than pre-frail older people, although about half of frail people met real-world use recommendations.
supporting_passage: The median age of the sample was 82.0 years (IQR: 79-85); 65% (n = 78) were women, and 36.7% (n = 44) were frail. Overall, 20.0% (n = 24) met the Clarity-AD eligibility criteria, while 50.8% (n = 61) and 47.5% (n = 57) were potentially eligible according to the American and French AURs, respectively. Only 9.1% (n = 4) of frail individuals met the Clarity-AD criteria, compared to 26.3% (n = 20) of pre-frail participants (p = 0.042). In contrast, 50.0% (n = 22) and 45.5% (n = 20) of frail individuals were potentially eligible according to the American and French AURs, respectively.
safe_wording: Among 120 older people (median age 82) with amyloid and early memory problems, 1 in 5 would have qualified for the lecanemab trial. Among the 44 who were frail, only 4 would have qualified. Under the looser rules now used in clinics, about half of the frail group could be considered for treatment.
qualifications: Small study; 44 frail people. The contrast shows that trial evidence says little about frail people, not that frail people cannot be treated. Keep trial rules and clinic rules clearly separate.

claim: In Clarity AD (people aged 50 to 90 with early Alzheimer's disease), lecanemab slowed decline on the 18-point CDR-SB by 0.45 points over 18 months compared with placebo; brain swelling or fluid on MRI (ARIA-E) occurred in 12.6% of people on lecanemab.
supporting_passage: We conducted an 18-month, multicenter, double-blind, phase 3 trial involving persons 50 to 90 years of age with early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease) with evidence of amyloid on positron-emission tomography (PET) or by cerebrospinal fluid testing. ... The primary end point was the change from baseline at 18 months in the score on the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; range, 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater impairment). ... The adjusted least-squares mean change from baseline at 18 months was 1.21 with lecanemab and 1.66 with placebo (difference, -0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.67 to -0.23; P<0.001). ... Lecanemab resulted in infusion-related reactions in 26.4% of the participants and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%.
safe_wording: In the main trial, people on lecanemab declined a little more slowly than people on a dummy drip: 0.45 points less on an 18-point scale of memory and daily function over 18 months. About 1 in 8 people on lecanemab had brain swelling or fluid on their scans, and about 1 in 4 had reactions to the drip.
qualifications: Optional context only; the editor asked the post to lead with access. Do NOT use the placebo ARIA-E rate (1.7%), which was not verified. Give the difference on the 18-point scale; do not convert to a percentage slowing. ARIA-E is mostly seen on scans; do not describe all cases as symptomatic.

claim: The UK medicines regulator (MHRA) approved lecanemab in August 2024.
supporting_passage: The decision by the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) to approve lecanemab in August 2024 followed similar regulatory decisions in the US and Japan. ... The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has not recommended lecanemab for use in early AD amid concerns, including treatment cost and the translation of efficacy outcomes into clinically meaningful improvement.
safe_wording: Lecanemab was licensed in the UK in August 2024.
qualifications: Optional. State only the dated licensing fact. Do not state NICE's current position or imply any view on NHS funding (editor's values concern); the NICE statement reflects early 2025 and could not be checked against current NICE guidance.

claim: An English cohort study followed 9,324 people with dementia aged 65 or over for a year, comparing those who saw the same GP most consistently with those who saw the same GP least consistently.
supporting_passage: A retrospective cohort study with 1 year of follow-up anonymised medical records from 9324 patients with dementia, aged ≥65 years living in England in 2016. ... At the study start date, all patients were aged ≥65 years, registered with a practice, and had at least three consultations (required for calculating continuity) during a 1-year lead-in period (1 January 2015 until 31 December 2015). ... There were 9324 individuals who were diagnosed with dementia before the study start date (age mean 84.5 years, SD 7.4, 65.7% female) and met the inclusion criteria.
location: Abstract, Design and setting; full text, Method (Population) and Results
safe_wording: A study of 9,324 people with dementia in England (average age 84) compared those who saw the same GP most often with those who saw the same GP least often.
qualifications: Continuity was measured with established indices (for example the share of consultations with the most-seen GP), not a simple count of different GPs; the post's 'count the doctors' idea is a practical proxy, not the study's measure. People with fewer than 3 GP consultations were excluded.

claim: People in the highest continuity quarter had fewer prescribed medicines (mean 8.5 vs 9.7) and fewer potentially inappropriate prescriptions (mean 2.1 vs 2.5) than those in the lowest quarter.
supporting_passage: Patients in the HQ of the UPC had fewer prescriptions (mean 8.52, SD 4.75) than those in the LQ (mean 9.67, SD 5.31,<0.01). A fully adjusted negative binomial regression model confirmed a dose–response relationship with fewer medications by increasing quartiles of UPC (). ... Patients in the HQ of the UPC had significantly fewer instances of PIP (mean 2.09, SD 2.06) compared with the LQ (mean 2.50, SD 2.28,<0.01). Negative binomial regression models confirmed this reduction in PIP was statistically significant (). Higher levels of CGPC were not associated with the likelihood of having ≥1 PIP. Table 2 (Usual Provider of Care Index, High quartile): number of prescriptions IRR 0.96 (0.93 to 0.98); potentially inappropriate prescribing IRR 0.93 (0.88 to 0.97); footnote: IRRs estimated using negative binomial regression model, stratified by quartile of CGPC and adjusted for age, sex, 14 comorbidities, and frailty status.
location: Full text, Results ('Treatment of patients with dementia') and Table 2
safe_wording: People with dementia who saw the same GP most consistently were prescribed fewer medicines on average: 8.5 compared with 9.7 in those with the least consistency. They also had fewer prescriptions that are often unsafe in older age: 2.1 compared with 2.5. After allowing for age, other illnesses and frailty, the difference was smaller but remained.
qualifications: The 8.5 vs 9.7 and 2.1 vs 2.5 figures are UNADJUSTED averages; the candidate's visual label 'linked with, after adjustment' is wrong for these bars. Label them 'average, before adjustment' and state that the adjusted difference was smaller (about 4% fewer medicines and about 7% fewer inappropriate prescriptions). Continuity was not linked with whether a person had at least one inappropriate prescription. Link, not proof of cause.

claim: Highest continuity was associated with lower odds of newly recorded incontinence (OR 0.42) and emergency hospital admission (OR 0.90) over a year, after adjustment for age, sex, deprivation, 14 conditions, frailty and number of consultations.
supporting_passage: Patients in the HQ of the UPC, compared with those in the quartile with least continuity (LQ), displayed reduction in risk of delirium by 34.8% (odds ratio [OR] 0.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.51 to 0.84,<0.01), reduction in risk of incontinence by 57.9% (OR 0.42, 95% CI = 0.31 to 0.58,<0.01), and reduction in risk of emergency admission to hospital by 9.7% (OR 0.90, 95% CI = 0.82 to 0.99,= 0.03). ... Censoring the first 6 months of follow-up did not significantly alter the association with delirium and incontinence, although emergency admission to hospital became non-significant (Supplementary Table S7). ... All models were adjusted for age (squared), sex, quintiles of multiple deprivation, diagnosis of 14 chronic conditions (listed in), frailty classification based on the Electronic Frailty Index, and the number of consultations during the lead-in period (a proxy of medical needs).
location: Full text, Results ('CGPC and AHOs') and Method (Statistical analysis)
safe_wording: Over the following year, people who saw the same GP most consistently were less likely to have new incontinence recorded and slightly less likely to be admitted to hospital as an emergency. The study shows a link; it does not prove that seeing the same GP caused these differences.
qualifications: Relative measures only; do not convert OR 0.42 into 'less than half as likely' or into '58% less' and do not derive absolute differences. The admission link was small and lost statistical significance when the first 6 months were excluded, so present it as weak. Incontinence here means a new diagnosis recorded in GP notes (3.5% of the whole cohort had one), so recording practices may contribute. Do not use the delirium result (collection excludes delirium as a topic).

claim: The study is observational and cannot show that continuity causes these differences.
supporting_passage: The observational nature of this study provides data on statistical associations but cannot indicate causation. ... Study design and sensitivity analyses excluding the first 6 months of follow-up minimise the potential role of reverse-causation driving the findings.
safe_wording: This kind of study shows a link, not proof that seeing the same GP causes fewer problems. People who are more unwell may also see more different doctors.
qualifications: The authors elsewhere write that continuity 'leads to better health outcomes'; do not repeat that causal wording.

claim: A separate Canadian study of 22,060 community-dwelling people with dementia found that those who saw the same primary care doctor at every visit had fewer hospital admissions and emergency department visits over the following year.
supporting_passage: Population-based sample of 22,060 community-dwelling 65 + persons with dementia on March 31st, 2015, with at least two primary care visits in the preceding year (mean age 81 years, 60% female). ... High primary care continuity on March 31st, 2015, i.e., having had every primary care visit with the same primary care physician, during the preceding year. ... Among the 22,060 persons, compared with the persons with low primary care continuity, the 14,515 (65.8%) persons with high primary care continuity had a lower risk of ACSC hospitalization (general population definition) (relative risk reduction 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94), ACSC hospitalization (older population definition) (0.87, 0.79-0.95), 30-day hospital readmission (0.81, 0.72-0.92), hospitalization (0.90, 0.86-0.94), and emergency department visit (0.92, 0.90-0.95).
safe_wording: A study of 22,060 people with dementia in Quebec found the same pattern: those who saw the same family doctor at every visit had somewhat fewer hospital admissions and emergency visits in the next year.
qualifications: Observational (propensity weighting). Effect sizes are modest; the abstract's labelling of the estimates is ambiguous ('relative risk reduction 0.82'), so describe in words ('somewhat fewer') rather than quoting numbers. Canada.

claim: Most UK general practices do not routinely measure continuity of GP care, although validated measures exist.
supporting_passage: Dineen 2025: "The Welsh Government has recognised that an important drawback is that most practices in the UK do not currently measure their continuity, despite the existence of several validated measures (for example, the Usual Provider of Care Index [UPC] or the St Leonard's Index of Continuity of Care [SLICC])." and "What the contract does not yet offer is any guidance or incentive for practices to deliver relational continuity of care to the patients that have been identified, nor is there any requirement to measure or evaluate the continuity that is already being delivered." Engamba 2026: "With the new GP contract in England highlighting the need for primary care providers to monitor and deliver relational continuity, it is more crucial than ever to understand how best to achieve it."
safe_wording: GP researchers wrote in 2025 that most UK practices did not measure how often patients see the same GP, even though simple measures exist.
qualifications: Attribute it ('GP researchers wrote in 2025'); it is an expert statement citing the Welsh Government, not a survey result. Do not say 'nobody counts it' or 'practices never measure it'. Policy is moving: the 2025-26 England contract encouraged practices to consider continuity, and a 2026 protocol says the new England contract highlights monitoring it.

claim: Having a named GP is not the same as seeing the same GP: England's named accountable GP policy for people over 74 (April 2014) was not followed by better continuity or fewer emergency admissions.
supporting_passage: National Health Service policy to introduce a named accountable GP for patients aged over 74 in April 2014. ... The intervention was associated with a decrease in continuity index-scores of -0.024 (95% CI -0.030 to -0.018, p<0.001) ... The introduction of the named GP scheme was not associated with improvements in either continuity of care or rates of unplanned hospitalisation.
safe_wording: In England, people over 75 were given a named GP from 2014, but a study found this did not increase how often they saw the same GP. So the useful request is to book with the same GP each time, not only to know who the named GP is.
qualifications: Observational policy evaluation; the policy was later extended but that extension was not verified here. The family action ('ask to book with the same GP each time and keep a note of who you saw') is a practical suggestion (judgement) that follows from the evidence, not a tested intervention.

claim: Continuity can be counted simply, for example as the percentage of appointments with the patient's own doctor.
supporting_passage: The percentage of face-to-face appointments for patients on each doctor's list, with the patient's personal doctor (the SLICC), was calculated monthly. ... Overall, 51.7% (95% confidence interval = 51.2 to 52.2) of GP appointments were with the patients' personal doctor. Patients aged ≥65 years had a higher level of continuity with 64.9% of appointments being with their personal doctor. ... This method could provide working GPs with a simple way to track continuity of care and inform practice management and decision making.
safe_wording: Practices can count continuity simply: the share of a person's appointments that are with their own GP.
qualifications: Single practice that organises care around personal lists; its percentages are not typical and should not be presented as a benchmark.

claim: In 89 nursing home residents with advanced dementia and frequent agitation in six Maryland nursing homes, raters identified about three unmet needs per resident; the commonest were loneliness or need for social contact and boredom, followed by need for meaningful activity.
supporting_passage: Participants were 89 NH residents (mean age=85.9) with a diagnosis of dementia, according to their medical chart, from 6 NHs in Maryland, USA. ... (b) The resident had been identified by nursing staff as exhibiting either verbal agitation or physical non-aggressive agitation several times a day ... The mean MMSE score was 7.6. ... The most common needs were loneliness/need for social contact and boredom/sensory deprivation, noted for about two thirds of the sample by RAs and for approximately half by NAs, followed by the need for a meaningful activity, which was noted for around half the sample by both sources. ... RAs reported an average of 2.9 unmet needs per participant (range 0–7, s.d.=1.3) and NAs reported an average of 2.6 unmet needs per participant (range 0–6, s.d.=1.4).
safe_wording: In one US study of 89 care home residents with advanced dementia who were often agitated, staff and researchers found about three unmet needs per person. The commonest were loneliness and boredom, each noted for about half to two thirds of residents, then having nothing meaningful to do, noted for about half.
qualifications: One small US study of people with advanced dementia and non-aggressive agitation (calling out, restlessness), not aggression. 'Unmet needs' are judgements by researchers and care staff, not measured causes. Name the study's limits in the post ('one US study of 89 residents').

claim: Pain and discomfort were also common and were probably under-detected by staff; boredom and loneliness sit alongside, not instead of, physical causes.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Based on results and independent ratings of pain, the authors estimate notable under-detection of discomfort and pain by both types of informants." Full text: "The following unmet needs were found for over half of the residents: loneliness/need for social contact, boredom, need for meaningful activity, pain, and discomfort. Moreover, each study participant was rated as having at least one unmet need."
location: Abstract; full text, Results 3.4 (authors' revised estimate)
safe_wording: The same study found that pain and physical discomfort were also common and were often missed. So checking for pain comes first, and asking about company and occupation comes next, not instead.
qualifications: The 'over half' figures are the authors' revised estimates, not direct ratings. Supports the judge's sharpening: state that this question follows a check for physical causes.

claim: The Unmet Needs Model proposes that distressed behaviour in dementia arises from needs the person can no longer communicate or meet for themselves.
supporting_passage: The Unmet Needs Model states that problem behaviors of people with dementia result from unmet needs stemming from a decreased ability to communicate those needs and to provide for oneself.
safe_wording: One way of understanding distressed behaviour in dementia is that it often signals a need the person can no longer put into words or meet for themselves.
qualifications: A model, not a proven law: say 'often' or 'one way of understanding'. Avoid 'problem behaviours' in the post; use 'distressed behaviour' (house style).

claim: The needs were raters' judgements and the two groups of raters agreed poorly on which residents had which need.
supporting_passage: The agreement rate between RAs and NAs averaged 86% for all types of needs, and kappas averaged .25. Based on our examination of the results, this indicates high agreement when most of the residents do not exhibit the need, but much lower agreement when determining which residents actually experience a specific unmet need.
safe_wording: Working out which need lies behind distress is hard: care staff and researchers often disagreed about which residents had which need.
qualifications: Include as the limitation, or omit the detail and say 'one small study'. Supports the practical point that several people who know the person should be asked.

claim: Care home residents spend much of the day inactive.
supporting_passage: Participants were 723 home residents in 7 nursing homes. ... Nursing homes in the Netherlands (19 psychogeriatric and 11 somatic wards). ... Nursing home residents of both psychogeriatric and somatic wards were mainly observed partaking in in activities, such as sleeping, doing nothing, and watching TV (range: 45%-77% of the 5 observation times). ... Residents were largely observed in a lying or sitting position (range: 89%-92%). ... Most of the psychogeriatric and somatic nursing home residents spend their day inactive in a lying or sitting position in the ward.
safe_wording: When researchers observed 723 residents of Dutch nursing homes at random times of day, residents were mostly asleep, doing nothing or watching television, in 45% to 77% of observations depending on the time of day.
qualifications: Netherlands, 2015; includes residents with and without dementia (psychogeriatric and somatic wards pooled). Say 'in one Dutch study'. Do not present as a UK figure.

claim: Addressing hypothesised unmet needs with individualised non-drug interventions reduced agitation in a randomised trial.
supporting_passage: Agitated nursing home residents with advanced dementia (from 9 nursing homes in 5 locations in Maryland, United States) were randomized into an intervention group (n = 89) and a placebo control group (n = 36). On the basis of data from baseline assessment, a systematic methodology for individualizing nonpharmacologic interventions, Treatment Routes for Exploring Agitation (TREA), was used with the intervention group: an unmet need was hypothesized, a corresponding treatment category was identified, and specifics of the treatment were chosen to fit the person's need, past identity, preferences, and abilities. ... TREA interventions were implemented for 2 weeks ... Relative to a control group, TREA interventions for unmet needs produced statistically significant declines in total (P < .001), physical nonaggressive (P < .001), and verbal agitation (P = .004) and significant increases in pleasure (P < .001) and interest (P < .05).
safe_wording: In a US trial, matching activities and company to each resident's likely unmet need reduced agitation and increased signs of pleasure over two weeks, compared with a control group.
qualifications: Short (2 weeks), small control group (36), US, by the same research team; effect sizes not given in the abstract. Say 'in a short US trial'.

claim: In 2016 the Mental Health Foundation published a UK inquiry, 'What is truth?', on truth and lying in dementia care.
supporting_passage: James and Caiazza 2018 (abstract): "Their use is complex and controversial, and a number of protocols have been produced to guide their usage (Mental Health Foundation, 2016)." Murray 2025 (full text): "investigated if, why, when and how non-truth telling is justified." Search extract (WebSearch summary, not verbatim from the page): the Mental Health Foundation page titled 'What is truth? An inquiry about truth and lying in dementia care'; report published December 2016; panel included people living with a diagnosis of dementia and family carers.
location: WebSearch results (mentalhealth.org.uk publication page); James and Caiazza 2018 abstract; Murray 2025 full text, Background
safe_wording: In 2016 a UK inquiry by the Mental Health Foundation looked at truth and untruths in dementia care.
qualifications: The report was not opened. Do not quote it or describe its panel or methods in detail. Title and year are corroborated by a peer-reviewed citation.

claim: The inquiry concluded that truth should be the starting point, that repeating a painful truth may not be in the person's interest, and that untruths should be a last resort, used with good intent.
supporting_passage: Murray 2025: "The report concludes that whilst telling the truth must always be the starting point, it may not be in a person's best interest, to continue to repeat that truth. In some instances, in order to reduce distress, it may be beneficial to consider a continuum from whole truth telling to lying, with lying being used as a last resort. What was repeated throughout the report was the significance of intent in relation to telling a lie, and the inquiry only focused on instances where lies would be told with best intent, whilst acknowledging that this may not always be the case." Search extract (not verbatim from the report): the report 'endorsed the use of untruths in dementia care if they are used in the best interests of people with dementia'; 'the choice to use an untruth in dementia care should not be taken lightly'.
location: Murray 2025 full text, Background (secondary description of the report); WebSearch extracts
safe_wording: A 2016 UK inquiry concluded that the truth should be the starting point. It also said that repeating a painful truth again and again may not be in the person's interest, and that an untruth should be a last resort, used only for the person's good.
qualifications: Secondary source: attribute as 'a 2016 UK inquiry concluded' and paraphrase; no quotation marks around the report's words. In the PMC text the reference name is stripped; the match to the Mental Health Foundation report rests on context and on search extracts that attribute the same wording to it.

claim: The inquiry described a specific range of responses: truth-telling, looking for the meaning of the question, going along with the person, and lying as a last resort.
supporting_passage: Only the ends of the range are verified: "... it may be beneficial to consider a continuum from whole truth telling to lying, with lying being used as a last resort." (Murray 2025, describing the report). The intermediate steps named in the candidate were not found in any opened source as the inquiry's words.
safe_wording: Do not present a named scale of responses as the inquiry's. The post may say the inquiry described a range from the whole truth to an untruth as a last resort. Middle options (responding to the feeling, going along with) can be described as approaches reported in other studies: staff in Spanish care homes described distraction and calming as responses 'in-between' (Villar 2025), and 'going along with' was one category observed on UK dementia wards (Murray 2025).
qualifications: The candidate's visual scale (gentle truth; look for the meaning; change the subject kindly; go along with; untruth as last resort) must not be credited to the inquiry. It can appear as an illustrative range labelled as such, or be replaced by the test 'What would help this person now?' (judgement).

claim: Repeating news of a death to a person with dementia causes fresh grief each time.
supporting_passage: No finding located. Background statements only: Murray 2025 (Background, citing others): "The difficulty is that telling the truth to patients with dementia can often cause major distress or do certain harm, for example, when a person with dementia is asking after a deceased relative." Casey 2020 (Abstract background): "A common symptom of cognitive decline in people living with dementia ... is the person repeatedly asking for loved ones who are deceased or making statements that are incorrect. Carers are then faced with a dilemma, do they avoid and distract or 'correct' the person and tell the 'truth', or tell a lie."
safe_wording: Do not state as fact that repeated news of a death causes fresh grief. Frame it as the carer's dilemma: 'Should I tell her again that he has died, or not?' The inquiry's view that repeating a painful truth may not be in the person's interest (C08-27-b) can carry the point.
qualifications: No empirical study located; Scite and Consensus were unavailable (usage limits) and PubMed searches found none.

claim: People with memory problems and their carers considered a 'good lie' to relieve distress acceptable only in some circumstances: with the intention to do good, by someone who knows the person, and never to deceive for harm.
supporting_passage: Three focus group's with a purposive sample of people with memory problems ( = 14) and three focus group's with informal/unpaid carers ( = 18) were undertaken. ... All participants considered that blatant lying with the intention to deceive and do harm is not acceptable. However, telling a 'good lie' or 'white lie' to alleviate distress was in certain circumstances considered acceptable. The intention behind the 'lie' in their view had to be to do good, and the informal/unpaid carer telling the lie had to really 'know the person' and be cognisant of family preferences. ... Lying was only considered acceptable in the context of knowing the person and when done with the intention not to harm or deceive, undertaken with empathy, and only for the purpose of mitigating the person living with dementia's distress.
safe_wording: In an Irish study, people with memory problems and family carers said that deceiving someone to harm them is never acceptable. A 'white lie' to ease distress could be acceptable, but only from someone who knows the person well and only to help them.
qualifications: Small qualitative study (32 people). Views, not outcomes. Valuable because people with memory problems themselves took part; say so.

claim: When staff told untruths on dementia wards, how and why they said it mattered: responses motivated by the person's needs, with empathy and validation of feelings, went well; those motivated by the carer's convenience were less effective. Asking for a relative who had often died was a frequent situation.
supporting_passage: Data were collected across the two sites over a period of 4 months which equated to 338 hours of observation time. 250 lies or untruths were recorded during this period from 63 participants. ... The study defined avoidance as not wanting to cause upset by confronting people with the truth. A frequent example was when a patient was looking for a relative, who was often deceased. ... Motivation and validation on the part of the teller are the indicative elements as to whether the lie is likely to be effective or therapeutic. When the teller demonstrates empathy and understanding with the aim of meeting the needs of the patient, the result of the interaction was always positive. ... If the motivation is to meet the needs of the nurse or carer, it is far less likely to be effective.
location: Full text, Methods (Data collection), Results (Avoidance; The Lie ARM) and Discussion
safe_wording: Researchers who watched staff on two UK dementia wards found that people often asked for a relative who had died. What helped was less the words chosen than the reason and the manner: responses aimed at the person's needs, given warmly and acknowledging their feelings, went well; those aimed at getting a task done went less well.
qualifications: Qualitative, one observer, hospital staff not families, moderate to severe dementia. 'Always positive' is the authors' observation in this sample; do not generalise it. Mark the post's position (any departure from the literal truth should serve the person, not the carer's convenience) as judgement, supported by this observation.

claim: Care staff are often unsure how to respond when a person with dementia believes they are living in the past, and practice varies.
supporting_passage: Forty-two staff members working in four Spanish long-term care facilities were interviewed. ... All the participants mentioned having experienced a situation similar to that described in the vignette. In the case of common practices, lying was the most frequently mentioned strategy. As for best practices, lying and telling the truth were mentioned as well as responses that lie in-between, such as distracting or relaxing. However, most assistant carers reported that they do not know how a challenging false belief should be managed.
safe_wording: In a Spanish study, all 42 care staff interviewed had faced a resident reliving the past. Most care assistants said they did not know how such a situation should be handled.
qualifications: Small qualitative study in Spain; staff views, not family carers.

claim: In a systematic review of capacity for treatment decisions in adult medical patients, MMSE scores below 20 made incapacity more likely, scores of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood, and scores above 24 made incapacity less likely.
supporting_passage: Although not designed to assess incapacity, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores less than 20 increased the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 6.3; 95% CI, 3.7-11), scores of 20 to 24 had no effect (LR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.53-1.2), and scores greater than 24 significantly lowered the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.06-0.34). ... The MMSE is useful only at extreme scores.
safe_wording: In a large review of studies of treatment decisions, an MMSE score below 20 made it more likely that a patient lacked capacity. A score of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood either way. A score above 24 made it less likely. The authors concluded the MMSE is useful only at extreme scores.
qualifications: Say 'decisions about treatment' (the studies were of treatment decisions in medical patients, not decisions about where to live). Say the MMSE was not designed to assess capacity. For practitioners the likelihood ratios (6.3, 0.87, 0.14) may be given; for the public say 'more likely', 'no change', 'less likely'. Do not convert the likelihood ratios into 'X times more likely' or into a probability without stating the starting probability.

claim: A score above 24 lowers but does not rule out incapacity; a decision-specific assessment is still needed.
supporting_passage: Sessums 2011: "scores greater than 24 significantly lowered the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.06-0.34)"; "Evaluation of the capacity of a patient to make medical decisions should occur in the context of specific medical decisions when incapacity is considered." Orr and Baruah 2018: "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Poole 2014 (Discussion): "The MMSE neither determines residence capacity, nor any other specific capacity [41]."
location: Sessums abstract (Context, Results); Orr 2018 full text ('Capacity: evolution of case law'); Poole 2014 full text, Discussion
safe_wording: A high score lowers the chance that someone lacks capacity, but it does not rule it out. Capacity is judged one decision at a time, so a test score can prompt an assessment but can't replace it.
qualifications: The judge asked for a link to executive impairment; the evidence opened here does not quantify how often people with high MMSE scores lack capacity because of executive problems (see C09-12-b on the thin evidence for the 'frontal lobe paradox'). Say 'can still lack capacity for a complex decision' as a reasoned point, not as a measured rate.

claim: In 37 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, MMSE scores of 21 to 25 did not separate those with and without capacity well.
supporting_passage: In this study of 37 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, a fairly wide range of MMSE scores (21 to 25, which includes an often used cutoff for "normal") did not discriminate capacity status well.
safe_wording: An earlier study of 37 people with Alzheimer's disease found the same pattern: scores of 21 to 25 did not reliably separate people who could consent from those who could not.
qualifications: The decision studied was consent to research, not treatment; the sample was small. Use as corroboration, not as the headline.

claim: Incapacity for treatment decisions was common among medical inpatients and often missed by clinicians; the Aid to Capacity Evaluation had useful test characteristics and is freely available.
supporting_passage: Incapacity was uncommon in healthy elderly control participants (2.8%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.7%-3.9%) compared with medicine inpatients (26%; 95% CI, 18%-35%). Clinicians accurately diagnosed incapacity (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] of 7.9; 95% CI, 2.7-13), although they recognized it in only 42% (95% CI, 30%-53%) of affected patients. ... The ACE was validated in the largest study; it is freely available online and includes a training module.
safe_wording: In the same review, about 1 in 4 medical inpatients lacked capacity for a treatment decision, and clinicians recognised it in about 4 in 10 of those patients. The Aid to Capacity Evaluation (ACE) had useful accuracy and is free to use.
qualifications: Optional context. '26%' is a pooled estimate across studies with a wide interval (18% to 35%); 'about 1 in 4' is a fair plain reading. The 42% is recognition among patients who lacked capacity, not among all patients.

claim: In CC v KK (Court of Protection, England and Wales, 2012) an 82-year-old woman with vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease and hemiplegia, whom several professionals had assessed as lacking capacity to decide where to live, was found by the judge to have that capacity.
supporting_passage: Hughes 2015: "The case concerned an 82-year-old woman, KK, who had hemiplegia, Parkinson's disease and vascular dementia. She was totally dependent on others for her personal care, frequently sought help by the use of a telecare alarm service and showed considerable anxiety. Finally, she was admitted to a nursing home with dehydration and a urinary tract infection. But she wanted to return home. Her case involved a number of professionals assessing her capacity on a number of occasions. They all found that she lacked residence capacity, but Mr Justice Baker determined otherwise." Ruck Keene 2019: "One of the other cases in which the judge showed clear commitment to fully articulating and applying the functional conception of capacity (and in doing so, overruled expert evidence) was CC v KK [2012] EWCOP 2136, concerning the capacity of an elderly woman with dementia to make decisions about her residence and care."
location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'Approaches to assessment: outcome v. functional'; Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Discussion
safe_wording: In a 2012 Court of Protection case in England, an 82-year-old woman with dementia wanted to go home from a nursing home. Professionals had repeatedly judged that she lacked capacity to decide where to live. The judge found that she had it.
qualifications: One first-instance judgment in England and Wales; it binds no other court and Scotland has different legislation (Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000). Say 'a judge found', not 'the law says'. Do not add details of her care or outcome beyond these sources.

claim: The judge said the person must be presented with detailed options so that their ability to weigh them can be fairly assessed.
supporting_passage: Moreover, different individuals may give different weight to different factors; and capacity assessors should not start with a blank canvas: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed" (CC v KK, para 68).
location: Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Discussion (quoting CC v KK para 68)
safe_wording: The judge said: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed."
qualifications: Quote exactly as above and attribute to CC v KK, para 68 (as quoted in Ruck Keene et al 2019). Do not paraphrase as 'the law requires'.

claim: For a decision about where to live, the information the person should be given includes why a move is proposed, the other options (for example home with extra help), and the likely consequences of each choice and of not deciding, stated honestly for the care home option too.
supporting_passage: Box 4: "The person should know why a change of residence is being proposed ... The person should know what is being proposed (e.g. they should know that it is being suggested they should move into a care home) The person should be informed if there are other options (e.g. that they could go home but extra help is recommended because of the risks identified) The person should understand the likely consequences of making any particular decision, including a decision not to follow the advice being given, as well as the consequences of making no decision at all". Worked example: "an alternative would be for him to go home with professional carers coming in to see him several times a day; and he should understand that if he goes into a care home it might well become the place he lives permanently and, alternatively, if he goes home and accepts the care package it cannot be guaranteed that he will not run into similar problems again in the future." Statute as quoted: "The person will be unable to make the required decision if, owing to the impairment or disturbance, he or she is unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information or to communicate the decision (MCA: section 3)."
location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'The ‘information’', Box 4 and vignette; 'Context' for MCA s3
safe_wording: Specialists in residence capacity recommend telling the person why a move is suggested, what the other options are, such as going home with carers several times a day, and what each choice could mean. That includes saying plainly that a care home may become permanent, and that going home with help carries no guarantee.
qualifications: This is an expert proposal in a peer-reviewed review, not the statute's wording; MCA s3(4) (reasonably foreseeable consequences) itself was not opened. Attribute as 'specialists recommend' or 'a review by residence-capacity researchers recommends'.

claim: On English hospital wards, professionals varied widely in what information they treated as relevant when assessing whether people with dementia could decide where to live, and legal standards were not routinely applied.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Our findings suggest that whilst professionals profess to be familiar with broad legal standards governing the assessment of capacity under the MCA, these standards are not routinely applied in practice in general hospital settings when assessing capacity to decide place of residence on discharge from hospital." Full text: "Our findings suggest that there is currently a wide inconsistency of approach amongst professionals when identifying 'information relevant to the decision' (section 3(1)(a) MCA) during the assessment of residence capacity." "Only by gathering this information can the assessor present the various options, alternatives and risks associated with a particular choice of residence to a patient so that they can understand and weigh those factors in the balance in order to demonstrate decisional capacity and make an informed choice."
location: Abstract (Results); full text (accepted manuscript), Introduction and 'Understanding Information Relevant to the Decision'
safe_wording: A study on English hospital wards found staff varied widely in what information they gave or tested when judging whether a person with dementia could decide where to live.
qualifications: Qualitative, 29 cases, fieldwork 2008 to 2009 (before CC v KK). Give no percentages. Say 'a study found', not 'assessments usually fail'.

claim: In video-recorded hospital capacity assessments, options were not always presented to the patient.
supporting_passage: Variation from this structure was observed across the dataset, notably in the way in which options were (or were not) presented. ... One phase, option listing, varied in practice and options were not always presented.
location: Abstract, Outcomes & Results; What this study adds
safe_wording: When researchers filmed four real capacity assessments in hospital, options were not always put to the patient.
qualifications: Four recordings only, in acquired brain injury rather than older people or dementia. Use only as an illustration, never as a rate.

claim: In a review of 40 disputed Court of Protection capacity cases, in one the judge found the person had not been given relevant information about care options at home.
supporting_passage: In one of these, the judge deemed P had not been provided with relevant information around care options at home.
location: Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Results (support principle)
safe_wording: Courts have criticised assessments where the person was not told what care would be available at home.
qualifications: Optional. One case among 40; do not present as frequent. The excerpt does not name the case.

claim: The judge warned that professionals may conflate capacity assessment with best interests and give more weight to the physical safety of a care home than to the emotional security of home.
supporting_passage: In para. 65, he reiterated the point about the importance of the objective test of capacity being made without reference to what might be best for the person and emphasised again the saliency of home: 'There is, I perceive, a danger that professionals, including judges, may objectively conflate a capacity assessment with a best interests analysis and conclude that the person under review should attach greater weight to the physical security and comfort of a residential home and less importance to the emotional security and comfort that the person derives from being in their own home'.
location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'Approaches to assessment: outcome v. functional'
safe_wording: The same judge warned that professionals can slip from asking 'can she decide?' into 'what is best for her?', and then expect the person to value a care home's safety over the security of being at home.
qualifications: Optional. If quoted, use the exact words above with para 65.

claim: About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia.
supporting_passage: Median frequencies for mixed stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic) were 30% and 34% for acute and rehabilitation settings, respectively. Frequencies by stroke type were lowest for acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (9%) and highest for acute ischemic stroke (62%) when arrival to the hospital was ≤3 hours from stroke onset. Articles monitoring aphasia for 1 year demonstrated aphasia frequencies 2% to 12% lower than baseline.
safe_wording: About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia, a difficulty with understanding or using language.
qualifications: 30% (acute) and 34% (rehabilitation) are median frequencies across studies of mixed stroke; frequency varies widely by stroke type and timing and falls somewhat over the first year.

claim: Aphasia is a disorder of language; it can hide a person's ability to decide, and some people with aphasia also have other cognitive problems, so aphasia alone does not show that the person lacks capacity or that they have it.
supporting_passage: Stipinovich 2023: "The presence of neurological pathology, for example, aphasia, and its associated difficulties with language and/or cognition, may affect an individual's capacity to make decisions, or their ability to reveal their capacity to make decisions." Kim 2020: "Because people with aphasia (PWA) have impaired language abilities and may also present with cognitive deficits, they may have difficulty during decision-making tasks." Hughes 2015 (Box 3): "Status Capacity is determined by the person's status as, for example, someone who is old, has an intellectual disability or dementia, has speech problems, has had a stroke"; "Professionals are mostly aware that assessments based on status should be avoided because they are unfairly discriminatory".
location: Stipinovich abstract (Background); Kim abstract (Purpose); Hughes 2015 full text, Box 3 and 'Approaches to assessment'
safe_wording: After a stroke, some people lose words but may keep their judgement. Aphasia can hide a person's ability to decide. Some people with aphasia also have problems with memory or reasoning, so the answer comes from a supported assessment, not from the diagnosis.
qualifications: Use 'may keep their judgement', never 'keep' (judge's note). Always pair with the point that some people with aphasia also have wider cognitive problems.

claim: In a small study, people with aphasia did worse than matched controls on a language-based decision task but did not differ clearly on non-verbal decision tasks.
supporting_passage: PWA differed significantly from control participants on linguistic decision making, particularly when required to verbalize their rationale for making their decision. PWA and control participants did not differ significantly on measures of nonlinguistic decision making. ... Decision-making tasks that are heavily dependent on language, such as those used in capacity assessments, may disadvantage PWA. Assessments of decision-making capacity should include communication supports for people with acquired communication disorders
safe_wording: In a study of 16 people with aphasia, they struggled most when a decision task relied on words, especially explaining their reasons aloud. On decision tasks without words, they did not score clearly differently from people without aphasia.
qualifications: Small study; laboratory tasks, not real capacity assessments; 'did not differ significantly' is not proof of equal ability.

claim: Communication supports (information in several forms, trained partners, extra time) can help people with aphasia take part in decisions.
supporting_passage: Decision-making by persons with aphasia (PWA) can be enhanced when communication partners are trained and if communication supports are provided, for example, supports that reduce the linguistic and cognitive demands of the task, and/or that facilitate expression. ... The most frequently listed strategies include augmenting information with different modalities, acknowledging the competence of the PWA, thereby inviting initiation and collaboration by the PWA, and the allocation of sufficient time for the decision-making process. ... Future research should focus on the effectiveness of the different strategies identified
safe_wording: Research on people with aphasia after stroke describes supports that help: key words written down, pictures of the options, trained conversation partners and more time.
qualifications: The review maps strategies; effectiveness of individual strategies is not established. Say 'can help', not 'proven to'. 'Key words written down' and 'pictures' are examples of 'augmenting information with different modalities'.

claim: In an international survey of 195 speech and language therapists, barriers to supporting decision-making for people with aphasia included other disciplines not seeking their involvement.
supporting_passage: One hundred ninety-five SLTs from 32 countries responded. Most respondents, especially those working in inpatient settings, had supported people with aphasia to make decisions as part of a general conversation or had enabled other professionals to provide decision-making support, including during capacity assessments. Fewer had been involved directly in capacity assessments. ... There are barriers to SLTs being able to provide this support, for example, other disciplines not seeking their involvement in decision-making processes.
safe_wording: In a 2026 survey of 195 speech and language therapists in 32 countries, one barrier they reported was that other professionals did not ask for their help with decisions.
qualifications: Self-selected respondents reporting their views; no proportion is given in the abstract, so do not say 'most' or 'often' for this barrier.

claim: Health professionals without speech and language therapy training had difficulty identifying communication difficulties before capacity assessments.
supporting_passage: Professionals reported they chose not to use the tool when they perceived patients' communication to be intact. Four of eight patients with a diagnosis of dementia or memory impairment, who professionals elected not to screen, were found to have significant communication needs. ... This study highlights that non-speech and language therapist health professionals have difficulty identifying and screening for communication difficulties.
safe_wording: In one English study, staff skipped communication screening when they thought a patient's communication was fine; half of the unscreened patients with dementia or memory problems (4 of 8) turned out to have significant communication needs.
qualifications: Very small numbers (4 of 8); present as counts, not a percentage. The finding concerns patients with dementia or memory impairment, not only aphasia.

claim: UK capacity law requires help with communication before concluding incapacity: in England and Wales, all practicable steps to help the person decide; in Scotland, an inability to communicate that can be overcome with human or mechanical aids is not incapacity.
supporting_passage: Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA 2005 s1): "A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help him to do so have been taken without success." Hughes 2015: "They must be able to hear and see adequately; if special means of communication are required, these should be available; and so on. In keeping with the principles of the MCA (Box 1), 'all practicable steps' must be taken to help the person make a decision." Orr 2018: "A person must be given all practicable help to make their own decision before being treated as lacking capacity." Edwardson 2018: "This incapacity must be resulting from a mental disorder or inability to communicate because of physical disability. If this inability to communicate can be overcome with human or mechanical aids, it does not constitute incapacity for the purposes of the Act."
location: Hughes 2015 full text, Box 1 and 'Delirium, time and the UN Convention'; Orr 2018 full text, Table 2; Edwardson 2018 full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
safe_wording: In England and Wales the law says a person can't be treated as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed. In Scotland, a communication difficulty that can be overcome with help or aids does not count as incapacity.
qualifications: Statutes were not opened directly; wording rests on published secondary sources quoting them. The Scottish provision concerns inability to communicate; where aphasia affects understanding, the general principles apply rather than this clause. The editor set aside posts resting only on statute text, so keep this as one supporting line alongside the empirical claims.

claim: A validated screening tool exists to identify stroke survivors' communication support needs before a capacity assessment.
supporting_passage: This unique screening tool for stroke survivors' communication support needs during mental capacity assessments is valid and reliable. Minor refinements to administration training will improve fidelity of use.
safe_wording: A screening tool now exists to help non-specialist staff spot which stroke survivors need communication support before a capacity assessment.
qualifications: Optional. Small samples; discriminant validity was poor. Do not call it 'the standard'.

claim: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person is unable to decide if, because of an impairment of mind or brain, they can't understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information, or communicate the decision.
supporting_passage: The person will be unable to make the required decision if, owing to the impairment or disturbance, he or she is unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information or to communicate the decision (MCA: section 3).
safe_wording: The capacity test in England and Wales asks whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh the information, and communicate a decision.
qualifications: England and Wales only; the Act was not opened directly.

claim: Some people with frontal or executive impairment can describe what they would do but fail to do it in everyday life (the 'frontal lobe paradox').
supporting_passage: The "frontal lobe paradox" highlights a phenomenon in which a subset of patients who possess frontal lobe damage and exhibit marked impairments in everyday life are still able to able to verbally describe a logical course of action relating to a task and perform well in interview and test settings. Such cases pose a challenge with regard to the assessment of mental capacity within clinical settings. ... Nearly 50% of all identified academic texts published since 2000 were position articles that cited a handful of case studies published between 1936 and 1986 as evidence for the phenomenon. ... Overall, our findings indicate a lack of readily accessible research specific to the frontal lobe paradox. In particular, there is a lack of contemporary research specific to the subject and an absence of clarification as to which syndromes and disorders are included within the term.
safe_wording: Some people with damage to the brain's planning systems can describe a task well in interview yet struggle to do it in daily life. The label for this, the 'frontal lobe paradox', is widely cited, but a 2022 review found it rests mostly on a handful of case reports from 1936 to 1986.
qualifications: The phenomenon is described, not measured: no frequency, no evidence specific to older people or dementia. Do not use the label as if it were an established diagnosis. The candidate's phrase 'often with impairment of planning and self-monitoring' should become 'some people'.

claim: Everyday decision-making ability in older people with cognitive impairment relates to executive function (ACED validation).
safe_wording: Do not use.
qualifications: Not searched in this batch to conserve usage; the lead (Lai 2008, ACED) was marked 'unsure' by the candidate.

claim: The Court of Protection has linked a deficit in executive functioning to inability to 'use or weigh' information, although how is unclear.
supporting_passage: In a later case, NCC v PB and TB [2014] EWCOP 14, a deficit in executive functioning was tied to the inability to 'use or weigh', but the nature of this relation remains unclear.
safe_wording: At least one Court of Protection judgment has tied problems with executive function to the 'use or weigh' part of the test, but legal commentators say the link is not yet clear.
qualifications: One named case via a secondary source; the judgment was not opened. Do not say 'courts recognise executive capacity' as settled law.

claim: For decisions about where to live, the person should be told what the concerns are (what has gone wrong or been observed), so observations from a practical assessment are information to put to the person, not a verdict.
supporting_passage: Box 4: "The person should know why a change of residence is being proposed: what have the problems been that have caused a concern (e.g. they should know why they had to come into hospital or what has caused a worry in the community)". Vignette: "An occupational therapy assessment in the ward kitchen showed that he was unsafe making a pot of tea." "From the information presented it is not possible to say with any certainty whether or not they have residence capacity. Careful assessments will be required to determine whether they do or not."
location: Hughes 2015 full text, Box 4 and 'Case vignettes'
safe_wording: A failed kitchen assessment does not by itself show that someone lacks capacity. Specialists recommend telling the person what the concerns are, then seeing whether they can weigh them.
qualifications: The OT kitchen example in the source is a fictional teaching vignette; label any visual 'Illustrative example'.

claim: Capacity is judged for a particular decision at a particular time; a person may lack capacity for one decision and still be able to make others.
supporting_passage: Orr 2018: "A patient may lack capacity to make decisions about some aspects of their care but retain the capacity to make decisions about more straightforward aspects." "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA 2005 s2): "'a person lacks capacity in relation to a matter if at the material time he is unable to make a decision for himself in relation to the matter because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in, the functioning of, the mind or brain' (MCA: section 2)." Ruck Keene 2019 abstract: "The subject P was determined to have capacity in 13 cases, to lack capacity in 22 cases, and in 5 cases P was found to have and lack capacity for different issues before the court."
location: Orr 2018 full text ('Consent: ethical principles'; 'Capacity: evolution of case law'); Hughes 2015 full text, 'Context'; Ruck Keene 2019 abstract
safe_wording: Capacity is judged one decision at a time. Someone who can't decide where to live may still be able to decide what to wear, what to eat and who visits. Courts have found the same person able to make some decisions and not others.
qualifications: Everyday examples (what to wear, eat, who visits) are illustrations consistent with the principle, not quoted from the sources. The Scottish Act (AWI 2000) was not shown in opened sources to use identical decision-specific wording; say 'UK capacity law' only for the general principle stated by Orr 2018.

claim: People must be given all practicable help to make their own decisions before being treated as lacking capacity.
supporting_passage: Orr 2018: "A person must be given all practicable help to make their own decision before being treated as lacking capacity." Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA s1): "A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help him to do so have been taken without success."
location: Orr 2018 full text, Table 2; Hughes 2015 full text, Box 1
safe_wording: The law in England and Wales says people must be given all practicable help to make their own decisions. So a follow-up question is: what help will she get to make the others?
qualifications: England and Wales statute via secondary sources.

claim: Under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, anyone acting must take account of the adult's past and present wishes (s1(4)) and encourage the adult to use existing skills (s1(5)).
