safe_wording: European palliative care guidance suggests a lower daily dose, a longer gap between doses, or a switch to an opioid less dependent on the kidneys, such as fentanyl or alfentanil, with specialist advice.
qualifications: Evidence is very low quality and from cancer pain; recommendations rest on pharmacokinetics and experience. Name only fentanyl and alfentanil (methadone needs specialist use). Do not name oxycodone as a safe swap (C10-19-d).

claim: Oxycodone's breakdown products are also cleared by the kidneys and can accumulate, so it is not a straightforward substitute.
supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "its hepatic metabolism produces multiple metabolites, including the noroxycodone and oxymorphone (further metabolized to noroxymorphone), which could accumulate in patients with renal failure, since oxycodone elimination is relatively impaired in ESRD patients." Owsiany 2019: "Oxycodone and its active metabolites are cleared renally, and this clearance may be greatly reduced in older, renally-impaired patients."
location: Coluzzi 2020 full text; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
safe_wording: Switching to oxycodone does not remove the problem: its breakdown products also depend on the kidneys.
qualifications: Both reviews say oxycodone can be used with dose adjustment and monitoring.

claim: Kidney function falls with age, and creatinine-based eGFR can overestimate kidney function in people with little muscle.
supporting_passage: Owsiany 2019: "Given the decreased kidney function associated with aging and chronic kidney disease, these patients are at increased risk for drug accumulation and adverse events." Hanna 2024: "Creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) may overestimate kidney function in patients with sarcopenia. While cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFR) is less affected by muscle mass, it may underestimate kidney function in patients with obesity." ... "After adjustment for potential confounders, CT-defined sarcopenia and high adiposity were both associated with >30% eGFR discordance (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12-3.24; aOR 2.01, 95% CI 1.15-3.52, respectively)" ... "A spline model demonstrated that as skeletal muscle index decreases, the predicted difference between eGFRand eGFRwidens considerably."
location: Owsiany 2019 abstract; Hanna 2024 abstract (Background and Results; subscripts cr/cys lost in the PubMed text)
safe_wording: A creatinine result in the normal range can hide low kidney function in someone with little muscle, because creatinine comes from muscle. In a study of people with low muscle mass, creatinine-based estimates often read well above cystatin C-based estimates.
qualifications: Hanna 2024 studied people with cancer (mean age 63), not frail older people specifically, and compared two estimates rather than measured GFR. The 'creatinine comes from muscle' explanation is standard physiology but was not stated verbatim in the opened sources beyond 'less affected by muscle mass'; keep it brief. Prefer 'can' to 'often' for the general statement.

claim: The clinical evidence linking morphine, kidney function and side effects is limited and partly conflicting.
supporting_passage: Sande 2016: "There is lack of consensus within the existing literature on the relationship between morphine, creatinine levels and morphine-related side effects. Based on the current evidence, morphine should be used with caution; however, more evidence is needed." Owsiany 2019: "Alternatively, two studies found no relationship between serum concentrations of morphine, M6G, and morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and pain intensity or adverse events."
location: Sande 2016 abstract, Conclusions; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 2
safe_wording: The studies are small and do not all agree, so the advice rests mainly on how the drug is handled by the body and on clinical experience.
qualifications: State as a named limitation, not a reason to ignore the risk.

claim: Among 18,343 surgical patients (mean age 52) in two US hospitals, 35.7% used no opioids in the 24 hours before discharge, and 45.6% of those were still prescribed opioids to take home.
supporting_passage: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures, there was wide variation in the amount of opioids prescribed at hospital discharge given a postoperative patient's 24-hour predischarge opioid use. A total of 6548 patients (35.7%) used no opioids in the 24 hours prior to hospital discharge; however, 2988 of these patients (45.6%) were prescribed opioids at hospital discharge, suggesting potential overprescription."
safe_wording: In a US study of over 18,000 surgical patients (average age 52), about 1 in 3 took no opioid in the last 24 hours before going home, yet almost half of that group were still given an opioid prescription to take home.
qualifications: Must state: surgical patients, average age 52, US hospitals; not older medical inpatients. 'Potential overprescription' is the authors' label; some may have needed pain relief at home.

claim: The amount of opioid prescribed at discharge varied widely for the same level of use in the last 24 hours.
supporting_passage: "...there was wide variation in the amount of opioids prescribed at hospital discharge given a postoperative patient's 24-hour predischarge opioid use." ... "Opioids are not regularly prescribed in a patient-specific manner to postoperative patients."
safe_wording: The amount prescribed to take home varied widely between people who had used the same amount in hospital.
qualifications: Surgical population.

claim: In general surgical patients, opioid use at home after discharge was best predicted by the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge.
supporting_passage: "For patients discharged after POD 1, in multivariate analysis, the number of opioid pills used at home was associated with the number taken the day before discharge (p < 0.0001) and patient age (p = 0.006), but not the type of surgery. Forty-one percent of patients took no opioids the day before discharge, 33% took 1 to 3, and 26% took more than 4 pills. Eighty-five percent of patients' home opioid requirements would be satisfied using the following guideline: if no opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, no prescription is needed; if 1 to 3 opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 15 opioid pills is given at discharge; and if 4 or more pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 30 opioid pills is given at discharge. If these guidelines were used, the number of opioid pills prescribed would decrease by 40%." ... "For patients admitted after surgical procedures, post-discharge opioid use is best predicted by usage the day before discharge."
safe_wording: In a US study of general surgical patients, the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge was the best guide to how much they used at home. A simple rule based on that count would have met the needs of 85 in 100 patients and cut the tablets prescribed by 40%.
qualifications: Single US centre, 333 surgical patients, not older-person specific. 85 in 100 means about 15 in 100 would have needed more: present 'none used' as a prompt to ask about pain at home, not an automatic no.

claim: A count of the last 24 hours is a rough guide: in a plastic surgery cohort, a 24-hour model predicted home opioid use much less well than a model using the whole inpatient course.
supporting_passage: "The POP model had the strongest association (R2 = 0.899; P < 0.0001) between model output and postdischarge opioid consumption when compared to a procedure-based (R2 = 0.226; P = 0.025) or a 24-hour (R2 = 0.152; P = 0.007) model."
safe_wording: The 24-hour count is a starting point, not a formula: look at the trend over the whole stay and ask the person what activity at home will involve.
qualifications: Small single-centre study; the 'look at the trend' advice is a judgement informed by it.

claim: In older adults, opioid use is linked with falls, fall injuries and fractures.
supporting_passage: "Thirty studies, providing 34 relevant effect sizes, met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis. Overall, opioid use was significantly associated with falls, fall injuries, and fractures, with effect sizes ranging from 0.15 to 0.71. In meta-regressions, no selected factors explained heterogeneity." ... "While heterogeneity is present, results suggest an increased risk of falls, fall injuries, and fractures among older adults who used opioids."
safe_wording: In older people, opioid use is linked with more falls and fractures.
qualifications: Observational; association, not proof of cause; do not quote the pooled effect sizes (log scale). An unneeded take-home supply adds risk without benefit is a judgement, not a measured finding.

claim: The evidence comes from surgical patients (mean age 52 in the largest study); applying the counting habit to older medical inpatients is a judgement.
supporting_passage: Chen 2018: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures..." Hill 2018: "We studied 333 inpatients discharged to home after bariatric, benign foregut, liver, pancreas, ventral hernia, and colon surgery."
safe_wording: These studies were in surgical patients, mostly younger than the people on a geriatric ward; using the count for older medical patients is sensible practice, not something these studies tested.
qualifications: Required caveat in every version.

claim: In a UK randomised trial of 608 adults on strong opioids for chronic non-cancer pain, a supported group programme helped far more people stop opioids (29% vs 7% at 12 months) and pain interference with daily life was no worse than with usual care.
supporting_passage: Sandhu 2023: "Of 608 participants randomized (mean age, 61 years; 362 female [60%]; median daily morphine equivalent dose, 46 mg [IQR, 25 to 79]), 440 (72%) completed 12-month follow-up. There was no statistically significant difference in PROMIS-PI-SF-8a scores between the 2 groups at 12-month follow-up (-4.1 in the intervention and -3.17 in the usual care groups; between-group difference: mean difference, -0.52 [95% CI, -1.94 to 0.89]; P = .15). At 12 months, opioid discontinuation occurred in 65 of 225 participants (29%) in the intervention group and 15 of 208 participants (7%) in the usual care group (odds ratio, 5.55 [95% CI, 2.80 to 10.99]; absolute difference, 21.7% [95% CI, 14.8% to 28.6%]; P < .001)." Sandhu 2026 (HTA): "The findings only apply to people willing to consider opioid reduction and may not apply to a more complex secondary care population. The results may not be applicable to people using very high opioid doses." ... "The I-WOTCH intervention helps substantially more people stop opioids than best usual care without adversely affecting pain interference."
location: Sandhu 2023 abstract, Results; Sandhu 2026 abstract, Limitations and Conclusions
safe_wording: In a UK trial in general practice, people on strong painkillers for long-term pain who got group sessions and nurse support to reduce them were much more likely to have stopped a year later (29 in 100, against 7 in 100 with usual care). Pain getting in the way of daily life was no worse than in the usual-care group.
qualifications: Mean age 61: few very old or frail people. Participants were willing to consider reduction; opioid use self-reported. 'No worse' = no clear difference (the trial did not show pain improved). Absolute figures first.

claim: In the same trial, serious adverse events were 8% with the programme vs 5% with usual care, and 1% of the programme group needed extra care for possible withdrawal symptoms.
supporting_passage: "Serious adverse events occurred in 8% (25/305) of the participants in the intervention group and 5% (16/303) of the participants in the usual care group. The most common serious adverse events were gastrointestinal (2% in the intervention group and 0% in the usual care group) and locomotor/musculoskeletal (2% in the intervention group and 1% in the usual care group). Four people (1%) in the intervention group received additional medical care for possible or probable symptoms of opioid withdrawal (shortness of breath, hot flushes, fever and pain, small intestinal bleed, and an overdose suicide attempt)."
safe_wording: Reducing was not free of risk even with support: serious health problems were reported in 8 in 100 people in the programme and 5 in 100 with usual care.
qualifications: Not all serious adverse events were due to reduction; no significance test is given in the abstract for this difference.

claim: A systematic review of 67 studies found very low quality evidence that pain, function and quality of life may improve after long-term opioid dose reduction.
supporting_passage: "Sixty-seven studies (11 randomized trials and 56 observational studies) examining 8 intervention categories, including interdisciplinary pain programs, buprenorphine-assisted dose reduction, and behavioral interventions, were found. Study quality was good for 3 studies, fair for 13 studies, and poor for 51 studies." ... "Among 40 studies examining patient outcomes after dose reduction (very low overall quality of evidence), improvement was reported in pain severity (8 of 8 fair-quality studies), function (5 of 5 fair-quality studies), and quality of life (3 of 3 fair-quality studies)." ... "Very low quality evidence suggests that several types of interventions may be effective to reduce or discontinue LTOT and that pain, function, and quality of life may improve with opioid dose reduction."
safe_wording: Older, weaker studies of people who reduced long-term opioids more often reported that pain and daily function improved than worsened, but most of those studies were small, uncontrolled and poor quality.
qualifications: Say clearly that the studies were weak. Many involved intensive pain programmes, so improvement may come from the programme rather than the lower dose. Use I-WOTCH (C10-24-a) as the lead evidence.

claim: In a large US cohort of people on stable higher-dose long-term opioids, tapering was linked with more emergency or hospital visits for overdose or withdrawal and for mental health crisis, and faster reductions were linked with higher risk (corrected figures).
supporting_passage: Corrected abstract (Scite record of the corrected article): "Posttapering patient periods were associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 6.3 overdose events per 100 person-years compared with 4.9 events per 100 person-years in non-tapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 1.4 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 0.7-2.1]; aIRR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.15-1.43]). Tapering was associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 7.4 mental health crisis events per 100 person-years compared with 4.3 events per 100 person-years among nontapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 3.1 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 2.1-4.1]; aIRR, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.50-2.01]). Increasing maximum monthly dose reduction velocity by 10% was associated with an aIRR of 1.05 for overdose (95% CI, 1.03-1.08) and of 1.14 for mental health crisis (95% CI, 1.11-1.17)." Erratum letter (Fenton 2022, 10.1001/jama.2022.0231): "After reanalyzing the data with corrected programming codes, the results showed that dose tapering remained significantly associated with both overdose and mental health crises, although the incidence rate ratios were reduced from 1.68 (95% CI, 1.53-1.85) to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.15-1.43) for overdose and from 2.28 (95% CI, 1.96-2.65) to 1.74 (95% CI, 1.50-2.01) for mental health crisis." Original abstract: "Although these findings raise questions about potential harms of tapering, interpretation is limited by the observational study design."
location: Corrected abstract, Results (via Scite); erratum letter JAMA 2022;327(7):687
safe_wording: Cutting down can carry risk if it is rushed or imposed. In US insurance records, periods after a dose reduction had about 6 emergency visits for overdose or withdrawal per 100 people a year, against about 5 without reduction, and about 7 mental health crises per 100 a year against about 4. Faster reductions were linked with higher risk.
qualifications: USE ONLY THE CORRECTED FIGURES; the PubMed abstract still shows the original (9.3 vs 5.5; 7.6 vs 3.3; aIRR 1.68 and 2.28), which were withdrawn by the authors. Observational; association, not proof that tapering caused the events; people who are tapered may differ. US population, mean age about 58, higher-dose users. The overdose outcome includes withdrawal encounters. Tapering was not separated into voluntary and imposed.

claim: In the SPACE trial of chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain, opioids were not better than non-opioid medicines for pain-related function over 12 months and caused more side effects.
supporting_passage: "Among 240 randomized patients (mean age, 58.3 years; women, 32 [13.0%]), 234 (97.5%) completed the trial. Groups did not significantly differ on pain-related function over 12 months (overall P = .58); mean 12-month BPI interference was 3.4 for the opioid group and 3.3 for the nonopioid group (difference, 0.1 [95% CI, -0.5 to 0.7]). Pain intensity was significantly better in the nonopioid group over 12 months (overall P = .03)" ... "Adverse medication-related symptoms were significantly more common in the opioid group over 12 months (overall P = .03)"
safe_wording: In a US trial in people starting treatment for long-term back, hip or knee pain, opioids did not improve daily function more than paracetamol, anti-inflammatories and other non-opioid medicines over a year, and caused more side effects.
qualifications: This trial was about starting opioids, not reducing them; participants were mostly middle-aged men. Use as background only.

claim: UK guidance recommends gradual, agreed tapering with review, at a specified rate (for example 10% every 1 to 2 weeks).
supporting_passage: Not found in opened sources. Faculty of Pain Medicine Opioids Aware and NICE NG193 pages could not be opened from this environment and no copy was found in Drive. CDC 2022 guideline (PMID 36327391) abstract opened: it contains no tapering rate; full text not read.
safe_wording: Do not state a tapering rate or cite UK guidance on rate. Say 'slowly, at a pace agreed with the person and reviewed regularly'; this is supported by I-WOTCH's supported approach and Agnoli's link between faster reduction and harm.
qualifications: Remove '[N to verify] weeks' from the visual.

claim: In adults with leg pain, having no pain when seated and symptoms that improve on bending forward are the most useful single history features pointing to the clinical syndrome of lumbar spinal stenosis.
supporting_passage: Four studies evaluating 741 patients were identified. [...] The most useful symptoms for increasing the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS were having no pain when seated (LR, 7.4; 95% CI, 1.9-30), improvement of symptoms when bending forward (LR, 6.4; 95% CI, 4.1-9.9), the presence of bilateral buttock or leg pain (LR, 6.3; 95% CI, 3.1-13), and neurogenic claudication (LR, 3.7; 95% CI, 2.9-4.8). Absence of neurogenic claudication (LR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.17-0.31) decreased the likelihood of the diagnosis. A wide-based gait (LR, 13; 95% CI, 1.9-95) and abnormal Romberg test result (LR, 4.2; 95% CI, 1.4-13) increased the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS. [...] Absence of pain when seated and improvement of symptoms when bending forward are the most useful individual findings.
safe_wording: In a review of 4 studies (741 people with leg pain), two answers were the strongest single pointers towards spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back): no pain when sitting, and symptoms that ease on bending forward. Leg pain on walking that goes away when the person sits, or leans forward on a shopping trolley, points towards the spine.
qualifications: Keep likelihood ratios out of lay text or describe them as 'strong pointers'; never 'X times more likely'. Estimates come mostly from specialist clinics and may be less accurate in primary care. Confidence interval for 'no pain when seated' is wide (1.9 to 30). No single feature confirms the diagnosis; it needs imaging as well.

claim: Worked example: if about 15 in 100 older adults with leg pain in primary care have the syndrome, symptoms easing on bending forward raises the probability to about 53 in 100 (73 in 100 if the starting figure is 30 in 100).
supporting_passage: Assuming a primary care clinic prevalence of 15% and using only the finding of symptom improvement with bending forward, the probability of the clinical syndrome of LSS increases to 53%. However, if the clinic prevalence of the syndrome of LSS is 30%, the posttest probability would be 73%.
safe_wording: The authors' own worked example: if 15 in 100 people with this kind of leg pain have spinal stenosis, relief on bending forward raises the chance to about 53 in 100. That is a strong pointer, not a diagnosis.
qualifications: The 15% and 30% starting figures are the authors' assumptions, not measured prevalence. Optional; useful for practitioners, not needed for the core post.

claim: Leg pain from the circulation (vascular claudication) is typically not eased by changes in posture such as bending forward, tends to come on after a more consistent walking distance, and when the clinical picture is uncertain it can be checked with ankle brachial pressure (ABI) or vascular imaging.
supporting_passage: Vascular intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease in particular is often considered when leg pain occurs with walking. Unlike neurogenic claudication, vascular claudication is typically not improved by changes in posture such as lumbar flexion.The discomfort of vascular claudication may be more consistently reproducible with a specific distance and time of ambulation than neurogenic claudication.When the diagnosis is uncertain by clinical evaluation, it can be confirmed by diagnostic testing including ankle brachial indices (ABIs), duplex ultrasound, computed tomographic angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography.
location: Full text, Differential Diagnosis of the Clinical Syndrome of LSS
safe_wording: Leg pain from narrowed arteries is usually not helped by bending forward, and it tends to come on after about the same walking distance each time. If the history leaves doubt, checking foot pulses and ankle blood pressure (ABI) helps sort it out.
qualifications: This is descriptive text in the review (citing other sources), not a pooled accuracy estimate.

claim: In patients with claudication, calf symptoms that ease on standing still strongly suggest a circulation cause, while buttock or thigh symptoms that start on standing alone, ease on sitting and are helped by leaning on a shopping trolley strongly suggest spinal stenosis; single features on their own are weak.
supporting_passage: We studied 53 patients. The most sensitive symptom attribute to rule out LSS was the absence of "triggering of pain with standing alone" (sensitivity 0.97, NLR 0.050). Pain alleviators and symptom location data showed a weak clinical significance for LSS and PVD. Constellation of symptoms yielded the strongest associations: patients with a positive shopping cart sign whose symptoms were located above the knees, triggered with standing alone and relieved with sitting had a strong likelihood of neurogenic claudication (PLR 13). Patients with symptoms in the calf that were relieved with standing alone had a strong likelihood of vascular claudication (PLR 20.0). [...] The classic symptom attributes used to differentiate neurogenic from vascular claudication are at best weakly valid independently. However, certain constellation of symptoms are much more indicative of etiology.
safe_wording: In a small study of 53 people with walking-related leg pain, calf pain that eased when the person simply stood still pointed strongly to the circulation. Pain above the knee that came on just from standing, eased on sitting and was helped by leaning on a shopping trolley pointed strongly to the spine. Any one of these features alone was a weak guide.
qualifications: Small single-centre study; likelihood ratios imprecise. Participants already had one diagnosis or the other; people with both conditions are not addressed. Keep figures out of lay posts; 'strong pointer' is the safe phrase.

claim: Spinal stenosis and peripheral arterial disease often coexist in older people, so the history points towards a cause but does not exclude the other; pulses or ankle brachial pressure should still be checked.
supporting_passage: Suri 2010: "The differential diagnosis of the clinical syndrome of LSS is complicated by the frequent coexistence of many of the above-described conditions in older adults." Uesugi 2012: "570 patients diagnosed with LSS using a clinical diagnostic support tool and MRI at 64 facilities were enrolled. [...] The LSSPAD group comprised 38 patients (6.7 %); 20 (3.5 %) had pre-diagnosised PAD while 18 (3.2 %) had undetected PAD. The clinical characteristics of these patients were advanced age, diabetes, and a history of ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disorder. [...] Pain in buttocks and legs improved less in the LSSPAD group than in the LSS group (p < 0.05). [...] clinicians should consider the coexistence of PAD in LSS patients."
location: Suri: full text, Differential Diagnosis; Uesugi: Abstract, Results and Conclusions
safe_wording: The two causes can occur together. In a Japanese study of 570 people with spinal stenosis, about 7 in 100 also had narrowed leg arteries, and in about half of those (3 in 100 overall) the artery disease had not been picked up before. So even when the story sounds like the spine, check the foot pulses or ankle blood pressure.
qualifications: Prevalence comes from Japanese specialist clinics and may differ in UK primary care. Coexisting PAD was more common with older age, diabetes and heart or stroke history.

claim: The diagnosis of spinal stenosis needs the typical clinical picture confirmed with cross-sectional imaging; narrowing on MRI is common in older people without symptoms, so a scan alone does not make the diagnosis. Hip osteoarthritis is among the other causes to consider.
supporting_passage: Suri 2010: "The diagnosis of the clinical syndrome of LSS requires the appropriate clinical picture and radiographic findings." and "The prevalence of radiographic LSS using qualitative criteria in asymptomatic older adults 55 years or older has been estimated at 21% to 30% for moderate stenosis and 6% to 7% for severe stenosis.These data make it clear that incidental radiographic LSS on spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is common in asymptomatic patients." and "Lower extremity pain can also be caused by other spinal and extraspinal musculoskeletal diagnoses, including lumbosacral radicular pain due to nerve root impingement, [...] lumbar vertebral compression fractures, and hip osteoarthritis." Katz 2022: "The diagnosis can generally be made based on a clinical history of back and lower extremity pain that is provoked by lumbar extension, relieved by lumbar flexion, and confirmed with cross-sectional imaging, such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)."
location: Suri: Abstract Conclusions and full text (Radiographic and Anatomic LSS; Differential Diagnosis); Katz: Abstract
safe_wording: The history makes spinal stenosis likely; a scan confirms it. Because many older people have some narrowing on a scan without any symptoms, the scan only means something alongside the story.
qualifications: The 21% to 30% asymptomatic figures are background data cited in Suri's introduction, not that review's own finding; if used, attribute them as 'studies of people without symptoms'. Do not quote Katz's prevalence figure (inconsistent in the abstract).

claim: In the PRECISE trial, pregabalin did not reduce sciatica leg pain more than placebo at 8 weeks or at 1 year, did not improve any secondary outcome, and caused more adverse events, dizziness most often.
supporting_passage: Mathieson 2017: "A total of 209 patients underwent randomization, of whom 108 received pregabalin and 101 received placebo; after randomization, 2 patients in the pregabalin group were determined to be ineligible and were excluded from the analyses. At week 8, the mean unadjusted leg-pain intensity score was 3.7 in the pregabalin group and 3.1 in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference, 0.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.2 to 1.2; P=0.19). At week 52, the mean unadjusted leg-pain intensity score was 3.4 in the pregabalin group and 3.0 in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference, 0.3; 95% CI, -0.5 to 1.0; P=0.46). No significant between-group differences were observed with respect to any secondary outcome at either week 8 or week 52. A total of 227 adverse events were reported in the pregabalin group and 124 in the placebo group. Dizziness was more common in the pregabalin group than in the placebo group." Enke 2018, Figure 3 (any adverse event): "Mathieson et al.: 68/106 (pregabalin) vs. 43/101 (placebo); RR 1.5 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0)"
location: Mathieson: Abstract, Results; Enke: Figure 3 (read via Undermind)
safe_wording: In a placebo-controlled trial of 207 adults with sciatica, leg pain at 8 weeks averaged 3.7 out of 10 with pregabalin and 3.1 with a dummy capsule, and the trial showed no clear difference at 8 weeks or at 1 year. About 64 in 100 people on pregabalin had at least one side effect, against about 43 in 100 on the dummy capsule; dizziness was the most common.
qualifications: Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'; the confidence interval (-0.2 to 1.2 points) runs from a slight benefit to slight harm and does not favour pregabalin. 227 vs 124 are adverse EVENTS, not people; use the per-person figures (68 of 106 vs 43 of 101) for people.

claim: PRECISE participants were adults of working age on average (mean ages 52 and 55); the trial took adults aged 18 or older and excluded people with estimated creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min, so many older people were not eligible.
supporting_passage: Enke 2018, Table 1: "207 participants with acute (7 d to < 3 mo) or chronic (≥ 3 mo) sciatica. Mean age ± SD: pregabalin group 52.4 ± 17.2 yr; placebo group 55.2 ± 16.0 yr." PRECISE protocol: "pain duration of current episode of at least 1 week and up to 1 year; age 18 years or older" and "contraindications to pregabalin (known allergy to pregabalin or significant renal impairment. Pregabalin is predominantly renally excreted, so patients with an estimated creatinine clearance of <60 ml/minute will be excluded)"
location: Enke: Table 1 (p E789); Protocol: Methods/Design, Participants and recruitment (read via Undermind)
safe_wording: The people in the trial were on average in their early to mid 50s, and anyone with reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min) was excluded. So the trial tells us little about how pregabalin works in older people, and nothing suggests it would work better.
qualifications: The last clause ('nothing suggests it would work better') is a reasoned inference, not a finding; mark as judgement if used. Applying the result to older people rests on the absence of benefit plus the known side-effect profile.

claim: Systematic reviews found gabapentinoids ineffective for low back pain and lumbar radicular pain (sciatica) compared with placebo, with a higher risk of adverse effects, most often drowsiness, dizziness and nausea.
supporting_passage: Enke 2018: "Nine trials compared topiramate, gabapentin or pregabalin to placebo in 859 unique participants. Fourteen of 15 comparisons found anticonvulsants were not effective to reduce pain or disability in low back pain or lumbar radicular pain; for example, there was high-quality evidence of no effect of gabapentinoids versus placebo on chronic low back pain in the short term (pooled mean difference [MD] −0.0, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.8 to 0.7) or for lumbar radicular pain in the immediate term (pooled MD −0.1, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.5). The lack of efficacy is accompanied by increased risk of adverse events from use of gabapentinoids, for which the level of evidence is high." Full text: "Pooled results indicate high-quality evidence that gabapentinoids were associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared with placebo (pooled risk ratio [RR] 1.4, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.7, 6 studies)." and "The most common adverse events reported in participants taking a gabapentinoid were drowsiness or somnolence, dizziness and nausea". Shanthanna 2017: "Compared with placebo, the following adverse events were more commonly reported with GB: dizziness-(RR = 1.99, 95% CI [1.17 to 3.37], I2 = 49); fatigue (RR = 1.85, 95% CI [1.12 to 3.05], I2 = 0); difficulties with mentation (RR = 3.34, 95% CI [1.54 to 7.25], I2 = 0); and visual disturbances (RR = 5.72, 95% CI [1.94 to 16.91], I2 = 0)."
location: Enke: Abstract and Results, Adverse events (full text via Undermind); Shanthanna: Abstract
safe_wording: Reviews that pooled the trials found that gabapentin and pregabalin did not ease back pain or sciatica more than a dummy tablet, and people taking them had more side effects, most often drowsiness, dizziness and nausea.
qualifications: Mostly working-age trial populations. Shanthanna is chronic low back pain (not sciatica specifically) with very low to moderate quality evidence for side effects. Use relative risks only with absolute figures, or not at all for the public.

claim: NICE NG59 recommends not offering gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for managing sciatica.
supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (nice.org.uk blocked): "Do not offer gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for managing sciatica as there is no overall evidence of benefit and there is evidence of harm." (reported as recommendation 1.2.16, 2020 update). Enke 2018 (opened): "Regarding sciatica, the 2016 UK guideline recommends following neuropathic pain guidelines, which endorse the use of gabapentinoids. However, the recommendation of gabapentinoids for sciatica should be reviewed in light of emerging evidence."
safe_wording: Do not state NICE's current position unless the NICE NG59 page is opened and the wording confirmed. If it is confirmed, the post may say: 'NICE advises against gabapentin and pregabalin for sciatica.' Without that check, say: 'The trial evidence does not support starting them for sciatica.'
qualifications: Search extract is not sufficient for an essential claim. The opened source (Enke 2018) records that the 2016 version of NG59 pointed to neuropathic pain guidance endorsing gabapentinoids; the change came in a 2020 update that could not be opened here. The recommendation concerns sciatica, not all nerve pain.

claim: For sciatica, guidelines consistently recommend explanation and education and commonly recommend physical activity; recommendations on medicines are inconsistent.
supporting_passage: "The consistent recommendation for 'should do' is: educational care [,,,,] and the common recommendation for 'should do' is physical activity [,,,,,,,]. Exercise/physical therapies [,,,,,] is consistently recommended as 'could do'." and "For all the other medications, such as paracetamol, Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants, antidepressants, corticosteroids and antibiotics, the recommendations are highly inconsistent." and "Referral to a specialist is recommended when conservative therapy fails or when steppage gait is present."
safe_wording: Guidelines agree on explaining the condition and helping the person stay active, with referral if things don't improve or there is foot weakness (foot drop).
qualifications: Review predates the 2020 NICE update; it is about adults generally, not older people specifically.

claim: In older people, dizziness and drowsiness from gabapentinoids raise the risk of falls.
supporting_passage: Chaitoff 2025: "Our analytic cohort included 57 086 older adults with a diagnosis of interest initiating treatment with gabapentin (= 52 152) or duloxetine (= 4934). [...] At 6-month follow-up, incident gabapentin users had lower hazard of falls (hazard ratio, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.43 to 0.64]), but there was no difference in the hazards of experiencing severe falls. [...] Claims may contain fewer frail adults and undercount falls. Compared with incident use of duloxetine, incident use of gabapentin was not associated with increased fall-related visits." Oh 2024: "gabapentin initiation was significantly associated with increased odds of new falls at the index + 2 visit (odds ratio [95% confidence interval] 2.5 [1.3, 4.6])."
safe_wording: Do not claim that gabapentinoids have been shown to raise falls risk in older people. Safe: 'Dizziness and drowsiness are the commonest side effects; for someone who is already unsteady, that is a reason not to start a medicine that has not been shown to help.' (judgement)
qualifications: Observational evidence conflicts. The link from dizziness to falls is plausible but the direct evidence is mixed; present the falls point as judgement, not finding.

claim: A 2012 systematic review found an unfavourable long-term pain outcome (moderate to severe pain, or pain not relieved) in about 10% to 34% of people after knee replacement and about 20% in the best-quality studies; definitions varied and the authors did not pool.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Total hip or knee replacement is highly successful when judged by prosthesis-related outcomes. However, some people experience long-term pain." and "The proportion of people with an unfavourable long-term pain outcome in studies ranged from about 7% to 23% after hip and 10% to 34% after knee replacement. In the best quality studies, an unfavourable pain outcome was reported in 9% or more of patients after hip and about 20% of patients after knee replacement." Methods: "Favourable outcome includes people with no pain or mild pain at follow-up, while unfavourable outcome includes those with moderate-to-severe pain or for whom surgery had not relieved pain." Discussion: "Although we have interpreted pain outcomes as favourable, unfavourable or uncertain, we do not believe that the data justify combination to provide summary values." and "While acknowledging probable underestimates of the extent of pain after surgery reported in the literature, we should recognise the effectiveness of replacement for many."
location: Abstract; Methods, Data synthesis; Discussion (full text via Undermind)
safe_wording: Background only. An earlier review (2012) put the figure at about 1 in 5 after knee replacement in the best studies. Prefer the 2025 update (C10-30-b) for current numbers, and do not give both figures unless the difference is explained.
qualifications: Superseded for current figures. The 'prosthesis-related outcomes' sentence is the authors' framing in the abstract background, not a result.

claim: Current best estimate: after knee replacement, about 22 in 100 people report unfavourable pain at 3 months, falling to about 13 to 15 in 100 at 1 to 2 years; about 14 in 100 after hip replacement at 6 to 12 months. Confidence is low and the figures are probably underestimates.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "For TKR, 68 studies with 89 time points, including 598 498 patients, were included. Multivariate meta-analysis showed a general decrease in pain proportions over time: 21.9% (95% CrI 15.6% to 29.4%) at 3 months, 14.1% (10.9% to 17.9%) at 6 months, 12.6% (9.9% to 15.9%) at 12 months and 14.6% (9.5% to 22.4%) at 24 months. Considerable heterogeneity, unrelated to examined moderators, was indicated by substantial prediction intervals in the univariate models. Substantial loss to follow-up and risk of bias led to low confidence in the results. For THR, only 11 studies were included, so it was not possible to describe the trend. Univariate meta-analysis estimated 13.8% (8.5% to 20.1%) and 13.7% (4.8% to 31.0%) of patients experiencing long-term pain 6 and 12 months after THR". Methods: "We adopted the term 'unfavourable pain' from the previous review, which serves as a collective label to include the various descriptions used by study authors—such as persistent pain, worsening pain, or residual pain—rather than as an indicator of dissatisfaction." Strengths and limitations: "These prevalence rates are likely underestimated due to loss to follow-up and the high risk of bias in the included studies." Results: "Patients in 52 studies with data had a mean age of 69.6 (SD 9.4) years, and 63% (58 to 69) were women."
location: Abstract; Methods, Outcome; Strengths and limitations; Results (full text via Undermind)
safe_wording: Knee replacement relieves pain for most people, but not all. In a 2025 review of 68 studies (nearly 600,000 people, average age about 70), about 13 in 100 still had troublesome knee pain a year after the operation. At 3 months the figure was about 22 in 100. The authors think these numbers are probably too low, because people with poor results are often missing from follow-up.
qualifications: Say 'troublesome' or 'persistent' pain, defined differently across studies; not 'severe' pain. Low confidence (authors' wording). Across individual studies the 12-month figure ranged from 3.3% to 43.3%. Do not also quote the 2012 'about 1 in 5' without explaining that it is an older, smaller evidence base.

claim: Most people are satisfied after knee replacement, but about 1 in 5 are not; satisfaction with pain relief varies by activity, and unmet expectations are the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction.
supporting_passage: "We performed a cross-sectional study of patient satisfaction after 1703 primary TKAs performed in the province of Ontario. Our data confirmed that approximately one in five (19%) primary TKA patients were not satisfied with the outcome. Satisfaction with pain relief varied from 72-86% and with function from 70-84% for specific activities of daily living. The strongest predictors of patient dissatisfaction after primary TKA were expectations not met (10.7x greater risk), a low 1-year WOMAC (2.5x greater risk), preoperative pain at rest (2.4x greater risk) and a postoperative complication requiring hospital readmission (1.9x greater risk)."
safe_wording: About 4 in 5 people in a Canadian survey were satisfied with their knee replacement. Satisfaction with pain relief ranged from about 7 in 10 to 9 in 10, depending on the activity. People whose expectations were not met were the most likely to be dissatisfied, which is a reason to ask about likely pain before the operation.
qualifications: Satisfaction is a different outcome from pain. Do not quote the '10.7x greater risk' figure. Older implants and one Canadian province.

claim: NICE recommends core non-surgical treatment for osteoarthritis and referral for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management has not helped.
supporting_passage: Not verified: NICE NG226 and NG157 pages could not be opened; the BMJ summary of NG226 (Wood 2023, PMID 36693668) has no abstract and no accessible PDF.
safe_wording: Omit NICE referral criteria. The post can still end with questions to ask the surgeon ('What are my chances of still having pain afterwards? What else could I try first?'); questions make no factual claim.
qualifications: Not essential for the revised angle.

claim: In population studies, knee X-ray changes and knee pain match poorly: 15% to 76% of people with knee pain had X-ray osteoarthritis, and 15% to 81% of people with X-ray osteoarthritis had pain, depending on definitions.
supporting_passage: "The proportion of those with knee pain found to have radiographic osteoarthritis ranged from 15-76%, and in those with radiographic knee OA the proportion with pain ranged from 15% - 81%. Considerable variation occurred with x ray view, pain definition, OA grading and demographic factors" and "Radiographic knee osteoarthritis is likewise an imprecise guide to the likelihood that knee pain or disability will be present. Both associations are affected by the definition of pain used and the nature of the study group. The results of knee x rays should not be used in isolation when assessing individual patients with knee pain."
safe_wording: Studies of the general population find that many people with arthritis changes on a knee X-ray have little or no pain, and many people with knee pain have X-rays that look fairly normal. The authors concluded that a knee X-ray should not be used on its own to judge a person's knee pain.
qualifications: Ranges are very wide and depend on definitions; avoid presenting a single figure. Use 'a poor guide', not 'no guide' (see C10-16-b).

claim: On average, worse X-ray changes do go with more pain: comparing a person's two knees, the knee with more severe X-ray osteoarthritis was far more likely to be the painful one.
supporting_passage: "696 people from MOST and 336 people from Framingham were included. Kellgren and Lawrence grades were strongly associated with frequent knee pain-for example, for Kellgren and Lawrence grade 4 v grade 0 the odds ratio for pain was 151 (95% confidence interval 43 to 526) in MOST and 73 (16 to 331) in Framingham (both P<0.001 for trend). [...] Joint space narrowing was more strongly associated with each pain measure than were osteophytes." and "Using a method that minimises between person confounding, this study found that radiographic osteoarthritis and individual radiographic features of osteoarthritis were strongly associated with knee pain."
safe_wording: The X-ray is not meaningless. When researchers compared each person's two knees, the knee with worse X-ray changes was much more often the painful one. So the X-ray is a poor guide to how much a particular person will hurt or what they can do, not no guide at all.
qualifications: Do not quote the odds ratios for the public and never turn them into 'times more likely'. Within-person design removes differences between people (such as mood or pain sensitivity), which is part of why X-rays match pain poorly across people.

claim: Specialist guidance says imaging is not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis in people with typical symptoms; imaging helps when the presentation is atypical or another diagnosis is suspected, or with unexpected rapid worsening, and plain X-ray is the first choice when imaging is needed.
supporting_passage: "17 011 references were identified from which 390 studies were included in the SLR. Seven recommendations were produced, covering the lack of need for diagnostic imaging in patients with typical symptoms; the role of imaging in differential diagnosis; the lack of benefit in monitoring when no therapeutic modification is related, though consideration is required when unexpected clinical deterioration occurs; CR as the first-choice imaging modality; consideration of how to correctly acquire images and the role of imaging in guiding local injections."
safe_wording: European rheumatology guidance (EULAR, 2017) says an X-ray is not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis when the symptoms are typical. Imaging helps when something is unusual, when another cause is possible, or when the knee gets worse unexpectedly.
qualifications: Exact recommendation wording not seen (abstract summary only). Surgical planning is not named in the abstract; if the post mentions it, say 'for example before surgery' only as general practice, or omit.

claim: NICE NG226 recommends diagnosing osteoarthritis clinically without imaging in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes.
supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (nice.org.uk blocked): "Diagnose osteoarthritis clinically without imaging in people who are 45 or over and have activity-related joint pain and have either no morning joint-related stiffness or morning stiffness that lasts no longer than 30 minutes." and "NICE recommends not to routinely use imaging to diagnose osteoarthritis unless there are atypical features or features that suggest an alternative or additional diagnosis."
safe_wording: Use only after opening the NICE NG226 page. Otherwise attribute the point to EULAR (C10-16-c) and omit the age 45 and 30-minute criteria.
qualifications: Search extract is not sufficient for an essential claim.

claim: People told their knee is 'bone on bone' often come to believe that loading the knee will damage it and that exercise and physiotherapy will make it worse, and some then set aside exercise-based treatment.
supporting_passage: "Thirty-seven patients were approached and 27 participated. Participants were 48% female; mean age was 67 years." and "All participants believed that their knee OA was "bone on bone" (identity beliefs) and most (> 14 participants) believed it was caused by "wear and tear" (causal beliefs). Most (> 14 participants) believed that loading the knee could further damage their "vulnerable" joint (consequence beliefs) and all believed that their pain would deteriorate over time (timeline beliefs). Many (>20 participants) believed that physiotherapy and exercise interventions would increase pain and could not replace lost knee cartilage." and "Once the participants in this study had been "diagnosed" with "bone-on-bone" changes, many disregarded exercise-based interventions which they believed would damage their joint, in favor of alternative and experimental treatments, which they believed would regenerate lost knee cartilage."
safe_wording: In interviews with 27 people waiting for a knee replacement in Australia, all described their knee as 'bone on bone'. Many believed exercise or physiotherapy would make it worse or damage the joint, and many had set exercise aside.
qualifications: Qualitative, small, one hospital, people already listed for surgery: describes beliefs, not how common they are, and does not show that the X-ray description caused the avoidance. Avoid causal wording ('the X-ray made them stop').

claim: After surgery, pain on movement is usually much worse than pain at rest, yet many trials measure only one kind of pain or do not say which.
supporting_passage: "Only 39% of trials measured MEP and 52% failed to identify pain outcome as pain at rest (PAR) or MEP. Temporal trending did not suggest that MEP measurement is becoming more frequent. Trials measuring both MEP and PAR suggest that MEP is 95-226% more intense than PAR in the first 3 postoperative days. Among trials measuring MEP, 38% did not specify the physical maneuver used to assess MEP. Five of 7 meta-analyses reviewed (71%) did not distinguish between PAR and MEP [...] This is an important problem because MEP is usually more severe than PAR; MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery and several current and novel pain treatments differentially affect MEP vs PAR."
safe_wording: After an operation, pain when moving is usually much worse than pain lying still. In surgical trials that measured both, pain on movement scored roughly 2 to 3 times higher in the first 3 days. Yet only about 4 in 10 trials measured pain on movement at all.
qualifications: Evidence is from postsurgical trials (including knee replacement), not older people or ward practice specifically. '2 to 3 times' is derived from '95 to 226% more intense' (1.95 to 3.26 times) and refers to average scores in trials that measured both; if in doubt, say 'much worse'. Fractures are not specifically covered.

claim: Pain on movement is the measure researchers now prioritise because it better reflects functional recovery.
supporting_passage: Srikandarajah 2011: "MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery". He 2025/2026: "We prioritized pain during movement over pain at rest, as it better reflects functional recovery."
safe_wording: Pain researchers now often put pain on movement first, because it is the pain that gets in the way of recovery.
qualifications: These are authors' statements of rationale, not measured comparisons of the two scores against function. Avoid 'proves' or 'shows' language.

claim: In older adults with chronic low back pain, more pain after standard movement tasks was linked with worse disability and physical function.
supporting_passage: "226 older adults with chronic LBP. [...] LBP intensity was collected before and after the repeated chair rise test, stair climbing test, and 6-minute walk test [...] Greater aggregated posttest MeP was independently associated with worse disability (b = 0.593, t = 2.913, P = .004), self-efficacy (b = -0.870, t = -3.110, P = .002), and physical function (b = -0.017, t = -2.007, P = .039). MeP change scores were not associated with any outcome (all P > .050)."
safe_wording: In a study of 226 older adults with long-term back pain, those who had more pain after standing up from a chair, climbing stairs and walking also had more disability and did less well on tests of physical function.
qualifications: Cross-sectional association; does not show that movement pain causes disability. One way of scoring movement pain (the change from before to after) showed no link. Effect sizes small.

claim: The most commonly used pain measures record pain at rest or recalled pain, which does not capture pain during movement; measuring movement-evoked pain has been slow to reach clinical care.
supporting_passage: "With musculoskeletal pain, the primary driver is often pain experienced during physical activity, commonly referred to as movement-evoked pain []. Yet, the most common used pain measures assess either spontaneous pain or pain recalled through the lens of questionnaires () []. Assessment of spontaneous pain, that does not involve physical activity, cannot discern pain related to movement." and "Burgeoning research supports movement-evoked pain measurement [;;], yet it remains slow to translate to clinical care []."
location: Full text, Introduction (empty brackets are stripped reference markers in the rendered PMC text)
safe_wording: A pain score taken while someone lies still does not tell you how much it hurts to stand, turn or walk. Asking about pain during those movements gives the missing information.
qualifications: Narrative expert review; the point is logical as much as empirical.

claim: UK national guidelines on assessing pain in older people ask for assessment of how pain affects function and activities, and for observation of pain behaviour during movement or care in people who can't self-report reliably.
supporting_passage: Section 15, United Kingdom (p i14): "Where pain is present, a detailed clinical assessment of the multidimensional aspects of pain should be undertaken including: • Sensory dimension: the nature, location and intensity of pain • Affective dimension: the emotional component and response to pain • Impact: on functioning at the level of activities and participation." and "In people with very severe impairment, and in situations where procedures might cause pain, an observational assessment of pain behaviour is additionally required." Glossary (p i4 to i5): "Checklist of Non-verbal Pain Indicators (CNPI) A summation score of pain behaviours at rest and on movement"; "Mobilization Observation Behaviour Intensity Dementia (MOBID) An observational tool for use in early morning by carers to assess pain behaviours on five movements". Section 10 (p i10): "Re-wording your question to elicit the presence of pain such as 'Do you hurt anywhere?' or 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?' can substantiate the presence or absence of pain."
location: Full text (PDF via Undermind): Section 15 UK subsection, p i14; Glossary, p i4 to i5; Section 10, p i10
safe_wording: UK guidance on assessing pain in older people asks how pain affects what the person can do, and for people who can't easily describe their pain, to watch them during movement or care. A practical question it suggests: 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?'
qualifications: The guidance does not explicitly require a separate 'pain on movement' score for every patient; recording pain at rest and on standing is the post's recommendation (judgement) built on this guidance and C10-21-a. Some UK text is the 2018 document's summary of earlier UK guidance.

claim: Acute pain guidance (ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence 2020) recommends assessing pain with movement and function.
supporting_passage: Not searched or opened in this batch.
safe_wording: Omit the ANZCA reference.
qualifications: Not essential; UK guidance and Srikandarajah cover the point.

claim: Compared with placebo, quinine reduces the number of cramps modestly: about 2 to 3 fewer cramps over two weeks from about 9 on placebo (about a quarter fewer), on low-quality evidence.
supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Effects of interventions: "Quinine resulted in a significant decrease in cramp number (-2.45 cramps, 95% CI -3.54 to -1.36, random-effects), equivalent to a 28% (95% CI 15% to 40%) reduction over placebo (see Analysis 1.2, Figure 2). It is worth noting the persistent heterogeneity (I2 = 71%) associated with this result." Summary of findings table: "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the control groups was 8.8 cramps"; "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the intervention groups was 2.45 lower (1.36 to 3.54 lower)" [952 participants, 13 studies, GRADE low]. Cramp days: "The remaining seven trials (n = 842) showed that quinine significantly reduced cramp days compared to placebo (-1.15 days, 95% CI -1.93 to -0.38, random-effects) (see Analysis 1.6). This represents a 20% (95% CI 6% to 33%) reduction in cramp days". Abstract: "There is low quality evidence that quinine (200 mg to 500 mg daily) significantly reduces cramp number and cramp days and moderate quality evidence that quinine reduces cramp intensity." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Abstract: "When individual patient data from all crossover studies were pooled, persons had 3.60 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.15, 5.05) fewer cramps in a 4-week period when taking quinine compared with placebo." Table 3: placebo "17.08 (15.40, 18.76)" cramps per 4-week period (n = 409).
location: Cochrane: Results (Effects of interventions, quinine versus placebo), Summary of findings table 1, Abstract. Man-Son-Hing: Abstract, Results, Table 3.
safe_wording: In pooled trials, people on a dummy tablet had about 9 cramps in two weeks. People on quinine had about 2 to 3 fewer, so roughly 6 or 7 instead of 9. That is about a quarter fewer cramps, and the evidence is low quality. Cramps were only slightly less painful.
qualifications: Give the absolute figures first; the 28% is relative. Say the evidence is low quality. Trials were short (up to 60 days) and included some middle-aged adults, not only older people. 'About 6 or 7' is derived by subtracting 2.45 from 8.8. The intensity effect was small (0.12 points on a 3-point scale, from 1.2).

claim: In trials, minor side effects (mainly stomach upset) were slightly more common with quinine; the trials were too small and short to measure rare serious harms.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "A significantly greater number of people suffered minor adverse events on quinine than placebo (risk difference (RD) 3%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0% to 6%), mainly gastrointestinal symptoms. Overdoses of quinine have been reported elsewhere to cause potentially fatal adverse effects, but in the included trials there was no significant difference in major adverse events compared with placebo (RD 0%, 95% CI -1% to 2%). One participant suffered from thrombocytopenia (0.12% risk) on quinine." Authors' conclusions: "There is moderate quality evidence that with use up to 60 days, the incidence of serious adverse events is not significantly greater than for placebo in the identified trials, but because serious adverse events can be rarely fatal, in some countries prescription of quinine is severely restricted." ... "Because serious adverse events are not common, large population studies are required to more accurately inform incidence."
safe_wording: In the trials, about 3 more people in every 100 had minor side effects on quinine than on a dummy tablet, mostly stomach upset. The trials lasted up to about two months and were too small to measure rare serious harms.
qualifications: The 3 in 100 is an absolute risk difference (95% CI 0 to 6). 'No significant difference in major adverse events' in short trials must not be read as 'safe'.

claim: Quinine can rarely cause serious harm, including immune reactions that destroy platelets (thrombocytopenia), heart rhythm problems especially in overdose, and death in overdose; dose-related side effects are a particular concern in older people.
supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Background: "Quinine may have potentially serious adverse effects including fatal hypersensitivity reactions, particularly quinine-induced thrombocytopenia (Barr 1990) which can occur idiosyncratically from the ingestion of even minimal amounts of quinine, such as are present in commercial tonic waters (Schneemann 2006). Other hypersensitivity reactions include angio-oedema, disseminated intravascular coagulation, pancytopenia (Maguire 1993) and haemolytic uraemic syndrome (McDonald 1997)." ... "Quinine can interfere with the conduction pathways in the heart giving rise to arrhythmias, especially in overdosage (White 2007). Acute intoxication (ingestion of 4 to 12 g quinine) can cause convulsions followed by coma; death from respiratory arrest often results with doses exceeding 8 g." Plain language summary: "Quinine can cause serious, even fatal adverse events, especially in overdosage." Discussion: "A case-control study in the USA estimated that quinine-induced thrombocytopenia occurs in 26 of every 1 million users (Kaufman 1993)." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "However, the degree of benefit from quinine is modest and the risks include rare but serious immune-mediated reactions and, especially in older people, dose-related side effects."
location: Cochrane: Background (Description of the intervention), Plain language summary, Discussion (Adverse events due to quinine). Rabbitt: Abstract.
safe_wording: Quinine can rarely cause serious reactions. These include a sudden fall in platelets, the blood cells that help clotting, and heart rhythm problems, especially after too many tablets. An overdose of quinine can kill. A review in Age and Ageing notes that older people are more prone to its dose-related side effects.
qualifications: These harms come from case reports, regulatory data and a case-control study summarised in the Cochrane background and discussion, not from the review's own trial results. If the 26 per million figure is used, attribute it to a US case-control study (Kaufman 1993) cited by the Cochrane review, and do not present it as a Cochrane finding. Do not quote the MHRA's list of harms (not opened).

claim: Guidance restricts quinine for cramps to severe symptoms, as a trial with regular review; UK advice reported in the Cochrane review allows up to 4 weeks to see an effect and a pause every 3 months to check benefit; the MHRA issued a quinine safety update in June 2010.
supporting_passage: Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Quinine treatment should be restricted to those with severe symptoms, should be subject to regular review and requires discussion of the risks and benefits with patients." Cochrane 2015, Discussion: "The British National Formulary (BNF) advises that it may take up to four weeks for the effect on cramp to become apparent and that if there is improvement, then quinine should be taken continuously with close monitoring for adverse events (BNF 2010). The BNF also advises interruption of treatment every three months for review of benefit." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Discussion: "If this fails and the patient's quality of life is significantly affected, then a trial of quinine (of at least 4 weeks) may be warranted. As with all potentially hazardous medications, physicians prescribing quinine need to closely monitor the benefits and risks in individual patients." Acheampong 2013, Abstract: "To ascertain the effects of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency's (MHRA) safety update in June 2010 on the volume of prescribing of quinine and on indices of quinine toxicity."
location: Rabbitt: Abstract. Cochrane: Discussion (Other considerations). Man-Son-Hing: Discussion. Acheampong: Abstract (Aims).
safe_wording: Specialists in older people's medicine advise keeping quinine for severe cramps, reviewing it regularly and talking through benefits and risks (Age and Ageing review, 2016). UK prescribing advice reported in the Cochrane review said the effect can take up to 4 weeks to show, and treatment should be paused every 3 months to check it is still helping. The UK medicines regulator issued safety advice on quinine for cramps in 2010.
qualifications: The MHRA 2010 Drug Safety Update was not opened: do not quote its wording (for example 'not for routine use' or 'stop after 4 weeks if no benefit') as MHRA text. The BNF advice is the 2010 edition as reported by Cochrane; the current BNF was not opened, so say 'UK prescribing advice' rather than quoting the current BNF.

claim: MHRA (June 2010): quinine not for routine use for nocturnal leg cramps; consider only when cramps severely disrupt sleep, are very painful or frequent, other causes are ruled out and non-drug measures have failed; review after 4 weeks.
supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not an opened document): "The update stated that quinine should not be used routinely for nocturnal leg cramps." ... "treatment with quinine should only be considered when cramps cause severe disruption of sleep, and should only be used when cramps are very painful or frequent, other treatable causes of cramp are ruled out and symptoms are not alleviated by non-drug measures, such as passive stretching exercises." ... "Treatment should be reviewed after 4 weeks to see whether there is any benefit and monitor for toxicity."
location: WebSearch result summary (GPonline, MIMS pages not opened)
safe_wording: Do not attribute this wording to the MHRA in the post. Use the wording in C10-03-d instead.
qualifications: search_extract only; not sufficient for an essential claim. Consistent with the opened sources (Rabbitt 2016, Cochrane 2015, Man-Son-Hing 1998).

claim: After the 2010 MHRA advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped growing but remained common; areas with comprehensive prescribing reviews saw much larger reductions.
supporting_passage: "Total prescribing continued to increase, but annual growth in quinine prescribing in England declined from 6.0 to -0.6% following the MHRA update [difference -0.04 (95% confidence interval -0.07 to -0.01) quinine prescriptions per 100 patients per quarter, P = 0.0111]. Much larger reductions were observed in Primary Care Trusts that introduced comprehensive prescribing reviews." ... "The MHRA advice was followed by limited reductions in the growth in quinine prescribing and in indicators of quinine overdose and toxicity. Quinine prescribing, however, remains common, and further efforts are needed to reduce availability and use."
safe_wording: After the 2010 UK safety advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped rising but stayed common, at least to 2012. Areas that ran thorough prescribing reviews saw much larger falls.
qualifications: Data end in 2012; current prescribing levels were not checked. Ecological before-and-after data: the review programmes are linked with larger falls, not proven to cause them. This contradicts the draft opening line that quinine 'is no longer a routine prescription in the UK'.

claim: In a UK primary care trial, advising people on long-term quinine to try stopping it led more of them to stop, without a clear difference in cramps at 12 weeks.
supporting_passage: "One hundred and ninety-one patients prescribed quinine for night cramps were randomised to one of four groups defined by two 'advice' factors: undertake exercises and stop quinine." ... "At 12 weeks there was no significant difference in number of cramps in the previous 4 weeks (exercise = 1.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -3.01 to 6.90; quinine cessation = 3.45, 95% CI = -1.52 to 8.41) nor symptom burden or severity of cramps. However, after 12 weeks 26.5% (95% CI = 13.3% to 39.7%) more patients who had been advised to stop quinine treatment reported taking no quinine tablets in the previous week (odds ratio [OR] = 3.32, 95% CI = 1.37 to 8.06)" ... "Advising those on long-term repeat prescriptions to try stopping quinine temporarily will result in no major problems for patients, and allow a significant number to stop medication."
safe_wording: In a trial in 28 English general practices, people on long-term quinine were randomly given advice to try stopping it, or not. At 12 weeks, about 1 in 4 more of those advised to stop were taking none, and the trial did not show a clear difference in how many cramps people had.
qualifications: The cramp comparison had wide confidence intervals and cannot rule out some rise in cramps for some people. Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'. 26.5% is a difference in percentage points. Do not use the 3.45 figure (direction of the difference is not clear from the abstract).

claim: Stretching before bed is a low-risk option, but evidence that it reduces night cramps is limited and mixed.
supporting_passage: Hawke 2021, Abstract: "A combination of daily calf and hamstring stretching for six weeks may reduce the severity of night-time lower limb muscle cramps (measured on a 10 cm visual analogue scale (VAS) where 0 = no pain and 10 cm = worst pain imaginable) in people aged 55 years and older, compared to no intervention (mean difference (MD) -1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.74 to -0.86; 1 RCT, 80 participants; low-certainty evidence). The certainty of evidence was very low for cramp frequency" ... "Calf stretching alone for 12 weeks may make little to no difference to the frequency of night-time lower limb muscle cramps in people aged 60 years and older" ... "No participant in these three studies reported adverse events. The evidence for adverse events was of moderate certainty as the studies were too small to detect uncommon events." Coppin 2005, Conclusions: "Calf-stretching exercises are not effective in reducing the frequency or severity of night cramps." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "There is conflicting evidence regarding the efficacy of prophylactic stretching exercises in preventing cramps."
location: Hawke: Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions). Coppin: Abstract (Conclusions). Rabbitt: Abstract.
safe_wording: Evidence on stretching is limited and mixed. In one small trial in people aged 55 and over, calf and hamstring stretches before bed for six weeks may have made cramps less painful; whether they came less often is very uncertain. In another, calf stretches alone made little or no difference. No one in these trials reported harm, so stretching is reasonable to try, but it is not a proven treatment.
qualifications: The candidate's claim that stretching 'reduced the frequency and severity' (Hallegraeff 2012 alone) overstates the evidence; present stretching as low-risk to try. Do not use the Hallegraeff '1.2 cramps per night' figure (very low certainty).

claim: Some medicines are linked with night cramps, particularly thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics and long-acting beta-agonist inhalers.
supporting_passage: Garrison 2012, Abstract: "Adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) for the 3 drug classes were 1.47 (1.33-1.63 [P < .001]) for diuretics, 1.16 (1.04-1.29 [P = .004]) for statins, and 2.42 (2.02-2.89 [P < .001]) for LABAs. For diuretic subclasses, adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) were 2.12 (1.61-2.78 [P < .001]) for potassium sparing, 1.48 (1.29-1.68 [P < .001]) for thiazidelike, and 1.20 (1.00-1.44 [P = .07]) for loop." ... "Cramp treatment was substantially more likely in the year following introduction of LABAs, potassium-sparing diuretics, or thiazidelike diuretics, and 60.3% of quinine users (individuals experiencing cramp) received at least 1 of these medications during a 13-year period. In contrast, statin and loop diuretic associations were small." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Recent evidence suggests that diuretic and long-acting beta-agonist therapy predispose to leg cramps."
safe_wording: Some medicines are linked with night cramps. In a large Canadian study of adults aged 50 and over, new treatment for cramps was more common in the year after starting some water tablets (thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics) or long-acting inhalers for the lungs. The link with statins and loop diuretics was small. This kind of study shows a link, not proof that the medicine caused the cramps.
qualifications: Observational; quinine starts are a proxy for cramps. Do not convert sequence ratios into 'X times more likely'. Never suggest stopping a diuretic or inhaler without advice; the action is to ask a doctor or pharmacist.

claim: Co-codamol (codeine with paracetamol) and co-dydramol (dihydrocodeine with paracetamol) contain paracetamol; co-codamol 8/500 is sold in UK pharmacies without prescription.
supporting_passage: Methods, Definitions: "compound overdose described overdose of compound tablets which included paracetamol such as co-proxamol or co-dydramol." Results: "Of the 48 subjects who had consumed an overdose of compound analgesics, the majority (21/48, 43.8%) had used codeine phosphate/paracetamol compounds (co-codamol), an analgesic available over the counter (OTC) in pharmacies in the UK at a dose of 8/500 mg, and only by prescription at higher doses. A total of 14 subjects had overdosed on prescribed compound analgesics, namely dextropropoxyphene/paracetamol (co-proxamol, n = 7) and dihydrocodeine tartrate/paracetamol (co-dydramol, n = 7)."
location: Methods (Definitions); Results (Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain)
safe_wording: Co-codamol is codeine plus paracetamol. Co-dydramol is dihydrocodeine plus paracetamol. The lowest-strength co-codamol can be bought in UK pharmacies without a prescription.
qualifications: OTC status is as described in 2012; not rechecked against current UK rules. Do not name brands.

claim: Some cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol.
supporting_passage: Chidiac 2024, Table 1 (Paracetamol involved): "Cold and flu preparations: Entire cohort: 1726 (12.0%)"; Results 3.1: "This was closely followed by combinations with opioids (primarily consisting of paracetamol and codeine with just 0.7% paracetamol and tramadol) and cold and flu preparations (which often include other ingredients including decongestants and sedating antihistamines)." Wolf 2012, Table 3 secondary products shown in the double-dipping scenarios include "Brand Name Combination Cold & Cough (650 mg/dose)" [acetaminophen dose].
location: Chidiac: Table 1 and Results 3.1. Wolf: Methods and Table 3.
safe_wording: Some cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, so check the ingredients list on anything you buy for a cold.
qualifications: Sources describe Australian and US products; UK packs were not examined. Say 'some', not 'most' or 'many'.

claim: The usual maximum daily dose of paracetamol for adults is 4 g in 24 hours.
supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Introduction: "Although paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity at standard therapeutic doses (up to 4 g/d) is rare, cases have been reported." Craig 2012, Methods (Definitions): "a staggered overdose described ingestion of two or more supratherapeutic paracetamol doses over a time interval of greater than 8 h resulting in a cumulative dose of >4 g day-1." Wolf 2012, Abstract: "23.8 % of participants demonstrated they would overdose on a single over-the-counter acetaminophen product by exceeding a dose of four grams in a 24-hour period".
location: Reid: Introduction. Craig: Methods. Wolf: Abstract.
safe_wording: For most adults the usual maximum is 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours. With 500 mg tablets, that is 8 tablets a day, counting every product that contains paracetamol.
qualifications: The BNF and product labels were not opened; the 4 g standard is taken from published papers. '8 tablets' is derived arithmetic (4 g divided by 500 mg). Lower maximums may apply to some people (see C10-09-f).

claim: Taking two paracetamol-containing products at once is a recognised route to accidental excess: in a US study nearly half of adults said they would take two such products together, and about 1 in 5 accidental paracetamol overdose calls to an Australian poisons centre involved more than one product.
supporting_passage: Wolf 2012, Abstract: "In addition, 45.6 % of adults demonstrated they would overdose by 'double-dipping' with two acetaminophen-containing products." Table 4, Double-dipping with 2 products by age: "18-30 37.1; 31-45 44.1; 46-60 52.8; 61-80 40.0" (P = 0.05). Discussion: "Clearly, our study is limited by the fact that the assessments of individuals' misunderstanding and misuse of OTC acetaminophen products reflects hypothetical and not actual health behaviors." Chidiac 2024, Results 3.1: "Multiple paracetamol-containing products (which may include more than one brand of the same category) were taken in 2816 (19.6%) exposures"; Abstract: "The in-depth analysis of exposures recorded during 2021 revealed 1899 exposures (median age 46 years, 63.4% female) with 26.8% requiring hospitalisation." ... "6% of exposures developed hepatotoxicity." Table 1: "Elderly >=75 years: Entire cohort: 1733 (12.1%)".
location: Wolf: Abstract, Table 4, Discussion. Chidiac: Abstract, Results 3.1, Table 1.
safe_wording: Doubling up is easy to do. In a US study, nearly half of 500 adults, shown real shop products, said it would be safe to take two paracetamol-containing products together; among those aged 61 to 80 it was 4 in 10. At an Australian poisons centre, about 1 in 5 calls about accidentally taking too much paracetamol involved more than one paracetamol product.
qualifications: Wolf measured what people said they would do, not what they did, and used US products. Chidiac counts calls, not confirmed harm; hospitalisation and liver-injury figures apply to all ages in 2021, not older people specifically. Neither study is UK-based. Do not say accidental excess 'in older people is often' a counting problem: no source gives that proportion for older people.

claim: In a Scottish liver unit series of adults with severe paracetamol liver injury, about 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than at once, and pain relief was the commonest reason among them.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Between 1992 and 2008, 663 patients were admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury, of whom 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were significantly older and more likely to abuse alcohol than single time point overdose patients. Relief of pain (58.2%) was the commonest rationale for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion." ... "had higher mortality rates compared with single time point overdoses (37.3% vs. 27.8%, P= 0.025), although this overdose pattern did not independently predict death." Results: "Staggered overdose subjects were significantly older (median 39 (29-46) years) compared with single overdose patients (32 (24-43) years, P < 0.001)" ...
