"Information regarding the reasons for overdose was available for 134/161 (83.2%) of staggered overdoses. The most common (58.2%) rationale for overdose was for relief of pain" ... "A total of 46/134 (34.3%) of staggered overdoses were taken deliberately as a suicide attempt." Table 1: "Age (years): 34 (26-44)".
location: Abstract; Results (Single time point vs staggered overdoses; Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain); Tables 1 and 2
safe_wording: In a Scottish liver unit, 663 adults were admitted with severe liver damage from paracetamol between 1992 and 2008. About 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than all at once. Where the reason was known, the most common was trying to relieve pain (78 of 134). Most people in this series were young or middle-aged adults.
qualifications: State that this was a series of adults of all ages (median 34; staggered group median 39), not older people; do not use 'older' from the abstract. A third of the staggered group were suicide attempts and many misused alcohol. Do not imply that doubling up commonly causes liver failure in older people. Mortality difference was not independent of other factors; do not present it as caused by the staggered pattern.

claim: For people who are frail or weigh under 50 kg, a lower daily paracetamol maximum is often advised, though the safest dose has not been established; full adult doses are common in this group.
supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Abstract: "Paracetamol doses administered in hospital, and doses prescribed on discharge, were compared against consensus guidelines that recommended <=60 mg/kg/d for older people weighing <50 kg, and <=3000 mg/d for frail older people." ... "In total, 240 admissions (n = 229 patients, mean age 84.7 years) were analysed. During 150 (62.5%) admissions, higher than recommended paracetamol doses were prescribed. On 138 (57.5%) occasions, patients were prescribed paracetamol on discharge, and 112/138 (81.2%) doses were higher than recommended." Introduction: "For example, England's Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch, an organisation responsible for the investigating patient safety concerns, is conducting an investigation titled Unintentional overdose of paracetamol in adults with low body weight. This was prompted by reports of paracetamol overdose in patients with low body weight at therapeutic doses." Discussion: "Although there is limited evidence that the standard maximum therapeutic dose (4 g/d) leads to significant rates of liver injury in frail and low-weight older people, we believe that reduced doses should be considered for 3 reasons." Caparrotta 2018, Abstract: "The safe (and still effective) oral dose of paracetamol in patients weighing less than 50 kg has not been established." ... "There is no patient group that is unequivocally at elevated risk of paracetamol-induced liver toxicity."
location: Reid: Abstract, Introduction, Discussion. Caparrotta: Abstract.
safe_wording: If you weigh under 50 kg (about 7 stone 12 lb) or are frail, ask a pharmacist or doctor whether a lower daily maximum is right for you. Some guidelines advise a lower dose for people in this group, although research has not established the safest dose. In one Australian study of frail or low-weight hospital patients aged 70 and over, about 8 in 10 discharge prescriptions were above those guideline doses.
qualifications: Do not quote or cite the BNF: its exact wording for adults under 50 kg was not opened. The consensus guidelines in Reid are Australian. England's HSIB investigation is reported via Reid, not opened. Evidence that 4 g a day harms low-weight older people is limited (Reid; Caparrotta), so frame lower doses as a precaution, not as proven necessary. '7 stone 12 lb' is a unit conversion of 50 kg.

claim: Paracetamol packs advise against taking other paracetamol-containing products at the same time.
supporting_passage: No passage opened. UK pack labelling, the BNF and MHRA pages could not be opened from this environment.
safe_wording: Do not state what pack labels say. Advise readers to check the ingredients of every product and ask a pharmacist.
qualifications: Unverified; leave out.

claim: In randomised trials in people aged 60 and over with insomnia, sleeping tablets increased self-reported total sleep time by an average of about 25 minutes a night and reduced night-time awakenings by 0.63 compared with placebo.
supporting_passage: "24 studies (involving 2417 participants) with extractable data met inclusion and exclusion criteria. Sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14, P < 0.05), total sleep time increased (mean 25.2 minutes, P < 0.001), and the number of night time awakenings decreased (0.63, P < 0.001) with sedative use compared with placebo." Methods: "total sleep time (total amount of time participants perceive that they have slept, measured in minutes)... Ratings were made by patients and not an observer." Inclusion: "Interventions were pharmacological treatments for insomnia for at least five consecutive nights."
location: Abstract (Results); Methods, Outcome measures and Inclusion criteria (pages 1 to 2 of PDF)
safe_wording: In short trials in people aged 60 and over, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of sleep a night on average, as reported by the people taking them, and about one fewer waking every two nights (0.63 fewer wakings a night).
qualifications: Average, self-reported, short-term (trials lasted from 5 nights to 9 weeks); older drugs (trials to 2003); 'wakings' figure is per night. Say 'in short trials', not 'long term'.

claim: After correcting for possible publication bias, the estimated gain in total sleep time was smaller, about 15 minutes.
supporting_passage: "Funnel plot analyses indicated a possible publication bias on outcomes of sleep quality and total sleep time favouring positive results (rs = 0.78, P ≤ 0.05). The mean effect size did not change after “trim and fill” to correct estimates of effect size, and the result was still significant in favour of sedatives (d = 0.14, P ≤ 0.05 for sleep quality; mean increase in total sleep time = 15 minutes, P ≤ 0.05)."
safe_wording: The true average gain may be smaller still: allowing for unpublished negative trials, the authors' corrected estimate was about 15 minutes.
qualifications: Practitioner detail; optional for public posts. If used, say it is an adjusted estimate.

claim: About 13 people needed to take a sleeping tablet for one extra person to report better sleep quality, while about 6 needed to take one for one extra person to have an adverse event.
supporting_passage: "On the basis of four studies (1072 participants), the number of patients who would need to be treated with a sedative (zaleplon, brotizolam or nitrazepam, or loprazolam) for one to have an improvement in sleep quality is 13 (95% confidence interval 6.7 to 62.9)." "On the basis of all adverse events reported in 16 studies (2220 participants), the number needed to harm for sedative hypnotics compared with placebo is 6 (4.7 to 7.1)." Discussion: "The number needed to treat for improved sleep quality was 13 and the number needed to harm for any adverse event was 6. This ratio indicates that an adverse event is more than twice as likely as enhanced quality of sleep. This ratio can be used as a rough indicator only, as more than double the number of participants contributed to the “harm” data than to the “effectiveness” data (2220 v 1072). The effectiveness estimate is less precise (the confidence interval is wider)."
location: Results, Quality of sleep (page 2) and Adverse events (page 3); Discussion, Numbers needed to treat versus numbers needed to harm (page 4) of the PDF; confirmed by Scite full-text snippets
safe_wording: In these trials, for every 13 people who took a sleeping tablet, about 1 more reported better sleep than with a dummy pill. For every 6 who took one, about 1 more had a side effect, most often drowsiness or tiredness, headache, nightmares or stomach upset. The authors describe this comparison as a rough guide.
qualifications: The two figures come from different sets of trials and outcomes; the NNT is imprecise (could be anywhere from about 7 to 63). Icon arrays must be labelled 'about 1 in 13' and 'about 1 in 6', 'extra compared with a dummy pill', 'short trials', and must not imply the same people.

claim: Memory and thinking problems (memory loss, confusion, disorientation) and daytime tiredness were reported more often with sleeping tablets than with placebo; falls-type events were not clearly shown in this analysis.
supporting_passage: "Adverse events were more common with sedatives than with placebo: adverse cognitive events were 4.78 times more common (95% confidence interval 1.47 to 15.47, P < 0.01); adverse psychomotor events were 2.61 times more common (1.12 to 6.09, P > 0.05), and reports of daytime fatigue were 3.82 times more common (1.88 to 7.80, P < 0.001) in people using any sedative compared with placebo." Methods: "cognitive adverse events (memory loss, confusion, disorientation); psychomotor-type adverse events (reports of dizziness, loss of balance, or falls)". Results: "The most common adverse events were drowsiness or fatigue, headache, nightmares, and nausea or gastrointestinal disturbances."
location: Abstract; Methods, Outcome measures (page 2); Results, Adverse events (page 3)
safe_wording: Memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common with the tablets than with a dummy pill.
qualifications: Do not turn the odds ratios (4.78, 3.82) into 'times more likely' or absolute risks. Do not list 'unsteadiness' or falls as a finding of this paper: psychomotor events were reported as P>0.05 (with an inconsistent confidence interval). For falls and fractures use Beers (C11-16-f) and Berry (C11-16-e).

claim: In US nursing home residents, use of Z-drug sleeping tablets was linked with hip fracture, more strongly in new users.
supporting_passage: "The risk for hip fracture was elevated among users of a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic drug (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.45-1.90). The association between nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic drug use and hip fracture was somes greater in new users (OR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.76-2.74)"
safe_wording: In US care homes, hip fractures were more likely to happen in periods when residents had been taking a Z-drug sleeping tablet, especially when the tablet was newly started. This links the tablets with fractures; it does not prove they caused them.
qualifications: Association, not causation; US Z-drugs (not zopiclone); care home residents only. Do not state 'X times more likely'.

claim: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults.
supporting_passage: Table 2 (page 22): Benzodiazepines, rationale "In general, all benzodiazepines increase the risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle crashes in older adults." Recommendation "Avoid"; Quality of evidence "Moderate"; Strength "Strong". Nonbenzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics (“Z-drugs”) Eszopiclone, Zaleplon, Zolpidem: "have adverse events similar to those of benzodiazepines in older adults (e.g., delirium, falls, fractures, increased emergency room visits/hospitalizations, motor vehicle crashes); minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration." Recommendation "Avoid"; Quality of evidence "Moderate"; Strength "Strong". Discussion: "“Avoid” is not defined as an absolute contraindication unless specified in the medication’s label."
location: Table 2, page 22 of the published PDF (via Undermind read_pdfs); Discussion, Interpreting recommendations (PMC full text)
safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping tablets in people aged 65 and over, noting falls, fractures and confusion, and only small gains in sleep.
qualifications: US guideline; 'avoid' means avoid except in unusual circumstances, with shared decision-making; list excludes zopiclone only because it is not marketed in the US. Do not mention delirium as a topic in the post (collection excludes delirium).

claim: Major guidelines recommend CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for chronic insomnia at any adult age, with sleeping tablets reserved for short-term use if CBT-I is not enough.
supporting_passage: European guideline: "Cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either applied in-person or digitally (A). When cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia is not sufficiently effective, a pharmacological intervention can be offered (A). Benzodiazepines (A), benzodiazepine receptor agonists (A), daridorexant (A) and low-dose sedating antidepressants (B) can be used for the short-term treatment of insomnia (≤ 4 weeks)." ACP: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)."
safe_wording: European and American guidelines recommend CBT for insomnia (a structured talking and sleep-scheduling treatment) as the first treatment for long-term insomnia at any adult age. If it is not enough, a sleeping tablet can be discussed for short-term use.
qualifications: Say 'long-term insomnia' (chronic insomnia disorder). The position that a short course may be reasonable after discussion is consistent with both guidelines. Do not claim NICE wording (not opened).

claim: In hospital, patients sleep less than at home, and the most reported sleep disturbers are noise from other patients, medical devices, pain and toilet visits.
supporting_passage: "Compared with habitual sleep at home, the total sleep time in the hospital was 83 minutes (95% CI, 75-92 minutes; P < .001) shorter." "A total of 1344 patients (70.4%) reported having been awakened by external causes, which in 718 (35.8%) concerned hospital staff." "The most reported sleep-disturbing factors were noise of other patients, medical devices, pain, and toilet visits."
safe_wording: In a survey of 2,005 adults in 39 Dutch hospitals (median age 68), patients reported sleeping 83 minutes less than at home. Noise from other patients, medical equipment, pain and needing the toilet were the disturbances they reported most.
qualifications: Adults of all ages, self-report, one night; people unable to consent excluded. It lists reported disturbers, not proven causes of any one patient's wakefulness.

claim: In people over 60, sedative hypnotics give small sleep gains with more memory and thinking side effects and daytime tiredness than placebo.
supporting_passage: "Improvements in sleep with sedative use are statistically significant, but the magnitude of effect is small. The increased risk of adverse events is statistically significant and potentially clinically relevant in older people at risk of falls and cognitive impairment. In people over 60, the benefits of these drugs may not justify the increased risk, particularly if the patient has additional risk factors for cognitive or psychomotor adverse events."
location: Abstract, Conclusions (numbers in C11-16-a to d)
safe_wording: In trials in people over 60, sleeping tablets added only about 25 minutes of sleep, and memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common than with a dummy pill.
qualifications: Trials were of nightly use over at least 5 nights, not a single 'as required' dose on a ward.

claim: Corticosteroids can disturb sleep, and giving them as a single morning dose may reduce this.
supporting_passage: "GC use can lead to a wide range of psychiatric and cognitive disturbances, including memory impairment, agitation, anxiety, fear, hypomania, insomnia, irritability, lethargy, mood lability, and even psychosis." "GC therapy may also be associated with sleep disturbances and unpleasant dreams [72]; the risk of these events can potentially be decreased by modifying the timing of GC administration (e.g., a single morning dose) and/or night-time administration of drugs with sedative effects." Table 10: "Administer as single daily dose (given in the morning), if possible"
location: Adverse events, Adults, Psychiatric and cognitive disturbances (page 7); Table 10 (page 14) of the PDF, via Undermind read_pdfs
safe_wording: Steroid tablets such as prednisolone can disturb sleep. Expert guidance advises a single morning dose where possible, which may reduce this.
qualifications: Expert advice, not trial evidence; do not claim frequency. Split or evening dosing is sometimes clinically intended; the post should say 'check whether the evening dose is needed', not 'always move it'.

claim: Donepezil can cause insomnia and vivid dreams or nightmares, and moving the dose to the morning may help.
supporting_passage: Jackson 2004: "Although insomnia and other sleep disorders have been reported following administration of donepezil, lengthening the time period before increasing the dose of donepezil from 5 to 10 mg day(-1) or switching to morning dosing can reduce these events to the levels of placebo-treated patients." Moderie 2021: "Medications should also be reviewed, and time of administration should be optimized (diuretics and stimulating medications in the morning, sedating medications in the evening). Importantly, cholinesterase inhibitors (especially donepezil) may trigger insomnia. Switching to morning dosing or to an alternative drug may help." Singer 2005: "We observed a clear-cut relationship between the occurrence of nightmares and an evening dose of donepezil in eight patients with DAT. None of these patients reported nightmares when donepezil was taken in the morning."
location: Abstracts (Jackson: review; Moderie: English abstract of French review; Singer: English abstract of German case series)
safe_wording: Donepezil can cause sleeplessness and vivid dreams. Reviews suggest that taking it in the morning instead may help; this is worth raising with the prescriber the next day.
qualifications: Evidence is from reviews and a case series of 8, not a randomised trial of timing. Frame as a question for the day team, not an overnight change.

claim: A loop diuretic given at teatime or in the evening increases urine output during the night (candidate wording).
supporting_passage: Oelke 2017: "The timing of diuretics is an important consideration, and they should be taken mid-late afternoon, dependent on the specific serum half-life." Reynard 1998: "a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of an afternoon dose of the diuretic frusemide, used to establish an early evening diuresis and so diminish nocturnal voiding frequency and voided volume in elderly men" ... "40 mg of frusemide or placebo, taken 6 h before their usual bedtime" ... "there was a significant reduction in night-time frequency (-0.5 and 0) and percentage night-time voided volume (-18% and 0%) in those taking frusemide compared with placebo." Getaneh 2025: "Limitation of fluid intake, especially in the evening; addressing timing of diuretic intake; and sleep hygiene are recommended." Moderie 2021: "time of administration should be optimized (diuretics and stimulating medications in the morning, sedating medications in the evening)".
safe_wording: Check when any diuretic ('water tablet') is given. Guidance on night-time urination advises taking it earlier in the day, no later than mid to late afternoon, rather than in the evening.
qualifications: The candidate's example of a teatime loop diuretic as a culprit is not supported: in a small trial, furosemide taken about 6 hours before bed (roughly teatime) reduced night-time urination in men with nocturnal polyuria. Only a late-evening or bedtime dose should be named as a possible cause, and even that is expert advice rather than a measured finding.

claim: In Parkinson's disease, symptoms can return overnight when levodopa wears off, and night-time dosing needs review (NICE NG71).
location: Not searched to a usable source: NICE NG71 is not openable from this environment and no published source was opened.
safe_wording: Leave out of the post.
qualifications: Drop this element, as the judge advised keeping only the timing fixes with citable sources.

claim: In the EMPOWER trial, older long-term benzodiazepine users given written information on the risks and a step-by-step tapering plan were far more likely to have stopped at 6 months than those with usual care (27% versus 5%).
supporting_passage: "Participants (303 long-term users of benzodiazepine medication aged 65-95 years, recruited from 30 community pharmacies)" ... "The active arm received a deprescribing patient empowerment intervention describing the risks of benzodiazepine use and a stepwise tapering protocol. The control arm received usual care." ... "Benzodiazepine therapy discontinuation at 6 months after randomization, ascertained by pharmacy medication renewal profiles." ... "At 6 months, 27% of the intervention group had discontinued benzodiazepine use compared with 5% of the control group (risk difference, 23% [95% CI, 14%-32%]; intracluster correlation, 0.008; number needed to treat, 4). Dose reduction occurred in an additional 11% (95% CI, 6%-16%)."
safe_wording: In a Quebec trial of 303 people aged 65 to 95 who had taken benzodiazepines for a long time, those given a booklet on the risks and a step-by-step plan for cutting down were far more likely to have stopped 6 months later: about 27 in 100, against about 5 in 100 with usual care. A further 11 in 100 had cut their dose.
qualifications: 'Stopped' means no further pharmacy refills, not confirmed abstinence. Say 'given', not 'sent' or 'posted' (delivery method not in the abstract). Denominators for the percentages are the randomised groups analysed; 86% completed follow-up. Benzodiazepines for any indication, not only sleep.

claim: Most people who received the EMPOWER booklet started a conversation about stopping with their doctor or pharmacist themselves.
supporting_passage: "Of the recipients in the intervention group, 62% initiated conversation about benzodiazepine therapy cessation with a physician and/or pharmacist."
safe_wording: About 62 in 100 people who got the booklet raised stopping with their doctor or pharmacist themselves.
qualifications: Self-reported by participants.

claim: In the D-PRESCRIBE trial, 43% of sedative-hypnotic users stopped at 6 months with a pharmacist-led educational approach versus 9% with usual care.
supporting_passage: "Pharmacists in the intervention group were encouraged to send patients an educational deprescribing brochure in parallel to sending their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to recommend deprescribing." ... "discontinuation of inappropriate medication occurred among 63 of 146 sedative-hypnotic drug users (43.2%) vs 14 of 155 (9.0%), respectively (risk difference, 34% [95% CI, 25% to 43%])"
safe_wording: In a second Quebec trial, pharmacists sent people a brochure and sent their doctors a recommendation to stop. Among people taking sleeping tablets or similar sedatives, 43 in 100 had stopped at 6 months, against 9 in 100 with usual care.
qualifications: Subgroup result; the intervention included a message to the doctor, so it is not a leaflet alone. Outcome by pharmacy renewal records.

claim: About 4 in 10 people who tapered sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms, but no adverse events needing hospital care were reported.
supporting_passage: "No adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported, although 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms."
safe_wording: Cutting down can be uncomfortable: 29 of 77 people who tried to taper reported withdrawal symptoms, though none needed hospital care. Tapering slowly, with a plan agreed with a doctor or pharmacist, is the approach tested in these trials.
qualifications: Small denominator; self-reported symptoms.

claim: Both trials were in Quebec, and the authors say results may differ elsewhere.
supporting_passage: D-PRESCRIBE: "Among older adults in Quebec, a pharmacist-led educational intervention compared with usual care resulted in greater discontinuation of prescriptions for inappropriate medication after 6 months. The generalizability of these findings to other settings requires further research." EMPOWER: "recruited from 30 community pharmacies" (Montreal, Quebec author affiliations; trial in Quebec).
safe_wording: Both trials were run through community pharmacies in Quebec, and the researchers say the results need testing elsewhere.
qualifications: EMPOWER abstract does not itself state 'Quebec'; D-PRESCRIBE does. Safer to attribute the generalisability statement to D-PRESCRIBE.

claim: Mailed education alone, without pharmacist involvement, did not reduce use of sedatives in later US trials.
supporting_passage: Singh 2024: "Patients were randomized to 1 of 3 arms: (1) a mailing of educational materials specific to the medication targeted for deprescribing to both the patient and their prescribing clinician; (2) a mailing to the prescribing clinician only; or (3) a usual care arm." ... "The cumulative incidence of being dispensed a medication targeted for deprescribing was 76.7% (95% CI, 75.4-78.0) in the patient and prescriber mailing group, 77.9% (95% CI, 76.5-79.1) in the prescriber mailing only group, and 77.5% (95% CI, 76.2-78.8) in the usual care group." ... "These findings suggest medication-specific educational mailings targeting patients with AD or ADRD and their clinicians are not effective in reducing the use of high-risk medications." Mak 2022: "Arm 1 was a mailed brochure about BZRA risks that also included information about a free, online cognitive behavioral therapy for the insomnia (CBTI) program. Arm 2 was a mailed brochure (same as arm 1) and telephone reinforcement call. Control: Arm 3 was a mailed brochure without insomnia treatment information." ... "Mailing information about BZRA risks and CBTI did not affect BZRA prescriptions."
safe_wording: The same idea by post alone has not always worked. In a US trial of 12,787 people with dementia, mailing information to them and their prescribers did not reduce use of the targeted medicines, including sedatives.
qualifications: Singh combined three drug classes and people with dementia; Mak's control arm also got a risk brochure, so it tested extra CBT-I information, not brochure versus nothing. Present as 'the setting and follow-through seem to count', not as disproof of the Quebec trials.

claim: Prolonged-release melatonin can be used for short-term treatment of insomnia in people aged 55 and over (up to 3 months in the European guideline); fast-release melatonin is not recommended.
supporting_passage: European guideline: "Prolonged-release melatonin can be used for up to 3 months in patients ≥ 55 years (B). Antihistaminergic drugs, antipsychotics, fast-release melatonin, ramelteon and phytotherapeutics are not recommended for insomnia treatment (A)." Hajak 2015: "Prolonged-release melatonin (PRM; Circadin) was approved in Europe for the management of primary insomnia patients age 55 years or older suffering from poor quality of sleep."
safe_wording: The European insomnia guideline says prescribed slow-release melatonin can be used for up to 3 months in people aged 55 and over with insomnia. It does not recommend ordinary fast-release melatonin for insomnia.
qualifications: Use this in place of the candidate's UK licence wording. Grade B for prolonged-release melatonin (moderate strength).

claim: In the UK, prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (Circadin) is licensed for short-term treatment of primary insomnia in people aged 55 and over for up to 13 weeks, and melatonin is prescription-only.
supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (emc SmPC and PIL results): "Circadin is indicated as monotherapy for the short-term treatment of primary insomnia characterised by poor quality of sleep in patients who are aged 55 or over." "The recommended dose is 2 mg once daily, 1-2 hours before bedtime and after food, and this dosage may be continued for up to thirteen weeks." Search summary also stated the medicine can only be obtained with a prescription in the UK.
location: Search-engine extract; official page not opened
safe_wording: Do not use as an essential claim. If a UK licence detail is wanted, recheck the emc SmPC directly first; otherwise use C11-24-a.
qualifications: Access is search_extract only, which the evidence standard does not accept for an essential claim. The judge's suggested line 'melatonin is prescription-only in the UK' is not verified from an opened source.

claim: In people with Alzheimer's disease and sleep problems, melatonin up to 10 mg may make little or no difference to sleep over 8 to 10 weeks.
supporting_passage: "We found low-certainty evidence that melatonin doses up to 10 mg may have little or no effect on any major sleep outcome over eight to 10 weeks in people with AD and sleep disturbances. We could synthesise data for two of our primary sleep outcomes: total nocturnal sleep time (TNST) (MD 10.68 minutes, 95% CI -16.22 to 37.59; 2 studies, n = 184)" ... "There were no serious adverse effects of melatonin reported." Conclusions: "We found no evidence for beneficial effects of melatonin (up to 10 mg) or a melatonin receptor agonist. There was evidence of some beneficial effects on sleep outcomes from trazodone and orexin antagonists and no evidence of harmful effects in these small trials"
location: Abstract, Main results and Authors' conclusions
safe_wording: In trials in people with Alzheimer's disease and poor sleep, melatonin (up to 10 mg) may make little or no difference to sleep over 8 to 10 weeks. The evidence is limited, and no serious side effects were reported.
qualifications: Low-certainty evidence, small trials. Say 'may make little or no difference', not 'does not work'. Do not imply nothing helps: the same review found some benefit for trazodone (low certainty) and orexin antagonists (moderate certainty).

claim: Melatonin supplements bought without prescription have been found to contain amounts very different from the label.
supporting_passage: Cohen 2023: "The 30 unique brands entered into the database in 2021 were purchased online." ... "25 products were analyzed. One product did not contain detectable levels of melatonin but did contain 31.3 mg of CBD." ... "In products that contained melatonin, the actual quantity of melatonin ranged from 74% to 347% of the labeled quantity. Twenty-two of 25 products (88%) were inaccurately labeled, and only 3 products (12%) contained a quantity of melatonin that was within ±10% of the declared quantity." Erland 2017: "Melatonin content was found to range from -83% to +478% of the labelled content. Additionally, lot-to-lot variable within a particular product varied by as much as 465%." ... "Melatonin content did not meet label within a 10% margin of the label claim in more than 71% of supplements and an additional 26% were found to contain serotonin."
location: Cohen: Methods and Results (Scite full-text excerpts); Erland: Abstract
safe_wording: When melatonin supplements sold in the US and Canada were tested, most did not contain what the label said. In one US study, 22 of 25 gummy products were wrongly labelled, with actual amounts from about three quarters to more than three times the stated dose; one contained none.
qualifications: North American supplements, not UK prescribed products. Do not claim this about products sold in UK shops (not tested). 'Bought online' is accurate for the US study.

claim: In people with primary sleep disorders, melatonin modestly shortened the time to fall asleep and slightly increased total sleep.
supporting_passage: "Nineteen studies involving 1683 subjects were included in this meta-analysis. Melatonin demonstrated significant efficacy in reducing sleep latency (weighted mean difference (WMD) = 7.06 minutes [95% CI 4.37 to 9.75], Z = 5.15, p<0.001) and increasing total sleep time (WMD = 8.25 minutes [95% CI 1.74 to 14.75], Z = 2.48, p = 0.013)." ... "The effects of melatonin on sleep are modest but do not appear to dissipate with continued melatonin use."
safe_wording: In people with insomnia and other primary sleep problems, melatonin helped people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner and sleep about 8 minutes longer than a dummy pill, on average.
qualifications: Mixed ages including children; not older-specific; average effects.

claim: In a US cohort of new users (mean age 70), low sodium was diagnosed at 146 per 1,000 person-years with desmopressin versus 11 per 1,000 with oxybutynin.
supporting_passage: "We identified 3,137 adults who were newly prescribed desmopressin and matched them to 3,137 adults who were newly prescribed oxybutynin. Mean age was 70, 55% were male, 13% filled a prescription for a diuretic during the baseline time period, and the mean baseline sodium prior to receiving either study drug was 140 mmol/L (normal: 135-145). The rate of hyponatremia was 146 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed desmopressin compared to 11 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed oxybutynin, corresponding to a 13-fold higher rate (HR 13.19; 95% CI 6.69, 26.01; p < 0.01)." ... "Important limitations of our study include unmeasured confounding (for example, over-the-counter medication use, dietary intake), missing data (i.e., only 20% of patients had a baseline serum sodium), and a lack of data on the newer formulation of desmopressin." Methods: "we assessed hyponatremia as the primary position diagnosis ICD9 or ICD10 code (inpatient or outpatient) following prescription of desmopressin or oxybutynin."
location: Abstract; Methods, Study outcomes (page 4 of PDF, via Undermind read_pdfs)
safe_wording: In a US study of about 3,100 people newly prescribed desmopressin (average age 70), low sodium was diagnosed at a rate of about 146 per 1,000 people per year, against about 11 per 1,000 per year in similar people starting oxybutynin, another bladder medicine.
qualifications: Older formulation of desmopressin, not the newer low-dose products; association in observational data; outcome is a coded diagnosis; only about 20% had a baseline sodium. 'Per 1,000 person-years' can be glossed as 'per 1,000 people treated for a year'. The 13-fold figure is a hazard ratio: prefer the two rates.

claim: The 2023 Beers Criteria advise avoiding desmopressin for nocturia or nocturnal polyuria.
supporting_passage: Table 2 (page 24), Genitourinary, Desmopressin: Rationale "High risk of hyponatremia; safer alternative treatments for nocturia (including non- pharmacologic)." Recommendation "Avoid for treatment of nocturia or nocturnal polyuria." Quality of evidence "Moderate". Strength of recommendation "Strong".
location: Table 2, page 24 of the published PDF (via Undermind read_pdfs)
safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise avoiding desmopressin for night-time urination in people aged 65 and over, because of the high risk of low sodium and the availability of safer options, including non-drug ones.
qualifications: US guideline; 'avoid' is not an absolute contraindication.

claim: A review of nocturia in frail older adults concluded that desmopressin is not recommended in frail people because of the risk of low sodium.
supporting_passage: "No studies specific to the frail older adult support the use of pharmacotherapy." ... "Desmopressin may be effective in the older adult, but a high risk of hyponatremia raises concerns for its safety, and therefore it is not recommended in the frail."
safe_wording: A review of night-time urination in frail older people concluded desmopressin is not recommended for them because of the risk of low sodium, and noted that no drug studies have been done specifically in frail people.
qualifications: Narrative review, expert conclusion.

claim: If desmopressin is used, sodium should be checked before starting and early after starting, especially from age 65.
supporting_passage: Juul 2017: "A sodium monitoring plan is proposed whereby baseline sodium must be ≥135 mmol/L (especially important in the elderly), with additional monitoring at week 1 and month 1 for those at elevated risk because they are aged ≥65 years or receiving concomitant medication associated with hyponatraemia." Rembratt 2006: "Age was the best single predictor. Elderly patients (>or=65 years of age) with a baseline serum sodium concentration below normal range were at high risk (75%)." ... "Treatment of nocturia in elderly patients with desmopressin should only be undertaken together with careful monitoring of the serum sodium concentration. Patients with a baseline serum sodium concentration below normal range should not be treated." Ebell 2014: "a lower initial dose of 25 to 50 mcg is appropriate in elderly patients. All patients should be monitored for hyponatremia."
safe_wording: If desmopressin is used, published schemes advise checking sodium before starting (and not starting if it is low), then again at about 1 week and 1 month in people aged 65 or over or taking other medicines that lower sodium, using the lowest dose.
qualifications: Monitoring schemes come from manufacturer-authored analyses and a systematic review, not from the UK product information (not opened). Say 'published schemes advise', not 'the licence requires'.

claim: Desmopressin gives a modest benefit for nocturia.
supporting_passage: "A dose of 100 mcg provided just more than an hour of additional sleep before the first void compared with placebo as well as 0.72 fewer voids per night. Higher doses provided no significant increase in benefit. Hyponatremia (RR 5.1) and headache (RR 4.3) were the most common adverse effects." ... "Desmopressin appears to offer a modest benefit for treating nocturia in generally healthy adults with adequate safety."
safe_wording: In trials in generally healthy adults, desmopressin reduced night-time trips to the toilet by less than one a night on average (0.72 fewer at 100 micrograms) and gave just over an hour more sleep before the first trip.
qualifications: Generally healthy adults, several trials excluded non-responders in a run-in; benefit in frail older people untested.

claim: Low sodium is also common with the newer low-dose tablet: in Japanese men (mean age 75) it occurred in 13% over up to a year.
supporting_passage: "The mean age of the total population was 75.0 ± 9.6 years. A total of 351 adverse drug reactions (ADRs) were reported in 259 patients, including 11 serious ADRs in 7 patients (0.7%). The most common ADR was hyponatremia, which occurred in 140 patients (13.3%)." ... "Patients aged ≥ 75 years, those with underlying medical conditions, and those with abnormal clinical laboratory values, such as reduced renal function or a baseline serum sodium level of < 140 mmol/L, should be closely monitored for the development of hyponatremia during desmopressin treatment for nocturia due to NP."
safe_wording: Newer low-dose tablets still carry the risk: in a Japanese survey of 1,049 men with an average age of 75, about 13 in 100 developed low sodium within a year.
qualifications: Manufacturer-run survey without a comparison group; men only; Japan. Most cases were without reported severe symptoms (no confusion, seizures, stupor or coma recorded among the 19 with symptoms).

claim: Not every study finds a higher risk: a Korean cohort of men with enlarged prostate found no significant increase after matching.
supporting_passage: "After propensity score matching, desmopressin use was not significantly associated with an increased risk of hyponatremia (hazard ratio 1.273, 95% confidence interval 0.988-1.640; p=0.062). Significant predictors of hyponatremia included advanced age, chronic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, and renal disease." ... "clinicians should implement routine monitoring protocols, including serum sodium checks, particularly in high-risk populations"
safe_wording: Practitioner posts may add that a large Korean study in men with enlarged prostate did not find a clear increase after matching, while still advising sodium checks in high-risk people.
qualifications: Men only; comparator alpha-blockers; formulation not stated in abstract; upper confidence limit allows a 64% increase.

claim: In a randomised trial of 327 adults aged 60 and over with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, six 20 to 30 minute telephone sessions of CBT for insomnia over 8 weeks reduced insomnia severity more than education only, and at 12 months 56% versus 26% were in remission.
supporting_passage: "This is a randomized clinical trial of 327 participants 60 years and older who were recruited statewide through Kaiser Permanente Washington from September 2016 to December 2018." ... "Six 20- to 30-minute telephone sessions provided over 8 weeks. Participants submitted daily diaries and received group-specific educational materials. The CBT-I instruction included sleep restriction, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, and homework. The EOC group received information about sleep and OA." ... "Of the 327 participants, the mean (SD) age was 70.2 (6.8) years, and 244 (74.6%) were women. In the 282 participants with follow-up ISI data, the total 2-month posttreatment ISI scores decreased 8.1 points in the CBT-I group and 4.8 points in the EOC group, an adjusted mean between-group difference of -3.5 points (95% CI, -4.4 to -2.6 points; P < .001). Results were sustained at 12-month follow-up (adjusted mean difference, -3.0 points; 95% CI, -4.1 to -2.0 points; P < .001). At 12-month follow-up, 67 of 119 (56.3%) participants receiving CBT-I remained in remission (ISI score, ≤7) compared with 33 of 128 (25.8%) participants receiving EOC."
location: Abstract: Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
safe_wording: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over who had both insomnia and arthritis pain, six phone sessions of CBT for insomnia (20 to 30 minutes each, over 8 weeks) improved sleep more than information about sleep and arthritis. A year later, 56 in 100 in the phone CBT group had no clinically significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 in the information group.
qualifications: Everyone in the trial had osteoarthritis pain; one US health plan. The remission figures use the people with 12-month data (119 and 128), not all 327. Remission means a score of 7 or less on the Insomnia Severity Index. Pain improved after treatment but the difference was not sustained at 12 months.

claim: Telephone CBT-I needs only a phone for the sessions and was designed as an access route for people who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
supporting_passage: "Scalable delivery models of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), an effective treatment, are needed for widespread implementation, particularly in rural and underserved populations lacking ready access to insomnia treatment." ... Key Points, Meaning: "Telephone CBT-I may improve access to an individualized and effective treatment for chronic insomnia among older persons with osteoarthritis pain, including those in rural and medically underserved areas."
location: Abstract (Importance) and Key Points (Meaning), via PMC
safe_wording: The therapy sessions in this trial were delivered by telephone. The researchers present phone delivery as a way to reach older people in rural and underserved areas who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
qualifications: The trial did not measure access or compare uptake between formats. Participants also kept daily sleep diaries and received written materials; how the diaries were returned is not stated in the abstract, so do not say 'nothing but a phone is needed'. Say 'the sessions were by phone'.

claim: CBT for insomnia is the recommended first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults (ACP and AASM guidelines).
supporting_passage: ACP 2016, Abstract: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)." | AASM 2021, Abstract: "1. We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG)."
safe_wording: US guidelines from the American College of Physicians and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults.
qualifications: Both are US guidelines covering adults of all ages. UK (NICE) guidance was not openable from this environment, so do not cite NICE.

claim: A substantial share of older people in the UK do not use the internet.
supporting_passage: Discussion: "In contrast, comparable ELSA estimates (i.e., proportion of users of any frequency, aged 60 +) suggest that in England, this remained constant at 79% before and during the pandemic." | Results: "Weighted estimates from the nationally representative English Longitudinal Study of Ageing suggest that the prevalence of daily Internet use among adults aged 50 + in England increased from 52·9% in 2012/2013 (Wave 6), to 71·8% in 2018/2019 (Wave 9), and finally to 73·9% in June/July 2020" | "This discrepancy increased with age, with those aged 85 + being 17 percentage points less likely (or 22·1% relative to the June/July 2020 average) than those aged 50–64 to use the Internet daily." | Abstract: "Daily use in June/July 2020 was negatively related to age, neighbourhood deprivation, and loneliness, and positively related to partnership status, education, employment, income, and organisation membership." | Discussion: "It is also worth noting that older adults in care homes have been excluded by design. There could be an under-representation of infrequent or non-users in our sample, in which case, the rates of Internet use would be lower than estimated."
location: Results (Daily Internet use; Factors predicting use); Discussion
safe_wording: In England in 2020, about 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living in their own homes did not use the internet. Daily use was lower in the oldest age groups, in more deprived areas and among lonelier people.
qualifications: England only (not the whole UK); 2020 data; care home residents excluded, and the authors say non-users may be under-represented, so the real figure is probably higher. The 85+ gap (17 percentage points) is adjusted for other factors and past use.

claim: NICE recommends a digital CBT-I programme (Sleepio, MTG70) as an option in primary care.
safe_wording: Do not state this. The NICE page could not be opened and no PubMed-indexed source stating it was found.
qualifications: Non-essential; drop from the post.

claim: In the UK, CBT for insomnia components can be delivered without an app: in an English trial, general practice nurses delivered sleep restriction therapy in four sessions.
supporting_passage: "Adults with insomnia disorder were recruited from 35 general practices across England and randomly assigned (1:1) using a web-based randomisation programme to either four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet or a sleep hygiene booklet only." ... "Brief nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy in primary care reduces insomnia symptoms, is likely to be cost-effective, and has the potential to be widely implemented as a first-line treatment for insomnia disorder."
safe_wording: An English trial showed that practice nurses can deliver a core part of CBT for insomnia, called sleep restriction therapy, in four sessions in general practice. It is a practical, non-digital route to ask about.
qualifications: This is trial evidence of feasibility and benefit, not proof that the service is routinely available. The post may suggest asking the GP practice whether CBT for insomnia can be given by phone or in person; it must not state that the NHS routinely offers it. The HABIT population was mostly middle-aged (mean 55).

claim: The AASM suggests that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia, and recommends multicomponent CBT-I; stimulus control, sleep restriction and relaxation are suggested as single components.
supporting_passage: "1. We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG). 2. We suggest that clinicians use multicomponent brief therapies for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 3. We suggest that clinicians use stimulus control as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 4. We suggest that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 5. We suggest that clinicians use relaxation therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 6. We suggest that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL)."
safe_wording: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using sleep hygiene advice on its own to treat long-term insomnia. It recommends full CBT for insomnia, and suggests stimulus control, sleep restriction or relaxation therapy as single treatments.
qualifications: The advice against sleep hygiene alone is a conditional recommendation ('we suggest ... not'), as are the single-component recommendations; only multicomponent CBT-I is a strong recommendation. Covers adults of all ages. Sleep hygiene can remain part of a multicomponent treatment.

claim: In the HABIT trial in English general practice, four nurse-delivered sleep restriction sessions plus a sleep hygiene booklet reduced insomnia severity at 6 months more than the booklet alone, and were likely cost-effective.
supporting_passage: "We did a pragmatic, superiority, open-label, randomised controlled trial of sleep restriction therapy versus sleep hygiene. Adults with insomnia disorder were recruited from 35 general practices across England and randomly assigned (1:1) using a web-based randomisation programme to either four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet or a sleep hygiene booklet only." ... "we randomly assigned 642 participants to sleep restriction therapy (n=321) or sleep hygiene (n=321). Mean age was 55·4 years (range 19-88)" ... "At 6 months, mean ISI score was 10·9 (SD 5·5) for sleep restriction therapy and 13·9 (5·2) for sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3·05, 95% CI -3·83 to -2·28; p<0·0001; Cohen's d -0·74)" ... "The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2076, giving a 95·3% probability that treatment was cost-effective at a cost-effectiveness threshold of £20 000."
safe_wording: In a large English general practice trial, the comparison group received a sleep hygiene booklet. People who also had four sessions of sleep restriction therapy from a practice nurse had less severe insomnia at 6 months (average score 10.9 against 13.9 on a 0 to 28 scale), and the treatment was likely to be good value for the NHS.
qualifications: Not an older-adult trial: mean age 55 (range 19 to 88). Open label with a self-reported outcome. Pair with Buysse 2011 for older-adult evidence.

claim: In older adults with chronic insomnia, brief behavioural treatment produced a response in 67% versus 25% with printed educational material (RCT).
supporting_passage: "A total of 79 older adults (mean age, 71.7 years; 54 women [70%]) with chronic insomnia and common comorbidities were recruited from the community and 1 primary care clinic. Participants were randomly assigned to either BBTI, consisting of individualized behavioral instructions delivered in 2 intervention sessions and 2 telephone calls, or IC, consisting of printed educational material. Both interventions were delivered by a nurse clinician. The primary outcome was categorically defined treatment response at 4 weeks" ... "Categorically defined response (67% [n = 26] vs 25% [n = 10]; χ(2) = 13.8) (P < .001) and the proportion of participants without insomnia (55% [n = 21] vs 13% [n = 5]; χ(2) = 15.5) (P < .001) were significantly higher for BBTI than for IC. The number needed to treat was 2.4 for each outcome." ... "Improvements were maintained at 6 months."
safe_wording: In a trial of 79 older adults (average age 72) with long-term insomnia, about 2 in 3 improved after two nurse sessions and two phone calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 of those given printed information. The benefit was still there at 6 months.
qualifications: Small single-centre US trial; the primary outcome was at 4 weeks. The printed information control is comparable to a leaflet but not identical to a sleep hygiene leaflet. Use 'about 2 in 3 vs 1 in 4' rather than n values, as group denominators are not stated in the abstract.

claim: CBT for insomnia is the recommended initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults.
supporting_passage: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)."
safe_wording: The American College of Physicians recommends CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults.
qualifications: US guideline, adults of all ages.

claim: The trial randomised 291 adults aged 60 and over (mean 70.1) with insomnia and no current major depression to 2 months of CBT-I or sleep education therapy.
supporting_passage: "This assessor-blinded, parallel-group, single-site randomized clinical trial assessed a community-based sample of 431 people and enrolled 291 adults 60 years or older with insomnia disorder who had no major depression or major health events in past year." ... "Participants were randomized to 2 months of CBT-I (n = 156) or SET (n = 135)." ... "Among 291 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 70.1 [6.7] years; 168 [57.7%] female"
location: Abstract: Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
safe_wording: The trial included 291 people aged 60 and over (average age 70) who had insomnia but were not depressed. They had 2 months of either CBT for insomnia or sleep education.
qualifications: Single site in Los Angeles; people with a major health event in the past year were excluded.

claim: Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 12.2% of the CBT-I group and 25.9% of the sleep education group over follow-up (HR 0.51).
supporting_passage: "Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 19 participants (12.2%) in the CBT-I group and in 35 participants (25.9%) in the SET group, with an overall benefit (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95%, CI 0.29-0.88; P = .02) consistent across subgroups." ... "The findings of this randomized clinical trial indicate that treatment of insomnia with CBT-I has an overall benefit in the prevention of incident and recurrent major depression in older adults with insomnia disorder."
safe_wording: Over up to 3 years of follow-up, 12 in 100 people who had CBT for insomnia developed major depression, compared with 26 in 100 who had sleep education. The risk of depression over time was about half as high with CBT.
qualifications: The 12 vs 26 in 100 are crude proportions of everyone randomised (19/156 and 35/135), not adjusted for unequal follow-up; the primary analysis was the hazard ratio of 0.51 (confidence interval 0.29 to 0.88, so the true reduction could be smaller or larger). Label icon arrays 'up to 3 years' and 'people randomised'. Do not use the 82.6% figure for CBT-I remitters: that compares a subgroup defined after randomisation and is not a randomised comparison.

claim: Follow-up completion at 24 months was lower in the CBT-I group (73%) than the comparison group (87%); follow-up was extended from 24 to 36 months by protocol amendment; the sample was 83% White.
supporting_passage: "The trial protocol was modified to extend follow-up from 24 to 36 months, with follow-up completion in July 2018." ... "7 [2.4%] Asian, 32 [11.0%] Black, 3 [1.0%] Pacific Islander, 241 [82.8%] White, 6 [2.1%] multiracial, and 2 [0.7%] unknown" ... "A total of 140 participants (89.7%) completed CBT-I and 130 (96.3%) participants completed SET (χ2 = 4.9, P = .03), with 114 (73.1%) completing 24 months of follow-up in the CBT-I group and 117 (86.7%) in the SET group (χ2 = 8.4, P = .004). After protocol modification, 92 (59.0%) of the CBT-I participants and 86 (63.7%) of the SET participants agreed to extended follow-up (χ2 = 0.7, P = .41), with 81 (51.9%) of the CBT-I participants and 77 (57.0%) of the SET group completing 36 months of follow-up"
safe_wording: Read it with care: it was one trial at one site, more than 8 in 10 participants were White, and more people dropped out of follow-up in the CBT group (73 in 100 completed 2 years, against 87 in 100 with sleep education). Only just over half completed 3 years.
qualifications: Uneven drop-out could bias the result in either direction. Single site; excluded people with recent major health events, so frailer older people are under-represented.

claim: A meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,577 people aged 5 to 102) found that in adults total sleep time, sleep efficiency and deep sleep fell and time awake after sleep onset rose with age, but only sleep efficiency continued to fall significantly after 60; age effects were modified, sometimes diminished, by how well participants were screened for illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
supporting_passage: "65 studies representing 3,577 subjects aged 5 years to 102 years." ... "In adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, percentage of slow-wave sleep, percentage of REM sleep, and REM latency all significantly decreased with age, while sleep latency, percentage of stage 1 sleep, percentage of stage 2 sleep, and wake after sleep onset significantly increased with age. However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age. The magnitudes of the effect sizes noted changed depending on whether or not studied participants were screened for mental disorders, organic diseases, use of drug or alcohol, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, or other sleep disorders." ... "effect sizes for the different sleep parameters were greatly modified by the quality of subject screening, diminishing or even masking age associations with different sleep parameters."
safe_wording: In healthy adults, sleep gets somewhat shorter, lighter and more broken with age. An older review of sleep studies found that after 60 only sleep efficiency (the share of time in bed spent asleep) kept falling clearly, and that age effects looked smaller when studies screened out illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
qualifications: Do not paraphrase as 'most change has happened by 60': the abstract says only one measure continued to fall significantly after 60, which is not the same thing. Studies were mostly small and published 1960 to 2003.

claim: In healthy adults, measured sleep changes gradually with age: for each decade, total sleep time falls by about 10 minutes and time awake after sleep onset rises by about 10 minutes.
supporting_passage: "Of 3712 articles, 169 studies, comprising 5273 participants, were eligible for inclusion." ... "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4), sleep onset latency increased by 1·1 min (0·3 to 1·9), arousal index increased by 2·1 events per h (1·5 to 2·6), percentage of N1 sleep increased by 0·5% (0·1 to 0·8), apnea-hypopnea index increased by 1·2 events per h (0·9 to 1·4)" ... "Changes with age in the percentage of N2 sleep (0·0%, 95% CI -0·1 to 0·1), N3 sleep (-0·1%, -0·1 to 0·0), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (0·0%, -0·1 to 0·0) were not significant."
safe_wording: In healthy adults, a large review of overnight sleep studies found that each extra decade of age brought about 10 minutes less sleep and about 10 minutes more time awake during the night. That is a gradual, modest change, not a collapse of sleep.
qualifications: Laboratory sleep of healthy volunteers; averages, not individual limits. Linear per-decade model; it does not show whether change speeds up or levels off in late life. Illustration: 40 years (for example 40 to 80) would be about 40 minutes less sleep on average, but only present this as arithmetic on the per-decade estimate if used at all.

claim: The US National Sleep Foundation recommends 7 to 8 hours for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults and adults.
supporting_passage: "For teenagers, 8 to 10 hours was considered appropriate, 7 to 9 hours for young adults and adults, and 7 to 8 hours of sleep for older adults." ... "The recommendations reported here represent guidelines for healthy individuals and those not suffering from a sleep disorder. Sleep durations outside the recommended range may be appropriate, but deviating far from the normal range is rare."
safe_wording: An expert panel for the US National Sleep Foundation suggests 7 to 8 hours a night for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults. So the saying that older people need less sleep is only slightly true: the recommended range drops by an hour at the top end, not at the bottom.
qualifications: Consensus opinion, not measured need. The abstract does not state the age at which 'older adults' starts; do not write '65 and over' unless it is checked in the full text.

claim: Sleep complaints in older people are common and are associated with health problems such as depression, pain, respiratory symptoms, disability and medicines.
supporting_passage: Foley 1995: "The frequencies of five common sleep complaints--trouble falling asleep, waking up, awaking too early, needing to nap and not feeling rested--were assessed in over 9,000 participants aged 65 years and older" ... "Less than 20% of the participants in each community rarely or never had any complaints, whereas over half reported at least one of these complaints as occurring most of the time. Between 23% and 34% had symptoms of insomnia" ... "In multivariate analyses, sleep complaints were associated with an increasing number of respiratory symptoms, physical disabilities, nonprescription medications, depressive symptoms and poorer self-perceived health. Sleep disturbances, particularly among older persons, oftentimes may be secondary to coexisting diseases." | Foley 2004: "Depression, heart disease, bodily pain and memory problems were associated with more prevalent symptoms of insomnia. Other conditions such as obesity, arthritis, diabetes, lung diseases, stroke and osteoporosis were associated with other sleep-related problems such as breathing pauses, snoring, daytime sleepiness, restless legs or insufficient sleep (<6 h nightly)." ... "These results suggest that the sleep complaints common in older adults are often secondary to their comorbidities and not to aging per se."
safe_wording: Sleep complaints are common in later life, and in large US surveys they were linked with low mood, pain, heart and lung problems, disability and some medicines. The researchers concluded that much of the poor sleep seen in older adults goes with these conditions rather than with age itself.
qualifications: Cross-sectional associations: they do not prove the conditions cause the poor sleep (the link can run both ways). US data from the 1980s and 2003.

claim: New insomnia in later life mostly occurs alongside identifiable health or life factors: in a 3-year cohort of people aged 65 and over, only 7% of new cases occurred without associated risk factors, and nearly half of chronic insomnia remitted.
supporting_passage: "Nearly 15% of the 4,956 participants without symptoms of insomnia at baseline reported chronic difficulty falling asleep or early morning arousal at follow-up, suggesting an annual incidence rate of approximately 5%. Incident insomnia was associated with depressed mood, respiratory symptoms, fair to poor perceived health, and physical disability." ... "Other factors associated with an increased risk of insomnia included use of prescribed sedatives, and widowhood. Only 7% of the incident cases of insomnia occurred in the absence of associated risk factors. Of the nearly 2,000 survivors with chronic insomnia at baseline, almost half no longer reported symptoms upon follow-up" ... "Because the vast majority of incident cases of insomnia were among persons with one or more of these risk factors, these data do not support a model of incident insomnia caused by the aging process per se."
safe_wording: In a large US study of people aged 65 and over followed for 3 years, only about 7 in 100 new cases of insomnia happened in people without a linked problem such as low mood, breathing symptoms, poor health, disability, sleeping tablet use or bereavement. Almost half of those with long-standing insomnia had improved 3 years later.
qualifications: Observational and old (1980s US data); self-reported insomnia. The factors are linked with insomnia, not proven causes. Sedative use may be a response to insomnia rather than a cause.

claim: Needing to pass urine at night (nocturia) is linked with insomnia in older adults.
supporting_passage: "A total of 5396 older adults were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled estimate of the OR was 1.958 (95% CI: 1.609-2.384) for nocturia in patients with insomnia based on 7 studies in a random effects model" ... "The overall odds for nocturia in older adults is higher in patients with insomnia than those without and is associated with worse sleep outcomes." ... "A limiting factor of our analysis was the scarcity of available data, potentially causing an important selection bias."
safe_wording: Getting up at night to pass urine is more common in older adults who have insomnia, and the two often go together, so it is worth asking about.
qualifications: Association only; the direction is unclear (waking may prompt voiding, or the bladder may wake the person). Do not convert the odds ratio into 'twice as likely'. Small evidence base.

claim: In healthy adults most age-related change in measured sleep has happened by about 60.
supporting_passage: Ohayon 2004: "However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age." | Boulos 2019: "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4)"
safe_wording: Do not say 'most change has happened by 60'. Say instead that in healthy people sleep changes gradually with age, by about 10 minutes less sleep per decade, so a large or sudden change is not explained by age alone.
qualifications: The candidate's paraphrase overstates Ohayon, and the more recent Boulos meta-analysis models a steady decline across adulthood.

claim: In 1,280 people with polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (mean age 66, 82.5% men), the rate of developing an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, and 73.5% had converted after 12 years.
supporting_passage: "Idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a powerful early sign of Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy." ... "We combined prospective follow-up data from 24 centres of the International RBD Study Group. At baseline, patients with polysomnographically-confirmed iRBD without parkinsonism or dementia underwent sleep, motor, cognitive, autonomic and special sensory testing." ... "Overall, 1280 patients were recruited. The average age was 66.3 ± 8.4 and 82.5% were male. Average follow-up was 4.6 years (range = 1-19 years). The overall conversion rate from iRBD to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting after 12-year follow-up."
safe_wording: Among 1,280 people whose dream enactment was confirmed as REM sleep behaviour disorder in specialist sleep centres, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition. By 12 years the estimate was about 3 in 4.
qualifications: Specialist-centre patients with sleep-study confirmation, mostly men; the 12-year figure is a Kaplan-Meier estimate (average follow-up was 4.6 years). It is not a personal prognosis for everyone who acts out dreams; people reporting dream enactment in the community are much less likely to have confirmed RBD (see C11-21-f). Conversion outcomes include Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.

claim: REM sleep behaviour disorder is a core clinical feature in the consensus diagnostic criteria for dementia with Lewy bodies.
supporting_passage: "RBD is now included as a core clinical feature because it occurs frequently in autopsy-confirmed cases compared with non-DLB (76% vs 4%). It often begins many years before other symptoms, may become less vigorous or even quiescent over time, and should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report." ... "If the PSG shows REM sleep without atonia in a person with dementia and a history of RBD, there is a ≥90% likelihood of a synucleinopathy,sufficient to justify a probable DLB diagnosis even in the absence of any other core feature or biomarker"
location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder; Indicative biomarkers
safe_wording: Acting out dreams (REM sleep behaviour disorder) is one of the four core features used to diagnose dementia with Lewy bodies. It often starts many years before other symptoms.
qualifications: The 76% vs 4% compares autopsy-confirmed DLB with other dementias; it is not the chance that someone who acts out dreams has DLB.

claim: RBD is often reported by the bed partner; conditions that mimic it (such as severe obstructive sleep apnoea) must be excluded, and doubt should prompt referral to a sleep clinic or polysomnography.
supporting_passage: "RBD is a parasomnia manifested by recurrent dream enactment behavior that includes movements mimicking dream content and associated with an absence of normal REM sleep atonia. It is particularly likely if dreams involve a chasing or attacking theme, and if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements." ... "should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report.Conditions mimicking RBD are common in people with dementia, e.g., confusional awakenings, severe obstructive sleep apnea, and periodic limb movements, all of which must be excluded by careful supplementary questioning to avoid a false-positive diagnosis. If there is any doubt whether a sleep disturbance is due to RBD, referral to a specialist sleep clinic should be made, or polysomnography (PSG) requested."
location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder
safe_wording: Ask the bed partner as well as the person: dreams with a chasing or attacking theme and injuries from movements in sleep make REM sleep behaviour disorder more likely. Other problems can look similar, including severe sleep apnoea, so if there is doubt, refer for a sleep study.
qualifications: Written for DLB assessment; the principle (partner history, exclude mimics, sleep study if doubt) applies generally. Access to sleep studies varies; do not imply everyone will get one quickly.

claim: Injuries to the person or bed partner occur, and bedroom safety measures are recommended.
supporting_passage: AASM 2023, Good Practice Statement: "It is critically important to help patients maintain a safe sleeping environment to prevent potentially injurious nocturnal behaviors. In particular, the removal of bedside weapons, or objects that could inflict injury if thrown or wielded against a bed partner, is of paramount importance. Sharp furniture like nightstands should be moved away or their edges and headboard should be padded. To reduce the risk of injurious falls, a soft carpet, rug, or mat should be placed next to the bed. Patients with severe, uncontrolled RBD should be recommended to sleep separately from their partners, or at the minimum, to place a pillow between themselves and their partners." | McKeith 2017: "if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements"
location: AASM abstract (Good Practice Statement); McKeith full text
safe_wording: US sleep specialists advise making the bedroom safe: remove objects that could hurt someone, move or pad sharp furniture and the headboard, put a soft rug or mat beside the bed, and, if episodes are severe, sleep apart or put a pillow between partners.
qualifications: Good practice statement based on expert consensus, not trial evidence.

claim: Antidepressants can bring on or worsen REM sleep behaviour disorder, so medicines should be reviewed; but antidepressant-associated RBD can still be a sign of early neurodegeneration.
supporting_passage: AASM 2023: "Adult patients with drug-induced RBD" ... "9. * The AASM suggests that clinicians use drug discontinuation (vs drug continuation) for the treatment of drug-induced RBD in adults. (CONDITIONAL)" | Haba-Rubio 2018: "Compared with RBD- participants, RBD+ took more frequently antidepressants and antipsychotics (23.8% vs. 5.4%, p = .005; 14.3% vs. 1.5%, p = .004, respectively)" | Postuma 2013: "Compared to matched controls, RBD patients taking antidepressants demonstrated significant abnormalities of 12/14 neurodegenerative markers tested" ... "However, on prospective follow-up, RBD patients taking antidepressants had a lower risk of developing neurodegenerative disease than those without antidepressant use (5-year risk = 22% vs. 59%, RR = 0.22, 95%CI = 0.06, 0.74)." ... "Development of RBD with antidepressants can be an early signal of an underlying neurodegenerative disease."
location: Abstracts: AASM recommendations; HypnoLaus Results; Postuma 2013 Results and Conclusions
safe_wording: Some medicines, including antidepressants, are linked with acting out dreams, and sleep specialists suggest stopping the drug where it is thought to be the cause. But in one specialist cohort, people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still showed early signs of Parkinson-type disease, so a medicines review should not end the assessment.
qualifications: The link in the general population is an association (people with RBD took antidepressants more often). The specific classes (for example serotonergic drugs) were not verified from the text read; say 'some antidepressants'. Do not use the 'up to 6% of users' figure, which is background in the Postuma 2013 abstract. Stopping an antidepressant needs its own risk-benefit decision.

claim: Dream enactment reported in the community often turns out not to be RBD on a sleep study, so the specialist-centre conversion figures cannot be applied to everyone who acts out dreams.
supporting_passage: "Full polysomnographic data from 1,997 participants (age = 59 ± 11.1 years, 53.6% women) participating in a population-based study (HypnoLaus, Lausanne, Switzerland) were collected." ... "Three hundred sixty-eight participants endorsed dream-enactment behavior on either of the two MUPS questions, and 21 fulfilled polysomnographic criteria for RBD, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 1.06% (95% CI = 0.61-1.50), with no difference between men and women."
safe_wording: In a Swiss population study, 368 of about 2,000 adults said they acted out dreams, but only 21 had REM sleep behaviour disorder on a sleep study. About 1 in 100 adults had it. A report of dream enactment is a reason to assess, not a diagnosis.
qualifications: One city; mean age 59, so younger than many geriatric patients. Screening was by two questionnaire items. 21 of 368 is roughly 1 in 18, but present the raw numbers rather than a derived ratio unless needed.

claim: Discussing what RBD may mean (risk disclosure) is valued by patients and professionals, but individual prognosis is uncertain.
supporting_passage: "For healthcare professionals, the main obstacles include uncertainty in formulating individualized prognoses, ethical challenges linked to the principle of beneficence and concerns about the possible emotional impact of disclosure. From the patients' viewpoint, there is a clear need for comprehensive and robust information about their condition, even though obtaining accurate and trustworthy sources can be difficult. Risk disclosure is considered essential by both patients and professionals, but a systematic step-by-step approach has yet to be implemented for people with iRBD on progression to neurodegenerative diseases."
safe_wording: A recent review found that both patients and professionals see discussing future risk as essential, while professionals find it hard to give an individual prognosis. The conversation needs time, honesty about uncertainty, and follow-up.
qualifications: Small scoping review (8 articles). The recommendation to have a careful, supported conversation is an ethical judgement and should be written as one ('we should').

claim: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, tested in deep sleep, the standard high-pitched (3100 Hz) smoke alarm at 75 dBA woke 56%, while a lower-pitched 520 Hz square-wave signal at the same level woke 92%.
supporting_passage: Three auditory signals, a bed shaker, a pillow shaker, and strobe lights were presented to 38 adults (aged 18 to 80 yr) with mild to moderately severe hearing loss of 25 to 70 dB (in both ears), during slow-wave sleep (deep sleep). ... The third auditory signal was the current 3100-Hz smoke alarm. All auditory signals were tested below, at, and above the decibel level prescribed by the applicable standard for bedrooms (75 dBA). ... The most effective signal was a 520-Hz square wave auditory signal, waking 92% at 75 dBA, compared with 56% waking to the 75 dBA high-pitched alarm.
safe_wording: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, a standard high-pitched smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 of them from deep sleep. A lower-pitched alarm sound at the same loudness woke about 92 in 100.
qualifications: Say who was studied: adults of all ages (18 to 80), not only older people; laboratory, deep sleep only; small sample. The abstract does not state whether hearing aids were worn; frame the post conditionally ('if you take your hearing aids out at night') rather than claiming participants had removed them. Do not tell readers to buy a 520 Hz alarm: UK availability was not checked.

claim: In the same study, bed and pillow shakers woke 80 to 84% at the intensity as purchased, while strobe lights woke only 27% even at an intensity above the US standard.
supporting_passage: In the case of bed and pillow shakers intensities below, at, and above the level as purchased were tested. For strobe lights three levels were used, all of which were above the applicable standard. ... Bed and pillow shakers awoke 80 to 84% at the intensity level as purchased. The strobe lights awoke only 27% at an intensity above the US standard. ... Strobe lights, even at high intensities, are ineffective in reliably waking people with mild to moderate hearing loss.
