safe_wording: After the first cataract operation, the two eyes can end up needing very different glasses. In one Belfast waiting list, about 1 in 3 people waiting for their first eye were judged at risk of this troublesome imbalance. Second-eye surgery helps even it out.
qualifications: The 32% is an estimated risk in one clinic sample, not measured symptoms. No source opened for the specific advice to remove or change the lens on the operated side; present it only as a question to ask the optician or eye team.

claim: In an RCT of 239 women over 70, expedited second-eye surgery improved visual function and confidence; the reduction in falls was not statistically significant.
supporting_passage: visual function (especially stereopsis) improved in the operated group. ... Rate of falling was reduced by 32% in the operated group, but this was not statistically significant (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.39, 1.19, P = 0.18). Confidence, visual disability and handicap all improved in the operated compared with the control group. ... The effect on rate of falling remains uncertain.
safe_wording: In a trial of 239 women over 70, having the second eye done within about a month rather than waiting a year improved their sight and confidence. Whether it reduced falls was uncertain.
qualifications: Women only; do not quote 32% as a benefit.

claim: NICE NG77 recommends access to cataract surgery is not restricted on visual acuity and that referral considers impact on daily life.
safe_wording: Not usable: NICE NG77 could not be opened (web blocked; not in Drive).

claim: In an RCT of 306 women over 70, expedited first-eye cataract surgery reduced the rate of falling by 34% and fewer had fractures.
supporting_passage: 306 women aged over 70, with cataract, were randomised to expedited (approximately 4 weeks) or routine (12 months wait) surgery. ... Rate of falling was reduced by 34% in the operated group (rate ratio 0.66, 95% confidence interval 0.45 to 0.96, p = 0.03). ... Four participants in the operated group had fractures (3%), compared with 12 (8%) in the control group (p = 0.04).
safe_wording: In a trial of 306 women over 70, those who had their first cataract removed within about a month had about a third fewer falls over the next year than women who waited about a year; 3 in 100 had a fracture compared with 8 in 100.
qualifications: Women only; proportion who fell at least once was not lower (49% vs 45%); the reduction was in rate of falls.

claim: Charles Bonnet syndrome: complex visual hallucinations in people with sight loss who keep insight; linked to acquired visual loss, often AMD.
supporting_passage: Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) is characterised by recurrent, complex and vivid visual hallucinations in the absence of cognitive dysfunction. Individuals with CBS usually maintain insight into the unreal nature of their hallucinatory experiences. There is a strong association between CBS and acquired visual loss and the most commonly described ocular pathology is age-related macular degeneration.
safe_wording: Some people with sight loss, most often from macular degeneration, see vivid images that are not there, and know they are not real. This is called Charles Bonnet syndrome.

claim: Teunisse 1996: 60 of 505 met criteria; all had full insight; correct diagnosis in 1 of 16 who saw a doctor; all glad to be told not mental illness.
supporting_passage: After screening 505 visually handicapped patients, 60 were found to meet proposed diagnostic criteria for CBS ... all patients had full insight into the unreal nature of their hallucinations. ... CBS caused considerable distress in only 17 (28%) patients. However, all patients were glad to be told that their hallucinations were not due to mental disease. The proper diagnosis had been made in only one of the 16 patients who had consulted a doctor.
safe_wording: In a Dutch study of 505 people attending with sight loss, 60 had these images. All knew the images were not real. Of 16 who had seen a doctor about them, only 1 had been given the right explanation. All were glad to hear it was not mental illness.
qualifications: Clinic population from 1996; do not generalise 60/505 to all people with sight loss.

claim: CBS is a diagnosis of exclusion; new hallucinations need assessment for other causes; information about benign nature is key treatment.
supporting_passage: It is widely agreed that CBS is an underreported diagnosis caused by patients' reluctance to admit their hallucinatory experience because of fear of being labelled mentally ill. CBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and careful assessment must be made to ensure that other etiologies causing the symptoms are ruled out. ... Thus, a major part of the treatment is careful information about the benign nature of the condition.
safe_wording: People often keep these images to themselves for fear of being thought mentally ill. New hallucinations should still be mentioned to a doctor, because other causes need to be ruled out. Explaining the condition is a large part of the help.
qualifications: Source does not list delirium, Lewy body dementia etc. specifically; keep to 'other causes' or source separately. Advice that eye clinics mention CBS at diagnosis is judgement, mark as 'we should'.

claim: Timolol eye drops enter the circulation and cause systemic beta-blockade; case reports describe complete heart block resolving on stopping.
supporting_passage: Despite its topical administration, ophthalmic timolol enters systemic circulation and produces a systemic beta-adrenergic blockade. ... Electrocardiography indicated a heart rate (HR) of 29 bpm with complete atrioventricular (AV) block ... The AV block and bradycardia resolved 48-h after timolol cessation.
safe_wording: Timolol eye drops get into the bloodstream and can act like a beta-blocker tablet. Case reports describe very slow heart rates and heart block that settled when the drops were stopped.
qualifications: Case reports show it can happen, not how often. In this case an underlying conduction problem was unmasked.

claim: Nasolacrimal occlusion (5 min) and tissue press method both lowered plasma timolol vs no intervention.
supporting_passage: These were: (a) nasolacrimal (punctal) occlusion for 5 min, (b) tissue press method or (c) no intervention. Timolol plasma levels were measured 1 h after drop application. ... Plasma timolol concentrations after tissue press method and NLO were significantly lower than those without intervention.
safe_wording: In a small cross-over study, pressing on the inner corner of the eye for 5 minutes after the drop, or a tissue press, lowered the amount of timolol reaching the blood.
qualifications: 21 adults, not older patients; surrogate outcome; clinical benefit not shown. Use '5 minutes' only as the trial's method.

claim: In one inner-city geriatric clinic population, 9% had unrecognised BPPV, and those with it were more likely to have had a fall in the previous 3 months.
supporting_passage: We performed a cross-sectional study to determine the prevalence of unrecognized benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and associated lifestyle sequelae in a public, inner-city geriatric population. Dizziness was found in 61% of patients, whereas balance disorders were found in 77% of patients. Nine percent were found to have unrecognized BPPV. ... Patients with unrecognized BPPV were more likely to have reduced activities of daily living scores, to have sustained a fall in the previous 3 months, and to have depression.
safe_wording: In one study of patients at a US inner-city clinic for older people, about 9 in 100 turned out to have BPPV that no one had recognised. Those patients were more likely to have had a fall in the previous three months. A snapshot study like this cannot show that the BPPV caused the falls.
qualifications: One clinic, one country, published 2000; not a general prevalence; association only; denominator and sample size not in abstract; do not say 'BPPV causes falls'.

claim: Posterior canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike test and should be treated, or referred for treatment, with a repositioning procedure; the guideline advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating vestibular suppressants and asks clinicians to assess mobility and falls risk.
supporting_passage: The update group made strong recommendations that clinicians should (1) diagnose posterior semicircular canal BPPV when vertigo associated with torsional, upbeating nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, performed by bringing the patient from an upright to supine position with the head turned 45° to one side and neck extended 20° with the affected ear down, and (2) treat, or refer to a clinician who can treat, patients with posterior canal BPPV with a canalith repositioning procedure. ... The update group made recommendations against ... (3) routinely treating BPPV with vestibular suppressant medications such as antihistamines and/or benzodiazepines. ... (3) assess patients with BPPV for factors that modify management, including impaired mobility or balance, central nervous system disorders, a lack of home support, and/or increased risk for falling
safe_wording: The 2017 US ENT guideline strongly recommends diagnosing the commonest type of BPPV with the Dix-Hallpike test (head turned 45 degrees, neck extended 20 degrees) and treating it, or referring for treatment, with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley. It recommends against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines, and asks clinicians to check mobility, balance and falls risk.
qualifications: US guideline. The named drug classes are antihistamines and benzodiazepines; prochlorperazine is not named in the abstract. The guideline also recommends against routine imaging when BPPV criteria are met.

claim: The Epley manoeuvre is effective for posterior canal BPPV.
supporting_passage: Complete resolution of vertigo occurred significantly more often in the Epley treatment group when compared to a sham manoeuvre or control (odds ratio (OR) 4.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.62 to 7.44; five studies, 273 participants); the proportion of patients resolving increased from 21% to 56%. ... Some patients were unable to tolerate the manoeuvres because of cervical spine problems. ... There is evidence that the Epley manoeuvre is a safe, effective treatment for posterior canal BPPV, based on the results of 11, mostly small, randomised controlled trials with relatively short follow-up. There is a high recurrence rate of BPPV after treatment (36%).
safe_wording: In trials, about 56 in 100 people had complete resolution of vertigo after the Epley manoeuvre, compared with about 21 in 100 after a sham manoeuvre or no treatment. BPPV often returns (about 36 in 100 in these trials), and a few people could not tolerate the manoeuvre because of neck problems.
qualifications: Mostly small trials, short follow-up; not specific to frail older people; 'complete resolution' is the stated primary outcome.

claim: A side-lying version of the test, with head and neck supported, can be used in older people when neck extension is limited.
supporting_passage: It is sometimes difficult to perform the Dix-Hallpike test in elderly persons, due to the limited range of motion when extending the neck. In this study, we used a side-lying test to stimulate the posterior semicircular canal, while the head and neck were fully supported on the examination table. ... A representative population sample of 675 persons completed a questionnaire about dizziness and 571 persons underwent side-lying, static balance and dynamic walking tests. ... BPPV was found in 11% and was significantly more common in women (p<0.01).
safe_wording: Because the usual test needs the neck tipped back, which some older people cannot manage, a Swedish study of 75-year-olds used a side-lying version with the head and neck fully supported on the couch. In that study about 11% of those tested were found to have BPPV.
qualifications: Shows the side-lying test was usable in a population sample of 75-year-olds. The abstract does not compare its accuracy with Dix-Hallpike and no guideline in this batch was opened that endorses it, so the post may describe it as a practical option used in research, not as an equal replacement. The 11% denominator is presumably the 571 tested (not stated explicitly).

claim: BPPV is common in the general population and most affected people do not receive effective treatment.
supporting_passage: The lifetime prevalence of BPPV was 2.4%, the 1 year prevalence was 1.6% and the 1 year incidence was 0.6%. The median duration of an episode was 2 weeks. In 86% of affected individuals, BPPV led to medical consultation, interruption of daily activities or sick leave. In total, only 8% of affected participants received effective treatment. On multivariate analysis, age, migraine, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and stroke were independently associated with BPPV.
safe_wording: In a German national survey of adults, about 2 in 100 people had had BPPV at some point in life, and only about 8 in 100 of those affected had received effective treatment. Age was one of the factors linked with having it.
qualifications: All adults, not only older people; older figures; the survey identified BPPV by structured interview, not an examination; 'effective treatment' is the authors' term.

claim: Prochlorperazine can cause drowsiness and movement side effects in older people (BNF).
location: Not checked (BNF and SmPC not openable in this environment)
safe_wording: Do not name prochlorperazine. Say the guideline advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines (C14-26-b).
qualifications: Claim dropped from the post.

claim: In a hospice EEG study, all 5 patients recorded when unresponsive showed a brain response to changes in simple tones; none showed the later response that goes with conscious detection of tone changes; 2 of the 5 showed it to changes in a pattern of tones.
supporting_passage: Consistent with control and responsive participants, all (5/5) showed some evidence of either an early fronto-central negativity (MMN), or a later fronto-central positivity (P3a), or both, to tone changes. None of the unresponsive patients showed a centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to the tone changes. One unresponsive patient (20%) showed evidence of a weak late fronto-central positivity (P3a) to pattern changes, and two patients showed stronger centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to pattern changes.
location: Full text, Results (Unresponsive, actively dying, hospice patients)
safe_wording: In a small Canadian hospice study, researchers played tones to 5 people who had stopped responding and were actively dying. All 5 showed a brain response to a change in the tones, which means their hearing system was still reacting. This does not show that they understood what they heard.
qualifications: Use the counts, not 'most': the abstract says 'most unresponsive patients showed evidence of MMN responses', but the Results give 5 of 5 with an MMN or P3a, and the sample is only 5 people. The P3b result in 2 of 5 (to pattern changes only, none to tone changes) is atypical, and the authors say it is 'plausible' these two were aware, not shown; do not report it as evidence of awareness. Time from recording to death is not given per patient; the study defines 'actively dying' as hours to days, so avoid 'hours before death' for these 5.

claim: These responses show part of the hearing system was working but do not show understanding or awareness; the authors say the result lends some credence to advice to keep talking to a dying relative.
supporting_passage: It is still unclear how the partial functioning of the auditory change detection system we have reported here relates to normal conscious awareness, in spite of arguments from the existing literature. ... We have presented evidence that at least a few actively dying hospice patients, when they are unable to respond to family or healthcare provider verbal stimuli, nonetheless seem to be hearing and giving neural responses to sequences of simple auditory stimuli. This is consistent with the trope that hearing is one of the last senses to lose function when a person is dying, and lends some credence to the advice that loved ones should keep talking to a dying relative as long as possible.
safe_wording: The study suggests that, in some people, the ear and brain keep reacting to sound close to death. It does not show that the person understood words or knew who was there. The authors say it gives some support to the advice to keep talking to a dying relative.
qualifications: Tones only, not speech or voices of relatives; 'hearing may be one of the last senses to lose function' is the authors' tentative conclusion; the Introduction also says the belief rests mostly on anecdote and near-death-experience reports and that 'the capacity for awareness ... remains unknown'.

claim: Study size and limits: 13 patients recruited, 4 excluded for noisy EEG, 9 analysed, 5 recorded when unresponsive; most on opioids; no delirium or cognitive impairment at entry.
supporting_passage: Data were collected initially from 13 participants, residing in a hospice facility in Vancouver, over a time period of more than two years. ... Data from four patients were excluded because of excessive noise in their EEG. The patient analysis to be described is based on nine patients (four female, age 28 to 88 years, mean age 68.2 years). Eight patients were recorded when they were responsive, five when they were unresponsive. ... Note that most patients were receiving various forms of opioids at both recording sessions.
safe_wording: State the size plainly: five people who had stopped responding.
qualifications: Patients were free of delirium and cognitive impairment when enrolled, so the findings may not apply to people with dementia or delirium at the end of life. Ages 28 to 88 apply to the nine analysed patients, not to the five unresponsive recordings alone.

claim: Care guidance for the last days of life advises continuing to talk to the dying person.
location: Not found (NICE NG31 and hospice or Marie Curie leaflets not openable; PubMed searches returned nothing usable)
safe_wording: Do not cite guidance. Present speaking to the person, saying who you are, and keeping a hearing aid in while comfortable as a judgement ('We think it is reasonable to ...') supported only by the authors' comment in Blundon 2020; the hearing-aid advice has no source in this batch and must be framed as common-sense practice, not as a finding.
qualifications: Claim dropped as a cited recommendation.

claim: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose glucocorticoid should be started immediately in active giant cell arteritis, and the diagnosis should be confirmed by imaging or histology.
supporting_passage: We recommend that a suspected diagnosis of LVV should be confirmed by imaging or histology. High dose glucocorticoid therapy (40-60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent) should be initiated immediately for induction of remission in active giant cell arteritis (GCA) or Takayasu arteritis (TAK).
safe_wording: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose steroid, 40 to 60 mg a day of prednisolone or equivalent, should start immediately in active giant cell arteritis, and that the diagnosis should be confirmed by scan or biopsy.
qualifications: The abstract does not say in so many words 'start before the test result' or 'same-day fast-track referral'. The practical order (treat first, confirm soon after) is a reasonable reading combined with C14-25-c but should be attributed to the guideline only as 'start immediately'. 'Active GCA' is the guideline's wording; the post should say 'strongly suspected' only when attributing to BSR (see C14-25-b) and BSR cannot yet be cited.

claim: BSR 2020 guideline: strongly suspected GCA treated immediately with high-dose glucocorticoid; specialist review same working day if possible and within 3 working days; new visual loss or double vision seen by an ophthalmologist the same calendar day; higher-dose or intravenous methylprednisolone for visual symptoms; ultrasound and biopsy time windows.
location: Guideline text not opened. Only a WebSearch summary (search extract) was seen: it paraphrased the BSR/NICE 2020 guideline as saying strongly suspected GCA should be treated immediately with high-dose glucocorticoids, with specialist evaluation ideally the same working day and within 3 working days, and new visual loss or double vision seen by an ophthalmologist the same calendar day. The same search found no confirmation of 'ultrasound within one week' or 'biopsy within two weeks' as BSR wording (attributed there to EULAR and the American College of Rheumatology) and no BSR wording on dose for visual symptoms.
safe_wording: Do not attribute any specific statement, time window or visual-symptom dose to the BSR guideline until the guideline text is opened. Alasdair can upload the BSR 2020 PDF (Rheumatology 2020;59:e1-e23) to Drive so the pass can be repeated.
qualifications: Search extract is not enough for an essential claim. The judge's suggested windows (ultrasound about 1 week, biopsy about 2 weeks) are NOT confirmed as BSR wording.

claim: Temporal artery ultrasound becomes less sensitive once glucocorticoid has started, so imaging should be done promptly.
supporting_passage: Before GC exposure, US sensitivity was 94% (95% CI: 83-99), 73% (95% CI: 58-85), and 71% (95% CI: 56-83) when assessing all vessels, TAs, and large vessels (LVs), respectively. At day 3 and 10, the overall US sensitivity was 92% (95% CI: 78-98, P = 0.16) and 83% (95% CI: 69-92, P = 0.10), respectively. At day 10, the TA-US and LV-US sensitivity was 53% (95% CI: 38-68, P < 0.01) and 60% (95% CI: 44-74, P = 0.13), respectively. ... Consistent with the EULAR recommendations, these findings encourage prompt US assessment, preferably within 3 days, to ensure an accurate diagnosis.
safe_wording: In a small Danish study of 48 people with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis, ultrasound of the temporal arteries picked up the disease in about 73 in 100 before steroids and about 53 in 100 after 10 days of steroids. The authors advise ultrasound as soon as possible after starting treatment, preferably within 3 days. Treatment should not wait for the scan.
qualifications: Small single-centre study; the last sentence ('treatment should not wait') comes from the EULAR statement in C14-25-a, not from this study. Whole-body ultrasound sensitivity fell less (94% to 83%, not clearly different). Temporal-artery drop was clear (P<0.01). The abstract does not name the reference standard. Cannot be used to say that ultrasound or biopsy remain informative for 1 or 2 weeks.

claim: Sight loss in giant cell arteritis can be permanent, and can still occur in a small number of people after treatment has started.
supporting_passage: Permanent visual loss is the main short-term complication. [Castaneda 2022, Abstract] ... Eleven out of 502 patients (2.2%) experienced a new PVL including 6 occurrences during the initial therapeutic phase and 5 during the tapering phase. [Curumthaullee 2022, Abstract] ... Headache and visual disturbances including loss of vision are characteristic of GCA. Constitutional symptoms and elevated inflammatory markers (>90%) are common in both diseases. [Buttgereit 2016, Abstract]
safe_wording: Giant cell arteritis can cause permanent sight loss, which is why it is treated as an emergency. Headache and sight problems are typical features, and tiredness, weight loss and other whole-body symptoms are also common.
qualifications: No opened source gives a proportion who lose sight permanently without treatment, and none says visual loss is 'usually' permanent; do not use 'usually'. Curumthaullee: new permanent sight loss after starting steroid was rare (2.2%, single French centre, 1976 to 2020), so 'treatment prevents all sight loss' must not be implied. 'Constitutional symptoms ... common' is from a statement that covers both PMR and GCA.

claim: Older people with giant cell arteritis may present with unusual features; people with only unusual features are treated later.
supporting_passage: Of 21,828 screened records, 429 studies corresponding to 746 individuals (median [IQR] age 72 [IQR, 66-78] years, 63% female) with at least one atypical feature of GCA were included. Eighty-two percent had both atypical and at least one concurrent typical giant cell arteritis feature, whereas 18% of patients with atypical signs and symptoms only presented with atypical features. ... Patients with atypical features only experienced greater delay in treatment initiation (p < 0.001). The most commonly reported atypical signs/symptoms were vertigo (11.9%), scalp necrosis/ulceration (7.9%), and dry cough (5.8%).
safe_wording: A review of published cases of giant cell arteritis found that some people, median age 72, have only unusual features such as vertigo, scalp ulceration or a dry cough, and these people had longer delays before treatment started. The authors advise checking inflammatory markers early in unexplained illness.
qualifications: Built from case reports, so it shows that atypical presentations exist and are linked with delay, not how common they are. The named atypical features do not include weight loss or jaw ache (jaw claudication is a typical feature), so the post should not list those as 'atypical' on this source.

claim: Intravenous glucocorticoid is used for people with ischaemic (including visual) complications.
supporting_passage: Glucocorticoids (oral, or intravenous in cases with ischaemic complications) remain the first line treatment for GCA.
safe_wording: A Swedish national guideline says steroids may be given intravenously when there are ischaemic complications, such as sight loss. The UK guideline wording on dose for visual symptoms has not been checked.
qualifications: Swedish guideline, not BSR; does not give a dose or say that visual symptoms alone trigger intravenous treatment. Do not describe it as the UK recommendation.

claim: Losing both sight and hearing is not rare in older people, and each loss makes it harder to follow speech.
supporting_passage: In combination dual sensory loss occurs. Dual sensory loss is becoming a more common condition seen by clinicians and previous research has shown that 6% of non-institutionalized older adults had a dual sensory impairment, whilst 70% of severely vision-impaired older adults also demonstrated a significant hearing loss. Decreased vision and/or hearing acuity interferes with reception of the spoken message and hence people with sensory loss frequently experience communication breakdown. [Heine and Browning 2002] ... Half of the participants had normal hearing and vision, 38% impaired hearing, 5% impaired vision, and 7% had dual-sensory impairment. [Dupuis 2015, 301 adults, mean age 71]
safe_wording: Losing both sight and hearing is not rare in later life, and poorer sight or poorer hearing each make speech harder to follow. Do not give a percentage.
qualifications: Heine and Browning figures are quoted from earlier research (2002). Dupuis 2015 is a single sample of 301 community adults (mean age 71), so 7% is not a population prevalence (the judge asked for a population estimate or omission). No UK population estimate was found in an opened source. The step 'lip-reading needs sight' is common-sense reasoning not stated in the abstracts.

claim: In England, the 2014 Care Act deafblind policy guidance requires councils to identify and keep a record of deafblind people and to arrange an assessment by a specifically trained person.
location: Not opened (GOV.UK blocked, HTTP 403 via proxy). Search extract only; it summarised the guidance as requiring councils to contact and keep a record of deafblind people and to have assessments done by someone with specific deafblind expertise; published 18 December 2014; issued under section 78 of the Care Act 2014 for adults.
safe_wording: Cannot be stated as fact in a post yet. If the guidance PDF is placed in Drive or opened by another route, a possible wording is: 'In England, government guidance under the Care Act says councils should identify deafblind people and arrange an assessment by a suitably trained person.' Current-version status also needs checking.
qualifications: Search extract is not enough for an essential claim; one of the extracts was a Sense (charity) summary, not the primary document.

claim: Scotland's See Hear framework covers services for people with sensory impairment, including dual sensory loss.
location: Not searched (reserve candidate; official web pages cannot be opened)
safe_wording: Omit.
qualifications: Not attempted because the statutory claim in C14-23-b already prevents 'ready'.

claim: US guidance for older people in long-term care defines fever as a single oral temperature above 37.8 C, repeated oral readings above 37.2 C (or rectal above 37.5 C), or a single temperature more than 1.1 C above the person's baseline from any site.
supporting_passage: Stone 2012: "The definition of fever was changed from a temperature of greater than 38°C (100.4°F), as in the original McGeer Criteria, to a definition consistent with the 2008 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guideline for evaluating fever and infection in older adults residing in LTCFs: either (1) a single oral temperature greater than 37.8°C (100°F) or (2) repeated oral temperatures greater than 37.2°C (99°F) or rectal temperatures greater than 37.5°C (99.5°F) or (3) a single temperature greater than 1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site." Table 2: "A. Fever 1. Single oral temperature >37.8°C (>100°F) OR 2. Repeated oral temperatures >37.2°C (99°F) or rectal temperatures >37.5°C (99.5°F) OR 3. Single temperature >1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site (oral, tympanic, axillary)"
location: Stone 2012, Definitions: Constitutional Criteria for Infection (p. 5) and Table 2 (p. 14)
safe_wording: US infection guidance for older people living in care homes counts as a fever: one oral reading above 37.8°C, repeated oral readings above 37.2°C, or any reading more than 1.1°C above the person's usual temperature. The rise-from-usual rule applies to ear, mouth or armpit readings.
qualifications: Say it comes from US guidance for care home residents (IDSA 2008, as restated in the 2012 revised McGeer surveillance criteria). The IDSA guideline full text itself was not opened. Do not present as UK guidance.

claim: Typical fever is often absent in older people with serious infection.
supporting_passage: High 2009 abstract: "Most residents are older and have multiple comorbidities that complicate recognition of infection; for example, typically defined fever is absent in more than one-half of LTCF residents with serious infection." Norman 2000 abstract: "Fever, the cardinal sign of infection, may be absent or blunted 20%-30% of the time." Stone 2012: "The lower threshold will increase sensitivity for detecting infection given the greater likelihood of a lower febrile response in the elderly."
location: High 2009 Abstract; Norman 2000 Abstract; Stone 2012 Definitions: Constitutional Criteria (p. 5)
safe_wording: Many older people with a serious infection do not develop a typical fever. US care home guidance says typical fever is absent in more than half of residents with serious infection; an earlier review put fever absent or blunted in 20 to 30 in 100 older people with infection.
qualifications: Either say 'often' without a number, or give both figures with their populations. Do not say 'more than half of older people' without 'living in care homes'.

claim: NEWS2 gives 0 points for temperatures from 36.1 to 38.0 C.
supporting_passage: Engebretsen 2020, Table 1 'NEWS2 and OUH-criteria', Temperature (°C) row: 3 points "≤35.0"; 1 point "35.1–36.0"; 0 points "36.1–38.0"; 1 point "38.1–39.0"; 2 points "≥39.1". NEWS2 is cited to: "Royal College of Physicians. National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2: Standardising the Assessment of Acute-Illness Severity in the NHS. London: RCP; 2017."
safe_wording: On NEWS2, any temperature from 36.1°C to 38.0°C scores 0. A temperature has to reach 38.1°C to score 1 point.
qualifications: Cite the Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart (2017) via this reproduction; the RCP document could not be opened here.

claim: NEWS2 has no adjustment for age, and a low score should never override a clinician's or carer's concern.
supporting_passage: Vardy 2022: "The National Early Warning Score (NEWS), published in 2012, made no specific adjustments for older people." "Insufficient evidence was available to apply weighting to the NEWS score to account for age." "Study of performance of the NEWS2 specifically in older people is important, as the physiological and vital sign changes seen in response to acute illness may differ for older adults, as well as their acute care preferences." Williams 2022: "An important point emphasised in the original NEWS report, and reiterated subsequently, is that a low score should never override a healthcare professional or carer's concern about a patient's clinical condition if they feel it is necessary to escalate care."
location: Vardy 2022 Abstract and 'NEWS2 in older people in hospital' (pp. 522-3); Williams 2022 p. 3
safe_wording: NEWS2 has no adjustment for age. Its developers say a low score should never override a professional's or carer's concern about a patient.
qualifications: Vardy is expert commentary; the Williams statement reports the RCP position.

claim: Illustrative example: for a person whose usual temperature is 36.0 C, a reading of 37.5 C scores 0 on NEWS2 but is a rise of 1.5 C, which meets the care home guidance definition of fever (more than 1.1 C over baseline).
supporting_passage: Engebretsen 2020 Table 1: 0 points "36.1–38.0". Stone 2012 Table 2: "3. Single temperature >1.1°C (2°F) over baseline from any site (oral, tympanic, axillary)"
safe_wording: Illustrative example: if someone's usual temperature is 36.0°C, a reading of 37.5°C scores nothing on NEWS2, yet it is 1.5°C above their usual, which US care home guidance would count as a fever.
qualifications: Must be labelled 'Illustrative example'. Do not state that older people typically run at 36.0°C (not supported).

claim: In an emergency department, adults with bloodstream infection but no fever were older and had higher 30-day mortality than those with fever.
supporting_passage: "The afebrile patients were older, have higher Charlson comorbidity index, and had poorer outcomes than the febrile patients." "Finally, the 30-day all-cause mortality was higher in the afebrile group than in the febrile group (45% versus 12%, log-rank P<0.001)."
safe_wording: In one emergency department study of adults with blood infection, those without a fever were older and more of them died within 30 days (45 in 100 versus 12 in 100).
qualifications: Single centre, retrospective, all adult ages; crude mortality comparison; absence of fever does not cause the deaths.

claim: Practical step: find the person's usual temperature in care home charts, GP records or previous admission records.
supporting_passage: No source found or opened for where baseline temperatures are recorded or how often they are available.
safe_wording: Offer as a suggestion only: 'If you can, find their usual temperature: care home charts and earlier hospital records may have it.' Do not claim these records usually contain it.
qualifications: Judgement, not a finding.

claim: In 6,481 medical patients with pneumonia in 43 Michigan hospitals, two thirds (67.8%) received more antibiotic days than needed.
supporting_passage: "6481 general care medical patients with pneumonia." "Two thirds (67.8% [4391 of 6481]) of patients received excess antibiotic therapy." Full text: "the median age was 70.2 years (interquartile range [IQR], 58.4 to 80.8 years)." "Patients with CAP were expected to have a treatment duration of at least 5 days, with longer courses expected only if time to clinical stability was longer" "treatment duration was considered to be appropriate if the actual duration was within 1 day of the expected duration." "The median excess duration was 2 days (IQR, 0 to 4 days) overall"
location: Abstract; full text Results (p. 7) and Methods, Primary Outcome (p. 5)
safe_wording: In 43 US hospitals, 2 in 3 adults treated for pneumonia (median age 70) got more days of antibiotics than they needed, usually about 2 extra days.
qualifications: US study of adults of all ages, not only older people. 'Needed' means the shortest effective duration set by the authors from guidelines (at least 5 days for community-acquired pneumonia, longer if slow to stabilise), with 1 day of leeway.

claim: Antibiotics prescribed at discharge accounted for 93.2% of the excess duration.
supporting_passage: "Antibiotics prescribed at discharge accounted for 93.2% of excess duration."
safe_wording: Almost all the extra days (93 in every 100) came from antibiotics prescribed at discharge.
qualifications: This is a share of excess days, not of patients.

claim: Only a third of discharge summaries documented the total antibiotic duration, and not documenting it was linked with more excess treatment.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Patients who ... did not have a total antibiotic treatment duration documented at discharge were more likely to receive excess treatment." Full text: "Only a third of patients (32.1% [2080 of 6481]) had a total treatment duration documented in their discharge summary." Table 2 row 'Documentation of total antibiotic treatment duration in discharge summary': No (n = 4401 [67.9%]) predicted excess days per patient 2.9, Reference; Yes (n = 2080 [32.1%]) predicted excess days 2.3, adjusted rate ratio 0.78 (0.70-0.87), P < 0.001.
location: Abstract; full text Results 'Prescribing at Discharge' (p. 7) and Table 2 (p. 32)
safe_wording: Only 1 in 3 discharge summaries said how many days of antibiotic in total. When the total was written down, patients got fewer extra days (about 2.3 versus 2.9 extra days per patient, after adjustment).
qualifications: Observational association; documentation may mark more careful prescribing rather than cause fewer days. Use 'linked with'.

claim: Each extra day was linked with 5% higher odds of patient-reported antibiotic side effects, and extra days were not linked with better outcomes.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Excess treatment was not associated with lower rates of any adverse outcomes, including death, readmission, emergency department visit, or Clostridioides difficile infection. Each excess day of treatment was associated with a 5% increase in the odds of antibiotic-associated adverse events reported by patients after discharge." Full text: "Of these, 60.4% (3592 of 5943) were reached." "Diarrhea, gastrointestinal distress, and mucosal candidiasis were the most common antibiotic-associated adverse events reported by patients" Table 3 patient-reported adverse events: appropriate duration "26/1132 (2.3%)"; excess duration "114/2460 (4.6%)"; adjusted OR per excess day 1.05 (1.02-1.08).
location: Abstract; full text Results 'Patient Outcomes' (p. 8), Table 3 (p. 33)
safe_wording: Extra days did not bring better results: no fewer deaths, readmissions or return visits. Each extra day was linked with slightly higher odds of side effects that patients reported, mostly diarrhoea and stomach upset. Among patients reached by phone, about 5 in 100 on too-long courses reported side effects, against about 2 in 100 on the right length.
qualifications: Observational; side effects known only for the 60% reached by phone; crude percentages (4.6% versus 2.3%) differ from the adjusted per-day estimate. Do not use causal verbs.

claim: The risk of C. difficile infection from antibiotics is higher in older people.
supporting_passage: No source opened supports the age claim. In Vaughn 2019 Table 3, C. difficile infection: appropriate duration "11 (0.5%)"; excess duration "22 (0.5%)"; adjusted OR per excess day "0.93 (0.81–1.07)", P = 0.30. Full text: "excess duration was not associated with C difficile infection or provider-documented adverse events".
safe_wording: Leave C. difficile out. In this study, extra antibiotic days were not linked with more C. difficile infection.
qualifications: Age-specific C. difficile risk was not sourced.

claim: Shorter courses work: in stable patients admitted with pneumonia, stopping antibiotics after 3 days was non-inferior to 8 days.
supporting_passage: "Among patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia who met clinical stability criteria, discontinuing β-lactam treatment after 3 days was non-inferior to 8 days of treatment." "In the ITT population, median age was 73·0 years (IQR 57·0-84·0)" "cure at day 15 occurred in 117 (77%) of 152 participants in the placebo group and 102 (68%) of 151 participants in the β-lactam group"
safe_wording: In a French trial of people admitted with pneumonia (median age 73) who were stable after 3 days, stopping antibiotics then worked as well as continuing to 8 days.
qualifications: Only for patients who met stability criteria at day 3 and were not in intensive care; one antibiotic regimen.

claim: UK (NICE) guidance recommends stopping antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia after 5 days unless the person is not clinically stable or microbiology suggests a longer course.
supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (not opened): "For adults with community-acquired pneumonia, stop antibiotic treatment after 5 days unless microbiological results suggest a longer course is needed or the person is not clinically stable, for example, if they have had a fever in the past 48 hours or have signs of clinical instability."
safe_wording: Do not quote NICE wording. If needed, say 'UK guidance favours short courses for most adults with pneumonia' only after the NICE page has been opened; otherwise rely on the trial (C15-01-f).
qualifications: Search extract only; NG138 has been incorporated into NG250 (September 2025) according to search results; exact current wording unverified.

claim: In UK trauma registry data, the mean age of major trauma patients rose from 36.1 in 1990 to 53.8 in 2013, people over 75 were 26.9% of cases in 2013, and low falls became the commonest mechanism (39.1%).
supporting_passage: "In 1990, the mean age of MT patients within the TARN database was 36.1, the largest age group suffering MT was 0-24 years (39.3%), the most common causative mechanism was road traffic collision (59.1%), 72.7% were male and 33.6% underwent CT. By 2013, mean age had increased to 53.8 years, the single largest age group was 25-50 years (27.1%), closely followed by those >75 years (26.9%), the most common mechanism was low falls (39.1%), 68.3% were male and 86.8% underwent CT." "the predominant mechanism that precipitates MT is a fall from <2 m."
safe_wording: In the national trauma registry for England and Wales, the commonest cause of major trauma changed from road collisions (59 in 100 cases in 1990) to falls from less than 2 metres (39 in 100 in 2013). By 2013, about 1 in 4 people with major trauma were over 75, and the average age had risen from 36 to 54.
qualifications: Registry data to 2013 only; say 'by 2013'. Shifts partly reflect changes in which hospitals submitted data and in CT use (33.6% to 86.8%), which finds more injuries.

claim: Older people with rib fractures have about twice the mortality and pneumonia of younger people with similar injuries, and each extra rib fracture is linked with higher odds of death.
supporting_passage: "Pneumonia occurred in 31% of elderly versus 17% of young (p < 0.01) and mortality was 22% for the elderly versus 10% for the young (p < 0.01). Mortality and pneumonia rates increased as the number of rib fxs increased with and odds ratio for death of 1.19 and for pneumonia of 1.16 per each additional rib fracture (p < 0.001)." Conclusions: "For each additional rib fracture in the elderly, mortality increases by 19% and the risk of pneumonia by 27%."
safe_wording: In one US trauma centre, people aged 65 or over admitted with rib fractures died more often than younger adults with similar injuries (22 in 100 versus 10 in 100) and got pneumonia more often (31 in 100 versus 17 in 100). Each extra broken rib was linked with higher odds of death.
qualifications: Single centre, old data (published 2000), admitted trauma patients only. Do not quote a per-rib pneumonia figure: the abstract gives 1.16 in Results and 27% in Conclusions. Do not turn the 1.19 odds ratio into '19% more likely to die' for the public.

claim: Older trauma patients are often under-triaged before reaching hospital.
supporting_passage: Alshibani 2021: "Current trauma triage guidelines have poor sensitivity to identify major trauma and the need for TC care for older adults." "This systematic review showed that under-triage is an ongoing issue for older trauma patients in prehospital care and its impact on their outcomes is still uncertain." Lupton 2022: "Among eight studies evaluating the entire FTG (steps 1-4), under-triage rates ranged from 1.6% to 72.0% and were higher for older (≥55 or ≥65 years) adults (20.1-72.0%) and pediatric (<15 years) patients (15.9-34.8%) compared to all ages (1.6-33.8%)."
location: Alshibani Abstract, Results and Conclusions; Lupton Abstract, Results
safe_wording: Reviews of ambulance triage rules find they miss serious injury in older people more often than in younger adults. Whether this changes outcomes is still uncertain.
qualifications: Mostly North American studies of prehospital triage, not UK emergency department practice. Ranges are wide.

claim: About 5 in 100 older people who come to an emergency department after a fall have bleeding inside the skull.
supporting_passage: "The pooled incidence of intracranial bleeding was 5.2% (95% CI 3.2-8.2%). A sensitivity analysis excluding studies with a high risk of bias gave a pooled estimate of 5.1% (95% CI 3.6-7.2%)." "The available literature suggests there is around a 5% incidence of intracranial bleeding in seniors who present to the ED after a fall."
safe_wording: Across studies, about 1 in 20 people aged 65 or over who came to an emergency department after a fall had bleeding inside the skull.
qualifications: Studies varied (some required head injury or a CT request); 8 of 11 at high risk of bias.

claim: Anticoagulant use should raise concern for serious head injury after a low fall.
supporting_passage: Dubucs 2025: "Preinjury anticoagulant was not a significant risk factor (OR: 0.8 [95% CI 0.7 to 1.0])." "Based on AOR, only focal neurologic signs (AOR: 4.4 [95% CI 3.0 to 6.5]), external sign of head trauma (AOR: 2.7 [95% CI 2.1 to 3.5]), loss of consciousness (AOR: 1.6 [95% CI 1.2 to 2.1]), and male sex (AOR: 1.4 [95% CI 1.2 to 1.6]) remained associated with traumatic ICH." Pandor 2022: "Heart rate and anticoagulant were not significant predictors."
location: Dubucs Abstract, Results; Pandor Abstract, Results
safe_wording: Do not tell readers that anticoagulants make a bleed after a low fall more likely: a 2025 meta-analysis did not find anticoagulant use to be a risk factor for bleeding inside the skull in this group. Keep the triage instruction to the injury and the person (look for head and chest injury after a low fall).
qualifications: This concerns the presence of a bleed, not how serious a bleed becomes; local head injury guidance on scanning people on anticoagulants was not opened.

claim: NICE major trauma guidance (NG39) applies regardless of mechanism.
supporting_passage: Not opened (NICE pages blocked).
safe_wording: Leave out any statement about NICE NG39.
qualifications: Unverified.

claim: The study included 5,249,891 patients admitted from type 1 emergency departments in England from April 2016 to March 2018; crude 30-day mortality was 8.71%.
supporting_passage: "A cross-sectional, retrospective observational study was carried out of patients admitted from every type 1 (major) ED in England between April 2016 and March 2018. The primary outcome was death from all causes within 30 days of admission." "Between April 2016 and March 2018, 26 738 514 people attended an ED, with 7 472 480 patients admitted relating to 5 249 891 individual patients, who constituted the study's dataset. A total of 433 962 deaths occurred within 30 days. The overall crude 30-day mortality rate was 8.71% (95% CI 8.69% to 8.74%)."
safe_wording: Researchers looked at over 5 million people admitted through major emergency departments in England between 2016 and 2018. About 9 in 100 died within 30 days.
qualifications: All adult ages, not older people only; admissions (7.47 million) relate to 5.25 million individuals.

claim: Mortality rose steadily with waits from 5 hours after arrival up to 12 hours; the largest change was an 8% increase in the standardised mortality ratio for waits of more than 6 to 8 hours.
supporting_passage: "A statistically significant linear increase in mortality was found from 5 hours after time of arrival at the ED up to 12 hours (when accurate data collection ceased) (p<0.001). The greatest change in the 30-day standardised mortality ratio was an 8% increase, occurring in the patient cohort that waited in the ED for more than 6 to 8 hours from the time of arrival."
safe_wording: The longer people waited beyond 5 hours from arrival, the higher their risk of dying within 30 days, compared with what the researchers' model expected. The rise continued up to 12 hours, where reliable timing data stopped.
qualifications: Association in observational data; do not use 'causes' even though the authors' conclusion does ('Between 5 and 12 hours, delays cause a predictable dose-response effect').

claim: The authors estimated one extra death for every 82 admitted patients delayed beyond 6 to 8 hours from arrival.
supporting_passage: "For every 82 admitted patients whose time to inpatient bed transfer is delayed beyond 6 to 8 hours from time of arrival at the ED, there is one extra death." Methods: "Observed mortality was compared with expected mortality, as calculated using a logistic regression model"
safe_wording: The authors estimated 1 extra death for every 82 people whose move to a ward bed was delayed beyond 6 to 8 hours after arrival. This is their estimate from comparing observed deaths with the deaths their model expected; it is a link in the data, not proof that the wait caused each death.
qualifications: The exact comparison group and calculation behind 1 in 82 could not be checked in the full text (not accessible). Do not state 'compared with people who waited less than 4 hours' or similar.

claim: The model adjusted for sex, age, deprivation, comorbidities, time of day, month, previous attendances and crowding, but not for acute illness severity.
supporting_passage: "expected mortality, as calculated using a logistic regression model to adjust for sex, age, deprivation, comorbidities, hour of day, month, previous ED attendances/emergency admissions and crowding in the department at the time of the attendance."
safe_wording: The researchers allowed for age, sex, deprivation, long-term conditions, time of day, month, earlier visits and how crowded the department was. They could not allow for how ill each person was on arrival.
qualifications: The absence of an acute severity measure is inferred from the listed variables in the abstract; do not write 'adjusted for illness' or 'illness severity'.

claim: Older people are more likely than younger adults to spend 4 hours or more in the emergency department.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Attendances of adults aged 65 to 74 years, 75 to 84 years and ≥ 85 years, respectively, had an increased risk (odds ratio (95% confidence interval) of length of ED stay ≥ 4 h of 1.52 (1.45-1.58), 1.65 (1.58-1.72), and 1.84 (1.75-1.93), compared to those of adults 18 to 64 years (all p < 0.001). These findings remained consistent in the subsets of attendances leading to hospital admission and those leading to discharge from ED." Table 3 (attendances with stay ≥4 h): 18-64 years "45,311 (43.6)"; 65-74 "9,027 (63.1)"; 75-84 "11,156 (71.4)"; ≥85 "10,142 (79.0)".
location: Abstract; full text Table 3 (p. 9) with denominators from Table 2
safe_wording: In one large English emergency department in 2019, 79 in 100 visits by people aged 85 or over lasted 4 hours or more, compared with 44 in 100 visits by adults under 65.
qualifications: Single hospital, one year, before the pandemic; attendances not people; adjusted odds ratios should not be turned into 'times more likely'. Longer stays may partly reflect more tests and assessment, not only waiting for a bed.

claim: In older people (75+) admitted through emergency departments, spending the night in the department was linked with higher in-hospital mortality in France, but a similar Spanish study did not find a clear difference.
supporting_passage: Roussel 2023: "The total sample comprised 1598 patients (median [IQR] age, 86 [80-90] years ...), with 707 (44%) in the ED group and 891 (56%) in the ward group. Patients who spent the night in the ED had a higher in-hospital mortality rate of 15.7% vs 11.1% (adjusted risk ratio [aRR], 1.39; 95% CI, 1.07-1.81). They also had a higher risk of adverse events compared with the ward group (aRR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.04-1.49)" "In a prespecified subgroup analysis of patients who required assistance with the activities of daily living, spending the night in the ED was associated with a higher in-hospital mortality rate (aRR, 1.81; 95% CI, 1.25-2.61)." Miro 2024: "In-hospital mortality for patients spending the night in the ED the ED group was 10.7% and 9.5% for patients transferred to a ward bed before midnight the ward group (adjusted OR: 1.12, 95%CI: 0.80-1.58)." "No increased risk of in-hospital mortality or prolonged hospitalization was found in older patients waiting overnight in the ED for admission."
location: Roussel Abstract, Results; Miro Abstract, Results and Conclusions
safe_wording: In France, older people (75 and over) who spent the night in the emergency department waiting for a bed died in hospital more often than those who reached a ward before midnight (about 16 in 100 versus 11 in 100). A similar study in Spain did not find a clear difference (about 11 in 100 versus 10 in 100).
qualifications: Observational; give both studies. Subgroup finding (people needing help with daily activities) is a subgroup, not the whole study.

claim: New pressure sores develop during emergency department stays, more often in people over 75; most are early (stage I) and on the heels and sacrum.
supporting_passage: A total of 27 patients developed new PU during their ED stay, among them 20 were aged over 75 years. The cumulative incidence was 4·9% and this rate increased to 15·7% in patients aged over 75 years. | Heels and sacrum were both the main sites of PUs, and new PUs were most often localised on these two sites with a greater tendency to appear on the heels. Stage I PUs were the most often stages registered among the 38 new PUs that occurred during the ED stay [i.e. 34 (89·5%) PUs]. | Length of stay, hours (mean ± SD) 9·1 (8·5) | A proportion of 165 (27·4%) patients were older than 75 years.
safe_wording: In one French emergency department, about 5 in 100 patients developed a new pressure sore during a stay that averaged 9 hours; among people over 75 it was about 16 in 100. Most were stage I, the earliest stage (reddened skin that is still unbroken), mostly on the heels and the base of the spine.
qualifications: One centre, two weeks in 2010; stage I included; 361 of 963 patients excluded for missing data. The incidence denominators appear to be patients without a sore on arrival (overall 602 minus 47 = 555 gives 27/555 = 4.9%; over-75s 165 minus 38 = 127 gives 20/127 = 15.7%): this is the checker's arithmetic, not a statement in the paper. 20 of 165 over-75s would be 12%, so do not compute any other percentage. Say 'in one French emergency department'.

claim: Older people are more likely than younger adults to have long emergency department stays.
supporting_passage: Attendances of adults aged 65 to 74 years, 75 to 84 years and ≥ 85 years, respectively, had an increased risk (odds ratio (95% confidence interval) of length of ED stay ≥ 4 h of 1.52 (1.45-1.58), 1.65 (1.58-1.72), and 1.84 (1.75-1.93), compared to those of adults 18 to 64 years (all p < 0.001). | Table 3 (stay ≥ 4 h, all attendances): Aged 18 to 64 years 45,311 (43.6); 65 to 74 years 9,027 (63.1); 75 to 84 years 11,156 (71.4); ≥ 85 years 10,142 (79.0)
safe_wording: At one large English emergency department in 2019, about 44 in 100 visits by adults aged 18 to 64 lasted 4 hours or more, compared with about 71 in 100 visits by people aged 75 to 84 and about 79 in 100 by people aged 85 or over.
qualifications: One hospital, one year; counts visits (a person can attend more than once), not people; 4 hours is the cut-off, so it says nothing about 12-hour waits. Percentages are the crude figures; the adjusted odds ratios should not be turned into 'times more likely'.

claim: Usual medicines can be given late or missed in hospital, and for time-critical medicines such as Parkinson's drugs this is linked with harm.
supporting_passage: Richard 2022: Time-critical medications were prescribed correctly on admission in 50% of admissions, with errors in medication timing most common (31.6%). Of all doses, 51.7% were administered >30 minutes late, and 29.7% of doses were administered >1 hour late. | Lertxundi 2017: Medication errors, affecting almost one third of admissions and half of patients, were associated with higher mortality: inappropriately omitted dopaminergic drug doses OR = 1.92 CI 95% (1.34-2.76). Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay.
safe_wording: For some medicines, such as Parkinson's drugs, timing matters. In one Dublin hospital, about half of Parkinson's doses were given more than 30 minutes late. In Spanish hospitals, missed Parkinson's doses were linked with longer stays and more deaths in hospital.
qualifications: Inpatient wards, not emergency department waits; Parkinson's only; observational (link, not proof). The sources do not cover medicines in general, and the NPSA 2010 report on omitted and delayed medicines was not opened, so do not cite it. Ask 'when are my usual medicines due?' as a question without claiming harm from a missed dose for all medicines.

claim: During a long wait an older person still needs a drink (if allowed), help to the toilet, and help to change position, and it is reasonable to ask for each.
supporting_passage: No source opened on dehydration, continence or repositioning during emergency department waits.
safe_wording: Present as a judgement and as questions ('Ask whether they are allowed to drink', 'Ask for help to the toilet', 'Ask whether they can be helped to change position'). Make no claim that any of these prevents harm in the emergency department.
qualifications: The pressure-sore data (C15-15-a) show the risk exists but do not test repositioning.

claim: Some patients must not eat or drink while awaiting tests or surgery, so the advice is to ask whether drinking is allowed.
supporting_passage: No source opened.
safe_wording: Keep as a question only: 'Ask whether they are allowed to drink.' Make no claim about harms of thirst or incontinence during waits.
qualifications: No evidence opened on dehydration or incontinence during emergency department waits.

claim: Living at home at 6 months similar with hospital at home vs admission
supporting_passage: At 6-month follow-up, 528 of 672 (78.6%) participants in the CGA HAH group versus 247 of 328 (75.3%) participants in the hospital group were living at home (relative risk [RR], 1.05 [95% CI, 0.95 to 1.15];= 0.36)
safe_wording: About 79 in 100 treated at home and 75 in 100 admitted were living at home six months later; the trial did not show a clear difference.
qualifications: Selected, physiologically stable people, mean age 83, mostly from acute medical assessment units; 2:1 randomisation.

claim: Deaths at 6 months similar
safe_wording: About 17 in 100 in each group had died by six months; no clear difference.
qualifications: Wide CI; not powered as equivalence on mortality.

claim: Fewer in long-term residential care at 6 months
supporting_passage: 37 of 646 (5.7%) versus 27 of 311 (8.7%) were in long-term residential care (RR, 0.58 [CI, 0.45 to 0.76];< 0.001)
safe_wording: About 6 in 100 treated at home and 9 in 100 admitted had moved into long-term residential care by six months.
qualifications: Use absolute figures only; the RR 0.58 does not match the crude proportions (adjusted), so do not quote it.

claim: Applicability: selected stable older people
supporting_passage: The findings are most applicable to older persons referred from a hospital short-stay acute medical assessment unit; episodes of delirium may have been undetected.
safe_wording: The trial included older people who were unwell but stable, mostly referred from short-stay acute medical assessment units; it applies to selected people, not everyone.

claim: Carer outcomes (what hospital at home asks of families)
safe_wording: Do not state any trial finding about carers or carer strain. The post may say, as judgement, that families should ask what help at home involves.
qualifications: Carer data not in abstract; full text/NIHR report not opened.

claim: Pathway halved hospitalisation in nursing home residents with pneumonia
supporting_passage: Thirty-four (10%) of 327 residents in the clinical pathway group were hospitalized compared with 76 (22%) of 353 residents in the usual care group. Adjusting for clustering of residents in nursing homes, the weighted mean reduction in hospitalizations was 12% (95% confidence interval [CI], 5%-18%; P = .001).
safe_wording: In a Canadian trial, about 10 in 100 residents treated in the home on the pathway went to hospital, against 22 in 100 with usual care.
qualifications: Population was lower respiratory tract infection including pneumonia; Canada, 2001-05; the 12% is a percentage-point difference adjusted for clustering.

claim: No clear difference in deaths, quality of life or function
supporting_passage: The mortality rate was 8% (24 deaths) in the clinical pathway group vs 9% (32 deaths) in the usual care group, with a weighted mean difference of 2.9% (95% CI, -2.0% to 7.9%; P = .23). There were no significant differences between the groups in health-related quality of life or functional status.
safe_wording: About 8 in 100 and 9 in 100 died; the trial did not show a clear difference in deaths, quality of life or function.
qualifications: Not powered to show a mortality difference; say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'.

claim: What the pathway included
supporting_passage: Treatment in nursing homes according to a clinical pathway, which included use of oral antimicrobials, portable chest radiographs, oxygen saturation monitoring, rehydration, and close monitoring by a research nurse, or usual care.
safe_wording: The home treatment included antibiotic tablets, chest X-rays taken in the home, oxygen level checks, fluids, and close checks by a dedicated research nurse.
qualifications: UK applicability to homes without this monitoring is a judgement and should be framed as such.

claim: Proportion of readmissions judged avoidable varies widely
supporting_passage: The median proportion of readmissions deemed avoidable was 27.1% but varied from 5% to 79%.
safe_wording: Across 34 studies, reviewers judged between 5 and 79 in 100 readmissions avoidable; the middle value was about 27 in 100.
qualifications: Denominator is readmissions, not patients.

claim: Methods mostly subjective, single centre, one reviewer; true proportion unclear
supporting_passage: Most of the studies were conducted at single teaching hospitals, did not consider information from the community or treating physicians, and used only one reviewer to decide whether readmissions were avoidable. ... All but three of the studies used subjective criteria to determine whether readmissions were avoidable. ... The true proportion of hospital readmissions that are potentially avoidable remains unclear.
safe_wording: Most studies relied on one reviewer's judgement at a single teaching hospital, so the true share of avoidable readmissions remains unclear.
qualifications: Position that a rate should prompt case review is judgement.

claim: Discharge planning slightly shortened initial stay for people admitted with a medical condition
supporting_passage: Participants allocated to discharge planning and who were in hospital for a medical condition had a small reduction in the initial hospital length of stay (MD - 0.73, 95% confidence interval (CI) - 1.33 to - 0.12; 11 trials, 2113 participants; moderate-certainty evidence)
safe_wording: Stays were on average about three quarters of a day shorter (moderate certainty).
qualifications: Medical-condition subgroup, 11 trials.

claim: Modestly fewer readmissions over about three months
supporting_passage: and a relative reduction in readmission to hospital over an average of three months follow-up (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.97; 17 trials, 5126 participants; moderate-certainty evidence)
safe_wording: Readmissions over about three months were somewhat lower, roughly a tenth fewer in relative terms (moderate certainty).
qualifications: Relative effect only; control rate not available, so no per-100 figure.

claim: Little or no difference in mortality and function; satisfaction may increase; costs uncertain
supporting_passage: There was little or no difference in participant's health status (mortality at three- to nine-month follow-up: RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.29; 8 trials, 2721 participants; moderate certainty) functional status and psychological health ... low certainty evidence). There was some evidence that satisfaction might be increased ... (very low certainty evidence). The cost of a structured discharge plan compared with routine discharge is uncertain
safe_wording: There was little or no difference in deaths or day-to-day function; satisfaction may be higher and costs are uncertain.
qualifications: Certainty low to very low for function and satisfaction.

claim: Medication errors and discrepancies are common after discharge
supporting_passage: For adult patients, the median rate of medication errors and unintentional medication discrepancies following discharge was 53% [interquartile range 33-60.5] (n = 5 studies) and 50% [interquartile range 39-76] (n = 11), respectively.
safe_wording: Studies commonly find medicine errors or unintended differences after leaving hospital; in most studies between a third and three quarters of patients were affected.
qualifications: Few studies (5 and 11), varying definitions; give as a range.

claim: Taking weekly methotrexate daily by mistake can cause serious harm; MHRA measures
supporting_passage: Intoxication with oral low-dose methotrexate (MTX) is a well-known and frequent problem, which is often discovered accidently. The major reason is error in the frequency of dosing, mostly of daily instead of weekly intake.
safe_wording: Taking a once-weekly medicine such as methotrexate every day by mistake can cause serious poisoning.
qualifications: Case-report level only; MHRA Drug Safety Update not opened, so do not cite MHRA.

claim: On discharge day the ward may already have given that day's doses, and a weekly medicine's day may change during admission, causing doubled or missed doses at home
safe_wording: No source found; cannot be stated as fact.
qualifications: Central premise of the post.

claim: Barriers to rapid (compassionate) discharge include getting equipment and medicines and poor communication between teams
supporting_passage: Process mapping, an Ishikawa diagram and a Pareto chart were used to identify barriers, which included timely acquisition of home equipment and medication and poor communication among stakeholders. | Barriers identified included sourcing of equipment, communication between teams and clunky paperwork.
safe_wording: Hospital improvement projects in England and Singapore found the usual hold-ups were getting equipment and medicines to the home, poor communication between teams, and paperwork.
qualifications: Two single-site QI projects; 'main' barrier ranking not claimed.

claim: Some people referred for rapid discharge die in hospital before discharge
supporting_passage: The average time to discharge was 6.3 days and 29% died in hospital, as median survival was only 15 days. ... In phase 2, we extended the pilot, and 104 patients were identified; 94 people were discharged to home, with a median of wait of 1 day (range 0-7) to discharge, and 10 (9.6%) died prior to discharge (median 1 day; range 0-4). Median survival from discharge for the 94 who achieved their wishes to go home to die was 9 days
safe_wording: In one English hospital project, 10 in 104 people (about 1 in 10) referred to a team set up to get them home to die within a day died before they could leave; in the first 13 people, 2 died before discharge. For the 94 who did get home, median survival was 9 days.
qualifications: Single hospital, uncontrolled, no comparison group. Do not use the 29% figure: it is background from earlier work quoted in the abstract, not a finding of this project, and the populations are not strictly comparable. Do not say the project reduced deaths before discharge.

claim: NICE NG31 covers anticipatory prescribing for last days of life
supporting_passage: This Concise Guideline overviews NICE Clinical Guideline (NG31), which addresses: recognising dying; communication and shared decision making; maintaining hydration; and pharmacological symptom control, including anticipatory prescribing.
safe_wording: National guidance on care in the last days of life includes planning medicines in advance for symptoms that may come.
qualifications: Recommendation text not opened; keep general. NICE is England-focused.

claim: NHS CHC Fast Track funds care quickly (England)
supporting_passage: assessment processes for care funding, through continuing healthcare fast-track funding often inhibit people being able to die at home.
safe_wording: Leave Fast Track out. If funding is mentioned at all: in England, waiting for a care-funding assessment can hold up going home to die (authors' background statement; Fast Track is England-only).
qualifications: Background statement in the abstract, not a finding; National Framework not opened; England-only, so not for Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish readers.

claim: In England, NHS Continuing Healthcare Fast Track funds care quickly for people who are rapidly deteriorating and may be entering a terminal phase.
supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (page not opened): the tool is for people whose condition is rapidly deteriorating and may be entering a terminal phase; it is the version integrated care boards and NHS England should use from 1 July 2022; a completed tool is sufficient on its own to establish eligibility.
safe_wording: Leave out. If the editor insists, say only 'In England, NHS Continuing Healthcare has a fast track route for people who are rapidly worsening', and label it England only.
qualifications: Access is search_extract, which is not enough for an essential claim. Scotland and other UK nations use different arrangements; no source opened for them. The post's same-day principle does not depend on this claim.

claim: In the Confidential Inquiry, median age at death of people with intellectual disabilities was 64; men 13 and women 20 years younger than the general population
supporting_passage: the median age at death was 64 years (IQR 52-75). The median age at death of male individuals with intellectual disabilities was 65 years (IQR 54-76), 13 years younger than the median age at death of male individuals in the general population of England and Wales (78 years). The median age at death of female individuals with intellectual disabilities was 63 years (IQR 54-75), 20 years younger than the median age at death for female individuals in the general population (83 years).
safe_wording: In an inquiry into 247 deaths in south-west England (2010 to 2012), men with a learning disability died a median of 13 years younger, and women 20 years younger, than the general population.
qualifications: Regional and more than a decade old; name place and years.

claim: 37% of deaths amenable to good-quality health care vs 13% in general population
supporting_passage: Avoidable deaths from causes amenable to change by good quality health care were more common in people with intellectual disabilities (37%, 90 of 244) than in the general population of England and Wales (13%).
safe_wording: About 37 in 100 of these deaths were from causes that good health care can usually treat, compared with 13 in 100 in the general population.
qualifications: Use 'amenable to good health care' definition; do not mix with LeDeR 'avoidable'.

claim: Contributory factors included advance care planning, Mental Capacity Act adherence, adjusting care as needs changed, carers not feeling listened to
supporting_passage: Contributory factors to premature deaths in a subset of people with intellectual disabilities compared with a comparator group of people without intellectual disabilities included problems in advanced care planning (p=0·0003), adherence to the Mental Capacity Act (p=0·0008), living in inappropriate accommodation (p<0·0001), adjusting care as needs changed (p=0·009), and carers not feeling listened to (p=0·006).
safe_wording: Problems found more often included not adjusting care as needs changed and carers not feeling listened to.
qualifications: Subset comparison; judgements by review panels.

claim: Recent national (LeDeR) data on age at death and avoidable deaths
supporting_passage: The median age at death was markedly lower in this group (57.9 years) compared to those with mild or moderate intellectual disability (65.0 years) and the general population (81.9 years) (p < 0.001). We classified two-fifths of deaths among adults with severe or profound intellectual disability as avoidable (39.5%)
safe_wording: In England in 2021 to 2023, adults with a mild or moderate learning disability died at a median age of 65 and those with a severe or profound learning disability at 58, compared with 82 in the general population.
qualifications: LeDeR covers deaths reviewed, not all; 39.5% avoidable refers only to severe/profound group, avoidable = before 75 from OECD causes. Not the official LeDeR annual report (not opened).

claim: Learning disability liaison nurses and hospital passports exist and help; liaison nurse input linked with more reasonable adjustments
supporting_passage: One-third of people with intellectual disability who died in hospital in England between 2016 and 2021 had input from an intellectual disability liaison nurse. ... associated with increased likelihood of reasonable adjustments being made to care (adjusted OR (aOR) 1.95, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.32) ... but was not associated with a rating of overall quality of care received (aOR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.12). | the use of the hospital passport and the intellectual disability liaison nurse to significantly improve the hospital experience for adults with intellectual disabilities was identified in two of the studies.
safe_wording: Only about 1 in 3 people with a learning disability who died in English hospitals (2016 to 2021) had seen a learning disability liaison nurse; when one was involved, care was more often adjusted to the person's needs. People with a learning disability have said hospital passports and liaison nurses made hospital easier.
qualifications: Association only; no difference in overall quality rating; do not convert OR to 'twice as likely'.

claim: Equality Act 2010 legal duty of reasonable adjustments
safe_wording: Omit the legal claim, or frame as 'hospitals should make reasonable adjustments' (judgement).
qualifications: Legislation not opened (official web pages unavailable). Equality Act 2010 does not apply in Northern Ireland. Frame as a judgement: hospitals should make reasonable adjustments.

claim: In Scotland the Key Information Summary is a shared electronic record available across settings, giving clinicians information for people likely to need emergency or out-of-hours care.
supporting_passage: Electronic care coordination systems, known as the Key Information Summary (KIS) in Scotland, enable the creation of shared electronic records available across healthcare settings. A KIS provides clinicians with essential information to guide decision making for people likely to need emergency or out-of-hours care.
safe_wording: In Scotland, the Key Information Summary is a shared record that out-of-hours and emergency clinicians can see, so a plan written there can reach the person who turns up at night.
qualifications: Source says 'available across healthcare settings'; do not list named services beyond that.

claim: Many KIS records lacked key content: 68% included resuscitation status and 55% preferred place of care.
supporting_passage: Overall, 68% (= 482) of KIS included resuscitation status and 55% (= 390) preferred place of care.
safe_wording: In one Scottish study of people who died in 2017, about 1 in 3 Key Information Summaries did not record resuscitation status and nearly half did not record preferred place of care.
qualifications: People with advanced progressive illness near death, not all care home or housebound people; 2017 data.

claim: Core hours 08:00-18:30 weekdays total 52.5 of 168 hours, so over two thirds of the week falls outside them.
safe_wording: Say 'most hours of the week fall outside weekday surgery hours' without citing contract hours, or omit.
qualifications: Contract definitions not opened; hours are not demand; England has extended access.

claim: Medication errors and unintentional discrepancies after hospital discharge are common.
supporting_passage: For adult patients, the median rate of medication errors and unintentional medication discrepancies following discharge was 53% [interquartile range 33-60.5] (n = 5 studies) and 50% [interquartile range 39-76] (n = 11), respectively.
safe_wording: Across studies in a systematic review, about half of adults had at least one unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital (median across 11 studies, with wide variation).
qualifications: Medians of few studies; definitions differ; not care-home specific; does not measure the repeat-list mechanism.

claim: Stopped medicines reappear via the GP repeat list and next monthly order; NICE SC1 reconciliation; Discharge Medicines Service; readmission reduction.
safe_wording: Present the repeat-list route as an illustrative example of how a change can be lost, not a measured frequency; do not cite NICE SC1, DMS or readmission effects.
qualifications: Official pages not opened.

claim: The INTERACT implementation trial did not show a clear reduction in hospital admissions overall.
supporting_passage: Training and support for INTERACT implementation as carried out in this study had no effect on hospitalization or ED visit rates in the overall population of residents in participating NHs.
