safe_wording: In a US trial across 85 nursing homes, training staff to use the INTERACT tools did not show a clear drop in hospital admissions overall.
qualifications: Potentially avoidable admissions fell but not robust to multiple-comparison correction; do not claim a high-engagement effect.

claim: RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is used in UK care homes; staff raised training concerns for night and temporary staff.
supporting_passage: there was strong support for using the RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) assessment tool to monitor residents; however, there were concerns about associated training requirements, especially for night and temporary staff.
safe_wording: RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is a UK care home tool; staff interviewed in one study worried about training night and temporary staff to use it.
qualifications: No effectiveness evidence opened; NEWS2/SBARD components and West Hampshire origin not sourced.

claim: Covert administration is common and often poorly documented.
supporting_passage: 11% of the patients in regular nursing home units and 17% of the patients in special care units for people with dementia received drugs mixed in their food or beverages at least once during seven days. ... The practice was documented in patients' records in 40% (96/241) of cases.
safe_wording: In a Norwegian study, about 1 in 9 nursing home residents, and 1 in 6 in dementia units, had medicines hidden in food or drink in one week, and this was written in the record in only 4 in 10 cases.
qualifications: Old Norwegian data; state place and that UK figures may differ.

claim: Tablets with special coatings or modified release, and bitter-tasting medicines, may be unsuitable for crushing or mixing.
supporting_passage: considerations included by consensus in the INGEST algorithm were the presence of special coating or modified release characteristics of the SODF medications, hazardous nature and taste of the active ingredients, manufacturer's advice and use of tube feeding.
safe_wording: Pharmacists check whether a tablet is coated or modified-release, and how it tastes, before it is crushed or mixed into food; ask a pharmacist for each medicine.
qualifications: Expert consensus tool, not harm data.

claim: NICE SC1 and Scottish AWI Act/MWC guide steps (capacity, best interests, section 47 certificate).
safe_wording: Do not attribute specific steps to NICE or MWC; state as professional judgement that hiding medicines should follow a documented capacity and best-interests decision with a pharmacist involved, and reference 'national guidance' without detail only if a later batch opens it.
qualifications: Official documents could not be opened.

claim: 'Potentially avoidable' (ambulatory care sensitive) admissions are defined by lists of diagnosis codes, and the lists vary, which changes how many admissions are counted as avoidable.
supporting_passage: The underlying ICD10 codes used to define ACSCs vary widely across subsets of ACSCs used in the NHS. This impacts on rates of admission, length of stay and costs attributable to ACSCs. ... different conceptual interpretations of the term 'ACSC' and use of differing definitions and diagnostic codes impact on the proportion of admissions that are attributed as ACSCs.
safe_wording: 'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes. Different lists give different totals.
qualifications: Study was of all emergency admissions, not care homes; it shows the classification is code-based, it does not itself state 'no case review' for any specific report.

claim: The measure is used to judge services: 'potentially avoidable emergency admissions' is an outcome in evaluations of support to care homes.
supporting_passage: Residents of participating residential care homes showed lower rates of potentially avoidable emergency admissions (rate ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.82), emergency admissions (rate ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.86) and Accident & Emergency attendances (0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.81) than matched controls.
safe_wording: Rates of 'potentially avoidable' admissions are used to compare services and programmes for care homes.
qualifications: Use only to show how the measure is used; do not quote the rate ratio as the post's point. Observational.

claim: Hospital admission from a care home is often necessary; blanket do-not-hospitalise approaches were problematic.
supporting_passage: While often necessary, such admissions can be distressing and provide an opportunity cost as well as a financial cost. ... Advance care planning was key to the success of most quality improvement programmes but do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.
safe_wording: A 2023 systematic review noted that admissions from care homes are often necessary, and that do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.
qualifications: 'Often necessary' is the authors' framing in the background, not a measured finding.

claim: Wolters et al. 2019 (Health Foundation): about 41 in 100 emergency admissions from care homes were potentially avoidable.
safe_wording: Do not give the proportion.
qualifications: No opened copy found in PubMed or Drive; per editor guidance, omit the figure.

claim: About 1 in 4 older care home residents died within one year; mortality was higher in nursing homes than residential homes, relative to the general population of the same age and sex.
supporting_passage: a total of 2,558 (26.2%) care home and 11,602 (3.3%) community residents died within 1 year. The age and sex standardised mortality ratio for nursing homes was 419 (95% CI: 396-442) and for residential homes was 284 (266-302).
safe_wording: In a study of care home residents in England and Wales in 2009, about 26 in 100 died within a year, so about 74 in 100 were alive a year later. Death rates were higher in nursing homes than in residential homes.
qualifications: People already living in homes, not people counted from the day they moved in; 2009 data. Higher mortality reflects how ill people are when they move in, not an effect of the home.

claim: A median is the value that half the group exceeds.
safe_wording: A median survival means half the group lived longer than that figure and half lived less.
qualifications: Standard statistical definition; no source needed.

claim: Median length of stay in UK care homes, with spread from weeks to years (Forder and Fernandez 2011).
safe_wording: Do not give a median length of stay or a histogram.
qualifications: PSSRU report not indexed or opened.

claim: Enhanced Health in Care Homes alignment and weekly home round; Scottish My Health My Care My Home; CQC Smiling Matters.
safe_wording: None.
qualifications: All are official web documents that cannot be opened; not searched further because C16-06 is a reserve and not needed (C16-12 is revise, not drop).

claim: Reablement is time-limited, goal-directed help at home to maximise independence.
supporting_passage: Unlike traditional home-care services, reablement is frequently time-limited (usually six to 12 weeks) and aims to maximise independence by offering an intensive multidisciplinary, person-centred and goal-directed intervention.
safe_wording: Reablement is short-term help at home, usually lasting weeks rather than months, that aims to help people do everyday things for themselves again, working towards goals set with them.
qualifications: Length varies by service ('usually six to 12 weeks').

claim: In England reablement is free for up to six weeks.
supporting_passage: No PubMed-indexed or opened source stating the charging rule was found (PubMed searches for reablement plus England and six weeks returned only a trial protocol that does not state it). The regulations and Care Act guidance could not be opened.
safe_wording: Do not state the six-week rule or that reablement is free. If needed: 'Ask the council whether there is any charge and how long the help will last.'
qualifications: Scotland and other nations differ; not verified.

claim: A 2016 Cochrane review found only two trials and very low certainty evidence.
supporting_passage: We are very uncertain as to the effects of reablement compared with usual care as the evidence was of very low quality for all of the outcomes reported.
safe_wording: A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials and was very uncertain whether reablement helps more than usual home care.
qualifications: Old searches (2015); a 2026 meta-analysis now exists (C16-28-e).

claim: A Norwegian trial found reablement improved self-rated performance of, and satisfaction with, chosen daily activities.
supporting_passage: There were significant improvements in mean scores favouring reablement in COPM performance at 3 months with a score of 1.5 points (p = 0.02), at 9 months 1.4 points (p = 0.03) and overall treatment 1.5 points (p = 0.01), and for COPM satisfaction at 9 months 1.4 points (p = 0.03) and overall treatment 1.2 points (p = 0.04). No significant group differences were found concerning COPM satisfaction at 3 months, physical capacity or health-related quality of life.
safe_wording: In one small Norwegian trial of 61 people, those offered 10 weeks of reablement rated their own performance of the everyday activities they had chosen as somewhat better at 3 and 9 months. It did not show a clear difference in physical capacity or quality of life.
qualifications: Single small trial; outcome self-rated; effects persisted to 9 months (contrary to the judge's note).

claim: The newest pooled evidence on reablement remains weak (evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit).
supporting_passage: Reablement-based interventions showed no significant effects on selected ADL tasks measured with Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) (n = 291, COPM performance MD 0.30, 95% CI - 0.25 to 0.86; COPM satisfaction MD 0.19, 95% CI - 0.04 to 0.42) or physical performance (n = 555, SMD 0.12, 95% CI - 0.05 to 0.28), with low to very low evidence according to GRADE. ... Evidence for other ADL outcomes and the Reablement-based remains limited.
safe_wording: A 2026 review that pooled reablement trials did not show a clear difference in chosen daily activities or physical performance, and the certainty of the evidence was low to very low. That means we do not know, not that it does not work.
qualifications: Small pooled numbers (291 and 555).

claim: The eFI was built from 36 deficits in routine GP records and predicts population outcomes.
supporting_passage: The eFI incorporates 36 deficits constructed using 2,171 CTV3 codes. ... The eFI score is calculated by the presence or absence of individual deficits as a proportion of the total possible. Categories of fit, mild, moderate and severe frailty were defined using population quartiles. ... with good to moderate discrimination but low calibration estimates.
safe_wording: The eFI counts 36 kinds of problem coded in GP records. It was built to sort a practice population by risk, and higher categories were linked with more deaths, hospital stays and care home moves.
qualifications: Validated for population risk prediction; 'low calibration'. Scores depend on what is coded (follows from the method; the abstract does not state it in these words).

claim: eFI agreement with in-person frailty assessment for individuals is limited.
supporting_passage: Brack 2023: "One study of 60 patients examined the eFI, reporting a sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI = 0.55, 0.98) and a specificity of 0.78 (0.64, 0.89)." ... "eFI is the best-performing VEFM; however, based on our analysis of an average UK GP practice, it would return a high number of false-positive results. In conclusion, existing electronic frailty tools may not be appropriate for primary care-based population screening." Barber-Fleming 2026: "Agreement was 'fair' between self-perceived frailty and eFI (linear weighted Kappa 0.25, quadratic weighted Kappa 0.37)."
safe_wording: Only one small study (60 people) has checked the eFI against an in-person frailty assessment. A 2023 review estimated that, across a typical practice, it would label many people as frail who are not. So an eFI category is a reason to review someone, not a diagnosis.
qualifications: Do not say 'moderate agreement' (no source gives that); self-perception study is not a clinical comparison.

claim: The GP contract in England since 2017/18 requires frailty identification using a tool such as the eFI.
supporting_passage: the use of tools that screen for frailty using electronic records (which we term as validated electronic frailty measures (VEFMs)) within primary care is incentivised by NHS England.
safe_wording: In England, NHS England encourages practices to use electronic record tools such as the eFI to find people who may be living with frailty.
qualifications: Year (2017) and contract wording not verified; background statement.

claim: Housebound older people are an under-researched group with complex needs who face challenges accessing primary care.
supporting_passage: Duncan 2026: "Housebound patients are an under-researched group who face challenges accessing primary health care and have complex needs." Winn 2023: "Older housebound people are a neglected group both in terms of research and clinical care."
safe_wording: UK researchers describe housebound patients as a group who find it hard to get GP care, have complex needs, and have been little studied.
qualifications: Authors' framing statements, not measured findings; CHiP results not found.

claim: Housebound people often miss routine long-term condition reviews at the practice.
supporting_passage: People who are housebound frequently miss general practice-based long-term condition (LTC) reviews. ... In total, twenty-three patients had missed 91 LTC reviews since becoming housebound and were prescribed a median of 14 regular medications (range 9-27).
safe_wording: In one small Glasgow study, 23 of 25 housebound people had missed routine reviews of their long-term conditions since becoming housebound.
qualifications: Small, Scottish, selected sample; not a prevalence estimate. Do not claim effects of the home visits.

claim: Home NHS sight tests and home vaccination are available for eligible housebound people.
supporting_passage: No source opened; NHS and UKHSA pages cannot be opened.
safe_wording: Leave out specific entitlements, or phrase as a question: 'Ask the practice what can be done at home, such as vaccines and medicine reviews.'
qualifications: Nation-specific rules unverified.

claim: The 3D trial of patient-centred multimorbidity reviews did not improve quality of life.
supporting_passage: In our intention-to-treat analysis, there was no difference between trial groups in the primary outcome of quality of life (adjusted difference in mean EQ-5D-5L 0·00, 95% CI -0·02 to 0·02; p=0·93).
safe_wording: In a UK trial of 1546 adults with three or more long-term conditions, longer six-monthly whole-person reviews did not show a difference in quality of life after 15 months.
qualifications: Adults of all ages. Better experience of care is not in the abstract and was not verified.

claim: A 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants) found people with stronger social relationships had higher odds of survival (OR 1.50); strongest for complex measures of social integration, weakest for living alone.
supporting_passage: "Across 148 studies (308,849 participants), the random effects weighted average effect size was OR = 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59), indicating a 50% increased likelihood of survival for participants with stronger social relationships. This finding remained consistent across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, and follow-up period. Significant differences were found across the type of social measurement evaluated (p<0.001); the association was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91; 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23) and lowest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone versus with others) (OR = 1.19; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44)." Full text (Results): "Participants were followed for an average of 7.5 years"
safe_wording: A 2010 review pooled 148 studies of about 309,000 people, followed for 7.5 years on average. People with stronger social relationships were more likely to be alive at the end of follow-up. The link was strongest when studies used measures combining several kinds of social ties, and weakest (not clearly different from no link) for simply living alone.
qualifications: Association from observational studies; the authors state causality is not easily established. OR 1.50 is an odds ratio for survival; do not convert it to '50% more likely to survive' or to an absolute difference. 'Social relationships' here is a composite of many measures, not loneliness.

claim: The 2010 paper compared its effect size in a figure with other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day, and described the effect as comparable with quitting smoking.
supporting_passage: Figure 6 bar label (as printed): "Smoking < 15 cigarettes daily". Figure 6 caption: "Comparison of odds (lnOR) of decreased mortality across several conditions associated with mortality. Note: Effect size of zero indicates no effect. The effect sizes were estimated from meta analyses: ; A = Shavelle, Paculdo, Strauss, and Kush, 2008 [205]; ..." Conclusion: "The magnitude of this effect is comparable with quitting smoking and it exceeds many well-known risk factors for mortality (e.g., obesity, physical inactivity)."
location: Figure 6 (bar labels and caption, read from the PDF via Undermind); Discussion/Conclusion (also in PMC full text)
safe_wording: A chart in the 2010 review set the size of this link beside other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day. The authors wrote that the effect was 'comparable with quitting smoking'. The chart compared numbers from different reviews of different people; it was not a head-to-head test.
qualifications: The comparator is 'fewer than 15' a day, not 15. The social relationships figure pooled marriage, networks, support, integration and other measures, not loneliness. The paper does not itself state the popular line 'loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day'; that the popular line derives from this chart was not confirmed from an opened source, so the post should say the comparison 'appears in' the 2010 review rather than that the slogan 'comes from' it.

claim: Most results pooled in the 2010 review measured social networks, marriage, support or integration rather than loneliness; loneliness contributed only 8 effect sizes.
supporting_passage: Introduction: "three major components of social relationships are consistently evaluated: (a) the degree of integration in social networks, (b) the social interactions that are intended to be supportive (i.e., received social support), and (c) the beliefs and perceptions of support availability held by the individual (i.e., perceived social support)." Results: "...which resulted in a total of 230 unique effect sizes across 116 studies" (structural measures); "We extracted 87 unique effect sizes that were specific to measures of functional social relationships within 72 studies"; "We extracted 64 unique effect sizes that evaluated combined structural and functional measures of social relationships within 61 studies." Table 2 lists 'Perception of loneliness: Feelings of isolation, disconnectedness, and not belonging' as one functional measure; Table 4, 'Loneliness (inversed)': k = 8, OR = 1.45 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.94).
location: Introduction; Results (metaregression sections, PMC full text); Tables 2 and 4 (read from PDF via Undermind)
safe_wording: Most of the studies measured things like marriage, the size of people's social networks, the support they had and how involved they were with others. Loneliness itself was measured in only 8 of the several hundred results in the review.
qualifications: k = 8 are effect sizes, not necessarily 8 separate studies. Within those 8, lower loneliness was linked with better survival (OR 1.45), so the review does not show loneliness is unimportant; it shows the headline figure is mostly about other social measures.

claim: A 2015 meta-analysis found loneliness associated with higher odds of death in adjusted studies (OR 1.26), similar to social isolation (1.29) and living alone (1.32).
supporting_passage: "Across studies in which several possible confounds were statistically controlled for, the weighted average effect sizes were as follows: social isolation odds ratio (OR) = 1.29, loneliness OR = 1.26, and living alone OR = 1.32, corresponding to an average of 29%, 26%, and 32% increased likelihood of mortality, respectively. We found no differences between measures of objective and subjective social isolation. ... Results also differ across participant age, with social deficits being more predictive of death in samples with an average age younger than 65 years."
safe_wording: A 2015 review of studies that allowed for other factors found loneliness linked with higher odds of dying during follow-up (odds ratio 1.26), about the same as for social isolation and living alone. These social measures predicted death more strongly in study groups whose average age was under 65.
qualifications: Odds ratio from observational studies: link, not proof of cause. The authors' own wording '26% increased likelihood' is a relative odds figure; do not present it as an absolute risk. The age finding applies to social deficits generally, not loneliness specifically.

claim: In ELSA (about 6,500 people aged 52 and over), loneliness was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for demographic factors and baseline health, while social isolation was.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "We found that mortality was higher among more socially isolated and more lonely participants. However, after adjusting statistically for demographic factors and baseline health, social isolation remained significantly associated with mortality (hazard ratio 1.26, 95% confidence interval, 1.08-1.48 for the top quintile of isolation), but loneliness did not (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval, 0.78-1.09)." Discussion: "These results do not imply that loneliness is not important but rather indicate that the experience of loneliness may be characteristic of people who already have major health and mobility problems." and "Reducing both social isolation and loneliness are important for quality of life and well-being, but efforts to reduce isolation would be likely to have greater benefits in terms of mortality."
safe_wording: In a study of about 6,500 people aged 52 and over in England, followed for about 7 years, lonely people were more likely to die at first. After allowing for their age, other background factors and their health at the start, loneliness was no longer linked with death, but social isolation (little contact with others) still was. The authors said loneliness still matters for quality of life and well-being.
qualifications: One cohort; loneliness measured once; observational (authors: causal conclusions cannot be drawn). 'Not independently associated' is not proof of no effect: the hazard ratio of 0.92 had a confidence interval from 0.78 to 1.09.

claim: Recent large meta-analyses, including one in older adults, still find loneliness linked with higher mortality, but less strongly than social isolation, with wide variation between studies.
supporting_passage: Wang 2023: "A total of 90 prospective cohort studies including 2,205,199 individuals were included. Here we show that, in the general population, both social isolation and loneliness were significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality (pooled effect size for social isolation, 1.32; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.26 to 1.39; P < 0.001; pooled effect size for loneliness, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.08 to 1.20; P < 0.001)". Nakou 2025: "Of 11,964 identified studies, 86 met the inclusion criteria. Loneliness was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.10-1.18), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 84.0%). Similar associations were found for social isolation (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.27-1.43) and living alone (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.13-1.30)."
safe_wording: The most recent large reviews, including one of older adults, still find that lonely people die somewhat earlier on average, but the link is smaller than for social isolation and varies a lot between studies.
qualifications: Relative effect estimates from observational studies; no absolute risks. Avoid '14% more likely to die' without saying it is a relative figure over each study's follow-up.

claim: Loneliness deserves attention because it is distressing and harms quality of life, whether or not the smoking comparison holds.
supporting_passage: "Reducing both social isolation and loneliness are important for quality of life and well-being, but efforts to reduce isolation would be likely to have greater benefits in terms of mortality."
safe_wording: Loneliness is worth taking seriously because it is painful to live with and affects quality of life. That case does not need a comparison with cigarettes.
qualifications: The first sentence is a value judgement and should read as one ('We should...'); the ELSA authors' statement supports the quality-of-life point. Do not claim evidence that treating loneliness lengthens life.

claim: The 2023 US Surgeon General's advisory repeated the smoking comparison.
location: Not opened (hhs.gov PDF appeared only as a search result; official pages cannot be opened from this environment)
safe_wording: Omit. If the post needs to show that the comparison is widely repeated, quote it as a popular claim without attributing it to a named body.
qualifications: Only a search-engine result list was available; no verbatim passage.

claim: The trial randomised 240 Meals on Wheels clients in Central Texas in 2020; aged 27 to 101, 63% aged 65 or over, 56% living alone, all with at least one chronic condition.
supporting_passage: "From July 6 to September 24, 2020, we recruited and followed up 240 adults who were assigned to receive calls (intervention group) or no calls (control group) via block randomization." "The study included MOWCTX clients who fit their service criteria, including being homebound and expressing a need for food." "The 240 participants were aged 27 to 101 years, with 63% aged at least 65 years (n = 149 of 232), 56% living alone (n = 135 of 240), 79% women (n = 190 of 240), 39% Black or African American (n = 94 of 240), and 22% Hispanic or Latino (n = 52 of 240), and all reported at least 1 chronic condition." Methods: "All MOWCTX clients were eligible except those with cognitive impairments, previously assessed through family report or via a case manager, or those in a hospice program."
safe_wording: A trial in Texas in 2020 randomly assigned 240 people who were getting Meals on Wheels at home to receive regular phone calls or no calls. They were aged 27 to 101, and about 6 in 10 were 65 or over. More than half lived alone, and all had at least one long-term condition. People with cognitive impairment were not included.
qualifications: About 4 in 10 participants were under 65, so this is not a trial of older people only. Mean age about 69 (Table 1). People with cognitive impairment or in hospice were excluded.

claim: Sixteen callers aged 17 to 23 had brief training in empathetic conversation: listen, and let the person choose the topics; no scripts or therapy training.
supporting_passage: Introduction: "Empathy was functionally defined as prioritizing listening and eliciting conversation from the participant on topics of their choice." Methods: "Sixteen people from ages 17 to 23 years, including 14 college undergraduates, 1 person entering community college, and 1 graduate student, were recruited to deliver calls to participants. Callers volunteered but were paid a stipend of $200 at the end of the program." "Callers were trained through a 1-hour videoconferenced session. The goal presented to callers was to learn from those they called by asking specific questions about topics raised by participants. No conversational prompts were provided nor training on CBT or its components. A short video was used to demonstrate techniques through role playing. Separately, callers received handouts and videotaped instructions on the logistics of the program (<1 hour)." Discussion: "our program required 2 hours of training for callers, no degree requirements"
safe_wording: The callers were 16 young people aged 17 to 23, mostly university students. They had about 2 hours of training in total. They were taught to listen, to let the person choose what to talk about, and to ask about the things the person raised. They were given no scripts and no therapy training.
qualifications: Callers were volunteers paid a $200 stipend at the end; they had a weekly optional feedback session with study staff and a route to report safety, food or money concerns to Meals on Wheels staff (34 escalations).

claim: Each caller had a panel of 6 to 9 participants; calls daily for the first 5 days, then at a frequency the participant chose (2 to 5 a week) for 4 weeks.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Each called 6 to 9 participants over 4 weeks daily for the first 5 days, after which clients could choose to drop down to fewer calls but no less than 2 calls a week." Methods: "Each caller supported a panel of 6 to 9 participants over 4 weeks. Calls were targeted to be less than 10 minutes; however, callers reported that calls could run longer. We did not limit time with the participant." "Calls were placed at the time of day participants requested. All participants were called 5 days during the first week. After this, participants chose the frequency of calls, with a minimum of 2 and maximum of 5 a week. Most (58%; n = 70 of 120) chose to continue to be called 5 times a week for the remaining 3 weeks". Randomization: "In the intervention arm, participants were assigned to a caller's panel once a sufficient number had consented so that each caller began with a full panel."
location: Abstract (Interventions); Methods (Intervention Program; Randomization and Blinding)
safe_wording: Each person was assigned to one caller, who looked after 6 to 9 people. Calls came every weekday for the first week, at a time the person chose. After that, people chose how often: between 2 and 5 calls a week. Most (58 in 100) kept 5 a week. Calls were meant to be under 10 minutes but could run longer.
qualifications: 'Same caller each time' is inferred from assignment to one caller's panel; the paper does not say in so many words that no other caller ever called. Prefer 'each person was assigned to one caller'. 'Daily for the first 5 days' (abstract) and 'called 5 days during the first week' (Methods) describe the same schedule.

claim: Loneliness improved by 1.1 points on the 3-item UCLA scale (range 3 to 9); a second loneliness scale did not show a clear difference; depression and anxiety improved; physical health did not change.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "Postassessment differences between intervention and control after 4 weeks showed an improvement of 1.1 on the UCLA Loneliness Scale (95% CI, 0.5-1.7; P < .001; Cohen d of 0.48), and improvement of 0.32 on De Jong (95% CI, -0.20 to 0.81; P = .06; Cohen d, 0.17) for loneliness; an improvement of 1.5 on the Personal Health Questionnaire for Depression (95% CI, 0.22-2.7; P < .001; Cohen d, 0.31) for depression; and an improvement of 1.8 on the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (95% CI, 0.44 to 3.2; P < .001; Cohen d, 0.35) for anxiety. General physical health on the Short Form Health Questionnaire Survey showed no change, but mental health improved by 2.6". Results: "Participants in the intervention group improved from a mean of 6.5 to 5.2 on the UCLA Scale and in the control group from 6.5 to 6.3". "Results were consistent with significant reductions in anxiety, with 50% of those with mild or greater anxiety (n = 60 of 120) in the intervention arm reducing to 36% (n = 38 of 107), while 49% of those with mild or greater anxiety (n = 59 of 120) in the control arm increased to 50% (n = 59 of 119)". "Although there was a reduction in those with mild or greater depression in the intervention arm relative to the control arm, it was not statistically significant (group difference of 9%; 95% CI, -3% to 23%". Statistical Analysis: "there are currently no prespecified clinically meaningful differences established for these measures."
location: Abstract (Results); Results (Main Analysis); Table 2; Methods (Statistical Analysis)
safe_wording: After 4 weeks, loneliness scores on a 3 to 9 scale fell from 6.5 to 5.2 in people who got calls, and from 6.5 to 6.3 in people who did not. A second loneliness questionnaire did not show a clear difference. Symptoms of depression and anxiety also improved. Among people with at least mild anxiety at the start, the share still anxious fell from 50 in 100 to 36 in 100 with calls, and stayed about 50 in 100 without. Physical health scores and the size of people's social networks did not change.
qualifications: The loneliness change is modest (about 1 point on a 7-point range); there is no agreed threshold for a meaningful change on these scales. The share with at least mild depression did not fall clearly. Short follow-up (4 weeks).

claim: Follow-up lasted only 4 weeks, during the COVID-19 pandemic; benefits beyond 4 weeks are unknown.
supporting_passage: Limitations: "A major limitation of this study is that it is unclear whether benefits are sustained after 4 weeks." "Another limitation is that we cannot distinguish between the effect of being called vs the empathetic nature of the engagement." "We also observed higher dropouts in the intervention arm (n = 13) relative to control (n = 1), 7 occurring after only 2 connections, citing time and interest." "Additionally, a strength and potential limitation of this study is that it was implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic."
safe_wording: The trial lasted 4 weeks, in the summer of 2020 during the pandemic. Nobody knows yet whether the benefit lasts once the calls stop. The comparison group got no calls, so the trial cannot say whether the listening style mattered or simply being called.
qualifications: More people dropped out of the call group (13) than the comparison group (1), several after only 2 calls.

claim: Across trials, the evidence for telephone-delivered loneliness interventions in older adults is still insufficient for a firm conclusion.
supporting_passage: "Evidence was insufficient to reach conclusions about group-based activities, individual in-person interactions, internet-delivered interventions, and telephone-delivered interventions."
safe_wording: Reviews of many loneliness programmes have not yet found enough evidence to judge telephone programmes as a group. This trial is one promising result, not a settled answer.
qualifications: The review's search ended in June 2021 and may not include this trial.

claim: In a US prospective study of 1,222 carer and patient pairs, carers' depression and anxiety did not fall after their relative with dementia moved into long-term care; effects were most pronounced in spouses; nearly half of spouses visited daily and still helped with physical care.
supporting_passage: "Prospective study from 1996 to 2000 of the placement transition in a sample of 1222 caregiver-patient dyads recruited from 6 US sites. A total of 180 patients were placed in a long-term care facility during the 18-month follow-up period." "Caregivers who institutionalized their relative reported depressive symptoms and anxiety to be as high as they were while in-home caregivers. Overall CES-D scores for depression did not change from before to after placement (median [IQR], 15.0 [8-24.5] and 15.0 [7.7-28]; P =.64). Overall anxiety scores on the State Trait Inventory also did not change significantly (median [IQR], 22.0 [19-27] before vs 21.1 [18-27] after; P =.21). These effects were most pronounced among caregivers who were married to the patient (P =.02 for depression), visited more frequently (P =.01 for depression and P<.001 for anxiety), and were less satisfied with the help they received from others (P =.003 for depression and P<.001 for anxiety)." "The use of anxiolytics before to after placement increased from 14.6% to 19% (P =.02), and nearly half of caregivers (48.3%) were at risk for clinical depression following placement of their relative." "The transition to institutional care is particularly difficult for spouses, almost half of whom visit the patient daily and continue to provide help with physical care during their visits."
safe_wording: In a US study of family carers of people with dementia, carers were just as depressed and anxious after their relative moved into a care home as before. Nearly half were at risk of clinical depression afterwards. Husbands and wives were hit hardest: almost half of spouses visited every day and still helped with their partner's physical care.
qualifications: US study from 1996 to 2000; dementia carers only; 180 placements. 'Did not fall' means no clear change in median scores, not a rise. 'Physical care' in the paper is general; do not add examples such as washing or dressing, which the opened abstract does not give.

claim: Carers commonly experience stress, guilt, grief and depression after placement, but trial evidence that specific interventions after placement reduce carer depression or burden is sparse and very low grade.
supporting_passage: "Many carers experience stress, guilt, grief and depression following placement of a relative with dementia into residential care." "Four studies were eligible for inclusion." "Meta-analyses indicated there was no overall effect at three to four months post-intervention on carer burden (weighted mean difference 2.38; 95% CI -7.72 to 12.48), and depression (weighted mean difference 2.17; 95% CI -5.07 to 9.40)." "There is insufficient evidence that individualized or group interventions improve carer depression, burden or satisfaction. However, due to substantial heterogeneity between studies and methodological flaws, the grade of this evidence is very low."
safe_wording: Offering the partner who stays at home their own conversation about how they are managing is a reasonable judgement. It has not been tested as a specific treatment: only a few small trials have looked at support for carers after a care home move, and they did not show clear effects on depression or burden.
qualifications: The first sentence of the passage is background in the review, not its finding. The recommendation to offer the spouse their own conversation must be written as a judgement ('should'), not as a proven intervention.

claim: In England, the value of the home is disregarded in the care home means test while a spouse or partner still lives there.
location: Care and Support Statutory Guidance (Annex B) could not be opened (gov.uk blocked; not found in Drive)
safe_wording: Do not state the rule. If money is mentioned, phrase it only as a question to ask before the move, for example: 'Ask how the fees assessment treats your home and your income if you are staying in the house.'
qualifications: Official guidance not opened.

claim: In Scotland, the home is similarly disregarded while occupied by a spouse or partner.
location: Charging for Residential Accommodation Guidance (CRAG) could not be opened
safe_wording: Omit, per editor's guidance.
qualifications: Official guidance not opened.

claim: In England, if a resident passes half of an occupational or personal pension to a spouse at home, that half is disregarded.
safe_wording: Omit. At most, ask: 'Ask whether any of the pension can stay with the partner at home.' Do not imply the answer.
qualifications: Official guidance not opened.

claim: In a US national probability sample of 3,005 adults aged 57 to 85, 26% of those aged 75 to 85 reported sexual activity in the previous year; about half of sexually active people reported at least one bothersome sexual problem.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "We report the prevalence of sexual activity, behaviors, and problems in a national probability sample of 3005 U.S. adults (1550 women and 1455 men) 57 to 85 years of age". "The prevalence of sexual activity declined with age (73% among respondents who were 57 to 64 years of age, 53% among respondents who were 65 to 74 years of age, and 26% among respondents who were 75 to 85 years of age); women were significantly less likely than men at all ages to report sexual activity. Among respondents who were sexually active, about half of both men and women reported at least one bothersome sexual problem." Methods: "In-home interviews were conducted in English and Spanish by professional interviewers between July 2005 and March 2006." Table 2, sexual activity with a partner in previous 12 months, aged 75 to 85: men 38.5% (95% CI 33.6 to 43.5), women 16.7% (12.5 to 21.0).
location: Abstract; Methods (Study Population); Table 2 (read via Undermind)
safe_wording: In a US national survey of people aged 57 to 85 (interviewed in 2005 to 2006), about 1 in 4 people aged 75 to 85 had been sexually active with a partner in the past year: about 4 in 10 men and 1 in 6 women. About half of those who were sexually active had at least one sexual problem that bothered them.
qualifications: US data about 20 years old; self-report; 'sexual activity' means with a partner. Women were less likely to have a partner. Use natural frequencies ('about 1 in 4'), not 'many'.

claim: In the same sample, 38% of men and 22% of women had discussed sex with a physician since age 50.
supporting_passage: Abstract: "A total of 38% of men and 22% of women reported having discussed sex with a physician since the age of 50 years." "Sexual problems are frequent among older adults, but these problems are infrequently discussed with physicians." Methods: "Communication with a physician about sex was ascertained in the leave-behind questionnaire with the following question: 'Since you turned 50, have you ever discussed sex with a doctor?'" Discussion: "Reasons for poor communication include the unwillingness of patients and physicians to initiate such discussions and sex and age differences between patients and their physicians."
safe_wording: In the same survey, only about 4 in 10 men and about 1 in 5 women said they had talked about sex with a doctor since turning 50. The authors noted that both patients and doctors were reluctant to raise it.
qualifications: Self-report over many years; the question asked whether sex had ever been discussed, not who raised it. US data, 2005 to 2006.

claim: In ELSA wave 6 (6,201 people aged 50 to over 90), a sizeable minority remained sexually active into their 70s and 80s; erectile difficulty was reported by 39% of sexually active men and arousal difficulty by 32% of sexually active women.
supporting_passage: "a total of 6,201 core ELSA participants (56 % women) aged 50 to >90 completed a comprehensive Sexual Relationships and Activities questionnaire (SRA-Q) included in ELSA Wave 6 (2012/13)." "Difficulties most frequently reported by sexually active women related to becoming sexually aroused (32 %) and achieving orgasm (27 %), while for men it was erectile function (39 %)." "Levels of sexual activity decline with increasing age, although a sizable minority of men and women remain sexually active until the eighth and ninth decades of life. Problems with sexual functioning were relatively common, but overall levels of sexual health concerns were much lower."
safe_wording: In England, a large survey of people aged 50 and over (2012 to 2013) found that a sizeable minority of men and women were still sexually active in their 70s and 80s. Among those who were sexually active, about 4 in 10 men reported erection problems and about 1 in 3 women reported difficulty with arousal.
qualifications: Exact percentages for people in their 80s were not available from the opened abstract; do not give a number for them. 'Eighth and ninth decades' means ages 70 to 89. Problems were common but fewer people were worried by them.

claim: Commonly prescribed antidepressants (SSRIs and SNRIs) often cause sexual side effects, which patients rarely report unless asked directly.
supporting_passage: "Sexual dysfunction (SD) is an important underestimated adverse effect of antidepressant drugs. Patients, in fact, if not directly questioned, tend to scarcely report them." "Our analyses indicated a significantly higher rate of total and specific treatment-emergent SD and specific phases of dysfunction compared with placebo for the following drugs in decreasing order of impact: sertraline, venlafaxine, citalopram, paroxetine, fluoxetine, imipramine, phenelzine, duloxetine, escitalopram, and fluvoxamine, with SD ranging from 25.8% to 80.3% of patients. No significant difference with placebo was found for the following antidepressants: agomelatine, amineptine, bupropion, moclobemide, mirtazapine, and nefazodone."
safe_wording: Sexual side effects are common with many widely used antidepressants, such as sertraline, citalopram and venlafaxine, and people tend not to mention them unless they are asked directly. Some antidepressants, such as mirtazapine, did not show a clear difference from placebo.
qualifications: Not specific to older adults; includes open-label studies and varied scales (authors' caveat); rates vary widely between drugs, so do not quote a single rate.

claim: Some blood pressure medicines are associated with sexual dysfunction.
supporting_passage: "Participants randomized to chlorthalidone reported a significantly higher incidence of erection problems through 24 months than participants randomized to placebo (17.1% versus 8.1%, P = .025). Incidence rates through 48 months were more similar among treatment groups than at 24 months, with nonsignificant differences between the chlorthalidone and placebo groups. Incidence was lowest in the doxazosin group but was not significantly different from the placebo group. Incidence for acebutolol, amlodipine, and enalapril groups was similar to that in the placebo group." "Similar incidence rates of erection dysfunction in placebo and most active drug groups caution against routine attribution of erection problems to antihypertensive medication."
safe_wording: In a blinded trial of blood pressure tablets, men on chlorthalidone (a water tablet) had more new erection problems over 2 years than men on placebo: about 17 in 100 compared with 8 in 100. The other four medicines did not differ clearly from placebo. So it is worth asking, but a new problem should not automatically be blamed on the blood pressure tablet.
qualifications: The candidate's wording 'some antihypertensives and antiandrogens' is only partly supported: this trial supports chlorthalidone (early effect), not beta-blockers in general (acebutolol was similar to placebo). No source was opened for antiandrogens; omit them. Trial participants were 45 to 69, younger than the post's audience.

claim: In a meta-analysis of 15 prospective cohort studies (about 2.26 million people), the relative risk of death after widowhood was 1.41 in the first six months and 1.14 after six months.
supporting_passage: "A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to calculate the overall relative risk (RR) for subsequent mortality among 2,263,888 subjects from 15 prospective cohort studies. We found a statistically significant positive association between widowhood and mortality, but the widowhood effect was stronger in the period earlier than six months since bereavement (overall RR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.26, 1.57) compared to the effect after six months (overall RR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.10, 1.18)."
safe_wording: When pooled across 15 studies of over 2 million people, the rise in the risk of death after a husband or wife died was largest in the first six months, and much smaller after that.
qualifications: Relative risks only; no absolute risks. Judge's advice: describe in words rather than as RR labels on the visual. If numbers are used, say 'about 4 in 10 higher, in relative terms, in the first six months' and make clear it is relative to people who stayed married.

claim: The widowhood effect was clear in men (RR 1.23) but small and not clearly different from no effect in women (RR 1.04, CI 1.00 to 1.08), and did not differ between people under and over 65.
supporting_passage: "Meta-regression showed that the widowhood effect was not different for those aged younger than 65 years compared to those older than 65 (P = 0.25). There was, however, a difference in the magnitude of the widowhood effect by gender; for women the RR was not statistically significantly different from the null (overall RR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.08), while it was for men (overall RR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.18, 1.28)."
safe_wording: The link was clear in men. In women it was small and not clearly different from no link. It was similar in people under and over 65.
qualifications: Call the women's figure 'small' rather than 'absent' (judge's note): the interval runs from no difference to 8% higher in relative terms. Relative risks only.

claim: The association is observational; proposed explanations include grief-related stress, loss of support and of a partner who encouraged healthy behaviour and medicine-taking, material resources, and shared risks.
supporting_passage: Moon 2011, Discussion: "marriage could provide additional social and emotional support, which may act as a buffer against harmful effects of various psychosocial stress. The guardian role theory suggests that spouses monitor each other, encouraging healthy behaviors of the partner, such as compliance with medical regimens, as well as discouraging unhealthy and risky ones" and "A final hypothesis is that grief associated with the loss of a loved one increases mortality risk directly via psychoneuroimmune pathways. This is especially plausible given that widowhood effect is markedly stronger in the months immediately following the spouse's death than in the years following." Limitations: "Most prior studies have inadequately controlled for socioeconomic confounders ... thus leading to uncertainty about whether the widowhood effect is causal." Elwert 2008: "Increased mortality following the death of a spouse (the 'widowhood effect') may be due to (1) causation, (2) bias from spousal similarity (homogamy), or (3) bias from shared environmental exposures." "These results strengthen the causal interpretation of the widowhood effect by suggesting that the widowhood effect is not due to homogamy bias to any substantial degree." Stroebe 2007: "bereavement is associated with excess risk of mortality, particularly in the early weeks and months after loss." "Although grief is not a disease and most people adjust without professional psychological intervention"
location: Moon: Discussion (read via Undermind); Elwert: Abstract; Stroebe: Abstract
safe_wording: Nobody knows exactly why the risk rises. Suggested reasons include the stress of grief, losing emotional support, and losing the partner who encouraged healthy habits and taking medicines. One large study found the pattern was not explained by spouses simply sharing the same risks, which makes a real effect of the loss more likely, but it is still not proven. Most bereaved people adjust without professional help.
qualifications: Loss of practical care (cooking, medicines, money, driving) is a plausible hypothesis, closest to the 'guardian role' idea; it is not a measured finding. Label it as a hypothesis.

claim: Widowhood is linked with changes in diet, particularly in men.
supporting_passage: "In 3.6 years of follow-up and relative to men who stayed married, widowed men showed significant declines (mean difference, 95% CI) in all four indicators of healthy eating including fruit quantity (-47.7, -80.6 to -14.9 g/d), fruit variety (-0.6, -1.1 to -0.2 no/month), vegetable quantity (-27.7, -50.5 to -4.9 g/d), and vegetable variety (-1.6, -2.2 to -0.9 no/month)." "Among women, only those who became separated/divorced or stayed single showed declines in one indicator, vegetable variety."
safe_wording: In a UK study, men whose wives died ate less fruit and fewer vegetables, and less variety, over the next few years than men who stayed married. This was not seen in widowed women.
qualifications: Observational; fruit and vegetables only; not a whole-diet or nutrition outcome; cohort includes middle-aged people.

claim: No trial evidence exists for a structured check on the surviving partner.
location: Brief PubMed search (widowed/bereaved spouses, older, RCT, support) returned 26 trials of bereavement support, not screened; no systematic search done
safe_wording: Do not state an evidence gap as a finding. Present the checklist (who now does the cooking, medicines, money, driving and appointments) as a practical suggestion: 'This is a practical step, not one tested in a trial.'
qualifications: Absence of evidence was not established.

claim: People over 90 and people in the most deprived areas were more likely to miss multiple GP appointments, after allowing for appointments made; young adults also at higher risk; practice factors mattered.
supporting_passage: After controlling for the number of appointments made, patterns of non-attendance could be differentiated, with patients who were aged 16–30 years (relative risk ratio [RRR] 1·21, 95% CI 1·19–1·23) or older than 90 years (2·20, 2·09–2·29), and of low socioeconomic status (Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation decile 1: RRR 2·27, 2·22–2·31) significantly more likely to miss multiple appointments. [Results:] ...more likely to miss multiple appointments than the reference group (patients aged 0–15 years).
safe_wording: In Scottish GP records from 2013 to 2016 (550,083 patients), people over 90 and people in the most deprived areas were among the most likely to miss appointments repeatedly, even after allowing for how many appointments they made. Young adults aged 16 to 30 were also at higher risk, and how the practice ran its appointments mattered too.
qualifications: Say 'over 90', not 'older people' generally; mention young adults; do not present RRR 2.20 as 'twice as likely' in lay text (comparison group is children 0-15). Scotland data.

claim: More long-term conditions linked with more missed appointments; missing appointments linked with higher all-cause mortality, especially with mental health conditions; a risk marker, not a cause.
supporting_passage: Patients with a greater number of long-term conditions had an increased risk of missing general practice appointments despite controlling for number of appointments made, particularly among patients with mental health conditions. These patients were at significantly greater risk of all-cause mortality, and showed a dose-based response with increasing number of missed appointments. ... Missed appointments represent a significant risk marker for all-cause mortality, particularly in patients with mental health conditions.
safe_wording: In Scottish GP records, people with more long-term conditions missed more appointments, and people who missed appointments were more likely to die in the following months, especially those with long-term mental health conditions. Missed appointments are a warning sign; the study does not show that missing them causes death.
qualifications: All ages, not older people specifically; observational; do not quote the 8-fold figure for older people (it concerns mental health conditions).

claim: 'Was not brought' is used in safeguarding for dependent adults.
safe_wording: Omit.
qualifications: Not searched to preserve budget; no opened source.

claim: Chicago 1995: bed confinement, not leaving home daily, top floor, living alone raised risk; social contacts, air conditioning, transport protective.
supporting_passage: The risk of heat-related death was increased for people with known medical problems who were confined to bed (odds ratio as compared with those who were not confined to bed, 5.5) or who were unable to care for themselves (odds ratio, 4.1). Also at increased risk were those who did not leave home each day (odds ratio, 6.7), who lived alone (odds ratio, 2.3), or who lived on the top floor of a building (odds ratio, 4.7). Having social contacts such as group activities or friends in the area was protective. In a multivariate analysis, the strongest risk factors for heat-related death were being confined to bed (odds ratio, 8.2) and living alone (odds ratio, 2.3); the risk of death was reduced for people with working air conditioners (odds ratio, 0.3) and those with access to transportation (odds ratio, 0.3).
safe_wording: In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, the people most likely to die were those confined to bed or who did not leave home each day; living on a top floor and living alone also raised the risk. Having friends nearby or group activities, working air conditioning and access to transport were linked with lower risk.
qualifications: Order by odds ratios (not leaving home 6.7, bed 5.5, top floor 4.7, alone 2.3 unadjusted). Note: in the multivariate model the authors named living alone as one of the two strongest factors (OR 2.3). Do not convert ORs to 'times more likely'. US 1995.

claim: France 2003: lack of mobility, no insulation, sleeping on top floor under roof linked with death; dressing lightly and cooling protective.
supporting_passage: Lack of mobility was a major risk factor along with some pre-existing medical conditions. Housing characteristics associated with death were lack of thermal insulation and sleeping on the top floor, right under the roof. The temperature around the building was a major risk factor. Behaviour such as dressing lightly and use of cooling techniques and devices were protective factors.
safe_wording: In the 2003 French heatwave, among people aged 65 and over living at home, being unable to get about, living in a poorly insulated home and sleeping on the top floor right under the roof were linked with dying; dressing lightly and using ways to cool down were linked with surviving.
qualifications: Associations from a case-control study; no numbers from abstract.

claim: UK heat-health guidance advises checking on older people living alone.
safe_wording: Omit attribution to UK guidance; present daily checks as a judgement drawn from the risk-factor studies.
qualifications: gov.uk pages cannot be opened.

claim: No trial has tested daily checks.
safe_wording: Say 'this advice comes from studies of who died, not from trials of checking' rather than asserting no trial exists.
qualifications: No search done.

claim: 14 UK studies of welfare advice co-located in health settings; all showed improved financial security; quality poor.
supporting_passage: The review identified 14 studies employing a range of study designs, including: one non-randomised controlled trial; one pilot randomised controlled trial; one before-and-after-study; three qualitative studies; and eight case studies. ... All studies demonstrated improved financial security for participants, generating an average of £27 of social, economic and environmental return per £1 invested. Some studies reported improved mental health for individuals accessing services. Several studies attributed subjective improvements in physical health to the service addressing key social determinants of health. ... However, given the generally poor scientific quality of the studies, care must be taken in drawing firm conclusions.
safe_wording: A 2022 review found 14 UK studies of welfare rights advice offered in GP surgeries and other health settings. All reported that people ended up better off financially. Some reported better mental health, and some people said their physical health improved, but most studies were small case studies of poor quality, so the health effects are not yet measured well.
qualifications: Studies covered all ages, not older people specifically. Omit £27 per £1 or state it is a modelled estimate built on weak studies. Evidence gap, not evidence of no health benefit.

claim: Earlier reviews found weak evidence on health outcomes; later review finds mental health improvements commonly attributed.
supporting_passage: Previous systematic reviews investigating the link between advice services and health outcomes have found a weak evidence base and cover the period up until 2010. ... Our synthesis suggested that improvements in mental health and well-being measures are commonly attributed to advice service interventions. However, there is little insight to explain these impacts... Co-locating services in health settings appears promising
safe_wording: A second 2022 review agreed: advice services are often linked with better mental health and wellbeing, earlier reviews found the evidence on health weak, and placing advice in health settings looks promising.
qualifications: Background statement about previous reviews is this paper's introduction, not its finding; cite as 'reviews have described the evidence as weak'.

claim: Some Scottish deprived-area practices embed advice workers.
safe_wording: Omit or keep generic ('some practices have advice workers on site'); no opened source.

claim: Driving cessation associated with declines in health and function, long-term care admission and death; pooled OR 1.91 for depressive symptoms.
supporting_passage: Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Driving cessation was reported to be associated with declines in general health and physical, social, and cognitive function and with greater risks of admission to long-term care facilities and mortality. A meta-analysis based on pooled data from five studies examining the association between driving cessation and depression revealed that driving cessation almost doubled the risk of depressive symptoms in older adults (summary odds ratio = 1.91, 95% confidence interval = 1.61-2.27).
safe_wording: A review of 16 studies found that older people who had stopped driving had worse general health, physical, social and mental function, and were more likely to move into a care home or die, than those still driving. Five studies together linked stopping driving with more depressive symptoms.
qualifications: Observational: say 'linked with'. Do not say 'twice as likely' or 'doubled' despite the authors' wording (odds ratio). Drivers aged 55+.

claim: Evidence on transport support or driving-retirement planning is sparse; UK transport options.
safe_wording: Omit; the review's own conclusion ('Intervention programs ensuring mobility and social functions may be needed') may be quoted as authors' suggestion.

claim: Healy 2003: Portugal 28%, Spain and Ireland 21%; milder climate and poorer housing thermal standards linked with higher excess winter mortality.
supporting_passage: Portugal suffers from the highest rates of excess winter mortality (28%, CI=25% to 31%) followed jointly by Spain (21%, CI=19% to 23%), and Ireland (21%, CI=18% to 24%). ... The strong, positive relation with environmental temperature and strong negative relation with thermal efficiency indicate that housing standards in southern and western Europe play strong parts in such seasonality.
safe_wording: Comparing 14 European countries in 1988 to 1997, winter deaths rose most, relative to the rest of the year, in Portugal, Spain and Ireland, countries with milder winters; countries with warmer winters and less heat-efficient housing had bigger winter rises.
qualifications: Country-level comparison, not individual risk; Finland claim not verified (not in abstract): omit.

claim: Wilkinson 2004: in 75+, winter mortality 31% higher; little variation by deprivation or financial worries; women and respiratory illness higher.
supporting_passage: The overall winter:non-winter rate ratio was 1.31 (95% confidence interval 1.26 to 1.36). There was little evidence that this ratio varied by geographical region, age, or any of the personal, socioeconomic, or clinical factors examined, with two exceptions: ... women compared with men was 1.11 (1.00 to 1.23), and those with a self reported history of respiratory illness had a winter:non-winter ratio of 1.20 (1.08 to 1.34) ... There was no evidence that socioeconomic deprivation or self reported financial worries were predictive of winter death. ... The lack of socioeconomic gradient suggests that policies aimed at relief of fuel poverty may need to be supplemented by additional measures
safe_wording: Among people aged 75 and over in Britain, death rates were about 31% higher in winter than the rest of the year, and this winter rise was much the same in richer and poorer areas. The authors concluded that helping people in fuel poverty may not be enough on its own.
qualifications: Not evidence that fuel poverty has no effect; area-level deprivation measure; data 1990s.

claim: Among older spouse carers, only those reporting strain had higher adjusted 4-year mortality than non-carers.
supporting_passage: participants who were providing care and experiencing caregiver strain had mortality risks that were 63% higher than noncaregiving controls (relative risk [RR], 1.63; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.00-2.65). Participants who were providing care but not experiencing strain (RR, 1.08; 95 % CI, 0.61-1.90) and those with a disabled spouse who were not providing care (RR, 1.37; 95% CI, 0.73-2.58) did not have elevated adjusted mortality rates
safe_wording: In a 1999 US study of older people caring for a spouse, the higher death rate over 4 years was seen only in carers who said caring caused them mental or emotional strain. Carers without strain did not show a clear difference from non-carers.
qualifications: Observational; adjusted for sociodemographic factors, prevalent disease and subclinical cardiovascular disease. Lower CI limit is 1.00, so borderline. Do not say 'X times more likely' or '63% higher' without saying it is a relative risk in a borderline estimate; the abstract itself says 'more likely to die'. Absolute figure available: 103 of 819 (12.6%) died in 4 years across the whole cohort, not by group. Spouse not helping despite disabled spouse: RR 1.37 (0.73 to 2.58), also not clearly raised.

claim: The 1999 study is widely cited; five later population studies found lower mortality for carers as a whole; most carers report benefits.
supporting_passage: A landmark study by Schulz and Beach that reported higher mortality rates for strained spouse caregivers has been widely cited as evidence for the physical health risks of caregiving ... However, 5 subsequent population-based studies have found reduced mortality and extended longevity for caregivers as a whole compared with noncaregiving controls. Most caregivers also report benefits from caregiving, and many report little or no caregiving-related strain.
safe_wording: Later population studies found carers as a whole lived as long as or longer than non-carers. This does not show that caring protects health.
qualifications: Observational. The 2015 review abstract does not explain why carers do better; the healthy-carer explanation comes from Janson 2022 (claim C18-11-c) and is stated there only as 'may be due to'.

claim: Cochrane review: 4 trials, 753 participants, very low quality, no significant effect on carer outcomes; may reflect lack of research rather than lack of benefit.
supporting_passage: Four trials are now included in the review, with 753 participants... Overall, the quality of the evidence was rated as very low. Re-analysis ... found no significant effects of respite care compared to no respite care on any caregiver variable... These results should be treated with caution, however, as they may reflect the lack of high quality research in this area rather than an actual lack of benefit.
safe_wording: A Cochrane review found only four trials of respite for dementia carers, with very low quality evidence. Taken together they did not show a clear benefit or harm. The authors say this may reflect a lack of good research rather than a lack of benefit.
qualifications: 2014 review; no later Cochrane update found on PubMed search 2026-10-08. No evaluable outcomes for people with dementia. Do not say respite 'does not work'. One comparison (respite vs polarity therapy, n=38) favoured polarity therapy for perceived stress: not needed in post.

claim: Respite is both a service and a psychological outcome; a positive experience depends on the carer perceiving mutual benefit.
supporting_passage: Respite is understood both as a service that provides a physical break for the carer and as a psychological outcome, i.e. a mental break for the carer... The key antecedent for a positive respite experience is that the carer perceives that mutual benefit is garnered from service use.
safe_wording: Research on carers' experiences suggests a break feels like a real rest when the carer believes the person they care for is benefiting too.
qualifications: Concept analysis of qualitative studies, not a trial.

claim: Of 217 US dementia carers, 72% said the death was a relief to them (and more than 90% believed it was a relief to the patient).
supporting_passage: Seventy-two percent of caregivers reported that the death was a relief to them, and more than 90 percent reported belief that it was a relief to the patient.
safe_wording: In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them. This followed a long and demanding period of care: half had spent at least 46 hours a week on care in the year before the death.
qualifications: Single US sample from a trial; self-reported; the study's own conclusion ties relief to 'a protracted and stressful period of caregiving'. The 'more than 90 percent believed relief to the patient' figure may read as a judgement that life with dementia is not worth living: use only with care (judge's values concern) or leave out.

claim: Depressive symptoms fell within three months of death and were substantially lower within a year; support was needed most before death.
supporting_passage: Within three months of the death, caregivers had clinically significant declines in the level of depressive symptoms, and within one year the levels of symptoms were substantially lower than levels reported while they were acting as caregivers... Intervention and support services were needed most before the patient's death.
safe_wording: On average, carers' depressive symptoms fell within three months of the death. The researchers concluded that carers needed support most before the death.
qualifications: Group averages; some carers do not follow this pattern.

claim: In 53 studies, positive aspects of caregiving were associated with lower depression and burden and better mental health and quality of life; not with self-rated health or personal strain; mostly cross-sectional.
supporting_passage: Fifty-three studies were included in the narrative synthesis. Most studies utilized a cross-sectional design... PAC was associated with lower depressive symptoms and burden. Conversely, PAC was associated with better mental health, quality of life, satisfaction with life, and competence/self-efficacy. PAC was not associated with self-rated health or personal strain/stress.
safe_wording: In studies of dementia carers, finding something worthwhile in caring was linked with lower depression and burden. Most studies measured both at one time, so we do not know which comes first.
qualifications: Association only; narrative synthesis.

claim: Lower mortality in carers compared with non-carers in longitudinal observational studies may reflect healthy people taking on caring (healthy-carer bias), and carers still show more depression and anxiety in cross-sectional studies.
supporting_passage: The lower mortality rates compared to non-caregivers may be due to a healthy-carer bias in longitudinal observational studies; however, these and other potential benefits of informal caregiving deserve further attention by researchers. ... In cross-sectional evaluations, informal caregiving seemed to be associated with a higher occurrence of depression and of anxiety (ranging from 4 to 51% and 2 to 38%, respectively), pain, hypertension, diabetes and reduced quality of life.
safe_wording: Carers as a whole do not die sooner than non-carers in population studies. That may be because healthier people take on caring, so it does not show that caring protects health. Carers still report more depression and anxiety.
qualifications: Use 'may be due to', as the authors do. Do not say caring is good for you. Cross-sectional links cannot show cause.

claim: A 2026 systematic review of 8 studies of respite care models found possible improvements in carer outcomes, but all studies were at high risk of bias or had some concerns.
supporting_passage: Eight studies (three randomized controlled trials, five quasi-experimental), including 1,420 care recipients and 1,610 caregivers, were analyzed. Four studies were judged to be at high risk of bias and four had some concerns. ... Home-based and day-care programs may be associated with improvements in caregiver outcomes, although evidence regarding their cost-related outcomes remains limited. Overall, the findings should be interpreted cautiously given the generally high risk of bias among included studies.
safe_wording: A 2026 review of eight studies found that respite programmes may be linked with better outcomes for carers, but every included study had a risk of bias concern, so the findings are preliminary.
qualifications: Mixed population (disability and dementia); only 3 of 8 were randomised trials. Optional: may be left out so the post stays on the Cochrane gap. If used, it must not be presented as confirming benefit.

claim: Respite services are often under-used and acceptability can be low.
supporting_passage: Respite services provide a break in the caregiving relationship for people with dementia and their carers, however they are often under-used and service acceptability can be low.
safe_wording: Do not use as a finding. If the post needs a point about what services should offer, the review's conclusions support: respite services need flexible, person-centred care with meaningful activity for people with dementia.
qualifications: Background sentence only, no figure or citation opened for it.

claim: Care Act 2014 s10(5) requires a carer's assessment to consider whether the carer is able and willing to continue caring.
safe_wording: Omit; legislation not opened and no published paper quoting it found on PubMed (three searches) or in Drive. Replace with C18-22 per editor.
qualifications: Re-checked 2026-10-08: a web search returned legislation.gov.uk section 10 links and a search-engine summary of s10(5) (able / willing, and likely to continue), but the page could not be opened; this is search_extract only and not sufficient for an essential claim. Scottish clause not verified at all.

claim: An adult carer support plan in Scotland must include the extent to which the carer is able and willing to provide care (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016).
supporting_passage: The Carers (Scotland) Act 2016 places responsibility on local authorities to implement such a plan, which will be fast-tracked for carers supporting someone at the end of life.
safe_wording: Drop the Scottish clause. The only opened source says the Act requires adult carer support plans, not what they must contain.
qualifications: Section number and content of the plan not verified.

claim: Legal or guideline basis for carer emergency planning (Carers (Scotland) Act, NICE NG150) and a named emergency card scheme.
safe_wording: Omit all legal, NICE and scheme claims; write as practical advice only (a one-page plan written in advance and shared), and at most suggest carers can ask about emergency planning when they have a carer's assessment, without saying it is a legal duty.
qualifications: No source opened for Carers (Scotland) Act, NICE NG150 or any emergency card scheme; none verified.

claim: NICE NG150 recommends that practitioners help carers plan for emergencies.
supporting_passage: [No passage found. Search summary of NG150 overview did not list emergency or contingency planning.]
safe_wording: Drop the claim. Do not cite NG150 for emergency plans.
qualifications: Guideline page not opened.

claim: Some councils or carers' centres run carer emergency card or contact schemes.
supporting_passage: [No scheme verified.]
safe_wording: Name no scheme. If the post mentions help, say 'ask your council or local carers' centre whether they can help you write a plan', which makes no claim that a scheme exists.
qualifications: Not verified; do not imply that every area has a scheme.

claim: Practical advice: a carer can write a one-page plan covering the person's needs, medicines, who to call, keys and access, routine, GP and pharmacy, and give copies to the people named.
supporting_passage: [Advice, not a research finding. No source opened and none needed if framed as a suggestion.]
safe_wording: 'You can write a one-page plan in advance and give copies to the people named in it.' Frame as a suggestion. Do not claim that having a plan improves outcomes, reduces hospital admissions or is a legal entitlement: no evidence was found or opened for those.
qualifications: Marked as judgement or advice. The medicines list and contact fields are sensible and uncontroversial but are not drawn from an opened source.

claim: In a meta-analysis of randomised trials, discharge planning that integrated family carers was linked with fewer readmissions at 90 and 180 days.
supporting_passage: Discharge planning interventions with caregiver integration were associated with a 25% fewer readmissions at 90 days (relative risk (RR) = 0.75, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.62-0.91) and 24% fewer readmissions at 180 days (RR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.64-0.90).
safe_wording: A review of randomised trials found that discharge plans that brought family carers in were linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions over the next 3 to 6 months (a relative reduction).
qualifications: Relative, not absolute; interventions were multicomponent so the carer part cannot be isolated; pooled from 6 and 5 trials; trial quality often unclear. Full text re-read 2026-10-08: 11 of 15 studies gave enough detail to calculate readmission rates (6 at 90 days, 5 at 180 days); text gives no pooled arm-level rates. Authors' own 'reduces the risk' conclusion is stronger than the trial quality supports; use 'linked with'.

claim: Common components included written care plans, demonstration of care tasks and teach-back.
supporting_passage: Of the 15 studies, 13 had an intervention component that linked caregivers to external or community resources ... and nine included written care plans. Caregiver assessment was a component in eight studies ... Live or video demonstrations of care tasks was included in five studies, and seven included so-called "teach back" techniques
safe_wording: The programmes that were tested often included a written care plan, linking carers to community services, and showing the carer how to do care tasks and having them show it back.
qualifications: Which component matters is unknown.

claim: NICE NG150 and the Carers (Scotland) Act require or recommend carer involvement in discharge.
safe_wording: Omit.
qualifications: Neither document could be opened.

claim: START, an eight-session coping programme for family carers of people with dementia, improved carers' anxiety and depression over six years.
