supporting_passage: A total of 260 self-identified family carers of people with dementia were randomised 2:1 to START, an eight-session manual-based coping intervention delivered by supervised psychology graduates, or to treatment as usual (TAU). ... Over 72 months, compared with TAU, the intervention group had improved scores on HADS-T (adjusted mean difference -2.00 points, 95% CI -3.38 to -0.63).
safe_wording: In a UK trial of 260 family carers, an eight-session coping programme left carers with fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression than usual care, and the benefit lasted six years. The average difference was modest.
qualifications: Average difference of 2 points on a 42-point scale; no MCID source verified, so describe as modest, not as clinically large.

claim: START did not show a clear difference in time to care home admission.
supporting_passage: Patient-related costs ... and carer-related costs ... were not significantly different between groups nor were group differences in time until care home (intensity ratio START:TAU was 0.88, 95% CI 0.58-1.35).
safe_wording: It did not show a clear difference in how soon the person with dementia moved into a care home.
qualifications: Secondary outcome; wide interval, so not evidence of no effect.

claim: A US counselling and support programme for spouse carers was linked with later nursing home placement.
supporting_passage: Patients whose spouses received the intervention experienced a 28.3% reduction in the rate of nursing home placement compared with usual care controls (hazard ratio = 0.717 after covariate adjustment, p = 0.025). The difference in model-predicted median time to placement was 557 days.
safe_wording: In a US trial of 406 spouse carers, counselling and support was linked with a later move to a nursing home: a model estimated the typical delay at about 18 months (557 days).
qualifications: Randomised, but 557 days is model-predicted and adjusted; different population, era and programme from START, so do not compare the programmes head to head.

claim: GMC guidance says listening to relatives' or carers' concerns is not a breach of confidentiality.
safe_wording: Do not quote or attribute to GMC; guidance could not be opened (Drive and PubMed searched).
qualifications: Re-checked 2026-10-08: web search returned only secondary summaries (MPS, Pulse, MDU) and the NHS Digital confidentiality guide; GMC paragraph not opened. Search_extract only; do not quote or attribute to GMC.

claim: Carers report being refused information on confidentiality grounds.
supporting_passage: the majority (56.3%) of respondents stated that they have specifically encountered difficulties accessing information from the treating mental health team. The main reasons given to them by the mental health team for withholding information include: lack of patient consent (46.2%) and unavailability of a team member (46.2%).
safe_wording: In an Irish survey of 159 carers of people with mental illness, over half had struggled to get information from the care team, and the commonest reason they were given was lack of the patient's consent.
qualifications: Mental health, not older people's services; self-selected sample.

claim: In a New York qualitative study, home care workers often lost both a close relationship and a job when a client died, and their grief was disenfranchised by employer and societal underestimation of the relationship.
supporting_passage: When a client dies, home care workers often lose both a close relationship and a job. ... Our findings suggest that home care workers' grief is disenfranchised via employer and societal underestimations of their relationships with clients and their losses when clients die, particularly job loss.
safe_wording: In a study of home care workers in New York, workers described losing both a close relationship and paid work when a client died, and felt employers and society underestimated that loss.
qualifications: Qualitative, US only; do not extend the job-loss point to England without workforce data.

claim: In interviews with 29 home care workers and 13 managers in England, a client's death left workers emotionally drained and under-prepared; peer support, manager acknowledgement, time off and encouragement to attend the funeral were supportive.
supporting_passage: Qualitative semi-structured interviews were conducted with 29 homecare workers and 13 homecare managers in England. ... When their work entailed high levels of emotion, such as a client's death or getting embroiled in a client's family conflict, they felt emotionally drained, under-prepared, and overwhelmed. Supportive elements include receiving encouragement and learning from experienced peers and their feelings being acknowledged by managers at their employing homecare agency. Some workers were offered time off or encouraged to attend the client's funeral as a means of supporting the process of bereavement.
safe_wording: In interviews with 29 home care workers and 13 managers in England, workers said a client's death could leave them drained and under-prepared. What helped: support from experienced colleagues, managers acknowledging their feelings, and for some, time off or encouragement to attend the funeral.
qualifications: Qualitative; dementia end-of-life context; 'told personally by the agency' is NOT in the abstract, so do not list it as a finding (it may appear only as the post's judgement).

claim: A substantial share of home care workers in England are on zero-hours contracts.
safe_wording: Omit. Skills for Care workforce data could not be opened and two PubMed searches for zero-hours contracts in English home care returned no papers. Do not state or imply that English care workers lose income when a client dies.
qualifications: Job loss on a client's death is a New York finding only.

claim: A systematic review of 13 studies found most barriers minority ethnic carers described were potentially relevant to all carers: not wanting to involve outsiders, not seeing the need, low awareness of services, service availability; specific issues were language barriers and concerns about cultural appropriateness; few studies compared with majority groups.
supporting_passage: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ... Few studies compared minority ethnic carers' perceptions with majority ethnic groups, making it difficult to identify issues specific to minority groups. Most barriers described were potentially relevant to all carers, irrespective of ethnic group. They included attitudinal barriers such as not wanting to involve outsiders or not seeing the need for services and practical barriers such as low awareness of services and service availability. Issues specific to minority ethnic groups included language barriers and concerns about services' cultural or religious appropriateness.
safe_wording: A review of 13 studies found most barriers minority ethnic carers described could apply to any carer: not knowing services exist, services not being available, not wanting outsiders involved, not seeing the need. Added barriers were language and services that did not fit the family's culture. Few studies compared groups directly.
qualifications: Say 'potentially relevant to all carers'; mention few direct comparisons; evidence to 2013. Source says 'cultural or religious'; per values note, may say 'cultural fit' without misquoting (do not present as a quotation).

claim: The phrase 'they look after their own' is used by services to explain low take-up.
safe_wording: Present only as a commonly voiced belief framed as the author's observation ('You may hear...'), with no claim about frequency or that services use it.

claim: Doctors' survival estimates at hospice referral were accurate in 1 in 5 and mostly too optimistic.
supporting_passage: Median survival was 24 days. Only 20% (92/468) of predictions were accurate (within 33% of actual survival); 63% (295/468) were overoptimistic and 17% (81/468) were overpessimistic. Overall, doctors overestimated survival by a factor of 5.3.
safe_wording: In a US study of 468 people referred to hospice, doctors' estimates were within a third of actual survival about 20 in 100 times; 63 in 100 were too optimistic and 17 in 100 too pessimistic.
qualifications: Define 'accurate' as within 33% of actual survival; US, one city, around 2000, mostly outpatient hospice referrals.

claim: Longer doctor-patient relationship was linked with less accurate prediction.
supporting_passage: As duration of doctor-patient relationship increased and time since last contact decreased, prognostic accuracy decreased.
safe_wording: In this one study, the longer the doctor had known the patient, and the more recently they had seen them, the less accurate the estimate tended to be.
qualifications: Association in one study; does not prove that knowing the patient causes the error.

claim: A systematic review found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care are frequently inaccurate, with no expert group.
supporting_passage: Studies of prognostic accuracy in palliative care are heterogeneous, but the evidence suggests that clinicians' predictions are frequently inaccurate. No sub-group of clinicians was consistently shown to be more accurate than any other.
safe_wording: A review of 42 studies found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care were often inaccurate, and no professional group was consistently better.
qualifications: Heterogeneous; no pooled accuracy figure.

claim: Give a range, name what would shorten it, seek a colleague's view.
safe_wording: Mark as professional recommendation: 'Our suggestion:'.
qualifications: Judgement, not tested remedy.

claim: Surprise question pooled performance.
supporting_passage: For the outcome of death at 6 to 18 months, the pooled prognostic characteristics were sensitivity 67.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] 55.7%-76.7%), specificity 80.2% (73.3%-85.6%), ... positive predictive value 37.1% (95% CI 30.2%-44.6%) and negative predictive value 93.1% (95% CI 91.0%-94.8%).
safe_wording: Pooled across 16 studies, the question picked up about 67 in 100 people who died within 6 to 18 months; of those flagged, about 37 in 100 died in that window, so most flagged people were still alive.
qualifications: PPV depends on how many in the group die, so varies by setting; window 6-18 months, not strictly a year.

claim: Worse in non-cancer illness; most studies at moderate-high risk of bias.
supporting_passage: The surprise question had worse discrimination in patients with noncancer illness (area under sROC curve 0.77 [95% CI 0.73-0.81]) than in patients with cancer (area under sROC curve 0.83 ... ). Most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias
safe_wording: It worked less well in illnesses other than cancer, and most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias.

claim: Surprise question is in Gold Standards Framework Proactive Identification Guidance.
safe_wording: Omit, or say 'widely used in UK identification tools' only if another batch verifies it.
qualifications: Official GSF document not opened.

claim: Use it as a prompt for conversation rather than prediction.
supporting_passage: The surprise question performs poorly to modestly as a predictive tool for death
safe_wording: The authors judged it a poor to modest predictor; using it to open conversations is our judgement.
qualifications: Mark 'prompt not prediction' as judgement.

claim: Course of advanced dementia over 18 months.
supporting_passage: Over a period of 18 months, 54.8% of the residents died. The probability of pneumonia was 41.1%; a febrile episode, 52.6%; and an eating problem, 85.8%.
safe_wording: In a US study of 323 care-home residents with advanced dementia, over 18 months about 86 in 100 developed eating problems, about 53 in 100 a fever, about 41 in 100 pneumonia, and about 55 in 100 died.
qualifications: US nursing homes, advanced (late-stage) dementia; probabilities over 18 months.

claim: Burdensome interventions in last 3 months and link with proxy understanding.
supporting_passage: In the last 3 months of life, 40.7% of residents underwent at least one burdensome intervention (hospitalization, emergency room visit, parenteral therapy, or tube feeding). Residents whose proxies had an understanding of the poor prognosis and clinical complications expected in advanced dementia were much less likely to have burdensome interventions in the last 3 months of life than were residents whose proxies did not have this understanding (adjusted odds ratio, 0.12; 95% confidence interval, 0.04 to 0.37).
safe_wording: About 41 in 100 who died had a hospital transfer, emergency visit, drip or tube feeding in their last 3 months. Those whose families understood the likely course were much less likely to have these.
qualifications: Observational; do not convert OR 0.12; does not prove that informing families causes the difference.

claim: Functional decline patterns differ by trajectory; frail decedents low function throughout last year and more dependent near death.
supporting_passage: cancer decedents were highly functional early in their final year but markedly more disabled 3 months prior to death ...; organ failure decedents experienced a fluctuating pattern of decline ...; and frail decedents were relatively more disabled in the final year and especially dependent during the last month (2.92 [2.24-3.60] vs 5.84 [5.33-6.35], P<.001). ... Trajectories of functional decline at the end of life are quite variable.
safe_wording: A large US study of older people found that those who died with frailty already needed help with daily activities a year before death and needed more near the end, while people dying of cancer often stayed independent until the last few months.
qualifications: Group averages from 1980s-90s US data; individuals vary widely; dementia grouped under frailty in this study only by inference - do not claim dementia specifically from Lunney.

claim: No clear moment; start conversations early.
safe_wording: Present as judgement drawn from the slow-decline pattern.
qualifications: Judgement.

claim: Early palliative care alongside cancer treatment improved quality of life and mood.
supporting_passage: We randomly assigned patients with newly diagnosed metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer to receive either early palliative care integrated with standard oncologic care or standard oncologic care alone. ... Patients assigned to early palliative care had a better quality of life ... (98.0 vs. 91.5; P=0.03). In addition, fewer patients in the palliative care group than in the standard care group had depressive symptoms (16% vs. 38%, P=0.01).
safe_wording: In a trial of 151 people with advanced lung cancer, palliative care given alongside cancer treatment from diagnosis improved quality of life, and fewer had depressive symptoms at 12 weeks (16 in 100 vs 38 in 100).
qualifications: One small US trial in lung cancer; do not generalise benefit to non-cancer illness; survival was secondary and should not lead; do not describe age as 'younger'.

claim: WHO definition: palliative care applicable early alongside life-prolonging therapy.
safe_wording: Omit the WHO attribution; the Temel trial itself shows palliative care given alongside treatment.
qualifications: WHO page not openable here; PubMed record of Sepulveda 2002 (PMID 12231124, WHO global perspective) has no abstract, so the definition wording could not be checked. Official WHO web pages cannot be opened from this environment.

claim: In interviews, people with advanced cancer and their caregivers initially associated palliative care with death and hopelessness.
supporting_passage: Participants' initial perceptions of palliative care in both trial arms were of death, hopelessness, dependency and end-of-life comfort care for inpatients. These perceptions provoked fear and avoidance, and often originated from interactions with health care professionals. During the trial, those in the intervention arm developed a broader concept of palliative care as "ongoing care" that improved their "quality of living" but still felt that the term itself carried a stigma.
safe_wording: In a Canadian interview study of 48 people with advanced cancer and 23 carers, many first thought of palliative care as meaning death and hopelessness, which led to fear and avoidance. After receiving early palliative care, participants described it as 'ongoing care' that improved their 'quality of living'.
qualifications: Small qualitative study in cancer; shows what these participants said, not how common the view is. Do not say 'most people' or give a percentage.

claim: In UK studies, missing preferences were common; once included, the proportion preferring home was unknown.
supporting_passage: Missing data were common. Across all health conditions when missing data were excluded the majority preference was for home: when missing data were included, it was not known what proportion of patients with cancer, non-cancer or multiple conditions preferred home. Caution should be exercised if asserting that most patients prefer to die at home.
safe_wording: A review of 61 UK studies found many people's preferences were never asked or recorded. Among those recorded, most chose home, but counting the missing views, we do not know what share of people prefer home.
qualifications: Must say that recorded preferences favoured home.

claim: Where people were asked was related to where they said they wished to die.
supporting_passage: Where patients wished to die was related to where they were asked their preference.
safe_wording: Where people were asked (for example in a hospice or at home) was linked with the place they said they preferred.
qualifications: Association.

claim: Most people who state a preference choose home, but estimates vary widely and about 1 in 5 changed preference.
supporting_passage: There was moderate evidence that most people prefer a home death-this was found in 75% of studies, 9/14 of those of high quality. Amongst the latter and excluding outliers, home preference estimates ranged 31% to 87% for patients (9 studies)... 20% of 1395 patients in 10 studies (2 of high quality) changed their preference, but statistical significance was untested.
safe_wording: A large international review found most people who state a preference choose home, but estimates in patients ranged from about 3 in 10 to nearly 9 in 10. In 10 studies, about 1 in 5 patients changed their preference as illness progressed.
qualifications: Change data from few studies, mostly low quality.

claim: US survey ranked dying at home lowest of 9 attributes (Steinhauser 2000).
safe_wording: Do not use.
qualifications: Not verified in this batch; old US ranking exercise.

claim: Home death / preferred place achieved is a UK quality indicator.
safe_wording: Do not state as fact; say 'home death is often treated as a mark of good care' as opinion only, or omit.
qualifications: OHID/PHS pages not openable.

claim: England census survey of cancer carers: over 90% gave care in last 3 months, median 69 h 30 min per week; median GBP 370 spent.
supporting_passage: In all, 1504 completed surveys were returned (28.5%). Over 90% of respondents reported spending time on care-giving in the last 3 months of the decedent's life, contributing a median 69 h 30 min of care-giving each week. Those who reported details of expenditure (72.5%) spent a median £370 in the last 3 months of the decedent's life.
safe_wording: In a survey of 1504 family carers of people who died of cancer in England in 2015, over 9 in 10 said they gave care in the last 3 months, a median of about 69 and a half hours a week. Those who gave spending details spent a median of £370.
qualifications: Say 'reported caregiving'; do not say whether hours are active care or on call (not in abstract); cancer only; 28.5% response; self-report.

claim: Carers' contributions are often underestimated or overlooked in evaluations.
supporting_passage: However, the value of care-givers' contributions is often underestimated or overlooked in evaluations.
safe_wording: The authors note that carers' contributions are often overlooked in evaluations.
qualifications: Authors' background statement, not a finding.

claim: Most vs least deprived neighbourhoods: more likely hospital death vs home, acute hospital care in last 3 months, and not receiving specialist palliative care; gradient across quintiles.
supporting_passage: Compared to people living in the least deprived neighbourhoods, people living in the most deprived neighbourhoods were more likely to die in hospital versus home (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23-1.38, p < 0.001), to receive acute hospital-based care in the last 3 months of life (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25, p < 0.001), and to not receive specialist palliative care (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.07-1.19, p < 0.001). For every quintile increase in area deprivation, hospital versus home death was more likely (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05-1.08, p < 0.001)
safe_wording: A review of studies from high-income countries found people in the poorest neighbourhoods were more likely than those in the richest to die in hospital rather than at home, to have hospital care in their last 3 months, and less likely to get specialist palliative care. The gap grew step by step with deprivation.
qualifications: Describe in words only; observational; modest effects; causes not established; mostly North American studies (53.5%).

claim: Evidence that anticipatory medicines improve symptom control or prevent admissions is inadequate; professionals believe they help.
supporting_passage: Healthcare professionals believe anticipatory prescribing provides reassurance, effective symptom control, and helps to prevent crisis hospital admissions. The attitudes of patients towards anticipatory prescribing remain unknown. It is a low-cost intervention, but there is inadequate evidence to draw conclusions about its impact on symptom control and comfort or crisis hospital admissions.
safe_wording: Professionals believe 'just in case' medicines help, but research has not yet shown whether they improve comfort or prevent hospital admissions.
qualifications: Say "professionals believe"; the review found the evidence inadequate, not evidence of no benefit. Review concerns injectable medicines in the community, searches to May 2017.

claim: NICE NG31/QS144 recommend anticipatory prescribing; usual symptom classes covered.
safe_wording: Not verified; NICE pages could not be opened.

claim: On TV dramas most people given CPR survive.
supporting_passage: Diem: There were 60 occurrences of CPR in the 97 television episodes... Seventy-five percent of the patients survived the immediate arrest, and 67 percent appeared to have survived to hospital discharge. Portanova: CPR was depicted 46 times in the 91 episodes, with a survival rate of 69.6%. Among those immediately surviving following CPR, the majority (71.9%) survived to hospital discharge
safe_wording: In 1990s US TV dramas, about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital. In Grey's Anatomy and House (2010-11), about 7 in 10 survived the CPR itself.
qualifications: Compare Diem's 67% (discharge) with the audit; Portanova's 69.6% is immediate survival, not discharge. Diem TV patients were mostly young with trauma.

claim: UK in-hospital arrest survival to discharge 18.4%; 10.5% for non-shockable rhythms (72.3% of arrests).
supporting_passage: Overall unadjusted survival to hospital discharge was 18.4%. The presenting rhythm was shockable (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) in 16.9% and non-shockable (asystole or pulseless electrical activity) in 72.3%; rates of survival to hospital discharge associated with these rhythms were 49.0% and 10.5%, respectively, but varied substantially across hospitals.
safe_wording: In UK hospitals, fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR by the hospital team survived to leave hospital. For the most common kind of arrest, about 1 in 10 did.
qualifications: Unadjusted; audit data about a decade old; all ages 16+, so older frailer people likely lower (not shown here).

claim: Anticipatory medicines are often not all used: use after prescription varies by setting.
supporting_passage: Use in nursing homes appears to be less common: one retrospective study reported that 'less than a third' of patients required the administration of prescribed medications, and a qualitative study of nursing home nurses reported that very few dying patients required the administration of prescribed drugs. Much higher proportions of use have been reported at home, ranging from 70%-77%. [Table, home study:] A significant amount of medicines went unused, but 77% of boxes issued had at least one drug used.
safe_wording: In studies reviewed, the box was used in most home deaths (about 7 in 10 to 3 in 4 of those studied) but less often in nursing homes (fewer than 1 in 3 patients), and many individual medicines in the box go unused. Having a box does not mean death is close or that every medicine will be given.
qualifications: Few, low-to-medium quality studies; use data are limited (review says literature on use after prescription is limited); the 70%-77% for home is the range reported by the review, not a national figure. 'Boxes' study is a single service evaluation.

claim: What families should do with unused anticipatory medicines after the death.
safe_wording: Do not state. Official guidance (NICE, local policy) could not be opened; the Bowers review gives costs of unused medicines, not disposal advice.

claim: A hand-held fan blown at the face reduced breathlessness compared with the fan on the legs.
supporting_passage: Fifty participants were randomized to use a handheld fan for five minutes directed to their face or leg first and then crossed over to the other treatment. ... There was a significant difference in the VAS scores between the two treatments, with a reduction in breathlessness when the fan was directed to the face (P=0.003).
safe_wording: In a small trial of 50 people with advanced illness, five minutes of a hand-held fan blowing on the face eased breathlessness more than the same fan blowing on the legs.
qualifications: Small, short-term (5 minutes) study.

claim: In people without low oxygen levels, oxygen through nasal tubes gave no more relief than room air; both groups improved.
supporting_passage: From baseline to day 6, mean morning breathlessness changed by -0.9 points (95% CI -1.3 to -0.5) in patients assigned to receive oxygen and by -0.7 points (-1.2 to -0.2) in patients assigned to receive room air (p=0.504). ... Since oxygen delivered by a nasal cannula provides no additional symptomatic benefit for relief of refractory dyspnoea in patients with life-limiting illness compared with room air, less burdensome strategies should be considered after brief assessment of the effect of oxygen therapy on the individual patient.
safe_wording: In a trial of 239 people with serious illness whose blood oxygen was not low, oxygen through nasal tubes eased breathlessness no more than room air given through the same tubes; both groups felt a little better.
qualifications: Excluded people with low blood oxygen; outpatients, not dying people; 7 days.

claim: In 32 people near death, oxygen, medical air and no flow made no difference to observed respiratory distress; 91% tolerated the protocol.
supporting_passage: Most (91%) patients tolerated the protocol with no change in respiratory comfort. Three patients (9%) displayed distress and were restored to baseline oxygen ... Repeated-measure analysis of variance revealed no differences in the Respiratory Distress Observation Scale under changing gas and flow conditions. ... The n-of-1 trial of oxygen in clinical practice is appropriate in the face of hypoxemic respiratory distress.
safe_wording: In a small study of people close to death who were not in distress, switching between oxygen, air and no flow made no difference to breathing distress for most; 3 of 32 became distressed and went back on oxygen.
qualifications: Small; people not distressed at start; distress rated by observers.

claim: Oxygen can cause nasal irritation and add cost.
supporting_passage: Campbell (background): "Oxygen may produce nasal irritation and increase the cost of care." Abernethy: "The frequency of side-effects did not differ between groups."
safe_wording: Oxygen tubing and equipment are a burden for some people; the post should not claim trial-proven extra side-effects.
qualifications: Campbell's statement is background, not a finding. In Abernethy nasal irritation was not more common with oxygen than air through the same tubes.

claim: The noise is presumed to come from secretions gathering in the airways that the dying person cannot clear.
supporting_passage: Cochrane: "The cause of death rattle remains unproven but is presumed to be due to an accumulation of secretions in the airways. It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs)." SILENCE: "Death rattle, defined as noisy breathing caused by the presence of mucus in the respiratory tract, is relatively common among dying patients."
safe_wording: The rattling sound is thought to come from saliva and mucus collecting in the throat and airways when a dying person can no longer cough or swallow it away.
qualifications: Mechanism presumed, not proven.

claim: The person is thought not to be distressed by the sound.
supporting_passage: The impact of death rattle on patients was less well described, although there was a consensus that death rattle is not distressing to affected patients (but may be distressing to other patients).
safe_wording: Experts generally agree the sound is unlikely to distress the dying person, but this has not been measured well.
qualifications: Consensus/inference, not measured.

claim: Some relatives are distressed by the sound, especially if they think the person is choking or drowning; others are not.
supporting_passage: Wee II: "Seventeen of the 25 bereaved relatives interviewed had heard the sound of death rattle. Ten relatives were distressed by the sound, but seven were not. Some relatives regarded the sound of death rattle as a useful warning sign that death was imminent. ... Relatives were distressed when they thought that the sound of death rattle indicated that the patient might be drowning or choking." Wee I: "almost half of the 12 relatives who had heard the sound of death rattle had been distressed by it. The others were either neutral about the sound or found it a helpful signal of impending death." Fagan 2025: "related distress was common amongst informal carers".
safe_wording: In interview studies, some relatives were upset by the sound, especially when they thought the person was choking or drowning; others were not, and some took it as a sign that death was close.
qualifications: Small qualitative studies; Wee I abstract says 'almost half of the 12' (the 5 of 12 figure is from Wee II's summary of study I).

claim: Repositioning is a recognised way to manage the sound; evidence that any treatment helps an established rattle is lacking.
supporting_passage: It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs). ... There is currently no evidence to show that any intervention, be it pharmacological or non-pharmacological, is superior to placebo in the treatment of death rattle. ... relatives need time, explanation and reassurance to relieve their fears and concerns.
safe_wording: Changing the person's position is a common first step; there is little trial evidence that medicines or other measures quiet the sound once it has started. Relatives need time and explanation.
qualifications: Do not claim repositioning is proven to reduce the sound. Review is from 2008.

claim: A preventive injection of hyoscine butylbromide reduced death rattle from 27% to 13% in Dutch hospices.
supporting_passage: A death rattle occurred in 10 patients (13%) in the scopolamine group compared with 21 patients (27%) in the placebo group (difference, 14%; 95% CI, 2%-27%, P = .02).
safe_wording: In a Dutch hospice trial, giving hyoscine butylbromide as soon as dying was recognised, before any rattle, meant about 13 in 100 developed the rattle compared with 27 in 100 on placebo.
qualifications: Prevention, not treatment of an established rattle; hospice setting; restlessness 28% vs 23%.

claim: Abrupt stopping of Parkinson's medicines can rarely cause parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a dangerous condition resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
supporting_passage: Beckers 2025 (full text, Introduction): "In rare cases, acute cessation causes parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. This potentially life-limiting syndrome is a specific form of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and consists of severe rigidity, autonomic dysfunction (e.g., hyperthermia, tachycardia), rhabdomyolysis and disturbances of consciousness." And: "Acute cessation of levodopa might result in a severe relapse of PD symptoms ... This includes a worsening of motor symptoms, such as akinesia, rigidity or tremor, and also of non-motor symptoms, such as anxiety and pain." End-of-life section: "If a person has sufficient symptom control with palliative treatments, including palliative sedation, one can opt to omit dopaminergic treatment altogether – although sudden cessation carries a risk of parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome." Also: "In the 72 h before death, severe motor symptoms were present in only 6% of persons in one study." Wang 2022 abstract (retained): "...caused by abrupt withdrawal of antiparkinsonian medication."
location: Beckers: Introduction; 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life'. Wang: Abstract
safe_wording: Stopping Parkinson's medicines suddenly can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety, and in rare cases a dangerous reaction with high fever. At the end of life, some people have good symptom control without them, so the decision is individual: ask what is making the person uncomfortable, and decide on purpose rather than by default.
qualifications: Withdrawal syndrome is rare. Expert review, not trial evidence. Reviewers note that tapering off dopaminergic medicine may be possible with limited harm in some people; terminal stiffness was documented in only 3 of 51 people in the 72 hours before death (Wilson 2024) and 6% in one study cited by Beckers. The post must not say that stopping is always harmful.

claim: A rotigotine skin patch is commonly used when oral Parkinson's medicines can no longer be swallowed at the end of life; conversion is approximate.
supporting_passage: Hindmarsh: "when oral administration of antiparkinsonian medications is no longer possible in dying patients, it is becoming common place to initiate transdermal rotigotine, despite a paucity of evidence to guide dosing. ... The majority of patients were converted to transdermal rotigotine (90%). Patients converted to a higher than equivalent dose of rotigotine were more likely to be agitated (p < 0.05)" Ibrahim: "25 (30%) patients were prescribed the recommended dose of Rotigotine; 31 (37%) higher and 28 (33%) lower than recommended. ... Inappropriate dosing may precipitate or worsen delirium/hallucinations. Use at end-of-life requires further evaluation." || Beckers 2025: "Based on these studies, transdermal rotigotine is the most widely used non-oral strategy at the end of life. In a UK-based cohort of 51 PwP at the end-of-life, 55% had dopaminergic medication substituted with transdermal rotigotine at death. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness is scarce" and "The equivalency factor from levodopa to transdermal rotigotine is 30:1 and the maximum dose of rotigotine is 16 mg/24 h, corresponding to 480 mg levodopa." and "it can sometimes induce psychotic symptoms or worsen autonomic symptoms" and "as many as 24% of subjects developed a delirium" (in a study of people with advanced PD started on a rotigotine patch). || Hewer 2024 abstract: "83% (n = 52) of PWP were eligible for rotigotine and, of those, 13% (n = 7) received the correct dose, 38% (n = 20) a lower dose, 12% (n = 6) a higher dose and 37% (n = 19) did not receive any. ... Rotigotine dose and admission LEDD were both associated with proxy measures of distress in the last 72 hours of life. This suggests cautious use of rotigotine at EOL." || Kim 2023 abstract: "Although rotigotine patch and apormorphine injections are most frequently recommended, there are no clinical trials in this patient population to support those recommendations."
location: Beckers: 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life' and Table 1; Hewer, Kim: Abstracts
safe_wording: When a person with Parkinson's can no longer swallow, a rotigotine skin patch is the most widely used non-oral option near the end of life, but no trials show it works there. Doses are approximate (about 30 mg of levodopa to 1 mg of rotigotine), the patch cannot replace high levodopa doses, and too high a dose is linked with confusion, hallucinations and agitation. In one Australian hospital, only 7 of 52 eligible people got the recommended dose. Agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team.
qualifications: Observational and expert-opinion evidence only. Absorption through skin can be reduced by sweating, weight loss and poor circulation. Apomorphine and subcutaneous levodopa are other non-oral routes but need specialist set-up and may be unavailable. Use the conversion ratio only if the practitioner audience is the target and label it approximate.

claim: Dopamine-blocking medicines (for example metoclopramide and haloperidol) are contraindicated in Parkinson's disease, including near the end of life, and are still prescribed.
supporting_passage: Hewer 2024 abstract: "Contraindicated dopamine antagonists were prescribed for 43% of PWP and administered in 31% of those cases." || Beckers 2025 (full text, surgery section): "certain drugs which are commonly used periprocedurally are contraindicated in PwP (examples include ketamine, metoclopramide and haloperidol)." || Lertxundi 2017 abstract: "...the administration of centrally acting antidopaminergics. ... inappropriate antiemetic administration OR = 2.15 CI 95% (1.36-3.39); and inappropriate antipsychotic administration OR = 1.91 ... Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay."
location: Hewer: Abstract (Results). Beckers: Surgery section. Lertxundi: Abstract
safe_wording: Metoclopramide and haloperidol block dopamine and are listed as contraindicated in Parkinson's disease. In an Australian audit of people with Parkinson's who died in hospital, 43% were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine blocker and 31% of those prescriptions were given. Check every anti-sickness, calming and sedative medicine on the chart against its dopamine-blocking effect.
qualifications: Beckers names metoclopramide and haloperidol (with ketamine) in a perioperative context, not specifically for the last days of life; the Hewer audit is end-of-life but its abstract does not list the drugs. Do not name safe alternatives or other drugs (for example levomepromazine, prochlorperazine) as unsafe or safe: not verified from an opened source. NICE NG71 and Scottish guideline text could not be opened. Lertxundi is observational and not end-of-life specific.

claim: About 1 in 10 bereaved adults develop prolonged grief disorder after non-violent loss; higher mean age linked with higher prevalence.
supporting_passage: Meta-analysis revealed a pooled prevalence of PGD of 9.8% (95% CI 6.8-14.0). Moderation analyses showed higher mean age to be associated with higher prevalence of PGD. ... Due to heterogeneity and limited representativeness, the findings should be interpreted cautiously
safe_wording: Studies suggest roughly 1 in 10 adults bereaved by a non-violent death develop grief that stays intense and disabling; it appears more common in older groups.
qualifications: Heterogeneous studies, pre-ICD-11 criteria; age link is across studies.

claim: In adults 50+, complicated grief treatment gave a response rate of 70.5% vs 32.0% with interpersonal psychotherapy.
supporting_passage: Response rate for CGT (52 individuals [70.5%]) was more than twice that for IPT (24 [32.0%]) (relative risk, 2.20 [95% CI, 1.51-3.22]; P < .001), with the number needed to treat at 2.56. ... Results were not moderated by participant age.
safe_wording: In a US trial of 151 people aged 50 and over, about 7 in 10 improved with a grief-specific therapy, compared with about 3 in 10 with a talking therapy proven for depression.
qualifications: One US trial; comparator is an active therapy.

claim: ICD-11 includes prolonged grief disorder with a 6-month criterion.
safe_wording: Do not state the ICD-11 duration unless verified; may say it was 'expected to be included in ICD-11' (Lundorff 2017).
qualifications: WHO page not opened.

claim: Guidance sets the as-needed opioid dose at one sixth (or one tenth to one sixth) of the 24-hour dose and advises recalculating when the regular dose changes.
qualifications: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines, PCF and EAPC text not opened in this batch.

claim: People with more positive self-perceptions of ageing lived 7.5 years longer in one cohort of 660.
supporting_passage: This research found that older individuals with more positive self-perceptions of aging, measured up to 23 years earlier, lived 7.5 years longer than those with less positive self-perceptions of aging. This advantage remained after age, gender, socioeconomic status, loneliness, and functional health were included as covariates. ... The sample consisted of 660 individuals aged 50 and older who participated in a community-based survey, the Ohio Longitudinal Study of Aging and Retirement (OLSAR).
safe_wording: In one US study of 660 people aged 50 and over, those with more positive views of their own ageing lived on average 7.5 years longer, after adjusting for age, sex, income, loneliness and health. This is a link, not proof of cause.
qualifications: Observational; single cohort; adjusted; do not say 'because of'; title's word 'increased' is the authors' causal framing.

claim: Meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found a small significant effect, stronger with shorter follow-up and younger samples.
supporting_passage: A systematic search ... resulted in 19 longitudinal studies ... The analyses revealed heterogeneity, with stronger effects for studies with a shorter period of follow-up, for studies of health versus survival, for studies with younger participants ... Subjective aging has a small significant effect on health, health behaviors, and survival.
safe_wording: When 19 long-term studies were pooled, how people view their own ageing had a small link with later health and survival, weaker with longer follow-up.
qualifications: Keep 'small'; effect larger for health than survival.

claim: Association may reflect reverse causation and confounding; the case against ageism is ethical.
supporting_passage: (methods interpretation; no source needed as general point; ethical position marked as judgement)
safe_wording: Studies like this cannot rule out that people who were already less well viewed ageing more negatively. We should oppose ageist treatment because it is unfair, whatever the survival figure.
qualifications: State as interpretation and judgement, not finding.

claim: Glass 1998 described discordance between hypothetical and enacted function in MacArthur data.
supporting_passage: Failure to attend to this distinction has obscured considerable discordance between what people say they are able to do in standard functional disability assessments, and what they actually do at home. To illustrate this point, data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging comparing the hypothetical to the enacted tenses are presented. These data show a consistent pattern of discordance between these two tenses.
safe_wording: A 1998 paper described three 'tenses' of function: what people say they can do, what they do in a test, and what they actually do at home. In US data, what people said they could do and what they did at home showed 'a consistent pattern of discordance'.
qualifications: No numbers available; do not quantify.

claim: Self-reported and performance-based function agree only moderately in older people.
supporting_passage: Cross-modal agreement was moderate, with by-criterion and frailty-wide Kappa statistics of 0.55-0.60 in all cases. ... Commonly used self-reported disability items cannot be assumed to stand in for performance-based criteria in the PFP. [Owens 2002:] Disagreement between the self-reported and performance-based measure of function was common (slight disagreement, 55.0%; substantial disagreement, 19.3%). Most women (95.4%) overreported their level of function.
safe_wording: In a large US study of older adults, self-reported walking and strength difficulty agreed only moderately with measured tests, and one could not simply stand in for the other.
qualifications: Owens is post-stroke women only; do not generalise its percentages.

claim: WHO ICF distinguishes capacity from performance.
supporting_passage: Not opened (WHO document not accessible from this environment).
safe_wording: Omit or state without attributing to WHO.

claim: Newcastle 85+: median diseases women 5, men 4; 77.6% rated health compared with others their age good or better.
supporting_passage: Overall, 77.6% (646/832) of participants rated their health compared with others of the same age as good, very good, or excellent. ... Women had significantly higher disease counts (medians: women 5, men 4; P=0.033) ... This large cohort of 85 year olds showed good levels of both self rated health and functional ability despite significant levels of disease and impairment.
safe_wording: In a study of 85-year-olds in Newcastle, the typical woman had 5 recorded diseases and the typical man 4, yet about 3 in 4 (78 in 100) rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age.
qualifications: Keep 'compared with others their age'; do not say disease lists 'say little' about life; cross-sectional.

claim: Most common conditions hypertension and osteoarthritis; hearing impairment ~60%.
supporting_passage: The most prevalent diseases were hypertension (57.5%, 592/1030) and osteoarthritis (51.8%, 534/1030). ... hearing impairment in 59.6% (505/848)
safe_wording: The commonest recorded conditions were high blood pressure (in over half) and osteoarthritis (about half); about 6 in 10 had hearing impairment.

claim: Time to benefit of screening can exceed remaining life, a legitimate reason for different advice.
supporting_passage: On average across included studies, it took 10.7 years (4.4 to 21.6) before one death from breast cancer was prevented for 1000 women screened. ... it took 10.3 years (6.0 to 16.4) before one death from colorectal cancer was prevented for 1000 patients screened. Our results suggest that screening for breast and colorectal cancer is most appropriate for patients with a life expectancy greater than 10 years.
safe_wording: For breast and bowel cancer screening, it took about 10 years before 1 death was prevented for every 1000 people screened, so researchers suggest screening suits people expected to live more than 10 years. That is a reason about expected benefit, not about age itself.
qualifications: Screening-specific example; life expectancy, not age, is the criterion.

claim: Age-based differences in access to treatment are widely documented.
supporting_passage: Ageism led to significantly worse health outcomes in 95.5% of the studies and 74.0% of the 1,159 ageism-health associations examined.
safe_wording: Omit, or say only that a large review found ageism linked with worse health in many studies worldwide, without causal wording.
qualifications: Review does not isolate treatment access in the abstract; causal wording must not be borrowed.

claim: Age discrimination in services unlawful in GB since Oct 2012 unless objectively justified.
supporting_passage: Not opened; official legislation pages not accessible.
safe_wording: Drop the legal claim.

claim: In >100,000 IAPT patients, older adults were more likely to recover (crude and adjusted) and less likely to drop out.
supporting_passage: At the end of treatment, older adults were more likely to reliably recover (52.5% vs 40.9%,<0.001), reliably improve (72% vs 66.4%,<0.001), and attrition was less likely (18.1% vs 31.6%,<0.001) compared to working-age adults. ... In adjusted models older adults were more likely to reliably recover (OR=1.33(95%CI=1.24-1.43)) ... There are potential selection biases affecting the characteristics of older people attending these services. Residual confounding cannot be ruled out
safe_wording: In NHS talking therapy services in London, about 53 in 100 people aged 65+ recovered, compared with 41 in 100 working-age adults, and fewer dropped out (18 vs 32 in 100). The difference held after allowing for how unwell people were at the start, but older people who reach these services may be a selected group.
qualifications: Observational; London services; after matching, the recovery advantage for depression alone was not clear (anxiety drove the effect).

claim: Older adults are under-represented in these services.
supporting_passage: We found that older people accounted for just 3.8% of patients treated at the services. This suggests that older adults were under-represented in the services that provided data here as over 65 year olds account for approximately 18% of the population ().
safe_wording: In these London services, fewer than 4 in 100 people treated were 65 or over, although about 18 in 100 of the population are that age.
qualifications: The 18% population figure is cited background; comparison is crude (need, not just population share, matters). National NHS Digital report not opened.

claim: Self-referral in England; different routes in Scotland.
supporting_passage: Not opened; official pages not accessible.
safe_wording: Omit specific referral routes; may say 'ask your GP about talking therapy'.

claim: Following US guidelines for 5 conditions in a hypothetical 79-year-old woman gives 12 medicines and a complicated non-drug regimen; most guidelines did not address older people with multiple conditions.
supporting_passage: Most CPGs did not modify or discuss the applicability of their recommendations for older patients with multiple comorbidities. ... If the relevant CPGs were followed, the hypothetical patient would be prescribed 12 medications (costing her 406 dollars per month) and a complicated nonpharmacological regimen. Adverse interactions between drugs and diseases could result.
safe_wording: A 2005 US analysis added up the guidelines for five common conditions for an imagined 79-year-old woman: she would be prescribed 12 medicines plus a complicated non-drug regimen.
qualifications: Hypothetical patient; US guidelines from 2005; not NICE. Daily dose count not verified (full text not opened) so do not state doses.

claim: Drugs recommended in NICE type 2 diabetes guideline had 133 potentially serious interactions with drugs recommended in guidelines for 11 other conditions; few highlighted.
supporting_passage: 133 drug-drug interactions for drugs recommended in the type 2 diabetes guideline, 89 for depression, and 111 for heart failure. Few of these drug-disease or drug-drug interactions were highlighted in the guidelines for the three index conditions.
safe_wording: A UK review found 133 potentially serious interactions between drugs recommended in the NICE type 2 diabetes guideline and drugs recommended in NICE guidelines for 11 other common conditions; few were flagged in the guideline.
qualifications: Potential interactions between recommendations, not observed harm in patients.

claim: Following five NICE guidelines for hypothetical patients gives considerable treatment burden and complex follow-up; guidelines give no guidance on prioritising.
supporting_passage: Explicitly following guideline recommendations for our two hypothetical patients would lead to a considerable treatment burden, even when recommendations were followed for mild to moderate conditions. In addition, the follow-up and self-care regime was complex ... current guideline recommendations rapidly cumulate to drive polypharmacy, without providing guidance on how best to prioritise recommendations
safe_wording: Applying five NICE guidelines to two imagined patients produced a heavy treatment burden and a complex follow-up and self-care routine, with no guidance on which recommendations to put first.
qualifications: Hypothetical patients; 2012 guidelines.

claim: Single-condition guidelines are not designed to weigh the combined effect of their recommendations in a person with several conditions, and give little guidance on prioritising them; the whole plan should be reviewed against the person's priorities.
supporting_passage: Current guidelines are not designed to consider the cumulative impact of treatment recommendations on people with several conditions, nor to allow comparison of relative benefits or risks. ... in people with multimorbidity current guideline recommendations rapidly cumulate to drive polypharmacy, without providing guidance on how best to prioritise recommendations for individuals in whom treatment burden will sometimes be overwhelming.
safe_wording: Single-condition guidelines are not built to weigh the combined effect of their advice for a person with several conditions, and give little help in deciding which advice to put first. We should review the whole plan as one plan against what the person most wants. (The review step is judgement, not a finding.)
qualifications: Supported: guidelines are not designed to consider cumulative impact (Hughes 2012, five NICE guidelines). NOT supported: the statement 'no trial tested the combined plan' (no source; do not state it as fact). Review-as-a-whole is ethical/clinical judgement. NICE NG56 not opened; do not cite it.

claim: Of 434 JAGS research articles 2008-09, at least 29% explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment; 6% gave justification; 14% discussed as limitation.
supporting_passage: Of 434 articles examined, 16% used recruitment methods likely to reduce participation by persons with cognitive impairment. At least 29% of studies (n = 127) employed explicit exclusion criteria. ... Few (6%) provided any justification for exclusion criteria used, only 43% gave any reason for exclusion, and only 14% discussed exclusion as a possible limitation.
safe_wording: In two years of a leading geriatrics journal, at least 127 of 434 studies (29%) explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment, and very few gave any justification for doing so.
qualifications: The abstract does not state whether 6% and 14% are of 434 or of the 127; avoid '6 in 100' unless full text confirms. One US journal, 2008-09.

claim: Few recently completed UK trials in conditions linked with cognitive impairment included adults who lacked capacity.
supporting_passage: We identified 81 trials in the conditions or populations searched for which were completed between 2015 and 2018, of which 15 trials (18%) allowed for the inclusion of adults who lacked capacity
location: Full text, Main text (abstract says 80 retrieved trials)
safe_wording: Of about 80 UK trials completed 2015-2018 in conditions where impaired capacity is common, only 15 allowed adults who lacked capacity to take part.
qualifications: Say 'about 80' or '15 of 81' given abstract/full-text discrepancy; search not comprehensive.

claim: UK law (England and Wales) allows adults lacking capacity to take part in research with safeguards via consultees/legal representatives.
supporting_passage: In England and Wales, the legal frameworks govern the inclusion of adults who lack capacity in clinical trials of medicinal products under the Medicines for Human Use (Clinical Trials) Regulations 2004 [], with other types of research governed by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 []. Under this legal framework, someone who knows the person who lacks capacity is approached by the researcher to act as their legal representative or consultee.
safe_wording: In England and Wales, the law already allows adults who lack capacity to take part in research: drug trials under the Clinical Trials Regulations 2004 with a legal representative's consent, and other research under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 with a consultee's advice.
qualifications: England and Wales only. Scottish law (Adults with Incapacity Act s51) not verified: do not state details; say only that Scotland has its own legislation, or omit.

claim: Adults with impaired capacity are frequently excluded partly because researchers are unfamiliar with legal frameworks; INCLUDE framework exists to help.
supporting_passage: adults with impaired capacity to consent are frequently excluded from trials - partly because researchers are unfamiliar with the legal and ethical frameworks and lack the necessary methodological expertise. ... The framework has two parts: a set of four key questions to help researchers identify who should be included in their trial, and a series of worksheets
safe_wording: A UK framework (INCLUDE Impaired Capacity to Consent) gives trial teams four key questions and worksheets to design trials that include people who lack capacity.
qualifications: Its effect on inclusion is not yet evaluated.

claim: In Scotland, onset of multimorbidity occurred 10-15 years earlier in the most deprived than most affluent areas.
supporting_passage: Onset of multimorbidity occurred 10-15 years earlier in people living in the most deprived areas compared with the most affluent
safe_wording: In a study of 1.75 million people in Scotland, having two or more long-term conditions became common 10 to 15 years earlier in the most deprived areas than in the most affluent.
qualifications: Population-level, cross-sectional 2007 data; not a statement about individuals. Chart values not verified (full text not opened): no chart figures.

claim: More people with multimorbidity were under 65 than over 65.
supporting_passage: the absolute number of people with multimorbidity was higher in those younger than 65 years (210,500 vs 194,996)
safe_wording: In that Scottish study, more people with two or more long-term conditions were under 65 (210,500) than 65 or over (194,996), although the proportion was highest in older people.

claim: Healthy life expectancy gap by deprivation.
safe_wording: Omit: no source opened.

claim: Standard survival analysis overestimated 5- and 10-year risk of second hip fracture vs competing-risk method.
supporting_passage: Using traditional survival analysis ... the incidence of second hip fracture at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years was 3%, 7%, 11%, and 21%, respectively. A competing risk approach resulted in a lower estimate of incidence: 3%, 6%, 8%, and 12%, respectively. ... During follow-up, a much greater proportion of subjects died without experiencing a second hip fracture (73%)
safe_wording: In 481 people after a first hip fracture, the usual method put the 10-year risk of a second hip fracture at 21 in 100; allowing for deaths from other causes gave 12 in 100. 73% died without a second fracture.
qualifications: One cohort; the gap grows with follow-up length and mortality. Do not imply FRAX shares the flaw.

claim: A trial with 80% power for the overall effect has only 29% power to detect an interaction of the same size; ~fourfold sample needed; subgroup-specific tests often give spurious results.
supporting_passage: a trial with 80% power for the overall effect had only 29% power to detect an interaction effect of the same magnitude. For interactions of this size to be detected with the same power as the overall effect, sample sizes should be inflated fourfold ... A significant effect in one subgroup only was observed in 7% to 64% of simulations
safe_wording: In simulations, a trial designed with 80% power for its main result had only 29% power to detect a subgroup difference of the same size; about four times the participants would be needed. Apparent effects in one subgroup only were also common by chance.
qualifications: Simulation; keep two-way caution.

claim: ADJUST-PE: in people 50 or over with a non-high/unlikely clinical probability, a D-dimer cut-off of age x 10 ug/L was used; of 331 people with a D-dimer between 500 ug/L and their age-adjusted cut-off who were left untreated, 1 had a clot event within 3 months.
supporting_passage: To prospectively validate whether an age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff, defined as age × 10 in patients 50 years or older, is associated with an increased diagnostic yield of D-dimer in elderly patients with suspected PE. ... Patients with a D-dimer value between the conventional cutoff of 500 µg/L and their age-adjusted cutoff did not undergo CTPA and were left untreated and formally followed-up for a 3-month period. ... The 3-month failure rate in patients with a D-dimer level higher than 500 µg/L but below the age-adjusted cutoff was 1 of 331 patients (0.3% [95% CI, 0.1%-1.7%]).
safe_wording: In a European study of 3346 emergency patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, people aged 50 or over whose clinical score was not high were not scanned if their D-dimer was below age x 10 (in ug/L). Of 331 people in that band between 500 and their age-based limit, 1 had a clot within 3 months.
qualifications: Only after a clinical probability score (simplified revised Geneva or 2-level Wells). Management study with no randomised comparator. Assay and units matter (highly sensitive assay, ug/L; check the lab's units). The upper confidence limit for the failure rate is 1.7%, so 'safe' should not be read as 'zero risk'.

claim: Among 673 people aged 75 or over with a non-high clinical probability, the share in whom PE could be excluded by D-dimer alone rose from 6.4% (43/673) with the 500 ug/L cut-off to 29.7% (200/673) with the age-adjusted cut-off, without any additional false-negative findings.
supporting_passage: Among the 766 patients 75 years or older, of whom 673 had a nonhigh clinical probability, using the age-adjusted cutoff instead of the 500 µg/L cutoff increased the proportion of patients in whom PE could be excluded on the basis of D-dimer from 43 of 673 patients (6.4% [95% CI, 4.8%-8.5%) to 200 of 673 patients (29.7% [95% CI, 26.4%-33.3%), without any additional false-negative findings.
safe_wording: Among 673 people aged 75 or over whose clinical score was not high, a clot could be ruled out by blood test alone in about 6 in 100 with the fixed cut-off and about 30 in 100 with the age-adjusted cut-off (a rise of about 23 percentage points), and no extra missed clots were found in that group.
qualifications: Subgroup (75+ with non-high probability, 673 people). 'No additional false negatives' means none found in the study; with about 200 people newly excluded, a small risk cannot be excluded (no confidence interval is given for this subgroup in the abstract). Differences are percentage points (29.7 minus 6.4 = 23.3). 'Ruled out' means no scan was needed after a negative score-plus-D-dimer pathway, not that clots are impossible.

claim: NICE NG158 advises considering an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold for people over 50.
supporting_passage: (Search-engine paraphrase, not verbatim) An NHS summary of the updated NICE guidance says it includes using an age-adjusted D-dimer when assessing people aged over 50.
safe_wording: Do not state what NICE or UK guidance says. The post can say the rule was validated in ADJUST-PE and leave guidance out, or add a UK guidance statement only after the NG158 text is opened by a human.
qualifications: Search extract only; NICE page cannot be opened; exact wording ('consider'), recommendation number and clinical-probability condition unconfirmed.

claim: In 209,622 US veterans with CKD stages 3 to 5, older patients had higher death rates and lower treated end-stage kidney disease rates than younger patients at comparable eGFR; among those aged 85 or over the risk of death always exceeded the risk of ESRD.
supporting_passage: However, among those with comparable levels of eGFR, older patients had higher rates of death and lower rates of ESRD than younger patients. ... Among those 85 years or older, the risk of death always exceeded the risk of ESRD in this cohort.
safe_wording: In a 2007 study of about 210,000 US veterans with reduced kidney function (stages 3 to 5), people aged 85 or over were more likely to die over roughly three years than to start dialysis or transplant, at every level of kidney function studied.
qualifications: All-cause death, not 'other causes'; 'treated ESRD' means dialysis or transplant, so untreated kidney failure is not counted; stages 3-5 combined, so not specific to stage 3 (the abstract does not give stage-3 figures); US veterans (sex mix not checked in the opened text, do not say 'mostly men' unless confirmed); observational; mean follow-up 3.2 years; 2007 data. It does not say kidney care is pointless: it says which outcome is likelier over a few years.

claim: Urine albumin gives risk information beyond eGFR at every age: higher albuminuria and lower eGFR were each linked with higher mortality and ESRD risk.
supporting_passage: Mortality (112,325 deaths) and ESRD (8411 events) risks were higher at lower eGFR and higher albuminuria in every age category. ... Both low eGFR and high albuminuria were independently associated with mortality and ESRD regardless of age across a wide range of populations.
safe_wording: In a pooled analysis of about 2 million people in 46 studies, both a lower kidney blood test (eGFR) and more albumin in the urine were each linked with a higher chance of dying and of kidney failure, in every age group, so the urine test adds information that the blood test alone does not.
qualifications: Association, adjusted; does not by itself show what happens to an individual with stage 3 and normal albumin.

claim: A stage 3 CKD result with normal urine albumin carries a low risk of kidney failure in older people.
supporting_passage: For example, even at age 75+ persons with eGFR 45–59 ml/min/1.73m and optimally low albuminuria had significantly increased mortality risk, though they had lower relative hazards and higher absolute risks than at younger ages.
safe_wording: Do not say a stable stage 3 result without albumin carries a low risk of kidney failure. Say instead that the urine albumin test adds information and that higher albumin goes with higher risk.
qualifications: The opened full text gives no absolute ESRD risk for stage 3 with normal ACR. The passage found shows increased mortality risk even with low albuminuria at 75+, so 'reassuring' framing is not supported.

claim: CKD is defined by kidney damage or reduced GFR persisting for 3 months or more, so a single result needs repeating (the 'is it stable?' question).
supporting_passage: CKD is defined as kidney damage or glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m(2) for 3 months or more, irrespective of cause. Kidney damage in many kidney diseases can be ascertained by the presence of albuminuria, defined as albumin-to-creatinine ratio >30 mg/g in two of three spot urine specimens.
safe_wording: Chronic kidney disease is defined by kidney function that is reduced for at least 3 months, so asking whether the result has been repeated and has stayed the same is a fair question.
qualifications: 2005 statement; current KDIGO 2024 and NICE NG203 wording not opened. The 'repeat before labelling' inference is mine from the definition; the statement does not say what a clinician must do after one test. 'Stage 3' means eGFR 30-59 in the standard staging (not stated in this abstract).

claim: Some medicines are dosed or chosen according to kidney function, so a kidney result can change prescribing.
supporting_passage: In clinical trials of dabigatran and rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF), drug eligibility and dosing were determined using the Cockcroft-Gault equation to estimate creatine clearance as a measure of renal function. ... Were the MDRD-derived eGFR to be used instead of Cockcroft-Gault in prescribing these new agents, many elderly patients with AF would either incorrectly become eligible for them or would receive too high a dose.
safe_wording: Some medicines, such as certain blood thinners for atrial fibrillation, are chosen or dosed by kidney function, so it is reasonable to ask whether any of your medicines depend on it.
qualifications: Evidence is for one drug class; do not generalise to all medicines or to a particular dose threshold. The kidney measure used for dosing is often creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault), not the eGFR on the lab report (see C06-19). The claim that stage 3 label changes heart or blood pressure care was not sourced and should be left out.

claim: Whether CKD should be defined by the same eGFR threshold at all ages is debated.
supporting_passage: Supporters of the former approach have cited a dramatic rise in the prevalence of nephrosclerosis with age in kidney biopsies, even among healthy kidney donors, and suggested the concept of natural inevitable senescence of the kidneys suggesting age specific cutoffs for defining normal kidney function. ... In contrast, our meta-analysis documents that risk of mortality and ESRD is increased at approximately 60 ml/min/1.73m, the threshold used for defining CKD over the last 10 years, across all age groups.
safe_wording: Doctors disagree about whether one kidney-function cut-off for 'kidney disease' suits every age; the post should take no side.
qualifications: Authors of Hallan argue for a common definition; Delanaye 2019 (age-adapted definition) not opened, so cite no one for the opposing view beyond saying the debate exists.

claim: KDIGO grades CKD risk by eGFR and albuminuria together; NICE NG203 recommends urine ACR alongside eGFR.
safe_wording: Do not attribute this to KDIGO or NICE. Hallan 2012 supports that the two measures are used together to stage CKD ('recently ... suggested that the definition and staging of CKD ... should be determined by the combination of estimated GFR and albuminuria', background statement) but the guideline text was not opened.
qualifications: KDIGO 2024 PubMed record has no abstract; NICE pages cannot be opened.
